Third: Punishment in this world does not indicate how grave or slight a sin is. This world is not the abode of recompense; rather, the Hereafter is. Nevertheless, punishments have been prescribed in this world to prevent corruption and aggression, as Allah Most High says:

“Whoever kills a soul, unless for a soul or for corruption in the land, it is as though he had killed all mankind.”

And the angels said:

“Will You place in it someone who will spread corruption there and shed blood?”

These two things mentioned by the angels are the very grounds on which Allah prescribed execution for the Children of Israel. This is why disbelievers under Muslim protection are allowed to remain upon payment of jizya, even though, by the consensus of the Muslims, their sin of failing to believe is greater than that of an adulterer or murderer whom we execute.

Abū Hanīfa held that, whatever the kind of disbelief, its adherents are fought only because they wage war; those who do not wage war are not to be fought. Accordingly, he accepts jizya from those other than the Arab People of the Book, even if they are idolaters. Mālik and, in one of his two opinions, Ahmad agreed with him on this. Nevertheless, execution is permissible in certain cases as a discretionary punishment and a measure of governance.

As for al-Shāfiʿī, he holds that disbelief itself makes a person’s blood lawful, but women and children are spared because they constitute property for the Muslims. An apostate is therefore executed because disbelief is present and, in his view, the grounds for sparing life are absent: disbelief remains without any benefit.

Ahmad, however, recognizes several grounds for permitting execution. In the case of someone who has never been Muslim, these are the harm he causes or the absence of any benefit in keeping him alive. The former consists of waging war through physical force or speech. Thus, women, children, monks, the blind, the chronically infirm and others like them who take no part whatsoever in warfare are not to be killed, as is the position of the majority of scholars.

As for an apostate, Ahmad holds that the ground for permitting his execution is disbelief after faith, which is a particular kind of disbelief. If such a person were not executed, someone could enter the religion and then leave it. Executing him therefore protects both the adherents of the religion and the religion itself: it guards against decline and deters them from leaving it. This differs from the case of someone who has never entered it.

If such a person belongs to the People of the Book or is accorded similar status, one of the two conditions for ending hostilities has been met in his case. If he is an idolater and jizya is accepted from him, the same applies. If it is not accepted, there is disagreement over whether he may be enslaved. Whenever his enslavement is permissible, it serves the same purpose as accepting jizya from him. Whenever neither enslaving him nor accepting jizya from him is possible, he remains a disbeliever whose continued life benefits neither himself—because he accumulates further sin—nor the believers. Killing him is therefore better than keeping him alive.

As for someone who abandons prayer and the payment of zakat, if he is executed, Ahmad regards him as belonging to the category of apostates, because by embracing Islam he committed himself to these acts; if he does not perform them, he has abandoned what he committed himself to

The seventh point:

According to the Sunnah and scholarly consensus, people of religious innovation are worse than those who commit sins driven by desire. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, commanded fighting the Khawārij and forbade fighting unjust rulers. Concerning the man who drank wine, he said:

“Do not curse him, for he loves Allah and His Messenger.”

Concerning Dhū al-Khuwaysira, he said:

“From this man’s progeny will emerge people who recite the Quran, yet it does not go beyond their throats. They will pass out of the religion—in another narration, ‘out of Islam’—as an arrow passes through its quarry. Any one of you would consider his own prayer insignificant compared with

their prayer, his fasting compared with theirs, and his recitation compared with theirs. Wherever you encounter them, kill them, for whoever kills them will have a reward with Allah on the Day of Resurrection.”

This principle has been established through abundant evidence in the principles discussed above. The sins of those who commit acts of disobedience consist in doing certain things they have been forbidden to do: theft, unlawful sexual intercourse, drinking wine, or consuming wealth wrongfully.

The sins of people of religious innovation, however, consist in neglecting what they have been commanded to do: following the Sunnah and the community of believers. The foundation of the Khawārij’s innovation is that they do not consider it necessary to obey and follow the Messenger in matters which, in their view, contradict the apparent meaning of the Quran. This is the neglect of a duty.

Likewise, the Rāfidah do not acknowledge the uprightness of the Companions or the duty to love them and seek forgiveness for them. This is the neglect of a duty. Likewise, the Qadariyyah do not believe in Allah Most High’s eternal knowledge, His all-encompassing will, and His perfect power. This is the neglect of a duty. Likewise, the Jabriyyah do not affirm the servant’s power and will, and they may invoke predestination to reject the divine command. This is the neglect of a duty.

The same applies to the moderate Murjiʾah, although their innovation is one of the innovations of the jurists and involves no disbelief, a point on which none of the leading scholars disagrees. Anyone from our school who has included it among the innovations for which he reported and upheld a verdict of disbelief has erred in doing so. Their innovation arose only because they do not consider deeds or utterances to be included in faith. This is the neglect of a duty.

As for the extremist Murjiʾah, who deny punishment and claim that the scriptural texts threatened people with something that has no reality, this is a grave assertion, and it constitutes the neglect of a duty.

translated_text:
And likewise, the Wa'īdiyyah do not accept belief that those who commit major sins will be brought out of the Fire, or that intercession on their behalf will be accepted. This is the neglect of a duty.

If it is said, “They may add to this a forbidden belief: declaring such people disbelievers or transgressors, or holding that they will remain in the Fire forever,” the response is:

“In this respect, their relationship with Ahl al-Sunnah is like that of disbelievers with believers. Simply failing to believe what the Quran, the Sunnah, and scholarly consensus establish is misguidance, even if it is not accompanied by an affirmative belief. If such a belief is added, both errors are combined. Had they possessed a foundation in the Sunnah, they would not have fallen into religious innovation.”

The eighth point:

If you reflect upon the misguidance and errors of the children of Adam concerning the foundations and subsidiary matters of their religion, you will find that most arise from failing to believe the truth, rather than from believing falsehood. In most questions over which people disagree, you will find that what each side affirms is correct; the misguidance arises instead from negation and denial.

For example, the disbelievers did not go astray through affirming the existence of the True One. Rather, their error arose from denying His Book, the Sunnah of His Messenger, and other truths. It was then that they fell into associating partners with Allah. Every community that associates partners with Allah does so fundamentally because it lacks a Book revealed from heaven; and every community devoted exclusively to Allah owes that devotion fundamentally to a Book revealed from heaven. For the children of Adam

need a revealed law to perfect their innate dispositions. Allah therefore began humanity with the prophethood of Adam, as He, the Exalted, said:

“He taught Adam all the names.”

And so it continued thereafter. Whoever departs from the teachings of the prophets falls into polytheism and other errors. This applies to every disbeliever who is not of the People of the Book: he is a polytheist, and his polytheism results from his lack of faith in the messengers, concerning whom Allah said:

“We certainly sent a messenger to every nation, saying, ‘Worship Allah and shun false gods.’”

Polytheism was not humanity’s original state. Rather, Adam and those of his descendants who followed his religion worshipped Allah alone because they followed prophethood. He, the Exalted, said:

“People were but one community, then they differed.”

Ibn ‘Abbās said: “Between Adam and Noah were ten generations, all following Islam.”

Thus, they fell into polytheism by abandoning adherence to the law of the prophets; it was not by falling into polytheism that they departed from the law of Islam. For Adam commanded them to do what Allah had commanded him, when He said to him:

“If guidance comes to you from Me, those who follow My guidance will have no fear, nor will they grieve.”

“But those who disbelieve and deny Our signs are the inhabitants of the Fire; they will remain there forever.”

And He said in the other passage:

“Whoever follows My guidance will neither go astray nor suffer.”

“But whoever turns away from My remembrance will have a life of hardship, and We will raise him blind on the Day of Resurrection.”

“He will say, ‘My Lord, why have You raised me blind when I used to see?’”

“He will say, ‘Just as Our signs came to you and you forgot them, so today you will be forgotten.’”

Thus, these words with which Allah addressed Adam and the others when He sent them down establish that He obligated them to follow His revealed guidance—the revelation conveyed to His prophets. They also establish that whoever turns away from it, even without denying it, will suffer humiliating punishment on the Day of Resurrection, and that his life will be one of hardship in this world, in the intermediate state after death, and in the Hereafter: a constricted, troubled existence filled with every kind of anxiety, distress, and sorrow. A good life, by contrast, belongs to whoever believes and does righteous deeds.

Whoever holds fast to this guidance will not associate partners with his Lord, for all the messengers commanded people to worship Allah alone and were themselves commanded to do so. He, the Exalted, said:

“We never sent a messenger before you without revealing to him: ‘There is no god but Me, so worship Me.’”

He thus made clear that He invariably reveals the command to worship Him alone to every messenger. He, the Exalted, also said:

“Ask those of Our messengers whom We sent before you: Have We appointed gods besides the Most Merciful to be worshipped?”

He thus made clear that He has never prescribed polytheism. These two texts demonstrate that He commanded every messenger to worship Him alone and never commanded the association of partners with Him. From the time Adam was sent down, He commanded him and his descendants to follow His guidance, which He reveals to the prophets. It is therefore established that polytheism arose from abandoning adherence to the prophets and messengers in what they commanded concerning worshipping Allah alone and following His religion—not that polytheism was the cause of disbelief in the messengers. In reality, associating partners with Allah and disbelief in the messengers necessarily accompany one another. This concerns the polytheists who disbelieve in the prophethoods. As for the People of the Book, the Jews were not led into error by what they affirmed

concerning Moses’ prophethood and belief in the Torah. Rather, in this they are rightly guided, and it is the foundation of their guidance. They were led into error only through what they did not acknowledge: the missions of the Messiah and Muhammad, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him. As the Exalted said of them:

“They incurred wrath upon wrath.”

Wrath for their disbelief in the Messiah, and wrath for their disbelief in Muhammad, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him. This falls under neglecting what has been commanded.

Likewise, the Christians were not led into error through what they affirmed of belief in the prophets of the Children of Israel and the Messiah. Rather, they were led into error through their disbelief in Muhammad, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him. As for their falling into the doctrines of the Trinity and union, through which they rejected monotheism and the prophetic message, this arose from their failure to follow the unambiguous passages of the Torah and the Gospel. These command the worship of Allah alone, without any partner, and make clear the Messiah’s servitude—that he is a servant of Allah. As Allah related his words:

“I told them only what You commanded me: ‘Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord.’ I was a witness over them as long as I remained among them. But when You took me, You were the Watcher over them, and You are a Witness over all things.”

When they abandoned following these passages in belief and practice, while still desiring worship and devotion, they invented monasticism and went to excess concerning the Messiah, following desires of their own. They clung to ambiguous expressions because of what they supposed them to mean and desires they followed, which led them away from the truth. Thus, “they follow nothing but conjecture and what their souls desire, although guidance has already come to them from their Lord.”

Hence, their distinguishing mark was going astray, as the Exalted said:

“Do not follow the desires of a people who went astray before, led many astray, and strayed from the straight path.”

One who is astray is the opposite of one who is rightly guided: he departs from the path of truth without knowledge. Lacking the knowledge one is commanded to acquire, and the guidance afforded by what is commanded, constitutes neglect of an obligation. Thus, the root of their disbelief is neglecting what is obligatory. They then divided over the Trinity and union, and enmity and hatred arose among them. They became Melkites, Jacobites, Nestorians, and other groups. The Quran has explained this point, which can also serve as an independent proof, since it shows that neglecting an obligation leads to committing what is forbidden. The Exalted said:

“From those who said, ‘We are Christians,’ We also took their covenant, but they neglected a portion of what they had been reminded of. So We stirred up enmity and hatred among them until the Day of Resurrection.”

This explicitly states that they abandoned some of what they had been commanded to do, and that abandoning it caused them to fall into forbidden enmity and hatred. This is evidence that neglecting an obligation can lead to committing what is forbidden, such as enmity and hatred; and the cause is stronger than its effect.

Likewise, He said concerning the Jews:

“For breaking their covenant, We cursed them and hardened their hearts. They distort words from their proper places and neglected a portion of what they had been reminded of.”

Breaking the covenant means abandoning what they were commanded to do, for the covenant includes obligations, as expressed in His words:

“Allah certainly took a covenant from the Children of Israel, and We appointed twelve leaders from among them. Allah said, ‘I am with you. If you establish prayer, give zakah, and believe in My messengers

and support them, and lend Allah a good loan, I will surely absolve you of your sins and admit you into gardens beneath which rivers flow. But whoever among you disbelieves after that has certainly strayed from the straight path.’”

“For breaking their covenant, We cursed them and hardened their hearts,”

and the verses that follow. The Exalted thus states that, by neglecting the duties He had imposed upon them through the covenant—even though these were also obligatory by His command—they incurred these punishments. These included falling into such forbidden things as hardness of heart, distorting words from their proper places, and neglecting a portion of what they had been reminded of.

Further into the surah, He states that He cast enmity and hatred among them, saying:

“The Jews said, ‘Allah’s hand is shackled.’ May their hands be shackled, and may they be cursed for what they said! Rather, both His hands are outstretched; He spends as He wills,”

and the rest of the verse. Quran commentators among the early generations, such as Qatāda and others, have said concerning the Christian sects what we have indicated.

Likewise, if you reflect on those within this community who have gone astray or fallen into error, you will find that the root cause is neglecting good deeds, rather than committing evil deeds. The foundation of what they affirm is sound; their error arises from what they deny. Affirmation amounts to performing a good deed, and negation to refraining from an evil deed. It thus becomes clear that neglecting good deeds is more harmful than committing evil deeds, and is its root cause.

An example of this is the Waʿīdiyya (those who insist on the fulfilment of divine threats of punishment), among the Khārijites and others, in the gravity they attach to

Likewise, the Murjiʾa have done well in affirming the faith of those who commit sins and the mercy shown to them. But the root of their error lies in their denial that deeds are part of faith and that those who commit major sins are subject to punishment. Affirmation consists in performing good deeds commanded as either obligatory or recommended, while negation consists in refraining from evil deeds or omitting commanded good deeds. Thus, their misguidance is rooted in abandoning what is obligatory and failing to affirm the truth.

In short, there are two categories: statements and non-declarative utterances. Statements divide into affirmation and negation—that is, positive and negative assertions—as in the classification of propositions as affirmative or negative. Non-declarative utterances include commands and prohibitions.

The foundation of guidance and the religion of truth is affirming what truly exists and carrying out the good that is intended; refraining from what is forbidden and rejecting falsehood follow from this.

The foundation of misguidance and the religion of falsehood is denying what truly exists and neglecting the good that is intended; committing what is forbidden and affirming falsehood then follow from that. Reflect on this, for it is a matter of great importance through which doors of guidance will open to you.

The ninth argument:

The comprehensive expressions in the Quran encompass compliance with what has been commanded and warnings of punishment for disobedience through neglecting it. An example is the saying of Allah Most High to His Prophet:

“So remain steadfast as you have been commanded, you and those who have repented

with you, and do not transgress.”

And He says:

“So call to this, remain steadfast as you have been commanded, and do not follow their desires.”

And He says:

“Say, ‘I have been commanded to be the first to submit,’ and do not be among those who associate partners with Allah.”

And He says:

“Say, ‘I have been commanded to worship Allah, devoting my religion sincerely to Him.’”

“‘And I have been commanded to be the first of the Muslims.’”

And He says:

“Nor do I tell you that I possess Allah’s treasuries, nor do I know the unseen, nor do I tell you that I am an angel. I follow only what is revealed to me. Say, ‘Are the blind and the sighted equal? Will you not then reflect?’”

And He says:

“Follow what is revealed to you, and be patient until Allah judges, for He is the best of judges.”

And He says:

“And this is My straight path, so follow it, and do not follow other paths, lest they lead you away from His path.”

There are many similar texts in which He enjoins adherence to what He has commanded, explains that steadfastness consists in this, that He has commanded nothing but this, and that abandoning it incurs punishment. These and similar statements show that compliance with commands is a general foundation, whereas avoiding what is forbidden is a particular branch of it.

The tenth argument:

The forbidden religious practices for which Allah censures the polytheists in the Quran are chiefly associating partners with Him and declaring things unlawful. This is also related of them in His saying:

“Those who associate partners with Allah will say, ‘Had Allah willed, neither we nor our forefathers would have associated partners with Him, nor would we have forbidden any

thing.’” This is also mentioned in al-Nahl, and in al-Zukhruf:

“They say, ‘Had the Most Merciful willed, we would not have worshipped them.’”

And He says:

“Or do they have partners who have ordained for them a religion that Allah has not authorized?”

And He says:

“Say, ‘Have you considered the provision Allah has sent down for you, some of which you have declared unlawful and some lawful?’ Say, ‘Has Allah authorized you, or are you fabricating lies against Allah?’”

And He says:

“Allah has not instituted any bahīrah, sā’ibah, wasīlah, or hām.”

And He says:

“Say, ‘Who has forbidden the adornment Allah has brought forth for His servants, and the good things He has provided?’”

As for those who neglect what they have been commanded to do, Allah has censured them, just as He has censured them for failing to believe in Him, His names, His signs, His angels, His Books, His messengers, resurrection after death, Paradise and Hell, and for neglecting prayer, zakah, jihad and other deeds. As explained earlier, associating partners with Allah is rooted in neglecting the command to worship Allah and follow His messengers. Declaring lawful things unlawful likewise entails neglecting the command to use them as a means of helping one worship Him.

Since the fundamental prohibitions they violated were associating partners with Allah and declaring things unlawful, it is reported in a hadith:

“I was sent with the way of pure monotheism and ease.”

Pure monotheism is the opposite of associating partners with Allah, and ease is the opposite of restriction and constraint. In Sahīh Muslim, Iyād ibn Himār relates that the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) narrated from his Lord:

“I created My servants as pure monotheists, but the devils drew them away from their religion, forbade them what I had made lawful for them, and commanded them to associate with Me that for which I had sent down no authority.”

The effects of these two sins have become evident among those who have gone astray among scholars, devout worshippers, rulers and ordinary people: they declare unlawful what Allah Most High has made lawful and practise forms of associating partners with Him that He has not prescribed. The former is prevalent among those devoted to jurisprudence and religious scrupulousness, while the latter is prevalent among Sufis and faqīrs. It thus becomes clear that the instances of neglecting obligations which Allah Most High has censured and punished are more numerous than the instances of committing forbidden acts which He has censured and punished.

The eleventh point:

Allah Most High created His creatures to worship Him, as He says:

“I did not create jinn and mankind except to worship Me.”

This is the foundation of what He commanded them through His messengers, as Noah, Hūd, Sālih, Abraham and Shuʿayb said:

“Worship Allah; you have no god other than Him.”

He also says:

“Who would turn away from the religion of Abraham except one who makes a fool of himself?”

Through to His words:

“one God, and to Him we submit.”

He said to Moses:

“Indeed, I am Allah. There is no god except Me, so worship Me.”

And the Messiah said:

“I said nothing to them except what You commanded me: ‘Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord.’”

What is commanded, however, is something that exists, and what exists can be good, beneficial and sought for its own sake. For whatever exists was created by Allah Most High, and Allah has created nothing except for a wise purpose. That wise purpose is an aspect of good, unlike what does not exist, which is nothing.

Thus, what exists is either wholly good or contains some good. What does not exist either contains no good whatsoever, or its good lies in preserving and safeguarding what exists. What is commanded is required to exist, whereas what is forbidden is required to be absent. It follows that what a command seeks is more perfect and nobler than what a prohibition seeks. It is the foundational objective, intended and desired for its own sake, and its absence is pure evil.

translated_text:
the Countenance of Allah Most High alone, love for Him and turning to Him, compassion for creation and kindness towards them, courage—which is strength and ability—and patience, which comes down to strength, restraint and self-control, among other things. All these are qualities, virtues and deeds through which the servant is set right and perfected. A thing can be sound and complete only through qualities actually present in it. Yet it may need the absence of whatever conflicts with them, so its need for that absence is incidental. Thus, what is commanded is foundational, while what is forbidden is secondary and subsidiary.

The fourteenth point:

People agree that what a command seeks is the existence of what is commanded, even if this entails the absence of its opposite. Jurists say, “Commanding something is forbidding its opposite,” but this is disputed.

The precise position is that its opposite is forbidden by implication; the one issuing the command may or may not intend this. As for what a prohibition seeks, one view is that it is simply the absence of what is forbidden.

Another view holds that this is not so, because absence is neither within one’s power nor an intended object. Rather, what is sought is to do the opposite of what is forbidden, namely to abstain, and this is something that actually exists.

The precise position is that the one issuing a prohibition may intend the mere absence of what is forbidden, or may intend doing its opposite. That absence is a specific, qualified absence that can be

This is because something is prohibited on account of the harm it entails, so the aim is its absence—as with prohibitions against killing a person or drinking wine. A prohibition may also be imposed solely to try and test the person subject to religious obligations, as Saul’s people were forbidden to drink except for a handful. Here, the aim is their obedience and submission, which is something that actually exists. As such, it is obedience of the same kind as carrying out what is commanded. What is forbidden is therefore subordinate to what is commanded: the aim is either the absence of something detrimental to what is commanded, or a component of what is commanded. Since it either encompasses what is commanded or is a branch of it, this establishes that what is commanded is more perfect and nobler, and is the primary objective.

The fifteenth point:

Commands are foundational, while prohibitions are subsidiary, for a prohibition is a kind of command. A command is a request, a call for something, or a demand; this includes both requesting an action and requesting that it be left undone. Prohibition, however, has been given a distinct name. This accords with the customary usage of the Arabs: when a general category has two kinds, one distinguished by a quality of perfection or deficiency, they give that kind a separate name and retain the general name for the other. Thus they speak of a Muslim and a hypocrite, and of a prophet and a messenger.

translated_text:
For this reason, the jurists have differed over the following question: if a man says to his wife, “If you disobey my command, you are divorced,” and she then disobeys a prohibition of his, has he broken his oath? Scholars of our school and others hold three views:

The first: he has broken his oath, because this constitutes disobedience to his command in customary usage, and because a prohibition is a kind of command.

The second: he has not broken his oath, because, as they claim, a prohibition does not fall within the linguistic meaning of a command.

The third: a distinction is drawn between someone who understands the true nature of commands and prohibitions and someone who does not. The first view is correct.

Everyone who disobeys a prohibition has therefore disobeyed a command, because a command is a verbal request for an action, made from a position of authority. One who prohibits seeks an action through his prohibition, either directly or by necessary implication. If prohibition is a kind of command, then command is more comprehensive, and what is more comprehensive is superior. If prohibition is not a kind of command, then command is the nobler of the two categories.

This is why the scholars agree on placing commands before prohibitions, and this is the order found in the Quran and Sunnah. Allah Most High says:

“He enjoins upon them what is right and forbids them what is wrong.”

And He says:

“Indeed, Allah commands justice, doing good, and giving to relatives, and forbids immorality, wrongdoing, and oppression.”

translated_text:
The sixteenth argument:

Allah has commanded nothing without having created within the servant’s innate constitution the cause and impulse for fulfilling it, and made him need it; in it lie his well-being and perfection. He has commanded belief in Him, and every child is born upon the natural disposition. Hearts therefore possess the strongest grounds for knowing their Creator and acknowledging Him. He has commanded knowledge, truthfulness, justice, maintaining ties of kinship, fulfilling trusts, and other things that hearts recognize and love. Hence these are called “recognized good.” He has forbidden disbelief, which is the root of ignorance and injustice, as well as lying, injustice, miserliness, cowardice, and other things that hearts reject.

A human being commits forbidden evil only because he is ignorant of it or needs it—in the sense that he desires it, takes pleasure in its presence, or suffers from its absence. Ignorance is the absence of knowledge. Thus, forbidden conduct caused by ignorance results from failing to acquire the knowledge one has been commanded to acquire. Conduct caused by a need arising from desire or aversion results from failing to perform the commanded action corresponding to that need. For example, someone commits unlawful sexual intercourse because he has not sought chastity through lawful marriage, or eats forbidden food because he has not kept himself from the unlawful through the lawful provisions he has been commanded to use. Otherwise, if he performs the commanded action that frees him of any need for the unlawful, he will not fall into it.

It is thus established that Allah has created within the servant the cause and impulse for what He has commanded, and that what is forbidden

It is like eating for the body—indeed, eating itself falls within what is commanded—and like marriage for humankind, which is also commanded. The cause of forbidden conduct arises within him only through the absence of what is commanded. Its occurrence therefore results from that absence. Hence, failing to do what is commanded is more harmful to him than committing what is forbidden, because that failure harms him in two ways. By neglecting what is commanded, he is also more deserving of blame and punishment, since he has within him an impulse toward it that helps him perform it. By contrast, there is originally no impulse within him toward what is forbidden except when what is commanded is absent. Its absence, in turn, is brought about only by performing what is commanded. Such is the case.

The seventeenth argument:

Doing good deeds entails abandoning bad deeds, whereas merely abandoning bad deeds does not entail doing good deeds. Refraining from bad deeds despite an impulse toward them can only occur through a good deed. Performing good deeds in the absence of such an impulse does not depend on refraining from a bad deed. One is rewarded for such restraint because one has refrained from bad deeds despite the impulse toward them.

This is because Allah created the son of Adam to be ever intent and ever active, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The truest names are Hārith and Hammām.”

A hārith is:

original_text:
الْعَامِلُ الْكَاسِبُ وَالْهَمَّامُ:
 الْكَثِيرُ الْهَمِّ.
 وَهَذَا مَعْنَى قَوْلِهِمْ:
 مُتَحَرِّكٌ بِالْإِرَادَةِ وَالْهَمِّ وَالْإِرَادَةُ لَا تَكُونُ إلَّا بِشُعُورِ وَإِحْسَاسٍ فَهُوَ حَسَّاسٌ مُتَحَرِّكٌ بِالْإِرَادَةِ دَائِمًا.
 وَلِهَذَا جَاءَ فِي الْحَدِيثِ:
 
" 
{لَلْقَلْبُ أَشَدُّ تَقَلُّبًا مِنْ الْقِدْرِ إذَا اسْتَجْمَعَتْ غَلَيَانًا}
 "
 وَ 
" 
{مَثَلُ الْقَلْبِ مَثَلُ رِيشَةٍ مُلْقَاةٍ بِأَرْضِ فَلَاةٍ}
 "
 وَ 
" 
{مَا مِنْ قَلْبٍ مِنْ قُلُوبِ الْعِبَادِ إلَّا بَيْنَ إصْبَعَيْنِ مِنْ أَصَابِعِ الرَّحْمَنِ}
 "
 وَإِذَا كَانَ كَذَلِكَ فَعَدَمُ إحْسَاسِهِ وَحَرَكَتِهِ مُمْتَنِعٌ فَإِنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ إحْسَاسُهُ وَحَرَكَتُهُ مِنْ الْحَسَنَاتِ الْمَأْمُورِ بِهَا أَوْ الْمُبَاحَاتِ وَإِلَّا كَانَ مِنْ السَّيِّئَاتِ الْمَنْهِيِّ عَنْهَا فَصَارَ فِعْلُ الْحَسَنَاتِ يَتَضَمَّنُ الْأَمْرَيْنِ فَهُوَ أَشْرَفُ وَأَفْضَلُ.
 وَذَلِكَ لِأَنَّ مَنْ فَعَلَ مَا أُمِرَ بِهِ مِنْ الْإِيمَانِ وَالْعَمَلِ الصَّالِحِ:
 قَدْ يَمْتَنِعُ بِذَلِكَ عَمَّا نُهِيَ عَنْهُ مِنْ أَحَدِ وَجْهَيْنِ: إمَّا مِنْ جِهَةِ اجْتِمَاعِهِمَا فَإِنَّ الْإِيمَانَ ضِدُّ الْكُفْرِ؛ وَالْعَمَلُ الصَّالِحُ ضِدُّ السَّيِّئِ فَلَا يَكُونُ مُصَدِّقًا مُكَذِّبًا مُحِبًّا مُبْغِضًا. وَإِمَّا مِنْ جِهَةِ اقْتِضَاءِ الْحَسَنَةِ تَرْكَ السَّيِّئَةِ؛
 كَمَا قَالَ تَعَالَى:
 
{إنَّ الصَّلَاةَ تَنْهَى عَنِ الْفَحْشَاءِ وَالْمُنْكَرِ}
 وَهَذَا مَحْسُوسٌ؛ فَإِنَّ الْإِنْسَانَ إذَا قَرَأَ الْقُرْآنَ وَتَدَبَّرَهُ كَانَ ذَلِكَ مِنْ أَقْوَى الْأَسْبَابِ الْمَانِعَةِ لَهُ مِنْ الْمَعَاصِي أَوْ بَعْضِهَا وَكَذَلِكَ الصَّوْمُ جُنَّةٌ وَكَذَلِكَ نَفْسُ الْإِيمَانِ بِتَحْرِيمِ الْمُحَرَّمَاتِ وَبِعَذَابِ اللَّهِ عَلَيْهَا بِصَدِّ الْقَلْبِ عَنْ إرَادَتِهَا.
translated_text:
one who works and earns, while a hammām is one who is ever intent. This is what is meant by saying that a person acts through volition and intention. Volition necessarily involves awareness and perception; thus, he is continually perceiving and acting through volition. Hence the following statements occur in hadith:

“The heart is more turbulent than a pot at a rolling boil.”

“The heart is like a feather lying on open desert ground.”

“There is no heart among Allah’s servants that is not between two of the fingers of the Most Merciful.”

Since this is so, it is impossible for the heart to be entirely without perception and activity. If its perception and activity do not fall within the good deeds that are commanded or within permissible acts, they must fall within the bad deeds that are forbidden. Doing good deeds thus encompasses both matters, making it nobler and more excellent.

This is because someone who fulfils what he has been commanded to do in terms of faith and righteous deeds may thereby refrain from what he has been forbidden in one of two ways. The first concerns their coexistence: faith is the opposite of disbelief, and righteous action is the opposite of evil action, so a person cannot simultaneously affirm and deny, or love and hate. The second is that a good deed leads one to abandon a bad deed, as Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, prayer restrains one from shameful and evil deeds.”

This is evident from experience. When a person reads the Quran and reflects upon it, this is among the strongest means of preventing him from committing sins, or at least some of them. Likewise, fasting is a shield. Similarly, belief itself that forbidden things are prohibited, and that Allah punishes people for them, turns the heart away from desiring them.

original_text:
فَالْحَسَنَاتُ إمَّا ضِدُّ السَّيِّئَاتِ؛ وَإِمَّا مَانِعَةٌ مِنْهَا فَهِيَ إمَّا ضِدٌّ وَإِمَّا صَدٌّ. وَإِنَّمَا تَكُونُ السَّيِّئَاتُ عِنْدَ ضَعْفِ الْحَسَنَاتِ الْمَانِعَةِ مِنْهَا كَمَا قَالَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ 
" 
{لَا يَزْنِي الزَّانِي حِينَ يَزْنِي وَهُوَ مُؤْمِنٌ؛ وَلَا يَسْرِقُ السَّارِقُ حِينَ يَسْرِقُ وَهُوَ مُؤْمِنٌ؛ وَلَا يَشْرَبُ الْخَمْرَ حِينَ يَشْرَبُهَا وَهُوَ مُؤْمِنٌ}
 "
 فَإِنَّ كَمَالَ الْإِيمَانِ وَحَقِيقَتَهُ يَمْنَعُ ذَلِكَ فَلَا يَقَعُ إلَّا عِنْدَ نَوْعِ ضَعْفٍ فِي الْإِيمَانِ يُزِيلُ كَمَالِهِ.
 وَأَمَّا تَرْكُ السَّيِّئَاتِ:
 فَإِمَّا أَنْ يُرَادَ بِهِ مُجَرَّدَ عَدَمِهَا فَالْعَدَمُ الْمَحْضُ لَا يُنَافِي شَيْئًا وَلَا يَقْتَضِيهِ بَلْ الْخَالِي الْقَلْبُ مُتَعَرِّضٌ لِلسَّيِّئَاتِ أَكْثَرَ مِنْ تَعَرُّضِهِ لِلْحَسَنَاتِ. وَإِمَّا أَنْ يُرَادَ بِهِ الِامْتِنَاعُ مِنْ فِعْلِهَا؛ فَهَذَا الِامْتِنَاعُ لَا يَكُونُ إلَّا مَعَ اعْتِقَادِ قُبْحِهَا وَقَصْدِ تَرْكِهَا وَهَذَا الِاعْتِقَادُ وَالِاقْتِصَادُ حَسَنَتَانِ مَأْمُورٌ بِهِمَا وَهُمَا مِنْ أَعْظَمِ الْحَسَنَاتِ. فَثَبَتَ بِذَلِكَ أَنَّ وُجُودَ الْحَسَنَاتِ يَمْنَعُ السَّيِّئَاتِ وَأَنَّ عَدَمَ السَّيِّئَاتِ لَا يُوجِبُ الْحَسَنَاتِ فَصَارَ فِي وُجُودِ الْحَسَنَاتِ الْأَمْرَانِ بِخِلَافِ مُجَرَّدِ عَدَمِ السَّيِّئَاتِ فَلَيْسَ فِيهِ إلَّا أَمْرٌ وَاحِدٌ وَهَذَا هُوَ الْمَقْصُودُ.
translated_text:
Thus, good deeds either stand in opposition to bad deeds or prevent them: they are either their opposite or a barrier against them. Bad deeds occur only when the good deeds that prevent them are weak, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“No adulterer is a believer while committing adultery; no thief is a believer while stealing; and no one who drinks wine is a believer while drinking it.”

Faith in its fullness and true reality prevents such acts. They therefore occur only when there is some weakness in faith that deprives it of its completeness.

As for leaving bad deeds, this may mean merely their absence. Pure absence neither excludes anything nor entails anything. Indeed, a person whose heart is unoccupied is more susceptible to bad deeds than to good ones. Alternatively, it may mean deliberately refraining from committing them. Such restraint requires believing that they are evil and intending to abandon them. This belief and moderation are two commanded good deeds, and they are among the greatest good deeds.

It is thus established that the presence of good deeds prevents bad deeds, whereas the absence of bad deeds does not necessarily bring about good deeds. The presence of good deeds therefore combines both benefits, unlike the mere absence of bad deeds, which involves only one. This is the point being made.

original_text:
الْوَجْهُ الثَّامِنَ عَشَرَ:
 أَنَّ فِعْلَ الْحَسَنَاتِ مُوجِبٌ لِلْحَسَنَاتِ أَيْضًا؛ فَإِنَّ الْإِيمَانَ يَقْتَضِي الْأَعْمَالَ الصَّالِحَةَ وَالْعَمَلُ الصَّالِحُ يَدْعُو إلَى نَظِيرِهِ وَغَيْرِ نَظِيرِهِ؛
 كَمَا قِيلَ:
 إنَّ مِنْ ثَوَابِ الْحَسَنَةِ الْحَسَنَةَ بَعْدَهَا. وَأَمَّا عَدَمُ السَّيِّئَةِ فَلَا يَقْتَضِي عَدَمَ سَيِّئَةٍ إلَّا إذَا كَانَ امْتِنَاعًا فَيَكُونُ مِنْ بَابِ الْحَسَنَاتِ كَمَا تَقَدَّمَ وَمَا اقْتَضَى فَرْعًا أَفْضَلُ مِمَّا لَا يَقْتَضِي فَرْعًا لَهُ وَهَذَا مِنْ نَمَطِ الَّذِي قَبْلَهُ.
الْوَجْهُ التَّاسِعَ عَشَرَ:
 تَرْجِيحُ الْوُجُودِ عَلَى الْعَدَمِ إذَا عُلِمَ أَنَّهُ حَسَنَةٌ وَأَمَّا الْمُخْتَلِطُ وَالْمُشْتَبِهُ عَلَيْهِ فَقَدْ يَكُونُ الْإِمْسَاكُ خَيْرًا لَهُ لِيَبْقَى مَعَ الْفِطْرَةِ فَهَذَا حَالُ الْمُهْتَدِي وَالضَّالِّ وَحَالُ. . . 
(١)
 فَإِذَا قَامَ الْمُقْتَضِي لِلْكُفْرِ وَالْفُسُوقِ وَالْعِصْيَانِ فِي قَلْبِهِ مِنْ الشُّبُهَاتِ وَالشَّهَوَاتِ لَمْ يَزَلْ هَذَا الْحِسُّ وَالْحَرَكَةُ إلَّا بِمَا يُزِيلُهُ أَوْ يَشْتَغِلُ عَنْهُ مِنْ إيمَانٍ وَصَلَاحٍ كَالْعِلْمِ الَّذِي يُزِيلُ الشُّبْهَةَ؛ وَالْقَصْدُ الَّذِي يَمْنَعُ الشَّهْوَةَ وَهَذَا أَمْرٌ يَجِدُهُ الْمَرْءُ فِي نَفْسِهِ وَهُوَ فِي كُلِّ شَيْءٍ؛ فَإِنَّ مَا وُجِدَ مُقْتَضِيهِ فَلَا يَزُولُ إلَّا بِوُجُودِ مُنَافِيهِ.
 فَإِنْ قِيلَ:
 فَقَدْ يَزُولُ ذَلِكَ بِمُبَاحِ. . . 
(٢)
.
original_footnote: (١، ٢) بياض بالأصل
translated_text:
The eighteenth point:

Doing good deeds also gives rise to further good deeds. Faith entails righteous deeds, and a righteous deed encourages others, both of the same kind and of different kinds. As has been said:

“Part of the reward for a good deed is another good deed that follows it.”

The mere absence of a bad deed, however, does not entail the absence of another bad deed, unless it involves deliberately refraining; in that case, it belongs among good deeds, as explained above. What produces a further outcome is better than what produces none. This argument is of the same kind as the preceding one.

The nineteenth point:

Doing is preferable to not doing when the act is known to be a good deed. For someone who is confused and uncertain, however, refraining may be better, so that he remains upon his natural disposition. Such is the condition of the rightly guided and the misguided, and the condition of . . . (1)

When doubts and desires arise in his heart, prompting disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience, this feeling and impulse will cease only through faith and righteousness that remove it or divert him from it—such as knowledge that dispels doubt and resolve that restrains desire. A person experiences this within himself, and it applies to everything: whatever has a cause sustaining it will cease only when something that counters it is present.

If it is said: “Yet that may cease through something permissible . . . (2).”
translated_footnote: (1, 2) Blank in the original.

original_text:
الْوَجْهُ الْعِشْرُونَ:
 أَنَّ اللَّهَ تَعَالَى بَعَثَ الرُّسُلَ وَأَنْزَلَ الْكُتُبَ فِي الْعُلُومِ وَالْأَعْمَالِ بِالْكَلِمِ الطَّيِّبِ وَالْعَمَلِ الصَّالِحِ بِالْهُدَى وَدِينِ الْحَقِّ وَذَلِكَ بِالْأُمُورِ الْمَوْجُودَةِ فِي الْعَقَائِدِ وَالْأَعْمَالِ فَأَمَرَهُمْ فِي الِاعْتِقَادَاتِ بِالِاعْتِقَادَاتِ الْمُفَصَّلَةِ فِي أَسْمَاءِ اللَّهِ وَصِفَاتِهِ: وَسَائِرِ مَا يَحْتَاجُ إلَيْهِ مِنْ الْوَعْدِ وَالْوَعِيدِ وَفِي الْأَعْمَالِ بِالْعِبَادَاتِ الْمُتَنَوِّعَةِ مِنْ أَصْنَافِ الْعِبَادَاتِ الْبَاطِنَةِ وَالظَّاهِرَةِ. وَأَمَّا فِي النَّفْيِ فَجَاءَتْ بِالنَّفْيِ الْمُجْمَلِ وَالنَّهْيِ عَمَّا يَضُرُّ الْمَأْمُورَ بِهِ فَالْكُتُبُ الْإِلَهِيَّةُ وَشَرَائِعُ الرُّسُلِ مُمْتَلِئَةٌ مِنْ الْإِثْبَاتِ فِيمَا يَعْلَمُ وَيَعْمَلُ.
 وَأَمَّا الْمُعَطِّلَةُ مِنْ الْمُتَفَلْسِفَةِ وَنَحْوِهِمْ:
 فَيَغْلِبُ عَلَيْهِمْ النَّفْيُ وَالنَّهْيُ؛
 فَإِنَّهُمْ فِي عَقَائِدِهِمْ الْغَالِبُ عَلَيْهِمْ السَّلْبُ:
 لَيْسَ بِكَذَا لَيْسَ بِكَذَا لَيْسَ بِكَذَا. .
 وَفِي الْأَفْعَالِ الْغَالِبُ عَلَيْهِمْ الذَّمُّ وَالتَّرْكُ:
 مِنْ الزُّهْدِ الْفَاسِدِ وَالْوَرَعِ الْفَاسِدِ: لَا يَفْعَلُ لَا يَفْعَلُ لَا يَفْعَلُ. . مِنْ غَيْرِ أَنْ يَأْتُوا بِأَعْمَالِ صَالِحَةٍ يَعْمَلُهَا الرَّجُلُ تَنْفَعُهُ وَتَمْنَعُ مَا يَضُرُّهُ مِنْ الْأَعْمَالِ الْفَاسِدَةِ؛ وَلِهَذَا كَانَ غَالِبُ مَنْ سَلَكَ طَرَائِقَهُمْ بَطَّالًا مُتَعَطِّلًا مُعَطِّلًا فِي عَقَائِدِهِ وَأَعْمَالِهِ.
translated_text:
The twentieth point:

Allah, Exalted is He, sent the messengers and revealed the scriptures concerning knowledge and action, bringing good words and righteous deeds, guidance and the religion of truth. All this involves positive content in belief and action. In matters of belief, He commanded detailed beliefs concerning Allah’s names and attributes and everything else one needs concerning promises of reward and threats of punishment. In matters of action, He commanded diverse forms of inward and outward worship. As for negation, the scriptures expressed it in general terms and prohibited whatever undermines what is commanded. Thus, the divine scriptures and the laws of the messengers abound in affirmations concerning what one is to know and do.

As for the negationists among the philosophical thinkers and their like, negation and prohibition predominate among them. Their beliefs are dominated by denial: “Not such-and-such, not such-and-such, not such-and-such…”

In matters of action, censure and abstention predominate, taking the form of corrupt asceticism and corrupt scrupulousness: “He does not do this, he does not do that, he does not do that…” Yet they offer no righteous deeds for a person to perform that would benefit him and keep him from harmful, corrupt deeds. Thus, most of those who follow their paths are idle and inactive, given to negation in both their beliefs and their actions.

The followers of the messengers, by contrast, possess knowledge, guidance, righteousness, and goodness in their beliefs and deeds. It is thus clear that command and affirmation predominate in what the messengers brought, whereas prohibition and negation predominate in the way of the disbelieving negationists and their like. This is among the clearest proofs of the superiority of command and affirmation over prohibition and negation.

The twenty-first point:

Negation and prohibition cannot stand independently; they must be preceded by something affirmed and a command. Command and affirmation, by contrast, can stand independently. This is because a person cannot conceive of the nonexistent from the outset, nor direct his intention toward it from the outset. I have established this earlier and explained that a person can conceive of the nonexistent only through conceiving of what exists. If he cannot conceive of it, then he is even less able to intend it, for intention and will are preceded by awareness and conception.

This dependence is more pronounced in intention and will than in awareness and knowledge. A person can conceive of both the existent and the nonexistent and make statements about them. As for willing the nonexistent, this is not conceivable in every respect. Rather, willing a thing’s nonexistence consists in hating and disliking it. A person either wills a thing’s existence, wills its nonexistence, or wills neither its existence nor its nonexistence. The first is the fundamental form of will and love.

As for the second—willing its nonexistence—it consists in hating and disliking it, which is preceded by conceiving of what is hated and disliked. Thus, hatred and dislike of a thing, which entail refraining from it—the aim of the one issuing the prohibition and what is required of the person addressed by it—are derivative in two respects:

This is because a person may know that something does not exist and report its nonexistence, as when we say: “I bear witness that there is no deity but Allah”; “There is no prophet after Muhammad”; “The Messiah is neither a deity nor a lord”; or “That is the Book in which there is no doubt.” Further examples include such statements as: “The mountain is not ruby, nor is the sea mercury,” and the like. These negative declarative statements are negative propositions. Without conceiving of the negation and the subject of that negation, a person could not assert the negation and make the judgment. He must therefore conceive of both the negation and its subject, as in conceiving of the mountain and the ruby.

What is negated is pure nonexistence. Yet the human soul, which is aware, knows, and perceives through its faculties and instruments, has neither found nonexistence, nor comprehended it, nor encountered it, nor sensed it through any of its inward or outward senses. It has been aware only of what exists. But once it becomes aware of something existent, the intellect and imagination begin to posit within the soul things derived from those existing things: either combinations of them or things resembling them.

Thus, a person perceives a ruby and a mountain, then combines them in his imagination into a mountain of ruby. He knows what prophethood is and knows the period following Muhammad’s being sent as a messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—then imagines a prophet in that later period. the worlds, then imagines that divinity existing in other beings. The believer then denies what has thus been posited: divinity in anyone other than Allah Most High, and prophethood in anyone after Muhammad—may Allah bless him and grant him peace. The disbeliever, however, may believe that what has been posited actually exists. He thus attributes divinity to the sun, the moon, the stars, the angels, the prophets or some of them, the righteous or some of them, other human beings, or idols fashioned as representations of some of these deities taken besides Allah, glorified be He.

The point is that a person cannot conceive of something’s nonexistence or report it without first conceiving of something existent, using it as the basis for an analogy, and thereby positing something else. He then negates what has been posited by analogy with it, then affirms it. The derivative thing posited by analogy depends upon the original that serves as the basis of the analogy and the supposition. Nonexistence can therefore be conceived of only through analogy, comparison, and derivation—not independently, as a directly apprehended reality or an original basis.

Although certain existing things can be conceived of in this world by people—or by some of them—only through analogy or comparison, some existing things are nevertheless perceived in their reality and actual existence, while others are perceived through analogy or comparison, as with things perceived in dreams. As for what does not exist, it can be perceived only through analogy or comparison, since it has no reality that a living, perceiving being can apprehend or that conscious beings can encounter directly. For the reality of each thing in the external world is identical with its essence. As for the essences and realities posited in the mind, they may have an actual reality in external, concrete existence in the world, or they may not.

translated_text:
And the same holds for intention, love, and will in two respects:

First, loving or hating an object—whether sought and loved or disliked and hated—is inconceivable without some prior awareness of it. Awareness of what exists is primary, while awareness of what does not exist is derivative; this applies all the more to the love and hatred that follow such awareness.

Second, a person loves only what suits him and accords with his nature, bringing him pleasure and delight. His soul is neither suited nor akin to sheer nonexistence and pure negation. In sheer nonexistence he finds neither pleasure nor joy, neither blessing nor bliss, no good whatsoever, and certainly no benefit. Indeed, loving sheer nonexistence is like the absence of love, and taking pleasure in sheer nonexistence is like the absence of pleasure. How can something that is nothing at all contain any benefit, pleasure, or good?

Rather, his soul loves what brings it benefit and pleasure: milk at birth, for example, and other foods; then the pleasures of sexual intimacy and the like; then the pleasures of honour, leadership, and similar things; and then the pleasures of reason, knowledge, and faith. He also loves what wards off harm, such as clothing, dwellings, and the good things that shield him from his foes—heat and cold, harmful human beings, harmful animals, and so forth. Thus, he loves the existence of what benefits him and the absence of what harms him. What benefits him is necessarily something that exists, as explained above. As for what harms him, sometimes

translated_text:
We reply:

This objection rests on two things: ignorance of the true nature of piety, scrupulousness, and asceticism; and ignorance of why these are praiseworthy.

First, we say:

Who said that piety consists merely in refraining from evil deeds? Rather, piety—as earlier and later generations have explained it—means doing what you have been commanded to do and refraining from what you have been forbidden. Thus, when strife broke out, Talq ibn Habīb said, “Protect yourselves against it through piety.” They asked, “What is piety?”

He replied:

“To obey Allah, guided by light from Allah, hoping for Allah’s reward; and to refrain from disobeying Allah, guided by light from Allah, fearing Allah’s punishment.”

Allah Most High says in the longest surah of the Quran:

“Alif Lām Mīm.”

“This is the Book about which there is no doubt, a guidance for the pious.”

“Those who believe in the unseen, establish prayer, and spend out of what We have provided for them.”

And so the passage continues. He thus describes the pious as carrying out what is commanded: faith and righteous deeds, including establishing prayer and giving zakah. He also says:

“O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you and those before you, so that you may become pious.”

And He says:

“Righteousness does not consist in turning your faces towards the east or the west. Rather, the righteous are those who believe in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Book, and the prophets, and give wealth, despite their love for it, to relatives, orphans, the needy, and the traveller

and those who ask, and for freeing slaves; establish prayer and give zakah; fulfil their pledges when they make them; and are patient in hardship, suffering, and battle. Those are the ones who are true, and those are the pious.”

This is a momentous verse of immense significance, among the greatest verses of the Quran and the most comprehensive in addressing the matters of religion. It has been reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked about the qualities of faith, whereupon this verse was revealed. In al-Tirmidhī, Fātimah bint Qays reports that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, “There is a due upon wealth besides zakah,” and recited this verse.

It indicates several things:

First, Allah declares that those who do these things are the pious, and most of these things consist of commanded actions.

Second, He declares that these things constitute righteousness, and that those who practise them are truthful—that is, in saying, “We believe.” Most of them involve actively performing commanded deeds. Thus, carrying out what is commanded is more integral to righteousness, piety, and faith than merely not doing what is forbidden.

It is by virtue of these three descriptions that Paradise is merited, as Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss, and indeed, the wicked will be in Hellfire.”

And He says:

“Or should We treat the pious like the wicked?”

“Indeed, the pious will be amid gardens and rivers.”

And He says:

“Is one who is a believer like one who is defiantly disobedient? They are not equal.”

“Worship Allah and associate nothing with Him, and be good to parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, the neighbour who is related to you, the neighbour who is unrelated, the companion at your side, the traveller, and those whom your right hands possess.”

And His words:

“Give relatives their due, and the needy and the traveller,”

in the surahs Subhān and al-Rūm.

Giving relatives their due means maintaining ties of kinship; giving the needy their due means feeding the hungry; and giving the traveller his due means offering hospitality to guests. Spending on freeing slaves includes securing the release of captives, while giving to orphans is a form of feeding the poor. In al-Bukhārī, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Visit the sick, feed the hungry, and free the captive.”

And in the hadith upon which Ahmad based his ruling:

“If the beggar were truthful, no one who turned him away would prosper.”

Furthermore, the messengers—such as Noah, Hūd, Sālih, and Shuayb—began their call, as related in Surah Hūd, with:

“Worship Allah; you have no god other than Him.”

And in al-Shuarā:

“Will you not fear Allah?”

“So fear Allah and obey me.”

Allah Most High also says:

“But righteousness is in one who fears Allah.”

And He says:

“Yes, whoever fulfils his covenant and fears Allah—indeed, Allah loves those who fear Him.”

And He says:

“Fulfil your treaty with them until the end of its term. Indeed, Allah loves those who fear Him.”

And He says:

“As long as they remain true to you, remain true to them. Indeed, Allah loves those who fear Him.”

He has thus made clear that fulfilling covenants is part of the piety that Allah loves. Fulfilling covenants encompasses everything commanded, for an obligation arises either from revealed law or from a stipulation, and all of this involves performing a commanded act. It constitutes fulfilment of the covenant with Allah and covenants with His servants.

Taqwā (piety) means either fearing Allah or guarding against His punishment, as He says:

“So fear the Fire whose fuel is people and stones.”

“And fear the Fire prepared for the disbelievers.”

Thus, taqwā means guarding against what is feared by doing what is commanded and refraining from what is forbidden, though it consists more in the former. This is called taqwā because neglecting what is commanded and doing what is forbidden is a means of safety from Allah’s censure, displeasure, and punishment. Its motivating force is therefore fear of sin. This differs from an act that brings benefit but whose omission causes no harm: that is a recommended act, which one may either perform or leave undone. He therefore described this as taqwā to make clear that it is obligatory and that the person concerned exposes himself to punishment by abandoning taqwā.

Secondly, we say: wherever taqwā is used to mean refraining from what is forbidden—if that interpretation is adopted—as in His words:

“Cooperate in righteousness and piety,”

concerning which some of the early Muslims said, “Righteousness means doing what you have been commanded, and piety means avoiding what you have been forbidden,” it is always coupled

with doing what is commanded, just as He mentions righteousness alongside it, and as in Noah’s words:

“Worship Allah, fear Him, and obey me.”

This is because such piety necessarily entails doing what is commanded.

Thirdly, we say: most people may perform some of what is commanded, but only the truly sincere refrain from what is forbidden, as Sahl said. This is because the soul has an inclination towards what is commanded, whereas refraining from what is forbidden requires opposing one’s desires and striving against oneself. It is therefore harder and more demanding, and few practise it. No one can do so without also doing what is commanded. Piety cannot be conceived as action [and] abstention alone. Whoever abandons associating partners with Allah, following misleading desires, and pursuing forbidden pleasures must necessarily perform many commanded deeds that keep him from these things. Their piety thus preserves the good deeds they have been commanded to perform and protects them from sins that harm them. This differs, for example, from someone who does both what he is commanded and what he is forbidden: committing forbidden acts corrupts whatever commanded deeds it corrupts, so that they do not remain intact for him.

This is why the ultimate good outcome belongs to piety, as Allah Most High says:

“And the ultimate good outcome belongs to piety.”

“And the ultimate good outcome is for those who fear Allah.”

“And if you are patient and fear Allah, their plotting will not harm you at all.”

Those who fear Allah are like someone who eats wholesome food and avoids harmful foods: his body becomes healthy, and his eventual condition is sound. Someone who lacks piety, however, is like a person who mixes different foods: although he gains nourishment from them, those mixtures may cause him

translated_text:
illnesses that are either harmful or fatal. Even so, no reasonable person would say that his need for, and benefit from, avoiding harmful foods is greater than his need for, and benefit from, wholesome foods. Rather, his need for and benefit from the foods he eats are greater than the benefit he derives from those he avoids. If he ate no food whatsoever, he would certainly perish. If, however, he eats both wholesome and harmful foods, there may be hope for his safety, but also fear for his life. If he eats wholesome foods and avoids harmful ones, he enjoys health and safety.

The first case is comparable to someone who abandons what he has been commanded to do. The second is comparable to someone who does both what is commanded and what is forbidden: someone who mixes righteous deeds with evil ones. The third is comparable to the person of piety who does what he has been commanded and avoids what he has been forbidden. Piety is therefore of such great importance because it combines safety with honour, not because it brings safety alone. In the Hereafter there is no abode other than Paradise or Hell: whoever is saved from Hell enters Paradise, and whoever is not granted bliss is punished. No human being is left without either punishment or bliss.

Reflect on this: every quality that Allah has commanded or praised necessarily involves doing what is commanded, either as an integral part of it or as its necessary consequence. Such qualities are praised for securing good rather than evil, and reward rather than punishment.

Likewise, scrupulousness and renunciation, as prescribed in Islam, are forms of the piety it prescribes. Some people, however, have misunderstood this. This includes performing obligatory acts and doubtful acts that appear to be obligatory, and avoiding prohibited acts and doubtful acts that appear to be prohibited. If disliked acts are included, I would say: “We fear that it may lead to deficiency and punishment.” Obligatory scrupulousness, however, means guarding against what leads to blame and punishment: performing what is obligatory and avoiding what is prohibited. The difference between the two concerns matters whose obligatory status is uncertain—whether they are obligatory or not—and matters whose prohibition is uncertain—whether they are prohibited or not. Refraining from what is unquestionably lawful is not scrupulousness, nor is performing what is unquestionably not required.

My qualification, “in the absence of an overriding consideration,” addresses cases in which a person can avoid something clearly prohibited or doubtful only by abandoning a good deed whose standing in Islamic law is greater than that of avoiding that evil. An example is someone who refuses to follow a sinful imam and consequently abandons Friday prayer, congregational prayer, Hajj and military campaigns. Likewise, a person may be able to perform a clear or possible obligation only by committing an evil more sinful than leaving that obligation unfulfilled. An example is someone who cannot fulfil the duties of enjoining right and forbidding wrong with respect to those in authority except through fighting that causes greater harm than the harm caused by the ruler’s injustice.

The basis for scrupulousness concerning doubtful matters is the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

However, errors concerning scrupulousness arise in three ways.

The first is that many people believe it consists in abstention. They therefore see scrupulousness only in avoiding the unlawful, not in fulfilling obligations. This afflicts many religiously observant and scrupulous people. You may see someone scrupulously avoiding a lie or a dirham of doubtful provenance because it comes from a wrongdoer’s wealth or an invalid transaction. He also scrupulously avoids inclining towards wrongdoers on account of religious innovations, and towards those given to immorality in worldly affairs.

Yet he neglects duties incumbent upon him, whether individual obligations or collective obligations that have become his personal responsibility: maintaining ties of kinship; fulfilling the rights of neighbours, the needy, companions, orphans and travellers; and fulfilling the rights of Muslims, those in authority and people of knowledge. translated_text:
and forbidding wrong, striving in Allah’s cause, and other duties incumbent upon him that benefit people in their religious and worldly affairs. Or he performs these duties not as worship of Allah Most High, but merely as an imposed obligation or the like.

Such scrupulousness may lead a person into grave religious innovations. The scrupulousness of the Khawārij, the Rāfidah, the Mu‘tazilah and others like them is of this kind. They scrupulously avoided injustice and what they believed to be injustice, such as associating with those they considered wrongdoers, until they abandoned major obligations: Friday and congregational prayers, Hajj, striving in Allah’s cause, sincere counsel to Muslims and compassion towards them. Those practising this kind of scrupulousness were censured by the leading scholars, including the four imams, and their case came to be discussed in expositions of the creed of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah.

The second source of error concerns unsound beliefs. When someone performs obligatory and doubtful acts, and refrains from forbidden and doubtful acts, his belief that something is obligatory or forbidden must rest on evidence from the Quran and Sunnah and on knowledge, not personal inclination. Many people feel an aversion to certain things because of habit or similar influences, which reinforces their belief that those things are forbidden or doubtful. Some harbour illusions and false suspicions, and these suspicions rest upon misguided scrupulousness. Such a person is among those of whom Allah Most High says:

“They follow nothing but conjecture and what their souls desire.”

This is the condition of those afflicted by obsessive doubts concerning ritual impurities. Their misguided scrupulousness combines a measure of religiosity with weakness of intellect and knowledge. The same applies to the scrupulousness of people who consider most people’s wealth unlawful

Some have gone so far as to deem it lawful for a ruler, on the grounds that he is entitled to it, and to hold that a thief’s hand should not be cut off for stealing it, nor should rulings concerning usurped property be applied to it. Imams such as Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others condemned these people’s conduct and censured those who go to excess in scrupulousness.

Muslim narrated in his Sahīh that ‘Abd Allāh ibn Mas‘ūd said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: ‘Those who go to excess are ruined.’ He repeated this three times.”

Much of the scrupulousness practised by the people of religious innovation belongs to this category. Indeed, the scrupulous refusal of Jews, Christians and other disbelievers to fulfil the obligations of Islam belongs to this category. So too does their scrupulous avoidance of things they themselves declared forbidden, although Allah Most High had not forbidden them—a practice Allah Most High censured in the Quran—such as the animals called bahīrah, sā’ibah, wasīlah and hām.

Another example is the scrupulousness censured by the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in the hadith recorded in the Sahīh. When he availed himself of certain concessions and learned that some people had scrupulously abstained from those things, he said:

of religion. Otherwise, his misguided scrupulousness may do more harm than good, as has happened among disbelievers and people of religious innovation, including the Khawārij, the Rāfidah and others.

The third consideration: a countervailing factor of greater weight.

This is more difficult than the preceding consideration. Something may have a harmful aspect that calls for avoiding it. A scrupulous person notices this but overlooks the greater good that weighs against it. The converse is subject to the same principle. It has become clear that someone who regards scrupulousness as abstention alone, includes within it the conduct of people who have good intentions but lack insight into their religion, and disregards the greater good they have forfeited through their scrupulousness, has missed more of the religion of Islam than he has grasped. Indeed, he may find fault with people who are closer to salvation and happiness. This principle is of great benefit in cases of this kind and others like them.

It benefits those whose scrupulousness is deficient or misguided, as well as those whose renunciation of worldly things is deficient or misguided. For the renunciation prescribed by Allah and His Messenger consists in having no desire for superfluous permissible things that bring no benefit. Forgoing superfluous permissible things that bring no religious benefit is renunciation, not scrupulousness. There is no doubt that craving and desire for this worldly life and its wealth and power are harmful. Al-Tirmidhī narrated that Ka‘b ibn Mālik said:

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Two hungry wolves let loose in a sheepfold are no more destructive to it than a man’s craving for wealth and honour is to his religion.”

Al-Tirmidhī said: “This is a good and authentic hadith.” Thus the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, condemned craving

for wealth and honour—the latter meaning leadership and authority—and stated that this corrupts religion as much as, or more than, two hungry wolves ravage a sheepfold. This shows that such craving is condemned precisely because it corrupts religion, which consists of faith and righteous deeds. Giving up this craving therefore serves righteous action. These two things are mentioned in Allah’s words:

“My wealth has availed me nothing. My authority has vanished from me.”

They are also the two things Allah mentions in Sūrat al-Qasas. He begins it with the account of Pharaoh and describes his exaltation on earth—that is, leadership, honour and authority. Then, towards its end, He mentions Qārūn and the wealth he had been given. He describes the ultimate fate of the authority of the one and the wealth of the other, then says:

“That abode of the Hereafter We assign to those who desire neither superiority on earth nor corruption.”

Such were the ways of Pharaoh and Qārūn. Accumulating wealth without spending it where one is commanded to, and acquiring it through improper means, are forms of corruption. Likewise, when someone seeks authority for himself without justice or right, he can attain it only through corruption and wrongdoing.

But simply possessing authority and wealth, when used to seek Allah’s countenance, uphold the truth and attain the abode of the Hereafter, and as an aid to obeying Allah—without the heart’s love for Allah, His Messenger and striving in His cause growing weak, as was the case with the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, Abū Bakr and ‘Umar, and without being distracted from remembering Allah—is among the greatest blessings Allah Most High bestows upon His servant, provided these conditions are met. Yet rarely does

one find a person of authority or wealth without finding that he is sluggish in obeying and loving Allah, discourages others from doing so, follows his own desires in using what Allah has given him, and shrinks from warfare, fighting in Allah’s cause, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong. Through these traits, he earns humiliation and blame in this world and the Hereafter.

Allah Most High said to His Prophet and his Companions:

“Do not lose heart or grieve, for you will have the upper hand.”

He thus declares that they have the upper hand, yet they desire neither superiority on earth nor corruption. Allah Most High also says:

“So do not lose heart and call for peace while you have the upper hand, and Allah is with you.”

“Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their wealth in exchange for Paradise.”

And He says:

“Do not entrust the foolish with your wealth, which Allah has made a means of support for you.”

Honour and wealth are therefore neither praised nor condemned unconditionally. Rather, whatever helps one obey Allah is praiseworthy. This may even be obligatory, when it is indispensable for fulfilling obligatory duties, or it may be recommended. It is praiseworthy only when accompanied by this intention. Whatever is used to disobey Allah or to hinder the fulfilment of obligations is blameworthy and forbidden. Its merit is diminished when it distracts from recommended deeds or leads to disliked acts.

And Allah knows best. As stated in the hadith:

“Whoever seeks this wealth to be independent of others, to refrain from begging, and to provide assistance to his vulnerable neighbour, the widow and the needy will meet Allah Most High with his face shining like the moon on the night when it is full. But whoever seeks it to show off and boast

and to outdo others in wealth will meet Allah while He is angry with him.”

He also said:

“The trustworthy, truthful merchant will be with the prophets, the steadfastly truthful, the martyrs and the righteous.”

And he said:

“How excellent is good wealth for a righteous man!”

Know that scrupulousness does not benefit a person or earn him a reward unless he fulfils the command to be sincere. With regard to scrupulousness expressed in doing what is commanded, this is clear: Allah Most High accepts only deeds done for His sake. As for refraining from what is forbidden—which some people call scrupulousness—if a person refrains from sins for a reason other than seeking Allah’s pleasure, he is not rewarded for refraining, although he is not punished for those sins. If he refrains for Allah’s sake, he is rewarded. This can only arise from the hope for Allah’s mercy or fear of His punishment that resides in his heart. Hope for His mercy and fear of His punishment are positive states that one is commanded to cultivate. Thus, scrupulousness is only a righteous deed when accompanied by the commanded acts of hope and fear. Mere abstention, as an absence of action, carries no reward.

As for renunciation, which is the opposite of desire, it is praised without qualification, while desire is condemned for leading one to neglect working for the Hereafter. Allah Most High says:

“Whoever desires the life of this world and its adornment—We will repay them in full for their deeds therein, and they will not be shortchanged.”

“Those are the ones who will have nothing in the Hereafter but the Fire.”

And He says:

“Whoever desires the harvest of the Hereafter—We will increase his harvest. And whoever desires the harvest of this world—We will give him some of it, but he will have no share in the Hereafter.”

And He says:

“Whoever desires the fleeting life of this world—We hasten for him therein whatever We will

for whomever We choose. Then We appoint Hell for him, where he will burn, condemned and banished.”

Whoever does not seek the Hereafter in word and deed, in preference, love, longing and devotion, will have no share in the Hereafter and gain no benefit in this worldly life. Rather, he is an unbeliever, accursed, distracted and tormented. Yet his renunciation of this world may afford him some immediate relief, although such renunciation is not sanctioned by the revealed law. He may also suffer from missing out on worldly pleasures. If he does not renounce them, however, he finds no relief in this regard.

Thus, whether someone renounces this world to find worldly ease or pursues it to obtain its pleasures, neither is engaged in a righteous deed or deserves praise for it according to the revealed law. Nevertheless, one course may sometimes be more advantageous in worldly terms, and the other at other times, just as one craft may be preferable to another, or one trade to another. Worldly pleasures are generally attained only through some effort. At times, the pleasure of foregoing them may outweigh the effort of pursuing them; at other times, the effort of pursuing them may be preferable to the pleasure of foregoing them. There is therefore no praise for abandoning this world unless it is for the sake of working for the Hereafter, just as there is no praise for pursuing it unless it is for the sake of working for the Hereafter.

It is thus established that merely renouncing this world deserves no praise, just as desiring it deserves no praise. Rather, praise is due to seeking Allah and the Hereafter, while blame attaches to the desire for this world that prevents one from seeking them, as explained above and as expressed in the words of Allah Most High:

“If you desire the life of this world and its adornment, then come: I will provide for you and release you graciously.”

“But if you desire Allah and His Messenger and the Hereafter, then Allah has prepared a tremendous reward for those of you who do good.”

For this reason, those with spiritual understanding customarily call such a person a seeker and aspirant;

What distinguishes the first, however, is that he fulfils something commanded while committing something forbidden, whereas the second does not fulfil that command. It is thus established that fulfilling the command to seek the Hereafter is beneficial, while renunciation without fulfilling this command is of no benefit.

Do not be swayed by how often people condemn this world on grounds unrelated to religion. Most ordinary people condemn it only because they have not obtained what they wanted from it. It has never afforded anyone untroubled happiness, however much he may have gained from it. No home has ever been filled with joy without also being filled with tears.

Sensible people therefore condemn the ignorant who place their trust in this world and imagine that their authority, wealth and enjoyment of its pleasures will endure. Yet they themselves still need its necessities, and most of them seek the very things in it that they condemn. Their condemnation of this world is, in reality, a worldly condemnation prompted by its worldly harms. It resembles sensible people’s condemnation of commerce or a craft that brings no profit but only toil, or your condemnation of keeping company with someone who harms you without benefiting you, as in marrying an ill-tempered woman, and similar matters whose harm and benefit concern this world alone.

There is no doubt that whatever causes harm in this world is blameworthy if it brings no benefit in the Hereafter, such as wasting wealth or undertaking arduous acts of worship that neither Allah nor His Messenger has commanded. Whatever brings benefit in this world is blameworthy if it causes harm in the Hereafter, such as enjoying forbidden pleasures and satisfying forbidden desires. The same applies to permissible pleasures and desires if they weaken a person’s resolve and hold him back in matters concerning the Hereafter and his pursuit of it. Whatever is harmful both in this world and in the Hereafter is evil and hardship. Whatever is beneficial in the Hereafter is praiseworthy, even if it causes harm in this world, such as sacrificing lives and wealth
