Whatever is beneficial in the Hereafter is praiseworthy, whether it causes harm in this world, brings benefit, or neither benefits nor harms. Whatever is harmful in the Hereafter is blameworthy, whether it brings benefit in this world, causes harm, or neither benefits nor harms.

Three categories remain: what is beneficial in this world without being harmful in the Hereafter, and what is harmful in this world without being beneficial in the Hereafter. The beneficial is praiseworthy, and the harmful is blameworthy.

There are two views concerning the third category. One holds that it merits neither praise nor blame; the other holds that it is blameworthy.

Most of people’s condemnation of this world is not because it distracts them from the Hereafter, but because of the harm they suffer in it. It is indeed blameworthy in that respect. The strongest grounds for condemning it, however, are that it distracts from the Hereafter. Yet a person may count his misfortunes and forget his blessings. He may condemn many things because of some harm he suffers, although they contain many benefits that he fails to mention. Such condemnation is a form of fretfulness and panic, as

the Exalted says:

“Indeed, mankind was created anxious:
when evil touches him, impatient,
and when good touches him, withholding—
except those who pray.”

What is truly blameworthy is whatever distracts one from the obligatory deeds that benefit one in the Hereafter. Whatever distracts from recommended deeds that benefit one there constitutes a shortcoming. Also blameworthy is whatever brings more harm than benefit in the Hereafter. These three principles settle the matter. Thus, it is clear that what is praiseworthy in this world may lie either in the presence of something or in its absence.

Errors may arise in renunciation, just as they do in scrupulousness:

First, some people renounce things that benefit them without causing harm, thereby neglecting obligatory or recommended acts—as when someone abstains from marriage to women, from meat, and the like. Yet the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: “But I fast and break my fast; I marry women and eat meat. Whoever turns away from my Sunnah is not of me.”

Second, a person’s renunciation may lead him to commit prohibited acts—as when someone forgoes wealth or benefits lawfully available to him, then needs them and obtains them unlawfully, begs from people in a forbidden manner, or looks expectantly to them; such expectation is disliked.

Third, some renounce things out of laziness, idleness, and a desire for ease, rather than to seek the abode of the Hereafter through righteous deeds and beneficial knowledge. For when a servant is given to renunciation but remains idle, he becomes utterly corrupt. Such people cultivate neither this world nor the Hereafter, as stated by

‘Abd Allāh ibn Mas‘ūd:

“I dislike seeing a man idle, occupied neither with the affairs of this world nor with those of the Hereafter.”

Such people are among the people of the Fire, as indicated by the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in the hadith narrated by Muslim in his Sahīh from ‘Iyād ibn Himār, who reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: “The people of Paradise are of five kinds.” Among them he mentioned “the weak man who lacks the judgment to restrain himself—those among you who merely follow others, seeking neither family nor wealth.”

Anyone whose renunciation leads him to abandon commanded good deeds—in which case what he abandons is better than his renunciation—or to commit forbidden sins or lapse into laziness and idleness is among “the greatest losers in their deeds,” “those whose efforts are wasted in this worldly life while they think they are doing good.”

Whoever renounces what distracts him from his obligations or leads him into forbidden acts is among those who follow a middle course, the people of the right. Whoever renounces what distracts him from recommended deeds and higher ranks is among those who are foremost, taking the lead in goodness.

This is a brief summary of renunciation. It has become clear that the primary aim is to do what has been commanded, since renunciation helps one to do so. This is the point intended here. And Allah knows best.

 إلَى قَوْلِهِ: 
{الْيَوْمَ أَكْمَلْتُ لَكُمْ دِينَكُمْ وَأَتْمَمْتُ عَلَيْكُمْ نِعْمَتِي}
 وَقَدْ ثَبَتَ أَنَّهَا نَزَلَتْ عَشِيَّةَ عَرَفَةَ فِي حِجَّةِ الْوَدَاعِ فَأَكْمَلَ اللَّهُ الدِّينَ بِإِيجَابِهِ لِمَا أَوْجَبَهُ مِنْ الْوَاجِبَاتِ الَّتِي آخِرُهَا الْحَجُّ وَتَحْرِيمِهِ لِلْمُحَرَّمَاتِ الْمَذْكُورَةِ فِي هَذِهِ الْآيَةِ هَذَا مِنْ جِهَةِ شَرْعِهِ وَمِنْ جِهَةِ الْفِعْلِ الَّذِي هُوَ تَقْوِيَتُهُ وَإِعَانَتُهُ وَنَصْرُهُ يَئِسَ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا مِنْ دِينِنَا وَحَجَّ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ حِجَّةَ الْإِسْلَامِ فَلَمَّا أَكْمَلُوا الدِّينَ قَالَ عَقِبَ ذَلِكَ:
translated_text:
And beware of being deceived by the renunciation of disbelievers and religious innovators. A sinful believer who seeks both the Hereafter and this world is better than the ascetics among religious innovators and disbelievers, because their beliefs are corrupt, their intentions are corrupt, or both are corrupt.

The twenty-second point:

Good deeds are a cause of things being made lawful, both in religious law and in the created order, while sins are a cause of things being forbidden in both respects. Prohibition may serve as protection or as punishment, while making things lawful may bring abundance or serve as punishment and a trial. Allah Most High says:

“Livestock have been made lawful for you, except what is recited to you, provided that you do not deem hunting lawful while in a state of pilgrimage consecration.”

Thus, He permitted livestock to them while they refrained from treating hunting as lawful—that is, while believing it to be forbidden and abstaining from it.

He also says:

“Forbidden to you are carrion, blood, and the flesh of swine,”

through to His words:

“Today I have perfected your religion for you and completed My favour upon you.”

It is established that this verse was revealed on the afternoon of the Day of ‘Arafah during the Farewell Pilgrimage. Allah thus perfected the religion by prescribing the obligations He prescribed, the last of which was Hajj, and by prohibiting the forbidden things mentioned in this verse. This was in terms of His legislation. As for His action—His granting strength, assistance, and victory—the disbelievers despaired of overcoming our religion, and the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, performed the pilgrimage prescribed in Islam. When they had completed their observance of the religion, He said immediately afterward:

“They ask you what has been made lawful for them. Say, ‘Lawful for you are all good things and game caught by the hunting animals you have trained,’”

through to His words:

“Today all good things have been made lawful for you.”

Thus, He made good things lawful on the day He perfected the religion. He perfected its prohibitions and permissions because they had perfected their compliance with it.

He also says:

“No blame rests upon those who believe and do righteous deeds…”

This verse clearly shows that righteous conduct, piety, and excellence in doing good are grounds for removing blame. A believer who does righteous deeds and excels in goodness incurs neither blame nor sin for what he consumes, for it provides him with help and strength to believe, do righteous deeds, and excel in goodness. Others remain subject to blame and sin, because Allah created blessings only so that they might be used to help people obey Him. This verse was revealed in Medina and is among the last passages of the Quran to be revealed.

Allah Most High also relates that Abraham said:

“And provide its people with fruits—those among them who believe in Allah and the Last Day.”

He also says:

“Say, ‘Who has forbidden the adornment Allah has brought forth for His servants, and the good things He has provided?’ Say, ‘They are for those who believe during the life of this world, and exclusively theirs on the Day of Resurrection.’”

He also says:

“If only the people of the towns had believed and feared Allah, We would have opened for them blessings from heaven and earth.”

He also says:

“If only the People of the Scripture had believed and feared Allah, We would have absolved them of their misdeeds and admitted them into Gardens of Bliss.”

“If only they had upheld the Torah, the Gospel, and what was revealed to them from their Lord, they would have received sustenance from above them and from beneath their feet.”

As for the other side of the matter, the Most High says:

“For the wrongdoing of the Jews, We forbade them good things that had been lawful for them, and for their frequent obstruction of Allah’s way,”

“and for their taking usury, though they had been forbidden it, and their wrongful consumption of people’s wealth.”

He also says:

“To the Jews We forbade every animal with claws,”

through to His words:

“That is how We repaid them for their transgression.”

The Most High also says:

“Ask them about the town by the sea, when they transgressed on the Sabbath,”

and so on to the end of the verses.

As for making things lawful and granting provisions being a test, He says:

“If they remained steadfast on the right path, We would give them abundant water,”

“to test them thereby.”

“And among them are those who pledged to Allah, ‘If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity and be among the righteous.’”

“But when He gave them of His bounty, they became miserly with it and turned away in aversion,”

and the following verses.

“We have made all that is on earth an adornment for it, to test which of them is best in deeds.”

“Eat and drink, but do not be excessive. Indeed, He does not love those who are excessive.”

“O Children of Israel, We delivered you from your enemy,”

through to His words:

“Eat of the good things We have provided for you, but do not transgress therein, lest My wrath descend upon you. Whoever incurs My wrath has indeed fallen into ruin.”

Whether something is lawful or unlawful also varies according to intention, as the Most High says:

“Their husbands have a greater right to take them back during that period, if they intend reconciliation.”

He also says:

“After carrying out any bequest made or paying any debt, without causing harm.”

وَقَدْ كَتَبْت فِي قَاعِدَةِ 
" الْعُهُودِ وَالْعُقُودِ "
 - الْقَاعِدَةِ فِي الْعُهُودِ الدِّينِيَّةِ فِي الْقَوَاعِدِ الْمُطْلَقَةِ وَالْقَاعِدَةِ فِي الْعُقُودِ الدُّنْيَوِيَّةِ فِي الْقَوَاعِدِ الْفِقْهِيَّةِ؛ وَفِي كِتَابِ النَّذْرِ أَيْضًا - أَنَّ مَا وَجَبَ بِالشَّرْعِ إنْ نَذَرَهُ الْعَبْدُ أَوْ عَاهَدَ اللَّهَ عَلَيْهِ أَوْ بَايَعَ عَلَيْهِ الرَّسُولَ أَوْ الْإِمَامَ أَوْ تَحَالَفَ عَلَيْهِ جَمَاعَةٌ فَإِنَّ هَذِهِ الْعُهُودَ وَالْمَوَاثِيقَ تَقْتَضِي لَهُ وُجُوبًا ثَانِيًا غَيْرَ الْوُجُوبِ الثَّابِتِ بِمُجَرَّدِ الْأَمْرِ الْأَوَّلِ فَتَكُونُ وَاجِبَةً مِنْ وَجْهَيْنِ بِحَيْثُ يَسْتَحِقُّ تَارِكُهَا مِنْ الْعُقُوبَةِ مَا يَسْتَحِقُّهُ نَاقِضُ الْعَهْدِ وَالْمِيثَاقِ وَمَا يَسْتَحِقُّهُ عَاصِي اللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِ. هَذَا هُوَ التَّحْقِيقُ.
 وَمَنْ قَالَ مِنْ أَصْحَابِ أَحْمَد:
 إنَّهُ إذَا نَذَرَ وَاجِبًا فَهُوَ بَعْدَ النَّذْرِ كَمَا كَانَ قَبْلَ النَّذْرِ بِخِلَافِ نَذْرِ الْمُسْتَحَبِّ فَلَيْسَ كَمَا قَالَ بَلْ النَّذْرُ إذَا كَانَ يُوجِبُ فِعْلَ الْمُسْتَحَبِّ فَإِيجَابُهُ لِفِعْلِ الْوَاجِبِ أَوْلَى وَلَيْسَ هَذَا مِنْ بَابِ تَحْصِيلِ الْحَاصِلِ بَلْ هُمَا وجوبان مِنْ نَوْعَيْنِ لِكُلِّ نَوْعٍ حُكْمٌ غَيْرُ حُكْمِ الْآخَرِ مِثْلَ الْجَدَّةِ إذَا كَانَتْ أُمَّ أُمِّ أُمٍّ وَأُمَّ أب أَبٍ فَإِنَّ فِيهَا شَيْئَيْنِ كُلٌّ مِنْهُمَا تَسْتَحِقُّ بِهِ السُّدُسَ.
وَكَذَلِكَ مَنْ قَالَ مِنْ أَصْحَابِ أَحْمَد:
 إنَّ الشُّرُوطَ الَّتِي هِيَ مِنْ مُقْتَضَى الْعَقْدِ لَا يَصِحُّ اشْتِرَاطُهَا أَوْ قَدْ تُفْسِدُهُ حَتَّى قَالَ بَعْضُ أَصْحَابِ الشَّافِعِيِّ: إذَا قَالَ: زَوَّجْتُك عَلَى مَا أَمَرَ اللَّهُ بِهِ مِنْ إمْسَاكٍ بِمَعْرُوفِ أَوْ تَسْرِيحٍ بِإِحْسَانِ كَانَ النِّكَاحُ فَاسِدًا؛ لِأَنَّهُ شَرَطَ فِيهِ الطَّلَاقَ. فَهَذَا
translated_text:
I have also written in my treatment of “Covenants and Contracts”—on religious covenants among the general principles, and on worldly contracts among the principles of jurisprudence—and in the Book of Vows, that when something is already obligatory under Islamic law, and a servant vows to perform it, makes a covenant with Allah to do so, pledges himself to the Messenger or the ruler to do so, or joins others in a mutual oath to do so, these covenants and solemn pledges impose a second obligation, distinct from the obligation established by the original command alone. The act thus becomes obligatory on two grounds: whoever neglects it deserves both the punishment due to someone who breaks a covenant or solemn pledge and that due to someone who disobeys Allah and His Messenger. This is the correct analysis.

Some jurists of Ahmad’s school say that when someone vows to perform an obligatory act, its status remains unchanged after the vow, unlike a vow to perform a recommended act. This is not correct. If a vow makes a recommended act obligatory, then it is all the more capable of imposing an obligation to perform an already obligatory act. This does not amount to bringing about what already exists. Rather, these are two obligations of different kinds, each with a legal effect distinct from the other. An example is a grandmother who is both one’s maternal grandmother’s mother and one’s paternal grandfather’s mother: she possesses two grounds of entitlement, each of which entitles her to one-sixth.

Likewise, some jurists of Ahmad’s school say that conditions inherent in a contract cannot validly be stipulated, or may even invalidate it. Some jurists of al-Shāfiʿī’s school have gone so far as to say that if someone says, “I give her to you in marriage on the terms Allah has commanded—keeping her on honorable terms or letting her go with kindness,” the marriage is invalid because he has stipulated divorce within it. This is

utterly unsound reasoning. The obligations arising from contracts become binding only because the contracting parties bind themselves to them. A contract expressed without qualification has a recognized meaning; when they express it without qualification, they thereby bind themselves to what is understood from it.

An obligation arising from a contract is binding by virtue of that contract, just as an obligation arising from a vow is binding by virtue of that vow. The Lawgiver did not impose it in the first instance; rather, He commanded the fulfillment of contracts, just as He commanded the fulfillment of vows. Thus, if a contract has an obligation known from its unqualified wording, or the contracting parties recognize its imposition through specific wording, this constitutes mentioning the particular after the general. The obligation has thus been imposed twice, or has been given a specific basis of obligation that dispenses with the general one.

There are parallels to this in the Quran, such as His saying:

“Whoever is an enemy to Allah, His angels, His messengers, Gabriel and Michael—then Allah is an enemy to the disbelievers.”

And His saying:

“And when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you, and from Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus, son of Mary.”

And His saying:

“Guard strictly the prayers, especially the middle prayer.”

And His saying:

“Say to your wives, your daughters, and the women of the believers.”

And His saying:

“Indeed, Allah commands justice, kindness, and giving to relatives, and forbids indecency, wrongdoing, and oppression.”

And His saying:

“Those who break Allah’s covenant after its solemn confirmation.”

For Allah proclaimed His covenant, which He commanded them to observe, after taking their solemn pledge to fulfill it. Thus, both grounds are combined in it: that of the covenant and that of the solemn pledge.

The Quran contains many covenants and solemn pledges concerning duties already made obligatory by Allah’s command. Among these are His words, Exalted is He:

“And when We took your covenant and raised the Mount above you,”

and the remainder of the verse; and His words:

“And when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel: ‘Worship none but Allah, and show kindness to parents,’”

through to the end of the passage; and His words:

“And when We took your covenant and raised the Mount above you: ‘Hold firmly to what We have given you, and listen.’ They said, ‘We hear and disobey.’”

And His words:

“Among the People of the Book are some who, if you entrust them with a great sum, will return it to you; and among them are some who, if you entrust them with a single dinar, will not return it to you,”

continuing to His words:

“Yes, whoever fulfills his covenant and fears Allah—indeed, Allah loves those who fear Him.”

“Indeed, those who exchange Allah’s covenant and their oaths for a small price will have no share in the Hereafter.”

His words, “Yes, whoever fulfills his covenant,” following His mention of faith, indicate that this means fulfilling the obligations arising from contracts in transactions and the like. Likewise, He says in the verse concerning sales:

“But if you trust one another, let the one entrusted discharge his trust.”

Discharging a trust means fulfilling the contractual obligations arising from transactions, such as taking possession and making delivery. This is obligatory by virtue of the contract alone. He then says:

“Indeed, those who exchange Allah’s covenant and their oaths…”

Allah’s covenant is what He has enjoined upon them, while their oaths are those they have solemnly sworn. The occasion of this verse’s revelation was the incident involving al-Ash‘ath ibn Qays, related in the two Sahīh collections, concerning his dispute with a Jewish man, when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever swears a false oath to appropriate a Muslim’s property will meet Allah while He is angry with him.”

Allah then revealed this verse. That property already had to be handed over to its rightful owner

original_footnote: (١) بياض بالأصل
translated_text:
by virtue of his covenant. If he then swears that he, rather than its rightful owner, is entitled to it, he has sinned in two respects. This is comparable to His words:

“Those who break Allah’s covenant after solemnly confirming it.”

Their opposites are those who fulfill Allah’s covenant and do not break the solemn pledge. And His words:

“And when Allah took the covenant of the prophets: ‘Whatever I give you of Scripture and wisdom, should a messenger then come to you confirming what is with you, you must believe in him and support him.’ He said, ‘Do you affirm this and accept My binding covenant on these terms?’ They said, ‘We affirm it,’”

and the remainder of the verse.

Ibn ‘Abbās said: “Allah never sent a prophet without taking a covenant from him that, if Muhammad were sent while he was still alive, he would believe in him and support him. He also commanded him to take a covenant from his people that, if Muhammad were sent while they were still alive, they would believe in him and support him.”

It is well known that if Allah sends Muhammad with a universal message, everyone whom his call reaches is obliged to believe in him and support him, even if no covenant to that effect had previously been taken from them. Thus, a covenant was taken from them concerning something already obligatory by Allah’s command, even without a covenant.

And His words, Exalted is He:

“They asked Moses for something even greater than that,”

through to His words:

“And We raised the Mount above them in connection with their covenant, and We said to them, ‘Enter the gate bowing humbly,’ and We said to them, ‘Do not transgress on the Sabbath,’ and We took from them a solemn covenant.”

“So for their breaking of their covenant, their disbelief in Allah’s signs, their killing of the prophets without right, and their saying, ‘Our hearts are covered,’”

and the subsequent verses. This, then, is a covenant that Allah took . . . (1).
translated_footnote: (1) A blank space in the original.

وَقَالَ شَيْخُ الْإِسْلَامِ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
تَنَازُعُ النَّاسِ فِي الْأَمْرِ بِالشَّيْءِ هَلْ يَكُونُ أَمْرًا بِلَوَازِمِهِ؟ وَهَلْ يَكُونُ نَهْيًا عَنْ ضِدِّهِ؟ مَعَ اتِّفَاقِهِمْ عَلَى أَنَّ فِعْلَ الْمَأْمُورِ لَا يَكُونُ إلَّا مَعَ فِعْلِ لَوَازِمِهِ وَتَرْكِ ضِدِّهِ. 
(*)
وَمَنْشَأُ النِّزَاعِ أَنَّ الْآمِرَ بِالْفِعْلِ قَدْ لَا يَكُونُ مَقْصُودُهُ اللَّوَازِمَ وَلَا تَرْكَ الضِّدِّ؛ وَلِهَذَا إذَا عَاقَبَ الْمُكَلَّفَ لَا يُعَاقِبُهُ إلَّا عَلَى تَرْكِ الْمَأْمُورِ فَقَطْ لَا يُعَاقِبُهُ عَلَى تَرْكِ لَوَازِمِهِ وَفِعْلِ ضِدِّهِ.
 وَهَذِهِ الْمَسْأَلَةُ هِيَ الْمُلَقَّبَةُ:
 بِأَنَّ مَا لَا يَتِمُّ الْوَاجِبُ إلَّا بِهِ فَهُوَ وَاجِبٌ.
وَقَدْ غَلِطَ فِيهَا بَعْضُ النَّاسِ فَقَسَّمُوا ذَلِكَ:
 إلَى مَا لَا يَقْدِرُ الْمُكَلَّفُ عَلَيْهِ؛ كَالصِّحَّةِ فِي الْأَعْضَاءِ وَالْعَدَدِ فِي الْجُمُعَة؛ وَنَحْوِ ذَلِكَ مِمَّا لَا يَكُونُ قَادِرًا عَلَى تَحْصِيلِهِ. وَإِلَى مَا يَقْدِرُ عَلَيْهِ كَقَطْعِ الْمَسَافَةِ فِي الْحَجِّ وَغَسْلِ جُزْءٍ مِنْ الرَّأْسِ فِي الْوُضُوءِ وَإِمْسَاكِ جُزْءٍ مِنْ اللَّيْلِ فِي الصِّيَامِ وَنَحْوِ ذَلِكَ.
 فَقَالُوا:
 مَا لَا يَتِمُّ الْوَاجِبُ الْمُطْلَقُ إلَّا بِهِ وَكَانَ مَقْدُورًا لِلْمُكَلَّفِ فَهُوَ وَاجِبٌ.

قال الشيخ ناصر بن حمد الفهد (ص ١٦٠):
وهنا أمور:
الأول: أن الذي يظهر من هذه الرسالة أنها ليست من صياغة الشيخ رحمه الله، بل قام بعضهم بتلخيصها من (درء التعارض) و (منهاج السنة)، وفي بعض المواضع منها تلخيض مخل.
الثاني: أن أكثر هذه الرسالة مأخوذ من مواضع من المجلدين الأول والثاني من (درء التعارض)، وآخر صفحة منه مأخوذة من موضعين من (منهاج السنة) كما سيأتي.
الثالت: قد حصل في هذه الرسالة بعض السقط والتصحيف، ويظهر هذا من مقابلة هذه الرسالة بأصولها المنقولة عنها كما يلي:
ثم نقل الشيخ - وفقه الله - نص الرسالة، فراجعها هناك من ص ١٦٠ إلى ص ١٦٩.
translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—said:

People disagree over whether commanding something also entails commanding its necessary requirements, and whether it entails prohibiting its opposite, although they agree that the commanded act cannot be performed without fulfilling its necessary requirements and refraining from its opposite. (*)

The disagreement arises because someone who commands an act may not intend its necessary requirements or the avoidance of its opposite. Thus, if he punishes the legally accountable person, he punishes him only for failing to perform the commanded act, not for omitting its necessary requirements or doing its opposite.

This issue is commonly expressed in the maxim: “Whatever is indispensable to fulfilling an obligation is itself obligatory.”

Some people have erred in this matter by dividing such requirements into two categories: those beyond the legally accountable person’s ability, such as soundness of the limbs, the requisite number of participants for Friday prayer, and similar matters that he cannot secure; and those within his ability, such as travelling the distance required for Hajj, washing a portion of the head during ablution, observing the fast for part of the night, and similar matters.

They therefore said: “Whatever is indispensable to fulfilling an unconditional obligation, and lies within the legally accountable person’s ability, is itself obligatory.”
translated_footnote:
Shaykh Nāsir ibn Hamad al-Fahd said (p. 160):

First: This treatise appears not to have been composed by the shaykh—may Allah have mercy on him—but rather abridged by someone from Dar’ al-ta‘ārud and Minhāj al-sunnah. In some places, the abridgment compromises the meaning.
Second: Most of this treatise is drawn from passages in the first and second volumes of Dar’ al-ta‘ārud. Its final page is drawn from two passages in Minhāj al-sunnah, as will be shown.
Third: Some omissions and textual corruptions have occurred in this treatise. This becomes apparent when it is compared with the sources from which it was drawn, as follows:”
The shaykh—may Allah grant him success—then reproduced the text of the treatise. Consult it there, pp. 160–169.

وَهَذَا التَّقْسِيمُ خَطَأٌ؛ فَإِنَّ هَذِهِ الْأُمُورَ الَّتِي ذَكَرُوهَا هِيَ شَرْطٌ فِي الْوُجُوبِ فَلَا يَتِمُّ الْوَاجِبُ إلَّا بِهَا وَمَا لَا يَتِمُّ الْوَاجِبُ إلَّا بِهِ يَجِبُ عَلَى الْعَبْدِ فِعْلُهُ بِاتِّفَاقِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ سَوَاءٌ كَانَ مَقْدُورًا عَلَيْهِ أَوْ لَا كَالِاسْتِطَاعَةِ فِي الْحَجِّ وَاكْتِسَابِ نِصَابِ الزَّكَاةِ؛ فَإِنَّ الْعَبْدَ إذَا كَانَ مُسْتَطِيعًا لِلْحَجِّ وَجَبَ عَلَيْهِ الْحَجُّ وَإِذَا كَانَ مَالِكًا لِنِصَابِ الزَّكَاةِ وَجَبَتْ عَلَيْهِ الزَّكَاةُ فَالْوُجُوبُ لَا يَتِمُّ إلَّا بِذَلِكَ فَلَا يَجِبُ عَلَيْهِ تَحْصِيلُ اسْتِطَاعَةِ الْحَجِّ وَلَا مِلْكُ النِّصَابِ؛
 وَلِهَذَا مَنْ يَقُولُ:
 إنَّ الِاسْتِطَاعَةَ فِي الْحَجِّ مِلْكُ الْمَالِ - كَمَا هُوَ مَذْهَبُ أَبِي حَنِيفَةَ وَالشَّافِعِيِّ وَأَحْمَد - فَلَا يُوجِبُونَ عَلَيْهِ الِاكْتِسَابَ وَلَمْ يَتَنَازَعُوا إلَّا فِيمَا إذَا بُذِلَتْ لَهُ الِاسْتِطَاعَةُ إمَّا بَذْلَ الْحَجِّ وَإِمَّا بَذْلَ الْمَالِ لَهُ مِنْ وَلَدِهِ. وَفِيهِ نِزَاعٌ مَعْرُوفٌ فِي مَذْهَبِ الشَّافِعِيِّ وَأَحْمَد وَلَكِنَّ الْمَشْهُورَ مِنْ مَذْهَبِ أَحْمَد عَدَمُ الْوُجُوبِ وَإِنَّمَا أَوْجَبَهُ طَائِفَةٌ مِنْ أَصْحَابِهِ؛ لِكَوْنِ الْأَبِ لَهُ عَلَى أَصْلِهِ أَنْ يَتَمَلَّكَ مَالَ وَلَدِهِ فَيَكُونُ قَبُولُهُ كَتَمَلُّكِ الْمُبَاحَاتِ. وَالْمَشْهُورُ مِنْ مَذْهَبِ الشَّافِعِيِّ الْوُجُوبُ بِبَذْلِ الِابْنِ بِالْفِعْلِ.
 وَالْمَقْصُودُ هُنَا:
 الْفَرْقُ بَيْنَ مَا لَا يَتِمُّ الْوَاجِبُ إلَّا بِهِ وَمَا لَا يَتِمُّ الْوُجُوبُ إلَّا بِهِ وَأَنَّ الْكَلَامَ فِي الْقِسْمِ الثَّانِي إنَّمَا هُوَ فِيمَا لَا يَتِمُّ الْوَاجِبُ إلَّا بِهِ كَقَطْعِ الْمَسَافَةِ فِي الْجُمُعَةِ وَالْحَجِّ وَنَحْوِ ذَلِكَ فَعَلَى الْمُكَلَّفِ فِعْلُهُ بِاتِّفَاقِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ لَكِنْ مَنْ تَرَكَ الْحَجَّ وَهُوَ بَعِيدُ الدَّارِ عَنْ مَكَّةَ؛ أَوْ تَرَكَ
translated_text:
This division is mistaken, for the matters they mentioned are conditions for an obligation to arise. The obligation cannot be fulfilled without them, and whatever is indispensable to fulfilling an obligation must, by agreement of the Muslims, be undertaken by the servant, whether it is within his ability or not—such as possessing the means for Hajj and acquiring the minimum amount of wealth liable to zakat. When a person possesses the means for Hajj, Hajj becomes obligatory upon him; and when he owns the minimum amount liable to zakat, zakat becomes obligatory upon him. The obligation does not arise without these conditions, but he is not required to acquire the means for Hajj or ownership of that minimum amount.

Hence, those who hold that possessing the means for Hajj means possessing sufficient wealth—as is the position of Abū Hanīfah, al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad—do not require a person to earn that wealth. Their disagreement concerns only the case in which the means are offered to him: either an offer to perform Hajj on his behalf or an offer of money from his child. There is a well-known disagreement over this in the schools of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad. The well-known position in Ahmad’s school is that it is not obligatory. Only a group of his followers held it obligatory, because, according to his underlying principle, a father is entitled to take ownership of his child’s wealth; accepting it would therefore be like taking possession of things freely available for ownership. The well-known position in al-Shāfiʿī’s school is that it becomes obligatory when the son offers to perform the act.

The point here is to distinguish between what is indispensable to fulfilling an obligation and what is indispensable for that obligation to arise. The discussion of the second category concerns only what is indispensable to fulfilling an obligation, such as travelling the necessary distance for Friday prayer, Hajj and the like. The legally accountable person must do this, by agreement of the Muslims. However, someone who neglects Hajj while living far from Mecca, or neglects

original_text:
الْجُمُعَةَ وَهُوَ بَعِيدُ الدَّارِ عَنْ الْجَامِعِ؛
 فَقَدْ تَرَكَ أَكْثَرَ مِمَّا تَرَكَ قَرِيبُ الدَّارِ وَمَعَ هَذَا فَلَا يُقَالُ:
 إنَّ عُقُوبَةَ هَذَا أَعْظَمُ مِنْ عُقُوبَةِ قَرِيبِ الدَّارِ.
 وَالْوَاجِبُ:
 مَا يَكُونُ تَرْكُهُ سَبَبًا لِلذَّمِّ وَالْعِقَابِ فَلَوْ كَانَ هَذَا الَّذِي لَزِمَهُ فِعْلُهُ بِطَرِيقِ التَّبَعِ مَقْصُودًا بِالْوُجُوبِ لَكَانَ الذَّمُّ وَالْعِقَابُ لِتَارِكِهِ أَعْظَمَ فَيَكُونُ مَنْ تَرَكَ الْحَجَّ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْهِنْدِ وَالْأَنْدَلُسِ أَعْظَمَ عِقَابًا مِمَّنْ تَرَكَهُ مِنْ أَهْلِ مَكَّةَ وَالطَّائِفِ وَمَنْ تَرَكَ الْجُمُعَةَ مِنْ أَقْصَى الْمَدِينَةِ أَعْظَمَ عِقَابًا مِمَّنْ تَرَكَهَا مِنْ جِيرَانِ الْمَسْجِدِ الْجَامِعِ فَلَمَّا كَانَ مِنْ الْمَعْلُومِ أَنَّ ثَوَابَ الْبَعِيدِ أَعْظَمُ وَعِقَابَهُ إذَا تَرَكَ لَيْسَ أَعْظَمَ مِنْ عِقَابِ الْقَرِيبِ: نَشَأَتْ مِنْ هَهُنَا الشُّبْهَةُ: هَلْ هُوَ وَاجِبٌ أَوْ لَيْسَ بِوَاجِبِ؟
 وَالتَّحْقِيقُ:
 أَنَّ وُجُوبَهُ بِطَرِيقِ اللُّزُومِ الْعَقْلِيِّ لَا بِطَرِيقِ قَصْدِ الْأَمْرِ؛ بَلْ الْأَمْرُ بِالْفِعْلِ قَدْ لَا يُقْصَدُ طَلَبُ لَوَازِمِهِ وَإِنْ كَانَ عَالِمًا بِأَنَّهُ لَا بُدَّ مِنْ وُجُودِهَا؛ وَإِنْ كَانَ مِمَّنْ تَجُوزُ عَلَيْهِ الْغَفْلَةُ فَقَدْ لَا تَخْطُرُ بِقَلْبِهِ اللَّوَازِمُ.
 وَمَنْ فَهِمَ هَذَا انْحَلَّتْ عَنْهُ شُبَهُ الْكَعْبِيِّ:
 هَلْ فِي الشَّرِيعَةِ مُبَاحٌ أَمْ لَا؟ فَإِنَّ الْكَعْبِيَّ زَعَمَ أَنَّهُ لَا مُبَاحَ فِي الشَّرِيعَةِ. . . إلَخْ،
 فَلَا تَجِدُ قَطُّ مُبْتَدِعًا إلَّا وَهُوَ يُحِبُّ كِتْمَانَ النُّصُوصِ الَّتِي تُخَالِفُهُ وَيُبْغِضُهَا وَيُبْغِضُ إظْهَارَهَا وَرِوَايَتَهَا وَالتَّحَدُّثَ بِهَا وَيُبْغِضُ مَنْ يَفْعَلُ ذَلِكَ كَمَا قَالَ بَعْضُ السَّلَفِ:
translated_text:
Friday prayer while living far from the congregational mosque has omitted more than someone who lives nearby. Yet it is not said that his punishment is greater than that of someone who lives nearby.

An obligatory act is one whose omission is grounds for blame and punishment. If what a person is required to do as a subsidiary matter were itself an intended object of the obligation, the blame and punishment for omitting it would be greater. Thus, someone from India or al-Andalus who neglected Hajj would face greater punishment than someone from Mecca or al-Tā’if who neglected it; and someone from the farthest part of the city who neglected Friday prayer would face greater punishment than someone living beside the congregational mosque who neglected it. Since it is known that the person who lives farther away receives a greater reward, yet does not face greater punishment for omission than someone who lives nearby, the following uncertainty arose: is this obligatory or not?

The precise distinction is that its obligatory character follows by rational necessity, not because it is an intended object of the command. Indeed, someone who commands an act may not intend thereby to demand its prerequisites, even though he knows that they must exist. If the person issuing the command is liable to inattention, those prerequisites may not even occur to him.

Whoever understands this will find al-Ka‘bī’s objections concerning whether the Sharia contains anything merely permissible resolved. Al-Ka‘bī claimed that nothing in the Sharia is merely permissible … etc.

You will never find an innovator who does not love to conceal the scriptural texts that contradict him, hate those texts, and hate their being made known, transmitted, and discussed. He also hates those who do so, as one of the early generations said:

original_text:
مَا ابْتَدَعَ أَحَدٌ بِدْعَةً إلَّا نُزِعَتْ حَلَاوَةُ الْحَدِيثِ مِنْ قَلْبِهِ. ثُمَّ إنَّ قَوْلَهُ الَّذِي يُعَارِضُ بِهِ النُّصُوصَ لَا بُدَّ أَنْ يُلْبِسَ فِيهِ حَقًّا بِبَاطِلِ بِحَسَبِ مَا يَقُولُ مِنْ الْأَلْفَاظِ الْمُجْمَلَةِ الْمُتَشَابِهَةِ؛ وَلِهَذَا قَالَ الْإِمَامُ أَحْمَد فِي أَوَّلِ مَا كَتَبَهُ فِي 
" الرَّدِّ عَلَى الزَّنَادِقَةِ وَالْجَهْمِيَّة فِيمَا شَكَّتْ فِيهِ مِنْ مُتَشَابِهِ الْقُرْآنِ وَتَأَوَّلَتْهُ عَلَى غَيْرِ تَأْوِيلِهِ "
 مِمَّا كَتَبَهُ فِي حَبْسِهِ - وَقَدْ ذَكَرَهُ الْخَلَّالُ فِي 
" كِتَابِ السُّنَّةِ "
 وَالْقَاضِي أَبُو يَعْلَى؛ وَأَبُو الْفَضْلِ التَّمِيمِيُّ؛ وَأَبُو الْوَفَاءِ ابْنُ عَقِيلٍ؛ وَغَيْرُ وَاحِدٍ مِنْ أَصْحَابِ أَحْمَد وَلَمْ يَنْفِهِ أَحَدٌ مِنْهُمْ عَنْهُ وَالْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ.
 وَالْمَقْصُودُ قَوْلُهُ:
 - يَتَكَلَّمُونَ بِالْمُتَشَابِهِ مِنْ الْكَلَامِ وَيَخْدَعُونَ جُهَّالَ النَّاسِ بِمَا يُشَبِّهُونَ عَلَيْهِمْ.
 فَإِنْ كَانُوا فِي مَقَامِ دَعْوَةِ النَّاسِ إلَى قَوْلِهِمْ وَالْتِزَامِهِمْ بِهِ أَمْكَنَ أَنْ يُقَالَ لَهُمْ:
 لَا يَجِبُ عَلَى أَحَدٍ أَنْ يُجِيبَ دَاعِيًا إلَّا إلَى مَا دَعَا إلَيْهِ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فَمَا لَمْ يَثْبُتْ أَنَّ الرَّسُولَ دَعَا الْخَلْقَ إلَيْهِ لَمْ يَكُنْ عَلَى النَّاسِ إجَابَةُ مَنْ دَعَا إلَيْهِ وَلَا لَهُ دَعْوَةُ النَّاسِ إلَى ذَلِكَ وَلَوْ قُدِّرَ أَنَّ ذَلِكَ الْمَعْنَى حَقٌّ؛ وَهَذِهِ الطَّرِيقُ تَكُونُ أَصْلَحَ إذَا لَبَّسَ مُلَبِّسٌ مِنْهُمْ عَلَى وُلَاةِ الْأُمُورِ وَأَدْخَلُوهُ فِي بِدَعِهِمْ.
 كَمَا فَعَلَتْ الْجَهْمِيَّة بِمَنْ لَبَّسُوا عَلَيْهِ مِنْ الْخُلَفَاءِ حَتَّى أَدْخَلُوهُ فِي بِدَعِهِمْ مِنْ الْقَوْلِ بِخَلْقِ الْقُرْآنِ وَغَيْرِ ذَلِكَ فَكَانَ مِنْ أَحْسَنِ مُنَاظَرَتِهِمْ أَنْ يُقَالَ:
 ائْتُونَا بِكِتَابِ أَوْ سُنَّةٍ حَتَّى نُجِيبَكُمْ إلَى ذَلِكَ وَإِلَّا فَلَسْنَا نُجِيبُكُمْ إلَى مَا لَمْ يَدُلَّ عَلَيْهِ الْكِتَابُ وَالسُّنَّةُ.
translated_text:
“No one introduces an innovation without the sweetness of hadith being taken from his heart.”

Moreover, the position with which he opposes the scriptural texts inevitably mixes truth with falsehood through the equivocal and ambiguous expressions he uses. Hence Imam Ahmad said, at the beginning of his Refutation of the Heretics and the Jahmiyyah concerning the Ambiguous Passages of the Quran about Which They Entertained Doubts and Which They Misinterpreted—a work he wrote during his imprisonment. Al-Khallāl mentioned it in his Book of the Sunnah, as did Judge Abū Yaʿlā, Abū al-Fadl al-Tamīmī, Abū al-Wafāʾ ibn ʿAqīl, and several other followers of Ahmad. None of them denied its attribution to him, and all praise belongs to Allah. The statement relevant here is:

“They speak in ambiguous language and deceive ignorant people through the confusion they create for them.”

If they are calling people to their doctrine and requiring them to adhere to it, they may be told:

“No one is obliged to answer any caller except when he calls to what the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, called to. Unless it is established that the Messenger called people to something, people are not obliged to answer anyone who calls to it, nor is he entitled to call people to it—even supposing that the meaning in question is true.”

This approach is more effective when one of their deceivers misleads those in authority and they draw them into their innovations. This is what the Jahmiyyah did to the caliphs whom they misled, drawing them into their innovations, such as the doctrine that the Quran is created and other such doctrines. One of the best ways to debate them was therefore to say:

“Bring us evidence from the Book or the Sunnah, and we will accept what you call us to. Otherwise, we will not accept from you anything for which the Book and the Sunnah provide no evidence.”

original_text:
وَهَذَا لِأَنَّ النَّاسَ لَا يَفْصِلُ بَيْنَهُمْ النِّزَاعَ إلَّا كِتَابٌ مُنَزَّلٌ مِنْ السَّمَاءِ وَإِذَا رَدُّوا إلَى عُقُولِهِمْ فَلِكُلِّ وَاحِدٍ مِنْهُمْ عَقْلٌ. وَمِنْ هُنَا يُعْرَفُ ضَلَالُ مَنْ ابْتَدَعَ طَرِيقًا أَوْ اعْتِقَادًا زَعَمَ أَنَّ الْإِيمَانَ لَا يَتِمُّ إلَّا بِهِ مَعَ الْعِلْمِ بِأَنَّ الرَّسُولَ لَمْ يَذْكُرْهُ وَمَا خَالَفَ النُّصُوصَ فَهُوَ بِدْعَةٌ بِاتِّفَاقِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ وَمَا لَمْ يُعْلَمْ أَنَّهُ خَالَفَهَا فَقَدْ لَا يُسَمَّى بِدْعَةً قَالَ الشَّافِعِيُّ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -: الْبِدْعَةُ بِدْعَتَانِ: بِدْعَةٌ خَالَفَتْ كِتَابًا وَسُنَّةً وَإِجْمَاعًا وَأَثَرًا عَنْ بَعْضِ أَصْحَابِ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فَهَذِهِ بِدْعَةُ ضَلَالَةٍ.
 وَبِدْعَةٌ لَمْ تُخَالِفْ شَيْئًا مِنْ ذَلِكَ فَهَذِهِ قَدْ تَكُونُ حَسَنَةً لِقَوْلِ عُمَرَ:
 نِعْمَتْ الْبِدْعَةُ هَذِهِ هَذَا الْكَلَامُ أَوْ نَحْوُهُ رَوَاهُ البيهقي بِإِسْنَادِهِ الصَّحِيحِ فِي الْمَدْخَلِ وَيُرْوَى عَنْ مَالِكٍ رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ أَنَّهُ قَالَ: إذَا قَلَّ الْعِلْمُ ظَهَرَ الْجَفَا وَإِذَا قَلَّتْ الْآثَارُ كَثُرَتْ الْأَهْوَاءُ. وَلِهَذَا تَجِدُ قَوْمًا كَثِيرِينَ يُحِبُّونَ قَوْمًا وَيُبْغِضُونَ قَوْمًا لِأَجْلِ أَهْوَاءٍ لَا يَعْرِفُونَ مَعْنَاهَا وَلَا دَلِيلَهَا بَلْ يُوَالُونَ عَلَى إطْلَاقِهَا أَوْ يُعَادُونَ مِنْ غَيْرِ أَنْ تَكُونَ مَنْقُولَةً نَقْلًا صَحِيحًا عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَسَلَفِ الْأُمَّةِ وَمِنْ غَيْرِ أَنْ يَكُونُوا هُمْ يَعْقِلُونَ مَعْنَاهَا وَلَا يَعْرِفُونَ لَازِمَهَا وَمُقْتَضَاهَا. وَسَبَبُ هَذَا إطْلَاقُ أَقْوَالٍ لَيْسَتْ مَنْصُوصَةً وَجَعْلُهَا مَذَاهِبَ يُدْعَى
translated_text:
This is because disputes among people can be settled only by a Book sent down from heaven; if they are referred to their own reason, each reasons in his own way. This reveals the misguidance of anyone who introduces a method or belief and claims that faith cannot be complete without it, despite knowing that the Messenger never mentioned it. Whatever contradicts the scriptural texts is an innovation by the agreement of the Muslims. Whatever is not known to contradict them, however, may not be called an innovation.

Al-Shāfiʿī—may Allah have mercy on him—said:

“Innovations are of two kinds: an innovation that contradicts the Book, the Sunnah, consensus, or a report from any of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace—this is an innovation of misguidance. An innovation that contradicts none of these may be good, as indicated by ʿUmar’s statement: ‘What an excellent innovation this is!’”

Al-Bayhaqī related these words, or words to this effect, with an authentic chain of transmission in his Introduction. It is also related from Mālik—may Allah have mercy on him—that he said:

“When knowledge becomes scarce, coarseness appears; and when transmitted reports become scarce, opinions born of desire proliferate.”

Thus, you find many people loving some and hating others because of views born of desire, whose meaning and supporting evidence they do not know. Rather, they base their loyalties and hostilities on the mere profession of these views, although they have not been authentically transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, or the early generations of the Muslim community, and although they themselves neither understand their meaning nor know what they imply and entail. The cause of this is the unqualified assertion of statements not set forth in the scriptural texts, making them into doctrines and calling people

to them and making them the basis of loyalty and hostility. It is authentically reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to say in his sermons:

“The truest speech is the speech of Allah,” and so on.

The religion of the Muslims is founded upon following the Book of Allah, the Sunnah of His Prophet, and the consensus of the Muslim community. These three are foundations protected from error. Whatever the community disputes is to be referred back to Allah and the Messenger.

No one may set up for the community any person other than the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, calling people to follow that person’s way and making it the basis of loyalty and hostility. Nor may anyone set up for them any statement as the basis of loyalty and hostility other than the words of Allah and His Messenger and that upon which the community has reached consensus. Rather, this is the practice of the proponents of religious innovation, who set up a person or a statement by which they divide the community, basing their loyalties and hostilities upon that statement or affiliation.

The Khawārij merely interpreted verses of the Quran according to their beliefs and declared those who disagreed with them to be disbelievers, because they believed that such people had contradicted the Quran. Thus, whoever introduces statements that have no basis in the Quran and declares those who disagree with them to be disbelievers holds a position worse than that of the Khawārij.

It must be understood that objections to matters known to be part of the Muslims’ religion must be answered decisively, leaving no room for doubt, unlike the approach followed by some speculative theologians. For whoever does not debate the heretics and proponents of religious innovation

translated_text:
in a manner that decisively refutes them has not given Islam its due or fulfilled the demands of knowledge and faith. His words have neither brought healing to hearts and reassurance to souls nor yielded knowledge and certainty. Allah has obliged the believers to believe in the Messenger and strive alongside him. Believing in him includes affirming the truth of everything he has conveyed, and striving alongside him includes repelling everyone who opposes what he brought and deviates concerning Allah’s names and signs.

It is well known that every question involving affirmation or denial must have an objectively true answer, or require distinctions to be drawn. But anyone unfamiliar with the reports of the early generations, the true meaning of their statements, the true import of the Book and the Sunnah, and what sound reason truly establishes—which cannot conceivably contradict them—cannot make pronouncements on the strength of the knowledge he possesses. Allah does not burden any soul beyond its capacity.

There is no doubt that errors concerning subtle points of knowledge are forgiven for this community, even when they concern theoretical matters. Were this not so, most of the community’s eminent scholars would have perished. If Allah forgives someone who was unaware that wine is forbidden because he grew up in a land of ignorance, even though he did not seek knowledge, then a person of virtue who diligently seeks knowledge according to what is accessible in his time and place, intending to follow the Messenger to the best of his ability, is all the more deserving of Allah accepting his good deeds, rewarding his earnest efforts, and not holding him accountable for his mistakes, in fulfilment of His words:

translated_text:
“Our Lord, do not take us to task if we forget or make a mistake.”

Ahl al-Sunnah affirm with certainty that everyone who fears Allah Most High will attain salvation, as the Quran explicitly declares. They withhold judgment only concerning a particular individual, because they do not know whether he is among the God-fearing.

Such is also the case of the other proponents of weak views who, when the matter is unclear to them, invoke the apparent wording of the Quran to support positions contrary to the Sunnah—even though nothing in the Quran’s apparent wording contradicts the Sunnah. Examples include those among the Khawārij who say, “One must pray only four units of prayer while travelling”; those who say that praying four is preferable; and those who say, “We do not issue judgments on the basis of one witness and an oath.”

What the apparent wording of the Quran indicates is true. It is not a general expression whose scope has been restricted, for the wording conveys no generality here; rather, it is unrestricted, as in His words:

“Kill the polytheists.”

This is general with respect to individuals and unrestricted with respect to circumstances. Likewise, His words:

“Allah instructs you concerning your children”

are general with respect to children and unrestricted with respect to circumstances.

The term “apparent” may mean what appears to a person, or it may mean what the wording itself indicates. The former depends on people’s understanding, and much in the Quran contradicts faulty understanding.

translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—said:

Section: Attributing a Single Ruling to Two Causes

This also concerns analogous questions, such as the existence of a single effect within the power of two agents, and a single act proceeding from two agents. We say:

Although disagreement over this is well known, most jurists, both of our school and others, allow a ruling to be attributed to two causes, while many jurists and theologians disallow this.

The disagreement ultimately amounts to variation in approach and wording, rather than mutually contradictory positions. A parallel is the disagreement over whether a cause admits exceptions. There is well-known disagreement about this among all the various groups, both within our school and outside it; indeed, two positions on it are reported from Ahmad.

The underlying point is that the term “cause” may mean a necessitating cause: a complete cause from which the ruling cannot fail to follow. Such a cause cannot conceivably admit exceptions; whenever a counterexample arises, it is invalidated. It includes what is called a constituent of the cause and a condition of the ruling;

and the absence of an impediment. Thus, everything on which the ruling depends falls within it.

“Cause” may also mean something that calls for a ruling: it contains a feature that warrants and calls for the ruling, without necessarily making it inevitable. The ruling associated with such a cause may depend on certain conditions being fulfilled and certain impediments being absent. If it admits an exception, and the ruling fails to follow because a condition is missing or an impediment is present, this does not undermine its validity. On this understanding, the deficiency is remedied by identifying the relevant distinction. But if the ruling fails to follow without any condition being missing or any impediment being present, this shows that it is not a cause. For, on this supposition, it is a complete cause, if it is deemed to be present in its entirety, with its conditions fulfilled and its impediments absent. A ruling cannot fail to follow from a complete cause; its failure to follow therefore shows that the cause is not complete.

The point of this comparison is that the objection raised against a cause by citing a counterexample rests on the question of whether a cause admits exceptions—that is, whether the attribute can be present without the ruling. The objection that an attribute has no effect is the reverse: the ruling is present without the attribute. This conflicts with the requirement that the ruling be absent when the cause is absent, just as the first objection conflicts with the requirement that the ruling be present whenever the cause is present. The former requirement turns on the question of attributing a ruling to two causes.

Although most jurists, both of our school and others, do not require the absence of the cause to entail the absence of the ruling in matters of Islamic law, and allow a single ruling to be attributed to two causes, they nevertheless say that a cause is invalidated by its lack of effect. The aim here is to show that the disagreement over attributing a ruling to two causes concerns diversity and terminology, rather than a substantive contradiction. There is no disagreement that a ruling considered as a single genus or species may be attributed to two causes: some of its types or individual instances arise from one cause, and others from another. Examples include inheritance, which arises through kinship, marriage, or the bond of manumission; ownership, which arises through sale, gift, or inheritance; the lawfulness of taking life, which arises through apostasy, murder, or unlawful sexual intercourse; the things that invalidate ablution; the things that necessitate a full ritual bath; and other such matters.

Their disagreement concerns a particular, individual instance of a ruling. For example, if someone touches women, touches his penis, and urinates, can it be said that his ablution has been invalidated by several causes, so that a single ruling is attributed to two causes? Other examples include someone who commits murder, apostatizes, and engages in unlawful sexual intercourse, or a stepdaughter whom one is also forbidden to marry because of a milk relationship. Thus, the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said concerning Durrah, the daughter of Umm Salamah, when Umm Habībah said to him, “We have been saying that you are going to marry Durrah, the daughter of Umm Salamah.”

He asked, “The daughter of Abū Salamah?”

She replied, “Yes.”

He said, “Even if she were not my stepdaughter under my care, she would not be lawful for me to marry, because she is the daughter of my brother through breastfeeding. Thuwaybah, the freedwoman of Abū Lahab, breastfed both me and Abū Salamah.”

in one of his remarks: “This is like the flesh of a dead pig, forbidden on two grounds.” There are other such examples.

We say: In such matters, neither party disputes that each cause independently establishes the ruling when present alone, or that one may say: “Two causes coincide in establishing this ruling, each of which independently establishes it when present alone.” This too is undisputed. It is what they mean when they say that a ruling may, without dispute, be attributed to either of two alternative causes.

Nor do reasonable people dispute that, when the two causes coincide, one cannot say that each independently establishes the same ruling while both are present. For a cause to establish a ruling independently means that the ruling is established by that cause to the exclusion of any other.

Thus, to say, “It is established by this cause to the exclusion of any other,” and, “It is established by the other cause to the exclusion of any other,” is to affirm two contradictory propositions. This amounts to saying: “It is established by this cause and is not established by it; and it is established by the other cause and is not established by it.” It therefore combines affirming that each is a cause of the ruling with denying that either is a cause of it. This is the meaning of the statement: “Attributing the ruling independently to each cause negates its being established by either of them; and whatever entails its own negation when affirmed is false.”

Here those who deny and those who affirm confront one another, but their dispute is verbal.

Those who deny say: “Establishing the ruling through this cause independently is incompatible with establishing it through the other independently.”

translated_text:
their concurrence. Rather, we mean that the ruling is established by each of them, and that each independently establishes it when present alone.”

Thus, the latter do not dispute the former’s contention that, when the two causes coincide, neither independently establishes the ruling. Nor do the former dispute the latter’s contention that each cause independently establishes it when present alone. This, then, is the discussion concerning two concurrent causes.

As for the ruling established when they coincide, it may differ according to the cause, as with the permissibility of execution on grounds of apostasy, unlawful sexual intercourse, or retribution. These rulings are distinct, not identical; none takes the place of another. The rulings may also be identical, as with the invalidation of ablution.

Those who reject attributing a ruling to two causes say: “What the causes establish is a plurality of rulings, not a single ruling.” This is especially so for those who concede to them—in accordance with one of the two views held by jurists among the followers of al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad, and others—that if someone intends, when performing ablution or a full ritual bath, to remove the ritual impurity arising from some of its causes, the other ritual impurity is not removed.

The disagreement over such concurrence in minor and major ritual impurity is well known. It relates to the coexistence of identical things in a single locus, and to whether identical things are mutually incompatible—a matter of well-known dispute.

translated_text:

Thus, when a single ruling is attributed to two causes in the words of the Lawgiver or the imams, this serves to emphasize how firmly the ruling is established and how strong it is. For example, Ahmad said concerning something whose prohibition is particularly severe: “This is like the flesh of a dead pig.” He said this to underscore the severity and strength of the prohibition.

This, too, comes back to the question of whether obligation, prohibition, and permissibility themselves admit of degrees: can one obligation be greater than another, and one prohibition greater than another? This is also disputed. The well-known position among most jurists, both those of our school and others, is that such variation is possible. A group, including Ibn ʿAqīl and others, denied this.

There is a similar dispute over whether one intellect can be more perfect than another. This resembles the dispute over whether the assent and knowledge within the heart admit of degrees. Two positions have been reported from Ahmad on this matter. The position of the imams of the Sunnah who oppose the Murjiʾah is that all these things vary in degree and excellence. The same applies to all the other attributes of a living being: love and hatred, will and aversion, hearing and sight, smell, taste, touch, satiety, the quenching of thirst, ability, inability, and so forth.

The dispute here resembles the dispute over whether two identical things can coexist, such as two instances of blackness or two instances of sweetness. There is no dispute that one instance of blackness may be more intense than another, or one instance of sweetness more intense than another. But should one say that two instances of blackness and two instances of sweetness coexist in the same locus, or that there is a single, intense blackness? This, too, is a merely verbal dispute.

translated_text:
Thus, saying that two rulings coexist in the same locus—two obligations, two prohibitions, or two permissions—is like saying that two instances of blackness coexist there. Saying that there is a single, reinforced ruling is like saying that there is a single, intense blackness. Both statements mean the same thing, for reinforcement does not preclude multiple identical instances: reinforcement may itself be achieved through repetition, as in the words of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“By Allah, I shall surely march against Quraysh! By Allah, I shall surely march against Quraysh! By Allah, I shall surely march against Quraysh!”

The same applies when someone says, “then, then,” or “Zayd has come, Zayd has come,” and similar expressions. Thus, affirming multiple rulings and affirming a strong, reinforced ruling amount to the same thing.

It is clear that, whether one speaks of multiple rulings or of a strong, reinforced ruling, that whole results only from the two causes together. Neither cause has independently produced it, nor can either do so, whether the causes occur together or separately. Each is therefore part of the cause of this whole, not its cause in its own right.

It is equally clear that each of the two causes, when occurring alone, independently establishes the single ruling in its basic form. Yet the term “single” is ambiguous, just as the term “independence” is ambiguous. Someone who affirms that a cause operates independently when it occurs alone does not contradict someone who denies its independence when it occurs together with another cause. Likewise, if someone says that a single ruling may be attributed to two causes, meaning that either independently establishes it when occurring alone, there is no dispute about this.

translated_text:
And if someone says that the single whole produced by the two causes together cannot be produced by either alone, there is no dispute about this. Someone who regards this whole as multiple rulings does not contradict someone who regards it as one, provided the latter means unity of type within a single locus. The point, then, is that a ruling of one type may have two individual instances in two different loci; this is clear. At other times, two instances of it coexist in a single locus: they are two types when considered in themselves, but a single instance when considered in relation to their locus.

Thus, if someone says that the ruling produced by two causes is a single ruling, he is correct if he means a single type within a single entity. Someone who means two instances of one type within a single entity is also correct.

It has thus become clear that two causes cannot each independently establish a single ruling when they occur together. This is self-evident once the matter is grasped, for independence is incompatible with joint participation: that which is independent has no partner. Hence, when two causes combine to produce a single effect, neither independently produces it.

It is also clear that the ruling established by two causes—whether described as multiple rulings or as a single, reinforced ruling—is not independently established by either of them. Rather, each is part of its cause, not a cause of it in its own right.

translated_text:
The same may be said when several proofs establish a single conclusion: they yield reinforced knowledge, or multiple instances of knowledge of the same kind. Hence, together they provide a clarity and strength that no single proof provides.

This falls under the general principle that whenever a causal factor—whether an agent acting by will and choice or by nature, or a motive prompting and impelling action—has a partner in its action and influence, that partner assists and supports it and prevents it from independently and exclusively producing the result. It follows that each needs the other and is not self-sufficient in its action. Joint participation thus entails dependence and precludes self-sufficiency, for two agents participating in an action assist one another in performing it.

Neither can, on its own, do what it does together with the other, provided that it remains unchanged whether acting jointly or alone. For if an agent produces something on its own, and we suppose that it remains unchanged and joins another like itself, their joint effect cannot be the same as the effect each produces alone. For if an effect owes its existence solely to its agent, and the agent produces an effect when acting alone, then, when the two combine, their joint effect must be greater in quantity or magnitude than the effect of either alone. Otherwise, the greater would be no different from the lesser.

It is different, however, when the agent undergoes a change. A person, for example, may lift a piece of timber or prepare food together with another person, and then do the same alone. This necessarily involves some change on his part in his will, movement, implements, or the like. Otherwise, if his condition remains the same in both cases, the effects produced when acting alone and when acting jointly cannot be equal.

A resolute will without power does not bring its object into existence, whereas a resolute will accompanied by complete power necessarily entails the existence of its object. Thus, if one of the two joint agents possessed complete power and complete will, the effect would necessarily be produced by it alone. Yet its being produced by that agent alone precludes its being produced by the other. This entails two contradictories being true together: the effect being produced by that agent alone and not being produced by it alone, and that agent being both an agent and not an agent. This is plainly impossible.

This mutual exclusion does not mean that each of the two agents prevents the other from acting, as when one is said to will to move a body while the other wills to keep it still, or one wills to cause a person’s death while the other wills to bring him to life. Rather, it is an intrinsic mutual exclusion: two partners, each possessing complete power and will, cannot jointly produce an effect over which each has complete power and which each fully wills. For whoever has complete power over something and fully wills it must necessarily produce the effect alone. If the other is likewise, the effect must necessarily be produced by it. These two consequences follow one another and exclude one another, since affirmation precludes negation and negation precludes affirmation, in an intrinsic relation of mutual exclusion and contradiction.

It is thus clear that acting jointly necessarily entails a deficiency in the partner’s power itself. If two agents are supposed to will some particular thing, one of two cases must obtain:

Either the effect produced by one is not the effect produced by the other, but each independently produces part of the effect.

الأول: أن هذا الفصل مذكور في (٢/ ٣٢ - ٣٨).
الثاني: الذي يظهر أن النسخة التي عنها طبع هذا الفصل في هذا الموضع تختلف عن نسخة هذا الفصل في المجلد الثاني، لأمور:

٥ - ٢٠/ ١٨١: (فلو كانت ذاته كافية)، ٢/ ٣٤: (كاملة)، وهو الأظهر.

translated_text:
Or the effect they jointly produce is something neither can produce alone unless it acquires a power more complete than the power it possessed while acting jointly. Thus, if the effect is a single whole whose parts are so intermingled that one agent cannot independently produce one part and another agent another part, joint action through distinct contributions is impossible—as occurs when human beings produce effects, one producing one part and another producing another. Joint action through intermingled contributions is likewise impossible unless one of the two agents is incapable, deficient in power, and lacks complete power over anything. This is what we meant when we said that joint action necessarily entails a deficiency in power.

Section

It may then be said:

This also entails that neither is necessary in itself, self-sufficient, and powerful. Rather, each depends upon another in its essence and attributes, just as it depends upon another in the effects it produces. (*)

For if each depends upon the other in producing its effects and is incapable of producing them alone—as joint action necessarily entails, as explained above—then either it can acquire the power to act independently, so that this is possible for it, or it cannot. The latter is impossible, because if it is impossible for something to be possible and within the power of one agent

Several points should be noted here:
First: This section also appears at 2/32–38.
Second: The manuscript used to print this section here appears to differ from the manuscript of this section in volume two, for the following reasons:
1. Here, the section forms part of a collection of sections, whereas in volume two it stands alone.
2. There are differences between the two versions—as will be shown, Allah willing—which indicate that the manuscripts differ.
3. The section in volume two is more complete than the section printed here.
Third: Comparing the two versions reveals several differences. Among the most important are:
1. 20/178: “is not necessary in itself, self-sufficient and powerful”; 2/32: “is not necessary in itself, qayyūm (ever-subsisting).” The latter reading appears more likely.
2. 20/179: “If it can be an effect within the power of two agents—it is possible—it can also be within the power of one”; 2/32: “and it is possible.” The latter reading appears more likely.
3. 20/179: “would be more perfect for them in being multiple and dispersed”; 2/33: “than being.” The latter reading appears more likely.
4. 20/180: “and to have another attribute; and if it is possible”; 2/34: “another attribute, if it is possible.” The latter reading appears more likely.
5. 20/181: “if its essence were sufficient”; 2/34: “perfect.” The latter reading appears more likely.
6. 20/182: “This is common, for no created being is without a partner and a counterpart”; 2/35: “It is the counterpart, for no created being is without a partner and a counterpart.” The latter reading appears more likely.
Fourth: The remainder of this section appears at 2/37–38.

it is impossible for it to be possible and within the power of two agents. For whether something is possible and within an agent’s power does not vary according to whether there is one agent capable of producing it or several. Thus, if it cannot be an effect within the power of one agent, it cannot be an effect within the power of two. Conversely, if it can be a possible effect within the power of two agents, it can also be within the power of one.

This is clear when possibility and impossibility arise from something in the possible effect itself, since its intrinsic attributes do not differ between the two cases. The same applies when they arise from something in the agent, for it is not impossible for the power possessed by two agents to be possessed by one. Indeed, the possibility of this is self-evident to reason. For reason knows self-evidently that all attributes, power and others alike, attain greater perfection when their bearer is unified and integrated rather than multiple and dispersed. This is why coming together and acting jointly give created beings a strength and power they do not possess when separated and acting individually, even if their conditions otherwise remain unchanged.

Indeed, individuals, bodily members, and other separate bodies each possess a power. If they are conceived as united and brought together, that power becomes stronger and more complete, because their union and coming together, to the extent possible, provide it with something it lacked when they were separate and multiple. This shows that, if the two agents possessing a power are conceived as one thing, that power becomes more complete. How, then, could it fail to be equal to the power

If it is known that two distinct subjects, each possessing a power, would undergo no diminution in power, but rather an increase, if they were conceived as a single subject possessing both powers, then the same holds for a possible effect within the power of two separate agents: if those very two agents were conceived as a single agent possessing whatever they both possessed, its power would not diminish but would increase. It is therefore clear that each could possess the power to act independently, for this is possible for it. Thus, when two agents jointly produce a single effect, it is not possible for each to be capable of producing it; rather, it is possible for them to be a single entity capable of producing it. It follows that each could be more perfect than it is and could possess a different attribute.

Now, if the essence and attributes of each can change, while it is known that it cannot perfect and change itself unaided—for, by hypothesis, it is incapable of independently producing an effect distinct from itself, and so it is all the more incapable of perfecting and changing itself—and if such a being can change and attain perfection but cannot do so by itself, then it cannot be necessarily existent in itself. Rather, it must involve contingency and dependence on another.

The hypothesis would therefore entail that it is both necessarily existent in itself and not necessarily existent in itself, making it both necessary and contingent. This is a contradiction. For whatever is necessarily existent in itself must itself suffice for the reality of its essence and attributes, without depending on another for anything pertaining to its essence, acts, or attributes, since all of these fall within what is denoted by its essence. Indeed, it must not depend on another for any of its acts or the effects it produces, for its acts, which subsist in it, fall within

 فَلَهُ شَرِيكٌ هُوَ لَهُ كَالشَّرْطِ وَلَهُ مُعَارِضٌ هُوَ لَهُ مَانِعٌ وَضِدٌّ وَقَدْ قَالَ سُبْحَانَهُ:
 
{وَمِنْ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ خَلَقْنَا زَوْجَيْنِ}
 وَالزَّوْجُ يُرَادُ بِهِ: النَّظِيرُ الْمُمَاثِلُ وَالضِّدُّ الْمُخَالِفُ.
translated_text:
what is denoted by its very being. Its dependence on another for some of the effects it produces entails dependence with respect to its act and the attribute subsisting in it, since its effect proceeds from these. If its essence were sufficient and self-sufficient, it would not depend on another for its action. Thus, its dependence on another in any respect demonstrates its lack of self-sufficiency and its need for another. This is precisely the contingency that contradicts its being necessarily existent in itself.

Since necessary existence and independence of all others are exclusive to the Lord of all worlds, independence in action is likewise exclusive to Him, as is freedom from any partner in His action or in what He produces. Nothing among created things independently produces any effect; nothing among them is, on its own, a complete cause; and nothing among them dispenses with a partner in producing any effect. Indeed, nothing in the world comes into existence through a cause without another cause sharing in its production. Thus, even if it is called a cause, it is a causal factor tending to produce the effect, not a complete cause, and each of the two is a condition for the other.

Likewise, there is no cause in the world without an impediment that prevents it from acting. Everything among created things described as a cause, a means, something possessing power, an agent, or something producing an effect has a partner that serves as a condition for it, and an opposing factor that serves as an impediment and an antagonist. He, glorified be He, has said:

“And of all things We created two mates.”

A “mate” may mean a similar counterpart or a contrasting opposite.

translated_text:
Instances of this abound: every created being has a partner and a peer. The Lord alone, glorified be He, has no partner, peer, or equal. Rather, whatever He wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass. Hence, none other than Him deserves to be called Creator or Lord without qualification, or to bear similar titles, for these imply independently and exclusively bringing about what is made and produced. This belongs to Allah alone.

Thus, although some people have disputed whether a cause can have several attributes, claiming that it can have only one, most people have disagreed with them and said that it may have several attributes. Indeed, it has been said that no cause among created things can have only one attribute, since nothing created can constitute a cause on its own. Every cause among created things must consist of two or more factors. Thus, there is no single created entity from which anything proceeds on its own, let alone grounds for saying, “From one, only one proceeds.” Rather, nothing proceeds from created things except through two or more of them.

As for the One who acts alone, that is none other than Allah. Just as oneness is necessary for Him and inseparable from Him, so shared agency is necessary for created beings and inseparable from them. Oneness entails perfection, and perfection entails oneness. Shared agency entails imperfection, and imperfection entails shared agency. Oneness entails independence of others, self-subsistence, and necessary existence in itself. And these attributes of independence and necessary existence in itself

translated_text:
and self-subsistence entail oneness. Shared agency entails dependence on others, contingency in itself, and a lack of self-subsistence. Likewise, dependence, contingency, and a lack of self-subsistence entail shared agency.

These and similar considerations are proofs and signs of Allah’s oneness in lordship. They also demonstrate the contingency and dependence of observable created things and their being subject to a Lord. They are therefore proofs of the Maker’s existence, for the separateness, multiplicity, and shared agency found in created things entail their dependence and contingency. Whatever is contingent and dependent must have One who necessarily exists and is independent in Himself; otherwise, it would not exist. Even if an infinite regress of contingent, dependent beings were posited, they would still be contingent collectively. It is self-evident that whatever is contingent depends on another for its existence. Thus, whatever is known to be contingent and dependent is also known to depend on another for its existence. There must therefore be One who is independent in Himself and necessarily existent in Himself; otherwise, nothing dependent and contingent could exist at all.

These considerations establish Allah’s oneness in lordship and His exclusive right to worship—the complete and obligatory affirmation of His oneness brought by the Quran—for reasons we have discussed elsewhere.

For example, things in motion must depend upon volitional motion, and volition must have something willed for its own sake: that is the deity. A created being cannot be willed for its own sake, just as it cannot act independently. Thus, just as there cannot be two independently acting agents, there cannot be two objects each willed for its own sake.

translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islām also said:

Section

Those followers of the imams who deviate in fundamentals and subsidiary matters—such as certain Khurāsānīs from Jīlān and elsewhere who affiliate themselves with Ahmad or other imams—deviate in several ways:

First: A view that neither the imam nor any of his followers known for their learning ever expressed. Examples include the claims made by some of them that the human soul and the light of the sun, the moon, and fires are beginningless. Some of their later followers also asserted that human speech is beginningless, that people will become mute when the Quran is taken away, that the adherents of legal reasoning are unbelievers, that Abū So-and-so should be cursed, and that the ink used in copies of the Quran is beginningless.

Second: A view expressed in error by one of the scholars among the imam’s followers, such as the claim that a person’s voice is beginningless, or the transmission of weak hadiths cited as evidence from the Sunnah concerning the divine attributes, divine decree, the Quran, virtues, and similar matters.
