الثَّالِثُ:
 قَوْلٌ قَالَهُ الْإِمَامُ فَزِيدَ عَلَيْهِ قَدْرًا أَوْ نَوْعًا كَتَكْفِيرِهِ نَوْعًا مِنْ أَهْلِ الْبِدَعِ كالْجَهْمِيَّة فَيَجْعَلُ الْبِدَعَ نَوْعًا وَاحِدًا حَتَّى يَدْخُلَ فِيهِ الْمُرْجِئَةُ وَالْقَدَرِيَّةُ أَوْ ذَمَّهُ لِأَصْحَابِ الرَّأْيِ بِمُخَالَفَةِ الْحَدِيثِ وَالْإِرْجَاءِ فَيَخْرُجُ ذَلِكَ إلَى التَّكْفِيرِ وَاللَّعْنِ أَوْ رَدِّهِ لِشَهَادَةِ الدَّاعِيَةِ وَرِوَايَتِهِ وَغَيْرِ الدَّاعِيَةِ فِي بَعْضِ الْبِدَعِ الْغَلِيظَةِ فَيَعْتَقِدُ رَدَّ خَبَرِهِمْ مُطْلَقًا مَعَ نُصُوصِهِ الصَّرَائِحِ بِخِلَافِهِ وَكَخُرُوجِ مَنْ خَرَجَ فِي بَعْضِ الصِّفَاتِ إلَى زِيَادَةٍ مِنْ التَّشْبِيهِ.
 الرَّابِعُ:
 أَنْ يَفْهَمَ مِنْ كَلَامِهِ مَا لَمْ يُرِدْهُ أَوْ يَنْقُلَ عَنْهُ مَا لَمْ يَقُلْهُ.
 الْخَامِسُ:
 أَنْ يَجْعَلَ كَلَامَهُ عَامًّا أَوْ مُطْلَقًا وَلَيْسَ كَذَلِكَ ثُمَّ قَدْ يَكُونُ فِي اللَّفْظِ إطْلَاقٌ أَوْ عُمُومٌ فَيَكُونُ لَهُمْ فِيهِ بَعْضُ الْعُذْرِ وَقَدْ لَا يَكُونُ كَإِطْلَاقِهِ تَكْفِيرَ الْجَهْمِيَّة الْخِلْقِيَّةِ مَعَ أَنَّهُ مَشْرُوطٌ بِشُرُوطِ انْتَفَتْ فِيمَنْ تَرَحَّمَ عَلَيْهِ مِنْ الَّذِينَ امْتَحَنُوهُ وَهُمْ رُءُوسُ الْجَهْمِيَّة.
 السَّادِسُ:
 أَنْ يَكُونَ عَنْهُ فِي الْمَسْأَلَةِ اخْتِلَافٌ فَيَتَمَسَّكُونَ بِالْقَوْلِ الْمَرْجُوحِ.
 السَّابِعُ:
 أَنْ لَا يَكُونَ قَدْ قَالَ أَوْ نُقِلَ عَنْهُ مَا يُزِيلُ شُبْهَتَهُمْ مَعَ كَوْنِ لَفْظِهِ مُحْتَمِلًا لَهَا.
translated_text:
Third:
A view expressed by the imam is extended in degree or scope. For example, he may declare a particular group of innovators, such as the Jahmiyya, to be unbelievers, but someone then treats all innovations as a single category, thereby including the Murji’a and the Qadariyya. Or his criticism of the adherents of legal reasoning for contradicting hadith and holding Murji’ite beliefs is taken further, to declaring them unbelievers and cursing them. Or his rejection of the testimony and narrations of those who propagate innovations—and, in certain grave innovations, even those who do not—is taken to mean that their reports must be rejected unconditionally, despite his explicit statements to the contrary. Another example is those who overstep concerning some of the divine attributes, going further in likening Allah to His creation.

Fourth:
Someone understands his words to mean something he did not intend, or attributes to him something he did not say.

Fifth:
Someone treats his words as general or unqualified when they are not. His wording may indeed contain an unqualified or general expression, giving them some excuse; or it may not. An example is his unqualified declaration that the Jahmiyya Khilqiyya are unbelievers, although this is subject to conditions that were not fulfilled in those upon whom he invoked mercy among the very people who subjected him to the ordeal, despite their being leaders of the Jahmiyya.

Sixth:
Differing positions are transmitted from him on a question, and they cling to the less well-founded position.

Seventh:
He may not have made a statement—or none may have been transmitted from him—that would dispel their misconception, while his wording admits of their interpretation.

original_text:
الثَّامِنُ:
 أَنْ يَكُونَ قَوْلُهُ مُشْتَمِلًا عَلَى خَطَأٍ. فَالْوُجُوهُ السِّتَّةُ تُبَيِّنُ مِنْ مَذْهَبِهِ نَفْسِهِ أَنَّهُمْ خَالَفُوهُ وَهُوَ الْحَقُّ وَالسَّابِعُ خَالَفُوا الْحَقَّ وَإِنْ لَمْ يَعْرِفْ مَذْهَبَهُ نَفْيًا وَإِثْبَاتًا وَالثَّامِنُ خَالَفُوا الْحَقَّ وَإِنْ وَافَقُوا مَذْهَبَهُ. فَالْقِسْمَةُ ثُلَاثِيَّةٌ؛ لِأَنَّهُمْ إذَا خَالَفُوا الْحَقَّ فَإِمَّا أَنْ يَكُونُوا قَدْ خَالَفُوهُ أَيْضًا أَوْ وَافَقُوهُ أَوْ لَمْ يُوَافِقُوهُ وَلَمْ يُخَالِفُوهُ لِانْتِفَاءِ قَوْلِهِ فِي ذَلِكَ وَكَذَلِكَ إذَا وَافَقُوا الْحَقَّ فَإِمَّا أَنْ يُوَافِقُوهُ هُوَ أَوْ يُخَالِفُوهُ؛ أَوْ يَنْتَفِيَ الْأَمْرَانِ. وَأَهْلُ الْبِدَعِ فِي غَيْرِ الْحَنْبَلِيَّةِ أَكْثَرُ مِنْهُمْ فِي الْحَنْبَلِيَّةِ بِوُجُوهِ كَثِيرَةٍ؛ لِأَنَّ نُصُوصَ أَحْمَد فِي تَفَاصِيلِ السُّنَّةِ وَنَفْيِ الْبِدَعِ أَكْثَرُ مِنْ غَيْرِهِ بِكَثِيرِ فَالْمُبْتَدِعَةُ الْمُنْتَسِبُونَ إلَى غَيْرِهِ إذَا كَانُوا جهمية أَوْ قَدَرِيَّةً أَوْ شِيعَةً أَوْ مُرْجِئَةً؛ لَمْ يَكُنْ ذَلِكَ مَذْهَبًا لِلْإِمَامِ إلَّا فِي الْإِرْجَاءِ؛ فَإِنَّهُ قَوْلُ أَبِي فُلَانٍ وَأَمَّا بَعْضُ التَّجَهُّمِ فَاخْتَلَفَ النَّقْلُ عَنْهُ وَلِذَلِكَ اخْتَلَفَ أَصْحَابُهُ الْمُنْتَسِبُونَ إلَيْهِ مَا بَيْنَ سُنِّيَّةٍ وجهمية؛ ذُكُورٍ وَإِنَاثٍ؛ مُشَبِّهَةٍ وَمُجَسِّمَةٍ؛ لِأَنَّ أُصُولَهُ لَا تَنْفِي الْبِدَعَ وَإِنْ لَمْ تُثْبِتْهَا. وَفِي الْحَنْبَلِيَّةِ أَيْضًا مُبْتَدِعَةٌ؛ وَإِنْ كَانَتْ الْبِدْعَةُ فِي غَيْرِهِمْ أَكْثَرَ وَبِدْعَتُهُمْ غَالِبًا فِي زِيَادَةِ الْإِثْبَاتِ فِي حَقِّ اللَّهِ وَفِي زِيَادَةِ الْإِنْكَارِ عَلَى مُخَالِفِهِمْ بِالتَّكْفِيرِ وَغَيْرِهِ؛ لِأَنَّ أَحْمَد كَانَ مُثْبِتًا لِمَا جَاءَتْ بِهِ السُّنَّةُ؛ مُنْكِرًا عَلَى مَنْ خَالَفَهَا مُصِيبًا فِي غَالِبِ الْأُمُورِ مُخْتَلِفًا عَنْهُ فِي الْبَعْضِ وَمُخَالِفًا فِي الْبَعْضِ.
translated_text:
Eighth:
His statement may contain an error.

The first six cases show, on the basis of his own teachings, that they have opposed him, while his position is the truth. In the seventh, they have opposed the truth, even if his own position, whether affirmative or negative, is unknown. In the eighth, they have opposed the truth even though they have agreed with his position.

The division is therefore threefold: when they oppose the truth, they may also have opposed him, agreed with him, or neither agreed with nor opposed him, because he made no statement on that matter. Likewise, when they agree with the truth, they may agree with him, oppose him, or neither.

Adherents of innovation are more numerous among non-Hanbalīs than among Hanbalīs, for many reasons. Ahmad’s explicit statements detailing the Sunnah and rejecting innovations are far more numerous than those of other imams. When innovators affiliated with another imam are Jahmīs, Qadarīs, Shīʿa, or Murjiʾa, their beliefs were not the imam’s position, except in the case of irjāʾ, which was the position of Abū So-and-so. As for certain elements of Jahmī doctrine, reports from him differ. Accordingly, those affiliated with him have differed, ranging from Sunnis to Jahmīs, male and female, anthropomorphists and corporealists. This is because his principles do not rule out innovations, even if they do not affirm them.

There are innovators among the Hanbalīs too, although innovation is more prevalent among others. Their innovation generally consists of excessive affirmation concerning Allah and excessive denunciation of their opponents, through declaring them unbelievers and other means. For Ahmad affirmed what the Sunnah brought and denounced those who opposed it. He was correct in most matters; on some, reports from him differed, and on others he held a contrary position.

original_text:
وَأَمَّا بِدْعَةُ غَيْرِهِمْ فَقَدْ تَكُونُ أَشَدَّ مِنْ بِدْعَةِ مُبْتَدِعِهِمْ فِي زِيَادَةِ الْإِثْبَاتِ وَالْإِنْكَارِ؛ وَقَدْ تَكُونُ فِي النَّفْيِ وَهُوَ الْأَغْلَبُ كالْجَهْمِيَّة؛ وَالْقَدَرِيَّةِ؛ وَالْمُرْجِئَةِ؛ وَالرَّافِضَةِ. وَأَمَّا زِيَادَةُ الْإِنْكَارِ مِنْ غَيْرِهِمْ عَلَى الْمُخَالِفِ مِنْ تَكْفِيرٍ وَتَفْسِيقٍ فَكَثِيرٌ.
 وَالْقِسْمُ الثَّالِثُ مِنْ الْبِدَعِ:
 الْخُلُوُّ عَنْ السُّنَّةِ نَفْيًا وَإِثْبَاتًا وَتَرْكُ الْأَمْرِ بِهَا وَالنَّهْيِ عَنْ مُخَالَفَتِهَا وَهُوَ كَثِيرٌ فِي الْمُتَفَقِّهَةِ وَالْمُتَصَوِّفَةِ.
translated_text:
As for innovation among others, it may exceed that of Hanbalī innovators in excessive affirmation and denunciation; or it may involve negation, which is more common, as with the Jahmīs, Qadarīs, Murjiʾa, and Rāfida. Excessive denunciation of opponents by others, through declaring them unbelievers or sinners, is also widespread.

The third category of innovation:

Being devoid of the Sunnah in both negation and affirmation, and failing to enjoin adherence to it or forbid opposition to it. This is common among students of jurisprudence and Sufis.

original_text:
وَقَالَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى -:
فَصْلٌ:
الْمُتَكَلِّمُ بِاللَّفْظِ الْعَامِّ لَا بُدَّ أَنْ يَقُومَ بِقَلْبِهِ مَعْنًى عَامٌّ؛
 فَإِنَّ اللَّفْظَ لَا بُدَّ لَهُ مِنْ مَعْنًى وَمَنْ قَالَ:
 الْعُمُومُ مِنْ عَوَارِضِ الْأَلْفَاظِ دُونَ الْمَعَانِي فَمَا أَرَادَ - وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَم - إلَّا الْمَعَانِيَ الْخَارِجَةَ عَنْ الذِّهْنِ كَالْعَطَاءِ وَالْمَطَرِ عَلَى أَنَّ قَوْلَهُ مَرْجُوحٌ فَإِذَا حَكَمَ بِحُكْمِ عَامٍّ لِمُسَمَّى مِنْ أَمْرٍ أَوْ نَهْيٍ؛ أَوْ خَبَرِ سَلْبٍ أَوْ إيجَابٍ فَهَذَا لَا بُدَّ أَنْ يَسْتَشْعِرَ ذَلِكَ الْمَعْنَى الْعَامَّ وَالْحُكْمَ عَلَيْهِ وَلَا يَجِبُ أَنْ يَتَصَوَّرَ الْأَفْرَادَ مِنْ جِهَةِ تَمَيُّزِ بَعْضِهَا عَنْ بَعْضٍ بَلْ قَدْ لَا يَتَصَوَّرُ ذَلِكَ إذَا كَانَتْ مِمَّا لَا يَنْحَصِرُ لِلْبَشَرِ وَإِنَّمَا يَتَصَوَّرُهَا وَيَحْكُمُ عَلَيْهَا مِنْ جِهَةِ الْمَعْنَى الْعَامِّ الْمُشْتَرَكِ بَيْنَهَا سَوَاءٌ كَانَتْ صِيغَةُ الْعُمُومِ اسْمَ جَمْعٍ؛ أَوْ اسْمَ وَاحِدٍ فَإِنَّهُ لَا بُدَّ أَنْ يَعُمَّ الِاسْمُ تِلْكَ الْمُسَمَّيَاتِ لَفْظًا وَمَعْنًى فَهُوَ يَحْكُمُ عَلَيْهَا بِاعْتِبَارِ الْقَدْرِ الْمُشْتَرَكِ الْعَامِّ بَيْنَهَا وَقَدْ يَسْتَحْضِرُ أَحْيَانًا بَعْضَ آحَادِ ذَلِكَ الْعَامِّ بِخُصُوصِهِ أَوْ بَعْضَ الْأَنْوَاعِ بِخُصُوصِهِ وَقَدْ يَسْتَحْضِرُ الْجَمِيعَ إنْ كَانَ مِمَّا يُحْصَرُ وَقَدْ لَا يَسْتَحْضِرُ ذَلِكَ بَلْ يَكُونُ عَالِمًا بِالْأَفْرَادِ عَلَى وَجْهٍ كُلِّيٍّ جُمْلَةً
translated_text:
He also said—may Allah Most High have mercy on him:

Section

Anyone who uses a general expression must have a general meaning in mind, for an expression must have a meaning. Whoever says, “Generality is a property of expressions, not meanings,” can only have intended—and Allah knows best—realities external to the mind, such as giving and rainfall, although his view is the weaker one.

When someone makes a general judgment concerning what an expression denotes—whether a command, a prohibition, or a negative or affirmative statement—he must be conscious of that general meaning and the judgment applied to it. He need not conceive of the individual instances in terms of what distinguishes them from one another. Indeed, he may be unable to do so if they are beyond human enumeration. Rather, he conceives of them and judges them in terms of the general meaning they share, whether the expression conveying generality is a collective noun or a singular noun. The noun must encompass those things it denotes both in wording and in meaning; thus, he judges them with regard to the general feature they share.

At times, he may bring to mind particular instances covered by that general expression, or particular categories. He may bring them all to mind if they can be enumerated. Alternatively, he may not bring them to mind, but know the individual instances in a general, comprehensive way

original_text:
لَا تَفْصِيلًا ثُمَّ إنَّ ذَلِكَ الْحُكْمَ يَتَخَلَّفُ عَنْ بَعْضِ تِلْكَ الْآحَادِ لِمُعَارِضِ.
 مِثْلَ أَنْ يَقُولَ:
 أَعْطِ لِكُلِّ فَقِيرٍ دِرْهَمًا فَإِذَا قِيلَ لَهُ: فَإِنْ كَانَ كَافِرًا أَوْ عَدُوًّا فَقَدَ يُنْهَى عَنْ الْإِعْطَاءِ. فَهَذَا الَّذِي أَرَادَ دُخُولَهُ فِي الْعُمُومِ إمَّا أَنْ يُرِيدَ دُخُولَهُ بِخُصُوصِهِ؛ أَوْ لِمُجَرَّدِ شُمُولِ الْمَعْنَى لَهُ مِنْ غَيْرِ اسْتِشْعَارِ خُصُوصِهِ؛ بِحَيْثُ لَمْ يَقُمْ بِهِ مَا يَمْنَعُ الدُّخُولَ مَعَ قِيَامِ الْمُقْتَضِي لِلدُّخُولِ.
 وَأَمَّا الْأَوَّلُ فَقَدْ أَرَادَ دُخُولَهُ بِعَيْنِهِ فَهَذَا نَظِيرُ مَا وَرَدَ عَلَيْهِ اللَّفْظُ الْعَامُّ مِنْ السَّبَبِ وَهَذَا إحْدَى فَوَائِدِ عَطْفِ الْخَاصِّ عَلَى الْعَامِّ وَهُوَ:
 ثُبُوتُ الْمَعْنَى الْمُشْتَرَكِ فِيهِ مِنْ غَيْرِ مُعَارِضٍ وَإِنْ كَانَ مِنْ فَوَائِدِهِ أَنْ يَتَبَيَّنَ دُخُولُهُ بِعُمُومِ الْمَعْنَى الْمُشْتَرَكِ: وَبِخُصُوصِ الْمَعْنَى الْمُمَيِّزِ وَإِنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ الْحُكْمُ ثَابِتًا لِلْمُشْتَرَكِ.
 وَأَمَّا الَّذِي لَمْ يُرِدْ دُخُولَهُ فِي الْعُمُومِ:

For example, someone may say, “Give every poor person a dirham.” If he is then asked, “What if he is an unbeliever or an enemy?” giving may be prohibited. An individual whom he intended to include within the general expression may have been intended specifically, or merely because the meaning encompasses him, without his particular circumstances being brought to mind, provided that nothing prevents his inclusion while the grounds for inclusion are present.

In the first case, he intended that particular individual to be included. This is analogous to the particular occasion that prompted the general expression. This is one benefit of mentioning the particular after the general: it establishes that the shared meaning applies to that particular instance without any countervailing factor. Another benefit, however, is to make clear that it is included both through the generality of the shared meaning and through the specificity of its distinguishing meaning, even if the ruling is not established for the shared meaning.

As for an individual whom he did not intend to include within the general expression, he may have been conscious, when uttering it, of a countervailing factor present in that individual. This prevents him from intending that individual’s inclusion under the ruling attached to the general meaning, even though the grounds for inclusion—namely, the general meaning—are present in him. Alternatively, he may have been conscious of that factor before uttering the general expression, but at the moment of speaking have overlooked that individual’s inclusion or exclusion. The first resembles a qualification accompanying the general expression, and the second a preceding qualification. That individual was included in the general expression without any qualification, and subsequently becoming conscious of what prevents his intended inclusion constitutes abrogation. This is because the grounds for his inclusion within the speaker’s intent consist in his possessing that meaning, which he does possess. The countervailing factor can prevent his intended inclusion only if the speaker is conscious of it when speaking; yet he was not conscious of it.

One who takes this view may also say of an earlier awareness of the preventing factor:

It has no effect unless it accompanies the utterance. Indeed, if, when making the general statement, he overlooks the exclusion of something, it falls within his general intent, just as it falls within his awareness of the general meaning. For qualification clarifies what he did not intend by the general expression, whereas this individual was intended by it. It is not necessary that he should have intended that individual specifically; all that is required is that he should have intended the shared meaning, and that is present.

It may, however, be said:

Rather, he did not intend this individual by the general designation, because he intended by it only those in whom no countervailing factor was present. In either case, even if the factor opposing that meaning had not been conceived of in detail, his intent is that the meaning provides grounds for intending to include the individual—not that the ruling necessarily applies to him merely because of that meaning, without regard to any countervailing factor. If his intent is that this meaning provides grounds for inclusion, then, when it is opposed by something he regards as a preventing factor, he did not intend that individual’s inclusion.

Thus, the issue turns on whether, within his intended meaning, the presence of the general meaning entails actual intent, unless it ceases to apply to some instances, or merely establishes grounds for intending the individual instances. Such grounds entail the inclusion of those instances when no countervailing factor opposes them.

translated_text:
On this basis, suppose he was not conscious of the countervailing factor that prevents inclusion, but, were he to become conscious of it, would know that he did not intend to include that individual. Can it be said that, in terms of meaning, his ruling and intent did not encompass that individual, even though his wording and its general meaning did? This may indeed be said. For he intended the universal, shared meaning in its general scope, but did not intend to include individuals possessing a feature that, in his judgment, opposes and outweighs that general meaning.

Moreover, he is not required to call to mind all preventing factors across kinds and individuals, given their great number. Even if he were conscious of some of them, it would not be appropriate to address each and every one explicitly to rule it out, for such speech would be ungainly, awkward, long-winded, and inarticulate. Knowing these preventing factors, explaining them, or both, may therefore be difficult or impossible. Here, the countervailing characteristics possessed by particular individuals prevent their intended inclusion by the speaker, even though his wording and its general meaning encompass them by virtue of what they share with the others.

Accordingly, if he might regard that factor as preventing inclusion, but might not, should we judge that the individual is included because the grounds for inclusion are present and the presumption is that no qualifying factor exists? Or should we suspend judgment because the grounds are present but a countervailing factor is possible? This requires consideration.

The proponent of the second view may say: “So long as this preventing factor is present, it prevents those grounds from actually entailing inclusion.”

The proponent of the first view may say: “Rather, their capacity to entail inclusion is established, whereas the preventing factor is doubtful.”

The more evident view is to suspend judgment concerning the speaker’s intent in such a case.

translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islām said:

Section

“A Principle”

Good deeds are deemed good on two grounds: first, the welfare and benefit they bring; and second, the corruption and harm they avert. Likewise, evil deeds are deemed evil on two grounds: first, the corruption and harm they entail; and second, the benefit and welfare they obstruct.

An example is His saying, Exalted is He:

“Indeed, prayer restrains one from indecency and wrongdoing, and the remembrance of Allah is greater.”

He thus explains both aspects. His saying:

“Indeed, prayer restrains one from indecency and wrongdoing”

explains how it averts corruption and harm. When the soul engages in remembering Allah and supplicating to Him—especially in a particular manner—this imparts to it a righteous disposition that restrains it from indecency and wrongdoing, as a person can sense within himself.

For this reason, He says, Exalted is He:

“Seek help through patience and prayer.”

For the heart experiences such joy, happiness, and contentment that it has no need for

reprehensible pleasures, and it acquires fear of Allah, reverence for Him, and awe. Its hope, fear, and love each serve to restrain it.

His saying:

“And the remembrance of Allah is greater”

explains the benefit and welfare that prayer brings. That is, the remembrance of Allah within prayer is greater than its restraining effect against indecency and wrongdoing, for remembrance is sought for its own sake, as He says:

“When the call to prayer is made on Friday, hasten to the remembrance of Allah.”

The former—its restraining effect—is secondary. This benefit and welfare are therefore greater than averting that harm. Thus, the sinful believer will ultimately receive mercy, whereas the hypocrite given to worship will ultimately come to misery. Faith in Allah and His Messenger is the sum and foundation of happiness.

Anyone who thinks the verse means that remembering Allah is greater than prayer is mistaken. Prayer is superior to remembrance on its own, according to both the scriptural texts and scholarly consensus. Prayer is itself remembrance of Allah, but remembrance in its most perfect form. How, then, could remembrance of Allah in general be deemed superior to its finest form?

A similar example is the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Keep to night prayer, for it draws you near to your Lord, is the practice of the righteous before you, restrains you from sin, expiates misdeeds, and dispels the urge to envy.”

He thus explains the benefit it brings through drawing near to Allah and following the example of the righteous, and the harm it averts through restraining future misdeeds and expiating past ones. This parallels the verse.

Likewise, He says:

“Establish prayer at the two ends of the day and in the early hours of the night. Indeed, good deeds do away with misdeeds.”

This describes the removal of harm. Then He says:

“That is a reminder for those who remember.”

This describes a benefit. The Quran and Sunnah contain many descriptions of the virtues of deeds, their rewards, benefits, and advantages that follow this pattern. For example, He says concerning jihad:

“He will forgive you your sins and admit you to gardens beneath which rivers flow,”

and continues as far as:

“And another blessing that you love: help from Allah and an imminent conquest.”

He thus explains how it removes the harm of sins and brings the benefit of mercy through admission to Paradise. This pertains to the Hereafter. In this world, there are help and conquest, which likewise involve averting harm and securing benefit. There are many similar examples.

As for evil deeds, an example is His saying:

“Satan only seeks to sow enmity and hatred among you through intoxicants and gambling, and to turn you away from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer.”

Here He explains the two reasons: first, the harm caused by outward enmity and inward hatred; and second, the obstruction of the benefit that is the foundation of happiness—namely, the remembrance of Allah and prayer. The result is to turn people away from what is commanded, whether as an obligation or a recommendation. This is also the rationale they gave for disapproving of forms of gambling, such as chess and similar games.

It thus encourages evil deeds and discourages good deeds, while offering no benefit. In the cases excepted from this, a countervailing factor removes its harm, as in comparable cases.

This is a vast subject; reflection upon it opens the way to understanding many meanings of the religion.

translated_text:
He also said:

Section: “A Principle of Islamic Law”

The fact that Allah and His Messenger prescribe an act in general and unrestricted terms does not entail that it is prescribed in a particular, restricted form. General and unrestricted wording does not indicate the particular features or restrictions pertaining to some of the instances it encompasses. It therefore does not entail that such specification or restriction is prescribed or commanded. If the evidence indicates that such specification or restriction is disliked, it is disliked; if it indicates that it is recommended, it is recommended. Otherwise, it remains neither recommended nor disliked.

An example of this is that Allah has prescribed supplication to Him and remembrance of Him in unrestricted, general terms. He says:

“Remember Allah with much remembrance.”

And He says:

“Call upon your Lord humbly and privately.”

There are other texts to the same effect. Thus, gathering for supplication and remembrance in a particular place or at a particular time—or the act of gathering for that purpose—is a restriction upon remembrance and supplication. The general, unrestricted indication of these texts does not establish that particular specification or restriction, although it does encompass the practice insofar as it shares the common underlying act. وَالْجَهْرِ بِبَعْضِ الْأَذْكَارِ فِي الصَّلَاةِ كَمَا جَهَرَ عُمَرُ بِالِاسْتِفْتَاحِ وَابْنُ عَبَّاسٍ بِقِرَاءَةِ الْفَاتِحَةِ. وَكَذَلِكَ الْجَهْرُ بِالْبَسْمَلَةِ أَحْيَانًا. وَبَعْضُ هَذَا الْقِسْمِ مُلْحَقٌ بِالْأَوَّلِ فَيَكُونُ الْخُصُوصُ مَأْمُورًا بِهِ كَالْقُنُوتِ فِي النَّوَازِلِ وَبَعْضُهَا يُنْفَى مُطْلَقًا فَفِعْلُ الطَّاعَةِ الْمَأْمُورِ بِهَا مُطْلَقًا حَسَنٌ وَإِيجَابُ مَا لَيْسَ فِيهِ سُنَّةٌ مَكْرُوهٌ. وَهَذِهِ الْقَاعِدَةُ إذَا جُمِعَتْ نَظَائِرُهَا نَفَعَتْ وَتَمَيَّزَ بِهَا مَا هُوَ الْبِدَعُ مِنْ الْعِبَادَاتِ الَّتِي يُشْرَعُ جِنْسُهَا مِنْ الصَّلَاةِ وَالذِّكْرِ وَالْقِرَاءَةِ وَأَنَّهَا قَدْ تُمَيَّزُ بِوَصْفِ اخْتِصَاصٍ تَبْقَى مَكْرُوهَةً لِأَجْلِهِ أَوْ مُحَرَّمَةً كَصَوْمِ يَوْمَيْ الْعِيدَيْنِ وَالصَّلَاةِ فِي أَوْقَاتِ النَّهْيِ كَمَا قَدْ تَتَمَيَّزُ بِوَصْفِ اخْتِصَاصٍ تَكُونُ وَاجِبَةً لِأَجْلِهِ أَوْ مُسْتَحَبَّةً كَالصَّلَوَاتِ الْخَمْسِ وَالسُّنَنِ الرَّوَاتِبِ. وَلِهَذَا قَدْ يَقَعُ مِنْ خَلْقِهِ الْعِبَادَةُ الْمُطْلَقَةُ وَالتَّرْغِيبُ فِيهَا فِي أَنْ شَرَعَ مِنْ الدِّينِ مَا لَمْ يَأْذَنْ بِهِ اللَّهُ كَمَا قَدْ يَقَعُ مِنْ خَلْقِهِ الْعِلْمُ الْمُجَرَّدُ فِي النَّهْيِ عَنْ بَعْضِ الْمُسْتَحَبِّ أَوْ تَرْكِ التَّرْغِيبِ. وَلِهَذَا لَمَّا عَابَ اللَّهُ عَلَى الْمُشْرِكِينَ أَنَّهُمْ شَرَعُوا مِنْ الدِّينِ مَا لَمْ يَأْذَنْ بِهِ اللَّهُ وَأَنَّهُمْ حَرَّمُوا مَا لَمْ يُحَرِّمْهُ اللَّهُ. وَهَذَا كَثِيرٌ فِي الْمُتَصَوِّفَةِ مَنْ يَصِلُ بِبِدَعِ الْأَمْرِ لِشَرْعِ الدِّينِ وَفِي الْمُتَفَقِّهَةِ مَنْ يَصِلُ بِبِدَعِ التَّحْرِيمِ إلَى الْكُفْرِ.
translated_text:
and reciting some remembrances aloud in prayer, as ʿUmar recited the opening supplication aloud and Ibn ʿAbbās recited al-Fātihah aloud. The same applies to occasionally reciting “In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful” aloud. Some cases in this category fall under the first category, so that the particular form itself is enjoined, as with the qunūt supplication during calamities. Others are ruled out altogether. Performing an act of obedience commanded in general is good, whereas making something obligatory without a basis in the Sunnah is disliked.

This principle is beneficial when its parallel cases are considered together. It distinguishes innovations within forms of worship whose general category is prescribed, such as prayer, remembrance, and recitation. Such acts may have a particular characteristic that renders them disliked or forbidden, as with fasting on the two Eid days or praying at prohibited times. Equally, they may have a particular characteristic that renders them obligatory or recommended, as with the five daily prayers and the regular Sunnah prayers.

Thus, someone whose disposition inclines toward worship in general and encouraging it may fall into instituting as religion what Allah has not authorized. Likewise, someone whose disposition inclines toward abstract knowledge may fall into forbidding certain recommended acts or failing to encourage them.

This is why Allah reproached the polytheists for instituting as religion what He had not authorized and for prohibiting what He had not prohibited. This occurs frequently: among those who pursue Sufism are some whose innovative prescriptions lead them to institute religious law, while among those who pursue jurisprudence are some whose innovative prohibitions lead them to disbelief.

He also said:

Section

“Making things obligatory and prohibiting them” may be a blessing, a punishment, or a test. The first includes making faith and good conduct obligatory and prohibiting disbelief and wrongdoing. This is what is affirmed by those who hold that reason can discern good and evil.

As for punishment, examples include His words:

“For wrongdoing on the part of the Jews, We forbade them good things that had been lawful to them.”

And His words:

“To those who were Jews, We forbade every animal with claws; and of cattle and sheep, We forbade them their fat,”

through to His words:

“Thus We recompensed them for their transgression.”

And His words:

“And he relieves them of their burden and the shackles that were upon them.”

Thus, He called them burdens and shackles: burdens concern obligations, while shackles concern prohibitions. And His words:

“And do not lay upon us a burden like that which You laid upon those before us.”

This is further supported by His words:

“And He has not placed upon you any hardship in religion.”

And His words:

“Allah does not intend to place you in any hardship.”

For this general negation excludes everything that may be called hardship,

 وَهُوَ مُطِيعٌ فِي ذَلِكَ هَذَا مِنْ جِهَةِ الشَّرْعِ وَقَدْ يَكُونُ مِنْ جِهَةِ الْكَوْنِ بِأَنْ يَخْلُقَ سُبْحَانَهُ مَا يَقْتَضِي وُجُودَ التَّحْرِيمِ الثَّابِتِ بِالْخِطَابِ وَالْوُجُوبِ الثَّابِتِ بِالْخِطَابِ كَقَوْلِهِ:
 
{وَاسْأَلْهُمْ عَنِ الْقَرْيَةِ الَّتِي كَانَتْ حَاضِرَةَ الْبَحْرِ إذْ يَعْدُونَ فِي السَّبْتِ إذْ تَأْتِيهِمْ حِيتَانُهُمْ يَوْمَ سَبْتِهِمْ شُرَّعًا وَيَوْمَ لَا يَسْبِتُونَ لَا تَأْتِيهِمْ كَذَلِكَ نَبْلُوهُمْ بِمَا كَانُوا يَفْسُقُونَ}
 فَأَخْبَرَ أَنَّهُ
translated_text:
and hardship means constraint. Thus Allah has imposed no obligation or prohibition that places people under such constraint. Its opposite is ease. Hardship resembles a shackle: something from which one cannot escape despite needing to do so.

As for testing, an example is His saying:

“Indeed, Allah will test you with a river,”

and the rest of the verse.

Such testing may occur through the revelation of divine instruction. This happens only in the time of the prophets and has now ceased. It may also occur when divine instruction becomes known to someone who had not previously heard it, but then hears it. Or it may occur through a belief that divine instruction has been revealed, or through a belief about its meaning, even if that belief is mistaken, because the outward ruling depends on the belief of the person subject to the law.

An obligation imposed by divine law may therefore apply both inwardly and outwardly, as with a command one knows with certainty to have been revealed by Allah. Alternatively, it may apply outwardly, as in the case of someone who believes that Allah’s ruling is obligation or prohibition—whether through independent legal reasoning, following another’s authority, or compound ignorance—because an indication has been presented that outwardly points to that ruling, without the countervailing evidence. This constitutes an outward obligation, for a jurist whose independent reasoning is mistaken is nevertheless correct, outwardly, in carrying out what he was commanded to do, and is obedient in that respect.

This concerns testing through divine legislation. Testing may also occur through His ordering of events, when He, glorified be He, creates circumstances that call for the application of a prohibition or obligation established by divine instruction, as in His saying:

“Ask them about the town that was by the sea, when they transgressed on the Sabbath: their fish would come to them openly on their Sabbath day, but would not come to them on the days when they did not observe the Sabbath. Thus We tested them because of their disobedience.”

He thus states that He

original_text:
بَلَاهُمْ بِفِسْقِهِمْ حَيْثُ أَتَى بِالْحِيتَانِ يَوْمَ التَّحْرِيمِ وَمَنَعَهَا يَوْمَ الْإِبَاحَةِ. كَمَا يُؤْتَى الْمُحْرِمُ الْمُبْتَلَى بِالصَّيْدِ يَوْمَ إحْرَامِهِ. وَلَا يُؤْتَى بِهِ يَوْمَ حِلِّهِ؛ أَوْ يُؤْتَى بِمَنْ يُعَامِلُهُ رِبًا وَلَا يُؤْتَى بِمَنْ يُعَامِلُهُ بَيْعًا.
 وَمِنْ ذَلِكَ مَجِيءُ الْإِبَاحَةِ وَالْإِسْقَاطِ نِعْمَةً وَهَذَا كَثِيرٌ كَقَوْلِهِ:
 
{الْآنَ خَفَّفَ اللَّهُ عَنْكُمْ}
 وَقَدْ تَقَدَّمَ نَظَائِرُهَا.
translated_text:
tested them because of their disobedience, bringing the fish on the day when fishing was forbidden and withholding them on the day when it was permitted. Likewise, someone in a state of pilgrimage consecration may be tested by having game brought before him while its restrictions apply, but not when he is free of them; or a person may encounter someone who will engage with him in usurious dealings, but no one who will engage with him in trade.

Another instance is the granting of permission and the waiving of obligations as a blessing. This occurs frequently, as in His saying:

“Now Allah has lightened your burden.”

Similar examples have already been mentioned.

original_text:
وَقَالَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
أَمَّا فِي الْمَسَائِلِ الْأُصُولِيَّةِ فَكَثِيرٌ مِنْ الْمُتَكَلِّمَةِ وَالْفُقَهَاءِ مِنْ أَصْحَابِنَا وَغَيْرِهِمْ مَنْ يُوجِبُ النَّظَرَ وَالِاسْتِدْلَالَ عَلَى كُلِّ أَحَدٍ حَتَّى عَلَى الْعَامَّةِ وَالنِّسَاءِ حَتَّى يُوجِبُوهُ فِي الْمَسَائِلِ الَّتِي تَنَازَعَ فِيهَا فُضَلَاءُ الْأُمَّةِ قَالُوا:
 لِأَنَّ الْعِلْمَ بِهَا وَاجِبٌ وَلَا يَحْصُلُ الْعِلْمُ إلَّا بِالنَّظَرِ الْخَاصِّ. وَأَمَّا جُمْهُورُ الْأُمَّةِ فَعَلَى خِلَافِ ذَلِكَ؛ فَإِنَّ مَا وَجَبَ عِلْمُهُ إنَّمَا يَجِبُ عَلَى مَنْ يَقْدِرُ عَلَى تَحْصِيلِ الْعِلْمِ وَكَثِيرٌ مِنْ النَّاسِ عَاجِزٌ عَنْ الْعِلْمِ بِهَذِهِ الدَّقَائِقِ فَكَيْفَ يُكَلَّفُ الْعِلْمَ بِهَا؟
 وَأَيْضًا فَالْعِلْمُ قَدْ يَحْصُلُ بِلَا نَظَرٍ خَاصٍّ بَلْ بِطُرُقِ أُخَرَ:
 مِنْ اضْطِرَارٍ وَكَشْفٍ وَتَقْلِيدِ مَنْ يَعْلَمُ أَنَّهُ مُصِيبٌ وَغَيْرِ ذَلِكَ.
وَبِإِزَاءِ هَؤُلَاءِ قَوْمٌ مِنْ الْمُحَدِّثَةِ وَالْفُقَهَاءِ وَالْعَامَّةِ قَدْ يُحَرِّمُونَ النَّظَرَ فِي دَقِيقِ الْعِلْمِ وَالِاسْتِدْلَالَ وَالْكَلَامَ فِيهِ حَتَّى ذَوِي الْمَعْرِفَةِ بِهِ وَأَهْلِ الْحَاجَةِ إلَيْهِ مِنْ أَهْلِهِ وَيُوجِبُونَ التَّقْلِيدَ فِي هَذِهِ الْمَسَائِلِ أَوْ الْإِعْرَاضَ عَنْ تَفْصِيلِهَا.
translated_text:
He—may Allah have mercy on him—also said:

Regarding questions of religious fundamentals, many speculative theologians and jurists, both within our school and elsewhere, require everyone to engage in rational inquiry and inference, including ordinary people and women. They even require this concerning questions disputed by the eminent scholars of the Muslim community. They argue: “Knowledge of these matters is obligatory, and such knowledge can only be attained through a specific process of rational inquiry.”

The majority of the Muslim community, however, holds otherwise. Knowledge of matters that must be known is obligatory only upon those capable of acquiring it. Many people are incapable of understanding these subtleties, so how can they be required to know them?

Moreover, knowledge may be attained without a specific process of rational inquiry, through other means: knowledge arising necessarily, unveiling, following someone whom one knows to be correct, and so forth.

At the opposite extreme are some hadith scholars, jurists, and ordinary people who may prohibit inquiry into subtle questions of knowledge, reasoning about them, and discussing them—even for those versed in them and those qualified people who need to address them. They require people either to follow others on authority in these matters or to refrain from examining their details.

original_text:
وَهَذَا لَيْسَ بِجَيِّدِ أَيْضًا؛ فَإِنَّ الْعِلْمَ النَّافِعَ مُسْتَحَبٌّ وَإِنَّمَا يُكْرَهُ إذَا كَانَ كَلَامًا بِغَيْرِ عِلْمٍ أَوْ حَيْثُ يَضُرُّ فَإِذَا كَانَ كَلَامًا بِعِلْمِ وَلَا مَضَرَّةَ فِيهِ فَلَا بَأْسَ بِهِ وَإِنْ كَانَ نَافِعًا فَهُوَ مُسْتَحَبٌّ فَلَا إطْلَاقُ الْقَوْلِ بِالْوُجُوبِ صَحِيحًا وَلَا إطْلَاقُ الْقَوْلِ بِالتَّحْرِيمِ صَحِيحًا.
 وَكَذَلِكَ الْمَسَائِلُ الفروعية:
 مِنْ غَالِيَةِ الْمُتَكَلِّمَةِ وَالْمُتَفَقِّهَةِ مَنْ يُوجِبُ النَّظَرَ وَالِاجْتِهَادَ فِيهَا عَلَى كُلِّ أَحَدٍ حَتَّى عَلَى الْعَامَّةِ وَهَذَا ضَعِيفٌ؛ لِأَنَّهُ لَوْ كَانَ طَلَبُ عِلْمِهَا وَاجِبًا عَلَى الْأَعْيَانِ فَإِنَّمَا يَجِبُ مَعَ الْقُدْرَةِ وَالْقُدْرَةُ عَلَى مَعْرِفَتِهَا مِنْ الْأَدِلَّةِ الْمُفَصَّلَةِ تَتَعَذَّرُ أَوْ تَتَعَسَّرُ عَلَى أَكْثَرِ الْعَامَّةِ.
 وَبِإِزَائِهِمْ مِنْ أَتْبَاعِ الْمَذَاهِبِ مَنْ يُوجِبُ التَّقْلِيدَ فِيهَا عَلَى جَمِيعِ مَنْ بَعْدَ الْأَئِمَّةِ:
 عُلَمَائِهِمْ؛ وَعَوَامِّهِمْ. وَمِنْ هَؤُلَاءِ مَنْ يُوجِبُ التَّقْلِيدَ بَعْدَ عَصْرِ أَبِي حَنِيفَةَ وَمَالِكٍ مُطْلَقًا ثُمَّ هَلْ يَجِبُ عَلَى كُلٍّ وَاحِدٍ اتِّبَاعُ شَخْصٍ مُعَيَّنٍ مِنْ الْأَئِمَّةِ يُقَلِّدُهُ فِي عَزَائِمِهِ وَرُخَصِهِ؟ عَلَى وَجْهَيْنِ. وَهَذَانِ الْوَجْهَانِ ذَكَرَهُمَا أَصْحَابُ أَحْمَد وَالشَّافِعِيِّ لَكِنْ هَلْ يَجِبُ عَلَى الْعَامِّيِّ ذَلِكَ؟ وَاَلَّذِي عَلَيْهِ جَمَاهِيرُ الْأُمَّةِ أَنَّ الِاجْتِهَادَ جَائِزٌ فِي الْجُمْلَةِ؛ وَالتَّقْلِيدَ
translated_text:
This, too, is unsound. Beneficial knowledge is recommended; discussion is objectionable only when it is undertaken without knowledge or causes harm. If one speaks with knowledge and without causing harm, there is nothing wrong with it; if it is beneficial, it is recommended. Thus, neither an unqualified declaration that it is obligatory nor an unqualified declaration that it is forbidden is correct.

The same applies to subsidiary questions of law. Some of the more extreme speculative theologians and jurists require everyone, even ordinary people, to engage in rational inquiry and independent legal reasoning concerning them. This position is weak: even if seeking knowledge of these matters were an individual obligation, it would be obligatory only for those capable of doing so. Yet acquiring knowledge of them from the detailed evidence is impossible or difficult for most ordinary people.

At the opposite extreme, some adherents of the legal schools require everyone who came after the imams—scholars and laypeople alike—to follow others on authority in these matters. Some require this without qualification after the era of Abū Hanīfa and Mālik. Must each person then follow one particular imam, adhering to both his strict rulings and his concessions? There are two views on this, both mentioned by the scholars of Ahmad’s and al-Shāfiʿī’s schools. But is this obligatory for the ordinary person?

The position held by the vast majority of the Muslim community is that independent legal reasoning is permissible in principle, and following others on authority

original_text:
جَائِزٌ فِي الْجُمْلَةِ لَا يُوجِبُونَ الِاجْتِهَادَ عَلَى كُلِّ أَحَدٍ وَيُحَرِّمُونَ التَّقْلِيدَ وَلَا يُوجِبُونَ التَّقْلِيدَ عَلَى كُلِّ أَحَدٍ وَيُحَرِّمُونَ الِاجْتِهَادَ وَأَنَّ الِاجْتِهَادَ جَائِزٌ لِلْقَادِرِ عَلَى الِاجْتِهَادِ وَالتَّقْلِيدَ جَائِزٌ لِلْعَاجِزِ عَنْ الِاجْتِهَادِ. فَأَمَّا الْقَادِرُ عَلَى الِاجْتِهَادِ فَهَلْ يَجُوزُ لَهُ التَّقْلِيدُ؟
 هَذَا فِيهِ خِلَافٌ وَالصَّحِيحُ أَنَّهُ يَجُوزُ حَيْثُ عَجَزَ عَنْ الِاجْتِهَادِ:
 إمَّا لِتَكَافُؤِ الْأَدِلَّةِ وَإِمَّا لِضِيقِ الْوَقْتِ عَنْ الِاجْتِهَادِ وَإِمَّا لِعَدَمِ ظُهُورِ دَلِيلٍ لَهُ؛ فَإِنَّهُ حَيْثُ عَجَزَ سَقَطَ عَنْهُ وُجُوبُ مَا عَجَزَ عَنْهُ وَانْتَقَلَ إلَى بَدَلِهِ وَهُوَ التَّقْلِيدُ كَمَا لَوْ عَجَزَ عَنْ الطَّهَارَةِ بِالْمَاءِ. وَكَذَلِكَ الْعَامِّيُّ إذَا أَمْكَنَهُ الِاجْتِهَادُ فِي بَعْضِ الْمَسَائِلِ جَازَ لَهُ الِاجْتِهَادُ فَإِنَّ الِاجْتِهَادَ مُنَصَّبٌ يَقْبَلُ التجزي وَالِانْقِسَامَ فَالْعِبْرَةُ بِالْقُدْرَةِ وَالْعَجْزِ وَقَدْ يَكُونُ الرَّجُلُ قَادِرًا فِي بَعْضٍ عَاجِزًا فِي بَعْضٍ لَكِنَّ الْقُدْرَةَ عَلَى الِاجْتِهَادِ لَا تَكُونُ إلَّا بِحُصُولِ عُلُومٍ تُفِيدُ مَعْرِفَةَ الْمَطْلُوبِ فَأَمَّا مَسْأَلَةٌ وَاحِدَةٌ مِنْ فَنٍّ فَيَبْعُدُ الِاجْتِهَادُ فِيهَا وَاَللَّهُ سُبْحَانَهُ أَعْلَمُ.
translated_text:
is permissible in principle. They do not require everyone to exercise independent legal reasoning while prohibiting following others on authority, nor do they require everyone to follow others on authority while prohibiting independent legal reasoning. Rather, independent legal reasoning is permissible for those capable of it, and following others on authority is permissible for those incapable of it. As for someone capable of independent legal reasoning, may he follow others on authority?

There is disagreement concerning this. The correct view is that he may do so when he is unable to exercise independent legal reasoning, whether because the evidence is evenly balanced, because there is insufficient time, or because no evidence has become apparent to him. Whenever he is unable to do something, the obligation to do what he cannot do falls away, and he turns to its alternative—in this case, following others on authority—just as when he is unable to purify himself with water.

Likewise, if an ordinary person can exercise independent legal reasoning in certain questions, he may do so. Independent legal reasoning is a scholarly qualification that admits subdivision; what matters is a person’s ability or inability. A man may be capable in some matters but incapable in others. However, the ability to exercise independent legal reasoning requires acquiring branches of knowledge that enable one to ascertain the answer sought. As for independent legal reasoning confined to a single question within a discipline, that is unlikely. And Allah, glorified is He, knows best.

original_text:
وَقَالَ شَيْخُ الْإِسْلَامِ
فَصْلٌ:
وَأَمَّا حَلِفُ كُلِّ وَاحِدٍ:

 وَالثَّانِي:
 يَحْنَثُونَ إلَّا وَاحِدًا مِنْهُمْ؛ فَإِنَّ حِنْثَهُ مَشْكُوكٌ فِيهِ؛
 يَجُوزُ أَنْ يَكُونَ صَادِقًا وَيَجُوزُ كَوْنُهُمْ سَوَاءً فَيَحْنَثُونَ كُلُّهُمْ وَإِذَا حَنِثُوا إلَّا وَاحِدًا مِنْهُمْ وَقَدْ وَقَعَ الشَّكُّ فِي عَيْنِهِ فَهِيَ كَمَا لَوْ قَالَ أَحَدُ الزَّوْجَيْنِ:
 إنْ كَانَ غُرَابًا فَزَوْجَتُهُ طَالِقٌ وَقَالَ الْآخَرُ: إنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ غُرَابًا فَزَوْجَتُهُ طَالِقٌ وَهَذِهِ فِيهَا قَوْلَانِ فِي مَذْهَبِ أَحْمَد وَغَيْرِهِ: أَحَدُهُمَا: لَا يَقَعُ بِوَاحِدِ مِنْهُمَا طَلَاقٌ وَهُوَ مَذْهَبُ الشَّافِعِيِّ وَغَيْرِهِ لَكِنْ يَكُفُّ كُلٌّ مِنْهُمَا عَنْ وَطْءِ زَوْجَتِهِ قِيلَ: حَتْمًا وَقِيلَ: رَدْعًا.
 وَالْقَوْلُ الثَّانِي:
 أَنَّهُ يَقَعُ بِأَحَدِهِمَا كَمَا لَوْ كَانَ الْحَالِفُ وَاحِدًا وَأَوْقَعَهُ
translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islām said:

Section

As for each person swearing that the best legal school is that of so-and-so: if each believes matters to be as he has sworn, there are two views. The stronger view is that none of them breaks his oath.

The second view is that they all break their oaths except one, whose having broken his oath remains uncertain: he may be speaking the truth. It is also possible that all the schools are equal, in which case they all break their oaths.

If all but one break their oaths, but his identity is uncertain, this resembles the case in which one of two married men says that if it is a crow, his wife is divorced, while the other says that if it is not a crow, his wife is divorced. There are two views concerning this within the school of Ahmad and elsewhere. The first is that neither man’s divorce takes effect. This is the position of al-Shāfiʿī and others. Each, however, must refrain from intercourse with his wife—according to one view, as an obligation; according to another, as a deterrent.

The second view is that divorce takes effect for one of them, just as if a single man had sworn and made the divorce apply

original_text: بِإِحْدَى زَوْجَتَيْهِ وَعَلَى هَذَا فَهَلْ تَخْرُجُ الْمُطَلَّقَةُ بِالْقَرْعَةِ؛ أَوْ يُوقَفُ الْأَمْرُ؟ عَلَى قَوْلَيْنِ أَيْضًا فِي مَذْهَبِ أَحْمَد وَالْوَقْفُ قَوْلُ الشَّافِعِيِّ. وَالصَّحِيحُ أَنَّ مَنْ حَلَفَ عَلَى شَيْءٍ يَعْتَقِدُهُ كَمَا لَوْ حَلَفَ عَلَيْهِ فَتَبَيَّنَ بِخِلَافِهِ فَلَا طَلَاقَ عَلَيْهِ وَأَمَّا مَالِكٌ فَإِنَّهُ يُحَنِّثُ الْجَمِيعَ وَلَوْ تَبَيَّنَ صِدْقُ الْحَالِفِ؛ بِنَاءً عَلَى أَصْلِهِ فِيمَنْ حَلَفَ عَلَى مَا لَا يَعْلَمُ صِحَّتَهُ كَمَا لَوْ حَلَفَ أَنَّهُ يَدْخُلُ الْجَنَّةَ وَالنِّزَاعُ فِيهَا كَالنِّزَاعِ فِي أَصْلِ تِلْكَ الْمَسْأَلَةِ. وَجُمْهُورُ الْعُلَمَاءِ لَا يُوقِعُونَ الطَّلَاقَ لِأَجْلِ الشَّكِّ وَمَالِكٌ يُوقِعُهُ لِعَدَمِ عِلْمِ الْحَالِفِ بِمَا حَلَفَ عَلَيْهِ فَهَذِهِ كَمَا لَوْ حَلَفَ وَاحِدٌ عَلَى مَا لَا يَعْلَمُهُ وَلَمْ يُنَاقِضْهُ غَيْرُهُ مِثْلَ أَنْ يَحْلِفَ أَنَّ مَذْهَبَ فُلَانٍ أَفْضَلُ وَهُوَ غَيْرُ عَالِمٍ بِذَلِكَ.
translated_text:
to one of his two wives. On this view, is the divorced wife to be identified by drawing lots, or should the matter remain unresolved? There are likewise two views within Ahmad’s school; leaving the matter unresolved is al-Shāfiʿī’s position.

The correct view is that no divorce takes effect for someone who swears to something he believes to be true, just as when he swears to something and it subsequently proves otherwise. Mālik, however, considers all of them to have broken their oaths, even if the person swearing is subsequently shown to have spoken the truth. This follows his principle concerning someone who swears to something whose truth he does not know—as when someone swears that he will enter Paradise. The disagreement here is the same as the disagreement over the underlying issue.

The majority of scholars do not hold that divorce takes effect on account of doubt, whereas Mālik holds that it does because the person swearing does not know the truth of what he has sworn to. This is therefore like the case of a person who swears to something he does not know, without anyone else contradicting him—for example, swearing that so-and-so’s legal school is the best, despite not knowing this.

original_text:
وَسُئِلَ:
عَمَّنْ يُقَلِّدُ بَعْضَ الْعُلَمَاءِ فِي مَسَائِلِ الِاجْتِهَادِ:
 فَهَلْ يُنْكَرُ عَلَيْهِ أَمْ يُهْجَرُ؟ وَكَذَلِكَ مَنْ يَعْمَلُ بِأَحَدِ الْقَوْلَيْنِ؟
فَأَجَابَ:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ،
 مَسَائِلُ الِاجْتِهَادِ مَنْ عَمِلَ فِيهَا بِقَوْلِ بَعْضِ الْعُلَمَاءِ لَمْ يُنْكَرْ عَلَيْهِ وَلَمْ يُهْجَرْ وَمَنْ عَمِلَ بِأَحَدِ الْقَوْلَيْنِ لَمْ يُنْكَرْ عَلَيْهِ وَإِذَا كَانَ فِي الْمَسْأَلَةِ قَوْلَانِ:
 فَإِنْ كَانَ الْإِنْسَانُ يَظْهَرُ لَهُ رُجْحَانُ أَحَدِ الْقَوْلَيْنِ عَمِلَ بِهِ وَإِلَّا قَلَّدَ بَعْضَ الْعُلَمَاءِ الَّذِينَ يُعْتَمَدُ عَلَيْهِمْ فِي بَيَانِ أَرْجَحِ الْقَوْلَيْنِ وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
translated_text:
He was asked:

“Should someone who follows a scholar’s opinion in matters open to juristic interpretation be censured or shunned? And what of someone who acts upon one of two scholarly views?”

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah.

In matters open to juristic interpretation, someone who acts upon a scholar’s opinion should neither be censured nor shunned. Likewise, someone who acts upon one of two scholarly views should not be censured. When there are two views on an issue, a person should follow whichever appears to him to be stronger. Otherwise, he should follow a scholar who can be relied upon to explain which of the two views is stronger. And Allah knows best.

original_text:
وَسُئِلَ - رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ -:
مَا تَقُولُ السَّادَةُ الْعُلَمَاءَ أَئِمَّةُ الدِّينِ - رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ أَجْمَعِينَ - فِي رَجُلٍ سُئِلَ إيش مَذْهَبُك؟
 فَقَالَ:
 مُحَمَّدِيٌّ أَتَّبِعُ كِتَابَ اللَّهِ وَسُنَّةَ رَسُولِهِ مُحَمَّدٍ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فَقِيلَ لَا: يَنْبَغِي لِكُلِّ مُؤْمِنٍ أَنْ يَتَّبِعَ مَذْهَبًا وَمَنْ لَا مَذْهَبَ لَهُ فَهُوَ شَيْطَانٌ فَقَالَ: إيش كَانَ مَذْهَبُ أَبِي بَكْرٍ الصِّدِّيقِ وَالْخُلَفَاءِ بَعْدَهُ - رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ -؟
 فَقِيلَ لَهُ:
 لَا يَنْبَغِي لَك إلَّا أَنْ تَتَّبِعَ مَذْهَبًا مِنْ هَذِهِ الْمَذَاهِبِ فَأَيُّهُمَا الْمُصِيبُ؟ أَفْتُونَا مَأْجُورِينَ
فَأَجَابَ:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ،
 إنَّمَا يَجِبُ عَلَى النَّاسِ طَاعَةُ اللَّهِ وَالرَّسُولِ وَهَؤُلَاءِ أُولُوا الْأَمْرِ الَّذِينَ أَمَرَ اللَّهُ بِطَاعَتِهِمْ فِي قَوْلِهِ:
 
{أَطِيعُوا اللَّهَ وَأَطِيعُوا الرَّسُولَ وَأُولِي الْأَمْرِ مِنْكُمْ}
 إنَّمَا تَجِبُ طَاعَتُهُمْ تَبَعًا لِطَاعَةِ اللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِ لَا اسْتِقْلَالًا ثُمَّ قَالَ: 
{فَإِنْ تَنَازَعْتُمْ فِي شَيْءٍ فَرُدُّوهُ إلَى اللَّهِ وَالرَّسُولِ إنْ كُنْتُمْ تُؤْمِنُونَ بِاللَّهِ وَالْيَوْمِ الْآخِرِ ذَلِكَ خَيْرٌ وَأَحْسَنُ تَأْوِيلًا}
 . وَإِذَا نَزَلَتْ بِالْمُسْلِمِ نَازِلَةٌ فَإِنَّهُ يَسْتَفْتِي مَنْ اعْتَقَدَ أَنَّهُ يُفْتِيهِ بِشَرْعِ اللَّهِ
translated_text:
He was asked—may Allah be pleased with him:

“What do the esteemed scholars, the imams of the religion—may Allah be pleased with them all—say about a man who was asked, ‘Which school of law do you follow?’

“He replied, ‘I am a follower of Muhammad. I follow the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.’

“He was told, ‘No! Every believer must follow a school of law. Whoever has no school of law is a devil.’

“He replied, ‘Which school did Abū Bakr al-Siddīq and the caliphs after him follow—may Allah be pleased with them?’

“He was told, ‘You must follow one of these schools.’ Which of the two is correct? Give us your ruling, and may you be rewarded.”

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah.

What is obligatory upon people is obedience to Allah and the Messenger. As for those in authority whom Allah has commanded people to obey in His words:

“Obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you,”

they must be obeyed only as part of obedience to Allah and His Messenger, not independently. Then He said:

“If you disagree over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger, if you believe in Allah and the Last Day. That is best and most favorable in outcome.”

When a Muslim faces an issue requiring a ruling, he should consult someone whom he believes will give him a ruling according to the law of Allah

original_text:
وَرَسُولِهِ مِنْ أَيِّ مَذْهَبٍ كَانَ وَلَا يَجِبُ عَلَى أَحَدٍ مِنْ الْمُسْلِمِينَ تَقْلِيدُ شَخْصٍ بِعَيْنِهِ مِنْ الْعُلَمَاءِ فِي كُلِّ مَا يَقُولُ وَلَا يَجِبُ عَلَى أَحَدٍ مِنْ الْمُسْلِمِينَ الْتِزَامُ مَذْهَبِ شَخْصٍ مُعَيَّنٍ غَيْرِ الرَّسُولِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فِي كُلِّ مَا يُوجِبُهُ وَيُخْبِرُ بِهِ بَلْ كُلُّ أَحَدٍ مِنْ النَّاسِ يُؤْخَذُ مِنْ قَوْلِهِ وَيُتْرَكُ إلَّا رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ. وَاتِّبَاعُ شَخْصٍ لِمَذْهَبِ شَخْصٍ بِعَيْنِهِ لِعَجْزِهِ عَنْ مَعْرِفَةِ الشَّرْعِ مِنْ غَيْرِ جِهَتِهِ إنَّمَا هُوَ مِمَّا يَسُوغُ لَهُ لَيْسَ هُوَ مِمَّا يَجِبُ عَلَى كُلِّ أَحَدٍ إذَا أَمْكَنَهُ مَعْرِفَةُ الشَّرْعِ بِغَيْرِ ذَلِكَ الطَّرِيقِ بَلْ كُلُّ أَحَدٍ عَلَيْهِ أَنْ يَتَّقِيَ اللَّهَ مَا اسْتَطَاعَ وَيَطْلُبَ عِلْمَ مَا أَمَرَ اللَّهُ بِهِ وَرَسُولُهُ 
(١)
 فَيَفْعَلَ الْمَأْمُورَ وَيَتْرُكَ الْمَحْظُورَ. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
original_footnote: (١) في المطبوعة: " ورسول " وأظن أن ما أثبتناه هو الصواب حتى يستقيم المعنى
translated_text:
and His Messenger, regardless of which school that scholar follows. No Muslim is obliged to follow any particular scholar in everything he says. Nor is any Muslim obliged to adhere to the teachings of any particular person other than the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in everything he prescribes and reports. Rather, anyone’s statements may be accepted or rejected, except those of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

Following a particular person’s school because one is unable to learn the revealed law except through him is permissible for that individual; it is not obligatory upon everyone if they can learn the revealed law by another means. Rather, everyone must fear Allah as much as he is able and seek knowledge of what Allah and His Messenger have commanded (1), so that he may do what is commanded and refrain from what is forbidden. And Allah knows best.
translated_footnote: (1) The printed edition reads wa-rasūl (“and a messenger”). I believe the reading we have adopted is correct, as it makes the meaning coherent.

وَسُئِلَ شَيْخُ الْإِسْلَامِ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَنْ رَجُلٍ تَفَقَّهَ فِي مَذْهَبٍ مِنْ الْمَذَاهِبِ الْأَرْبَعَةِ وَتَبَصَّرَ فِيهِ وَاشْتَغَلَ بَعْدَهُ بِالْحَدِيثِ فَرَأَى أَحَادِيثَ صَحِيحَةً لَا يَعْلَمُ لَهَا نَاسِخًا وَلَا مُخَصِّصًا وَلَا مُعَارِضًا وَذَلِكَ الْمَذْهَبُ مُخَالِفٌ لَهَا:
 فَهَلْ يَجُوزُ لَهُ الْعَمَلُ بِذَلِكَ الْمَذْهَبِ؟ أَوْ يَجِبُ عَلَيْهِ الرُّجُوعُ إلَى الْعَمَلِ بِالْأَحَادِيثِ وَيُخَالِفُ مَذْهَبَهُ؟
فَأَجَابَ:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ،
 قَدْ ثَبَتَ بِالْكِتَابِ وَالسُّنَّةِ وَالْإِجْمَاعِ أَنَّ اللَّهَ سُبْحَانَهُ وَتَعَالَى فَرَضَ عَلَى الْخَلْقِ طَاعَتَهُ وَطَاعَةَ رَسُولِهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَلَمْ يُوجِبْ عَلَى هَذِهِ الْأُمَّةِ طَاعَةَ أَحَدٍ بِعَيْنِهِ فِي كُلِّ مَا يَأْمُرُ بِهِ وَيَنْهَى عَنْهُ إلَّا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ حَتَّى كَانَ صِدِّيقُ الْأُمَّةِ وَأَفْضَلُهَا بَعْدَ نَبِيِّهَا يَقُولُ:
 أَطِيعُونِي مَا أَطَعْت اللَّهَ فَإِذَا عَصَيْت اللَّهَ فَلَا طَاعَةَ لِي عَلَيْكُمْ. وَاتَّفَقُوا كُلُّهُمْ عَلَى أَنَّهُ لَيْسَ أَحَدٌ مَعْصُومًا فِي كُلِّ مَا يَأْمُرُ بِهِ وَيَنْهَى
translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

A man studied jurisprudence according to one of the four schools and acquired a thorough understanding of it. He then devoted himself to hadith and encountered authentic hadiths for which he knew of no evidence that abrogated them, restricted their general scope, or contradicted them, yet his school’s position differed from them. Is it permissible for him to follow that school’s position, or must he instead act upon the hadiths and depart from his school’s position?

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah.

It is established by the Book, the Sunnah, and consensus that Allah, glorified and exalted is He, has obliged His creation to obey Him and His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. He has not obliged this community to obey any particular individual in everything he commands and forbids except the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Even the most truthful member of this community, and its best after its Prophet, used to say:

“Obey me so long as I obey Allah. If I disobey Allah, you owe me no obedience.”

They all agreed that no one is infallible in everything he commands and forbids

original_text:
عَنْهُ إلَّا رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَلِهَذَا قَالَ غَيْرُ وَاحِدٍ مِنْ الْأَئِمَّةِ:
 كُلُّ أَحَدٍ مِنْ النَّاسِ يُؤْخَذُ مِنْ قَوْلِهِ وَيُتْرَكُ إلَّا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ.
وَهَؤُلَاءِ الْأَئِمَّةُ الْأَرْبَعَةُ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ قَدْ نَهَوْا النَّاسَ عَنْ تَقْلِيدِهِمْ فِي كُلِّ مَا يَقُولُونَهُ وَذَلِكَ هُوَ الْوَاجِبُ عَلَيْهِمْ؛
 فَقَالَ أَبُو حَنِيفَةَ:
 هَذَا رَأْيِي وَهَذَا أَحْسَنُ مَا رَأَيْت؛ فَمَنْ جَاءَ بِرَأْيٍ خَيْرٍ مِنْهُ قَبِلْنَاهُ وَلِهَذَا لَمَّا اجْتَمَعَ أَفْضَلُ أَصْحَابِهِ أَبُو يُوسُفَ بِمَالِكِ فَسَأَلَهُ عَنْ مَسْأَلَةِ الصَّاعِ؛ وَصَدَقَةِ الْخَضْرَاوَاتِ؛ وَمَسْأَلَةِ الْأَجْنَاسِ؛
 فَأَخْبَرَهُ مَالِكٌ بِمَا تَدُلُّ عَلَيْهِ السُّنَّةُ فِي ذَلِكَ فَقَالَ:
 رَجَعْت إلَى قَوْلِك يَا أَبَا عَبْدِ اللَّهِ وَلَوْ رَأَى صَاحِبِي مَا رَأَيْت لَرَجَعَ إلَى قَوْلِك كَمَا رَجَعْت.
 وَمَالِكٌ كَانَ يَقُولُ:
 إنَّمَا أَنَا بَشَرٌ أُصِيبُ وَأُخْطِئُ فَاعْرِضُوا قَوْلِي عَلَى الْكِتَابِ وَالسُّنَّةِ أَوْ كَلَامًا هَذَا مَعْنَاهُ.
 وَالشَّافِعِيُّ كَانَ يَقُولُ:
 إذَا صَحَّ الْحَدِيثُ فَاضْرِبُوا بِقَوْلِي الْحَائِطَ وَإِذَا رَأَيْت الْحُجَّةَ مَوْضُوعَةً عَلَى الطَّرِيقِ فَهِيَ قَوْلِي.
 وَفِي مُخْتَصَرِ المزني لَمَّا ذَكَرَ أَنَّهُ اخْتَصَرَهُ مِنْ مَذْهَبِ الشَّافِعِيِّ لِمَنْ أَرَادَ مَعْرِفَةَ مَذْهَبِهِ قَالَ:
 مَعَ إعْلَامِهِ نَهْيَهُ عَنْ تَقْلِيدِهِ وَتَقْلِيدِ غَيْرِهِ مِنْ الْعُلَمَاءِ.
 وَالْإِمَامُ أَحْمَد كَانَ يَقُولُ:
 لَا تُقَلِّدُونِي وَلَا تُقَلِّدُوا مَالِكًا وَلَا الشَّافِعِيَّ
translated_text:
except the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Hence, more than one of the imams said:

“Anyone’s statements may be accepted or rejected, except those of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.”

These four imams, may Allah be pleased with them, forbade people to follow them unquestioningly in everything they said. This was their duty.

Abū Hanīfa said:

“This is my opinion, and it is the best view I have reached. If anyone brings a better opinion, we will accept it.”

Thus, when his foremost student, Abū Yūsuf, met Mālik, he asked him about the sāʿ measure, zakat on vegetables, and the question of categories. Mālik explained to him what the Sunnah indicated concerning these matters, whereupon he said:

“I have adopted your position, Abū Abd Allāh. Had my teacher seen what I have seen, he would have adopted your position just as I have.”

Mālik used to say:

“I am only human: sometimes I am right and sometimes I am wrong. So test my statements against the Book and the Sunnah”—or words to that effect.

Al-Shāfiʿī used to say:

“If a hadith is authentic, discard my opinion. Whenever you find the proof plainly before you, that is my position.”

In al-Muzanī’s Compendium, after explaining that he had abridged al-Shāfiʿī’s school of thought for anyone wishing to learn it, he said:

“While informing the reader that al-Shāfiʿī forbade following him or any other scholar unquestioningly.”

Imam Ahmad used to say:

“Do not follow me unquestioningly, nor Mālik, nor al-Shāfiʿī

nor al-Thawrī; learn as we have learned.”

He also used to say:

“It is a sign of a man’s limited knowledge that he follows others unquestioningly in matters of religion.”

And he said:

“Do not follow men unquestioningly in your religion, for they cannot be free of error.”

It is authentically reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever Allah intends good for, He grants him understanding of the religion.”

This necessarily implies that whoever Allah does not grant understanding of the religion, He has not intended good for him. Thus, gaining understanding of the religion is obligatory.

Understanding the religion means knowing the rulings of the revealed law together with their transmitted evidence. Whoever does not know these has not gained understanding of the religion. Some people, however, may be unable to learn the detailed evidence concerning all their affairs. They are therefore excused from learning what lies beyond their ability, but this inability does not exempt them from gaining religious understanding altogether. They remain obliged to learn what they can.

As for someone capable of reasoning from evidence, one view holds that following others unquestioningly is prohibited for him in all circumstances; another permits it in all circumstances; and a third permits it when necessary, as when there is insufficient time to examine the evidence. This third view is the most balanced.

Independent juristic reasoning is not an indivisible whole. A person may be qualified to exercise it in one discipline, chapter, or question, but not in another. Each person’s exercise of independent reasoning is according to his capacity. Thus, if someone examines a question over which scholars disagree and finds revealed texts supporting one of the two positions, without knowing of any countervailing evidence after examining the matter to the extent that someone of his ability can, he faces two alternatives:

either to follow the other scholar’s position merely because he is the imam whose school he has studied—yet this is not evidence recognized by the revealed law, but merely a habit, counterbalanced by someone else’s habit of studying another imam’s school—or to follow the position that, in his judgment, is stronger because of the revealed texts supporting it. In the latter case, he will be agreeing with an imam of equal standing to the other imam, while, as far as he is concerned, the revealed texts remain unopposed as a basis for action. This, then, is the proper course.

We have made this concession only because it may be said that this person’s examination is inadequate and that his independent reasoning in this question is not sound, owing to his insufficient qualifications for such reasoning.

If, however, he is capable of fully exercising independent reasoning and thereby concludes that the other position has no grounds sufficient to counter the revealed text, then he must follow the revealed texts. If he does not, he will be following conjecture and the desires of the soul, and will be among those most disobedient to Allah and His Messenger. This differs from the case of someone who says:

“The other position may have evidence that outweighs this text, of which I am unaware.”

Such a person should be told: Allah Most High has said:

“So fear Allah as much as you are able.”

And the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When I command you to do something, do as much of it as you can.”

The knowledge and religious understanding within your capacity concerning this question have shown you that this position is the stronger one, so you must follow it. If it later becomes clear to you that there is countervailing evidence that outweighs the text, your case will be like that of an independent jurist whose judgment changes. translated_text:
another because of the truth that has become clear to him is praiseworthy. By contrast, persisting in a position for which he has no proof, abandoning a position whose proof has become clear, or moving from one position to another merely out of habit or in pursuit of personal desire is blameworthy.

If the imam being followed has heard the hadith but has not acted upon it—especially if he has also narrated it—that alone does not justify setting aside the revealed text. In our work, “Lifting Blame from the Eminent Imams,” we explained some twenty excuses for the imams’ not acting upon certain hadiths, and showed that these excuses absolve them of blame for doing so. We, for our part, are excused in setting those excuses aside with respect to this position.

Someone may have set aside a hadith because he believed it was not authentic, or that its narrator was unknown, or for a similar reason, while another person knows that it is authentic and that its narrator is trustworthy. The former’s excuse no longer applies to the latter. Likewise, someone may have set aside a hadith because he believed that the apparent meaning of the Quran, analogical reasoning, or the practice of certain regions contradicted it. Yet another person may have come to understand that the apparent meaning of the Quran does not contradict it, and that the explicit wording of an authentic hadith takes precedence over apparent meanings, analogical reasoning, and established practice. The former’s excuse would then be no excuse for the latter.

The extent to which the grounds of the revealed law are clear or obscure to people’s minds cannot be precisely delimited. This is especially so when someone who sets aside a hadith believes that the Emigrants and the Helpers—the inhabitants of the Prophet’s city and elsewhere—had ceased to act upon it, and it is said of them that they would only set aside a hadith if they believed it had been abrogated or outweighed by stronger evidence, whereas someone coming after him has learned that the Emigrants

" هَذِهِ وَهَذِهِ سَوَاءٌ "
.
 وَقَدْ كَانَ بَعْضُ النَّاسِ يُنَاظِرُ ابْنَ عَبَّاسٍ فِي الْمُتْعَةِ فَقَالَ لَهُ:
 قَالَ أَبُو بَكْرٍ وَعُمَرُ فَقَالَ ابْنُ عَبَّاسٍ: يُوشِكُ أَنْ تَنْزِلَ عَلَيْكُمْ حِجَارَةٌ مِنْ السَّمَاءِ أَقُولُ قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَتَقُولُونَ قَالَ أَبُو بَكْرٍ وَعُمَرُ؟ .
translated_text:
and the Helpers had not abandoned it; rather, a group of them—or those among them who had heard it—had acted upon it, or he has learned something similar that undermines this objection to the revealed text.

If this person seeking guidance and right direction is asked, “Are you more knowledgeable, or is such-and-such an imam?” this is an invalid objection. That imam has been opposed on this issue by another imam of equal standing. I am not more knowledgeable than either of them. Yet the relationship of these scholars to the imams is like that of Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthmān, ʿAlī, Ibn Masʿūd, Ubayy, Muʿādh, and others like them to the imams and other scholars. These Companions were peers in matters of dispute: whenever they disagreed over something, they referred their disagreement to Allah and the Messenger, even though some might have been more knowledgeable in other matters. The same applies to matters disputed among the imams.

People set aside the position of ʿUmar and Ibn Masʿūd concerning dry ablution for someone in a state of sexual impurity, and adopted the position of someone below them in standing, such as Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī and others, because he supported his position with the Quran and Sunnah. They also set aside ʿUmar’s position concerning compensation for the loss of fingers and adopted Muʿāwiyah’s position because he had evidence from the Sunnah that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“This one and that one are equal.”

Someone once debated Ibn ʿAbbās concerning mutah and said to him, “Abū Bakr and ʿUmar said…” Ibn ʿAbbās replied:

“Stones may soon rain down upon you from heaven! I say, ‘The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said,’ and you say, ‘Abū Bakr and ʿUmar said’?”

{اتَّخَذُوا أَحْبَارَهُمْ وَرُهْبَانَهُمْ أَرْبَابًا مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ وَالْمَسِيحَ ابْنَ مَرْيَمَ وَمَا أُمِرُوا إلَّا لِيَعْبُدُوا إلَهًا وَاحِدًا لَا إلَهَ إلَّا هُوَ سُبْحَانَهُ عَمَّا يُشْرِكُونَ}
 وَاَللَّهُ سُبْحَانَهُ وَتَعَالَى أَعْلَمُ وَالْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ وَحْدَهُ.
translated_text:
Likewise, when Ibn ʿUmar was asked about it, he instructed them to practise it. They objected by citing ʿUmar’s statement. It then became clear to them that ʿUmar had not rejected what they were saying, but they persisted, so he said to them:

“Which is more deserving of being followed: the command of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, or the command of ʿUmar?”

This was despite everyone knowing that Abū Bakr and ʿUmar were more knowledgeable than even those who ranked above Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn ʿAbbās.

If this door were opened, it would require turning away from the command of Allah and His Messenger, and each imam would occupy among his followers the same position as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, occupied among his community. This would amount to altering the religion, resembling what Allah reproached the Christians for when He said:

“They have taken their rabbis and monks as lords besides Allah, and the Messiah, son of Mary, though they were commanded only to worship one God. There is no god but Him. Glory be to Him above what they associate with Him!”

Allah, glorified and exalted be He, knows best. All praise belongs to Allah alone.

original_footnote: (*) ما بين معقوفتين غير موجود في المطبوع، والمثبت من كتاب صيانة مجموع الفتاوى من السقط والتصحيف ص ٢٦٣
translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah sanctify his soul—was also asked:

“Does a necessary implication of a person’s position count as his own position, or not?”

He replied:

As for the question, “Does a necessary implication of a person’s position count as his own position, or not?” the correct answer is that the [necessary implication] (*) of a person’s position is not itself his position if he does not accept it. If he has rejected and denied it, attributing it to him would be a false allegation against him. Rather, it demonstrates the unsoundness of his position and the inconsistency of his assertions, not that he accepts implications which evidently entail disbelief or impossibility. Such cases are exceedingly numerous: people advance views that entail other views which they are known not to accept, without realizing that these follow from their position.

If a necessary implication of a position were itself counted as the person’s position, this would require declaring everyone who describes Allah’s rising above, or any other attribute, as figurative rather than literal to be a disbeliever. For this position necessarily implies that none of His names or attributes has a literal meaning. Likewise, for anyone who does not affirm a shared meaning between the two names, it would follow that nothing of faith in Allah, knowledge of Him, or acknowledgment of Him would constitute faith. For whatever the heart affirms, an argument analogous to that made about the other can be made about it. The necessary implications of these people’s position entail the position of the extreme heretics who deny the divine attributes, whose disbelief is greater than that of the Jews and Christians.
translated_footnote: (*) The text in square brackets is absent from the printed edition and has been supplied from Siyānat Majmū‘ al-Fatāwā min al-Saqt wa-l-Tashīf (Safeguarding the Collected Fatwas against Omissions and Textual Corruptions), p. 263.

 فَيُقَالُ لَهُ:
 أَصَبْت فِي تَنْزِيهِ اللَّهِ عَنْ مُمَاثَلَتِهِ خَلْقَهُ؛ لَكِنْ أَخْطَأْت فِي ظَنِّك أَنَّهُ إذَا كَانَ اللَّهُ سَمِيعًا حَقِيقَةً بَصِيرًا حَقِيقَةً مُتَكَلِّمًا حَقِيقَةً كَانَ هَذَا مُتَضَمِّنًا لِمُمَاثَلَتِهِ خَلْقَهُ.
 فَكَذَلِكَ لَوْ قَالَ الْقَائِلُ:
 إذَا قُلْنَا: إنَّهُ مُسْتَوٍ عَلَى عَرْشِهِ حَقِيقَةً لَزِمَ التَّجْسِيمُ وَاَللَّهُ مُنَزَّهٌ عَنْهُ فَيُقَالُ لَهُ: هَذَا الْمَعْنَى الَّذِي سَمَّيْته تَجْسِيمًا وَنَفَيْته هُوَ لَازِمٌ لَك إذَا قُلْت: إنَّ لَهُ عِلْمًا حَقِيقَةً؛
 وَقُدْرَةً حَقِيقَةً وَسَمْعًا حَقِيقَةً:
 وَبَصَرًا حَقِيقَةً؛ وَكَلَامًا حَقِيقَةً؛ وَكَذَلِكَ سَائِرُ مَا أَثْبَتَهُ مِنْ الصِّفَاتِ؛
 فَإِنَّ هَذِهِ الصِّفَاتِ هِيَ فِي حَقِّنَا أَعْرَاضٌ قَائِمَةٌ بِجِسْمِ فَإِذَا كُنْت تُثْبِتُهَا لِلَّهِ تَعَالَى مَعَ تَنْزِيهِك لَهُ عَنْ مُمَاثَلَةِ الْمَخْلُوقَاتِ وَمَا يَدْخُلُ فِي ذَلِكَ مِنْ التَّجْسِيمِ:
 فَكَذَلِكَ الْقَوْلُ فِي الِاسْتِوَاءِ؛ وَلَا فَرْقَ.
translated_text:
But we know that many who deny this are unaware of the necessary implications of their position. Indeed, many imagine that the literal meaning consists solely in the realities peculiar to created beings. Such people do not understand what literal and figurative meanings are, and their position misrepresents both language and revelation. Yet someone who denies a literal meaning may intend to deny that the attributes of the Lord—glory be to Him—resemble those of created beings. He should then be told:

“You are right to reject this false meaning, but mistaken in thinking that it is the literal meaning of the attributes with which Allah has described Himself.”

Such a person is therefore like someone who says: “Allah does not literally hear, see, or speak, because the literal meaning of these attributes is the familiar hearing, sight, and speech of created beings, whereas Allah Most High is far above that.”

He should be told:

“You are right to declare Allah free of resemblance to His creation. But you are mistaken in thinking that His literally hearing, seeing, and speaking would imply that He resembles His creation.”

Likewise, someone might say:

“If we say that He has literally risen above His Throne, this necessarily implies corporeality, whereas Allah is far above that.”

He should be told:

“This meaning which you have called corporeality and denied is also a necessary implication of your saying that He has knowledge in a literal sense, power in a literal sense, hearing in a literal sense, sight in a literal sense, and speech in a literal sense. The same applies to all the other attributes affirmed. For in our case, these attributes are accidents inhering in a body. If, then, you affirm them for Allah Most High while declaring Him free of resemblance to created beings and of the corporeality that such resemblance entails, the same holds for His rising above the Throne. There is no difference.”

فَإِنْ قُلْت:
 أَهْلُ اللُّغَةِ إنَّمَا وَضَعُوا هَذِهِ الْأَلْفَاظَ لِمَا يَخْتَصُّ بِهِ الْمَخْلُوقُ فَلَا يَكُونُ حَقِيقَةً فِي غَيْرِ ذَلِكَ.
 قُلْت:
 وَلَكِنَّ هَذَا خَطَأٌ بِإِجْمَاعِ الْأُمَمِ: مُسْلِمِهِمْ وَكَافِرِهِمْ وَبِإِجْمَاعِ أَهْلِ اللُّغَاتِ فَضْلًا عَنْ أَهْلِ الشَّرَائِعِ وَالدِّيَانَاتِ وَهَذَا نَظِيرُ قَوْلِ مَنْ يَقُولُ: إنَّ لَفْظَ الْوَجْهِ إنَّمَا يُسْتَعْمَلُ حَقِيقَةً فِي وَجْهِ الْإِنْسَانِ دُونَ وَجْهِ الْحَيَوَانِ وَالْمَلَكِ وَالْجِنِّيِّ أَوْ لَفْظَ الْعِلْمِ إنَّمَا اُسْتُعْمِلَ حَقِيقَةً فِي عِلْمِ الْإِنْسَانِ دُونَ عِلْمِ الْمَلَكِ وَالْجِنِّيِّ وَنَحْوِ ذَلِكَ بَلْ قَدْ بَيَّنَّا أَنَّ أَسْمَاءَ الصِّفَاتِ عِنْدَ أَهْلِ اللُّغَةِ بِحَسَبِ مَا تُضَافُ إلَيْهِ؛ فَالْقَدْرُ الْمُشْتَرَكُ أَنَّ نِسْبَةَ كُلِّ صِفَةٍ إلَى مَوْصُوفِهَا كَنِسْبَةِ تِلْكَ الصِّفَةِ إلَى مَوْصُوفِهَا فَالْقَدْرُ الْمُشْتَرَكُ هُوَ النِّسْبَةُ فَنِسْبَةُ عِلْمِ الْمَلَكِ وَالْجِنِّيِّ وَوُجُوهِهِمَا إلَيْهِ كَنِسْبَةِ عِلْمِ الْإِنْسَانِ وَوَجْهِهِ إلَيْهِ وَهَكَذَا فِي سَائِرِ الصِّفَاتِ وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
translated_text:
If you say:

“Speakers of the language coined these expressions only for what is peculiar to created beings, so they cannot have a literal meaning when applied to anything else.”

I reply:

But this is mistaken by the unanimous agreement of all peoples—Muslims and unbelievers alike—and of those versed in languages, let alone those versed in revealed laws and religions. This is like saying that the word “face” is used literally only for a human face, not for the face of an animal, an angel, or a jinn; or that the word “knowledge” is used literally only for human knowledge, not for the knowledge of an angel or a jinn; and so forth.

Rather, we have already explained that, in linguistic usage, terms denoting attributes are understood according to the beings to whom they are attributed. The common element is that each attribute bears the same relation to its possessor as the corresponding attribute bears to its own possessor. What is shared, then, is the relation: an angel’s or a jinn’s knowledge and face bear the same relation to that being as a human being’s knowledge and face bear to him. The same applies to all other attributes. And Allah knows best.

original_text:
وَسُئِلَ شَيْخُ الْإِسْلَامِ:
أَنْ يَشْرَحَ مَا ذَكَرَهُ نَجْمُ الدِّينِ بْنُ حَمْدَان:
 مَنْ الْتَزَمَ مَذْهَبًا أُنْكِرَ عَلَيْهِ مُخَالَفَتُهُ بِغَيْرِ دَلِيلٍ وَلَا تَقْلِيدٍ أَوْ عُذْرٍ آخَرَ؟ .
فَأَجَابَ:
هَذَا يُرَادُ بِهِ شَيْئَانِ:

translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islām was asked to explain the following statement by Najm al-Dīn ibn Hamdān:

“Anyone who commits himself to a school of law is to be censured for departing from it without evidence, reliance on a scholarly authority, or some other excuse.”

He replied:

This may mean two things.

The first is that someone commits himself to a particular school of law, then acts contrary to it without following another scholar who has given him a fatwa, without reasoning from evidence that supports a contrary conclusion, and without a valid excuse under Islamic law permitting what he has done. Such a person is following his own desires, acting neither on independent legal reasoning nor on scholarly authority, and committing a prohibited act without a valid excuse under Islamic law. This is reprehensible. This is the meaning intended by Shaykh Najm al-Dīn.

Imam Ahmad and others explicitly stated that no one may believe something to be obligatory or forbidden, then regard it as neither obligatory nor forbidden merely to suit his own desires. For example, someone claims a right of pre-emption on the grounds of being a neighbour and believes that he is entitled to it; yet when that same right is claimed against him, he believes that no such right exists. Or, when inheriting as a brother alongside a grandfather, he believes that siblings share the inheritance with the grandfather; but when inheriting as a grandfather alongside a brother, he believes that the grandfather does not share with the siblings. Or he has an enemy who engages in certain practices over which scholars differ, such as drinking nabīdh of disputed permissibility and playing chess

original_text:
وَحُضُورِ السَّمَاعِ أَنَّ هَذَا يَنْبَغِي أَنْ يُهْجَرَ وَيُنْكَرَ عَلَيْهِ فَإِذَا فَعَلَ ذَلِكَ صَدِيقُهُ اعْتَقَدَ ذَلِكَ مِنْ مَسَائِلِ الِاجْتِهَادِ الَّتِي لَا تُنْكَرُ فَمِثْلُ هَذَا مُمْكِنٌ فِي اعْتِقَادِهِ حِلُّ الشَّيْءِ وَحُرْمَتُهُ وَوُجُوبُهُ وَسُقُوطُهُ بِحَسَبِ هَوَاهُ هُوَ مَذْمُومٌ بِخُرُوجِهِ خَارِجٌ عَنْ الْعَدَالَةِ وَقَدْ نَصَّ أَحْمَد وَغَيْرُهُ عَلَى أَنَّ هَذَا لَا يَجُوزُ. وَأَمَّا إذَا تَبَيَّنَ لَهُ مَا يُوجِبُ رُجْحَانَ قَوْلٍ عَلَى قَوْلٍ إمَّا بِالْأَدِلَّةِ الْمُفَصَّلَةِ إنْ كَانَ يَعْرِفُهَا وَيَفْهَمُهَا وَإِمَّا بِأَنْ يَرَى أَحَدَ رَجُلَيْنِ أَعْلَمَ بِتِلْكَ الْمَسْأَلَةِ مِنْ الْآخَرِ وَهُوَ أَتْقَى لِلَّهِ فِيمَا يَقُولُهُ فَيَرْجِعُ عَنْ قَوْلٍ إلَى قَوْلٍ لِمِثْلِ هَذَا فَهَذَا يَجُوزُ بَلْ يَجِبُ وَقَدْ نَصَّ الْإِمَامُ أَحْمَد عَلَى ذَلِكَ.
 وَمَا ذَكَرَهُ ابْنُ حَمْدَان:
 الْمُرَادُ بِهِ الْقِسْمُ الْأَوَّلُ؛
 وَلِهَذَا قَالَ:
 مَنْ الْتَزَمَ مَذْهَبًا أُنْكِرُ عَلَيْهِ مُخَالَفَتَهُ بِغَيْرِ دَلِيلٍ أَوْ تَقْلِيدٍ أَوْ عُذْرٍ شَرْعِيٍّ فَدَلَّ عَلَى أَنَّهُ إذَا خَالَفَهُ لِدَلِيلِ فَتَبَيَّنَ لَهُ بِالْقَوْلِ الرَّاجِحِ أَوْ تَقْلِيدٍ يَسُوغُ لَهُ أَنْ يُقَلِّدَ فِي خِلَافِهِ؛ أَوْ عُذْرٍ شَرْعِيٍّ أَبَاحَ الْمَحْظُورَ الَّذِي يُبَاحُ بِمِثْلِ ذَلِكَ الْعُذْرِ لَمْ يُنْكِرْ عَلَيْهِ. وَهُنَا مَسْأَلَةٌ ثَانِيَةٌ قَدْ يُظَنُّ أَنَّهُ أَرَادَهَا وَلَمْ يُرِدْهَا لَكِنَّا نَتَكَلَّمُ عَلَى تَقْدِيرِ إرَادَتِهَا وَهُوَ أَنَّ مَنْ الْتَزَمَ مَذْهَبًا لَمْ يَكُنْ لَهُ أَنْ يَنْتَقِلَ عَنْهُ
translated_text:
and attending listening sessions—and he believes that this person should be shunned and censured. Yet when his friend does the same, he considers it a matter open to independent legal reasoning for which no censure is warranted. Someone of this kind, who allows his own desires to determine whether he regards something as lawful or forbidden, obligatory or no longer binding, is blameworthy for his departure and forfeits his standing as an upright person. Ahmad and others explicitly stated that this is impermissible.

If, however, something becomes clear to him that warrants preferring one opinion over another—whether through detailed evidence, if he knows and understands it, or because he considers one of two scholars more knowledgeable about that particular issue and more mindful of Allah in what he says—and he changes his opinion for such a reason, then this is permissible; indeed, it is obligatory. Imam Ahmad explicitly stated this.

What Ibn Hamdān mentioned refers to the first category. Hence his statement:

“Anyone who commits himself to a school of law is to be censured for departing from it without evidence, reliance on a scholarly authority, or a valid excuse under Islamic law.”

This indicates that he is not to be censured if he departs from it because of evidence that has made the stronger opinion clear to him; because he follows a scholarly authority whom he may legitimately follow in holding a contrary view; or because of a valid excuse under Islamic law that permits an otherwise prohibited act to which such an excuse applies.

There is a second issue that one might think he intended, though he did not. Nevertheless, we shall discuss it on the assumption that he intended it: namely, that whoever commits himself to a school of law may not depart from it.

original_text:
قَالَهُ بَعْضُ أَصْحَابِ أَحْمَد وَكَذَلِكَ غَيْرُ هَذَا مَا يَذْكُرُهُ ابْنُ حَمْدَان أَوْ غَيْرُهُ؛ يَكُونُ مِمَّا قَالَهُ بَعْضُ أَصْحَابِهِ وَإِنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ مَنْصُوصًا عَنْهُ وَكَذَلِكَ مَا يُوجَدُ فِي كُتُبِ أَصْحَابِ الشَّافِعِيِّ وَمَالِكٍ وَأَبِي حَنِيفَةَ كَثِيرٌ مِنْهُ يَكُونُ مِمَّا ذَكَرَهُ بَعْضُ أَصْحَابِهِمْ وَلَيْسَ مَنْصُوصًا عَنْهُمْ؛ بَلْ قَدْ يَكُونُ الْمَنْصُوصُ عَنْهُمْ خِلَافَ ذَلِكَ.
وَأَصْلُ هَذِهِ الْمَسْأَلَةِ أَنَّ الْعَامِّيَّ هَلْ عَلَيْهِ أَنْ يَلْتَزِمَ مَذْهَبًا مُعَيَّنًا يَأْخُذَ بِعَزَائِمِهِ وَرُخَصِهِ؟
 فِيهِ وَجْهَانِ لِأَصْحَابِ أَحْمَد وَهُمَا وَجْهَانِ لِأَصْحَابِ الشَّافِعِيِّ وَالْجُمْهُورُ مِنْ هَؤُلَاءِ وَهَؤُلَاءِ لَا يُوجِبُونَ ذَلِكَ وَاَلَّذِينَ يُوجِبُونَهُ يَقُولُونَ:
 إذَا الْتَزَمَهُ لَمْ يَكُنْ لَهُ أَنْ يَخْرُجَ عَنْهُ مَا دَامَ مُلْتَزِمًا لَهُ أَوْ مَا لَمْ يَتَبَيَّنْ لَهُ أَنَّ غَيْرَهُ أَوْلَى بِالِالْتِزَامِ مِنْهُ.
وَلَا رَيْبَ أَنَّ الْتِزَامَ الْمَذَاهِبِ وَالْخُرُوجَ عَنْهَا إنْ كَانَ لِغَيْرِ أَمْرٍ دِينِيٍّ مِثْلَ:
