This view was stated by some of Ahmad’s followers. Likewise, other views mentioned by Ibn Hamdān or others may be statements of some of Ahmad’s followers, without having been expressly stated by Ahmad himself. Much of what appears in the books of the followers of al-Shāfiʿī, Mālik, and Abū Hanīfa is similarly drawn from statements of some of their followers, rather than explicit statements of the imams themselves. Indeed, the views expressly reported from them may be contrary to those statements.

The underlying question is whether a layperson must commit himself to a particular school of law, following both its stricter rulings and its concessions. There are two positions among Ahmad’s followers on this, and likewise two among the followers of al-Shāfiʿī. The majority in both groups do not consider this obligatory. Those who do consider it obligatory say that once someone commits himself to a school, he may not depart from it so long as he remains committed to it, or unless it becomes clear to him that another school is more deserving of his commitment.

There is no doubt that if someone commits himself to a school of law or departs from it for a nonreligious reason—for example, committing himself to a school to obtain some worldly advantage, such as wealth, prestige, or the like—he deserves no praise for this. Rather, he is in fact blameworthy, even if the position he adopts is better than the one he leaves. He is like someone who embraces Islam solely for a worldly purpose, or migrates from Mecca to Medina for a woman he wishes to marry or some worldly gain he hopes to obtain.

During the Prophet’s lifetime, a man migrated for the sake of a woman called Umm Qays, and so he became known as “the migrant for Umm Qays.” The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said from the pulpit, as reported in the authentic hadith: “Deeds are judged only

If, however, he moves from one school of law to another for a religious reason—for example, because it becomes clear to him that one view is stronger than another, and he therefore adopts the view he considers closer to the guidance of Allah and His Messenger—he is rewarded for doing so. Indeed, whenever the ruling of Allah and His Messenger on a matter becomes clear to anyone, he must neither depart from it nor follow anyone in opposing Allah and His Messenger. For Allah has made obedience to His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, obligatory upon everyone in every circumstance. Allah Most High says:

“But no, by your Lord, they will not believe until they make you judge concerning that over which they dispute among themselves, and then find within themselves no discomfort from what you have judged and submit in full submission.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Say, ‘If you love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you and forgive you your sins.’”

And Allah Most High says:

“It is not for a believing man or a believing woman, when Allah and His Messenger have decided a matter, to have any choice in their affair.”

Imam Ahmad wrote a book on obedience to the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. This is a matter of agreement among the imams of the Muslims: obeying Allah and His Messenger, regarding as lawful what Allah and His Messenger have made lawful, regarding as forbidden what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden, and regarding as obligatory what Allah and His Messenger have made obligatory are duties incumbent upon all humankind and jinn; they are obligatory upon

everyone in every circumstance, in private and in public. However, since many people do not know certain rulings, they turn to someone who can teach them, because he knows better what the Messenger said and what he intended. The imams of the Muslims whom people follow thus serve as means, paths, and guides connecting them to the Messenger. They convey his words and explain his intended meaning to the best of their judgment and ability. Allah may grant one scholar knowledge and understanding that another does not possess, while the other may possess knowledge concerning another matter that the first does not.

Allah Most High says:

“And David and Solomon, when they judged concerning the field into which the sheep of a people had strayed by night; We were witness to their judgment.”

“And We gave Solomon understanding of the case, and to each We gave judgment and knowledge.”

These were two noble prophets who judged the same case. Allah singled one of them out for understanding, yet praised them both. Scholars are the heirs of the prophets, and their efforts to determine legal rulings resemble the efforts of those seeking to determine the direction of the Kaaba. If four people each lead a group in prayer, facing four different directions because each believes the direction of prayer lies that way, the prayers of all four are valid. Yet only one has prayed toward the Kaaba: he is the one who is correct and receives two rewards. As authentically reported from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, he said:

“When a judge exercises his independent judgment and reaches the correct decision, he receives two rewards; if he exercises his independent judgment and errs, he receives one reward.”

Most people have committed themselves to schools of law—indeed, to religions—on the basis of what has become clear to them

, for a person grows up following the religion of his father, his master, or the people of his town, just as a child follows his parents, his captor, and the people of his town in religion. Once he reaches adulthood, however, he must seek to obey Allah and His Messenger wherever that obedience lies. He must not be among those who, when told, “Follow what Allah has revealed,” say, “Rather, we follow what we found our fathers following.”

Anyone who turns away from following the Quran and Sunnah and obeying Allah and His Messenger, preferring his own customs and those of his father and his people, belongs to the people of ignorance who deserve the threatened punishment. Likewise, anyone to whom the truth with which Allah sent His Messenger becomes clear on a particular question, but who then abandons it in favour of his customary practice, deserves blame and punishment.

As for someone unable to ascertain the ruling of Allah and His Messenger, who follows a person of knowledge and religious integrity on that question, without it becoming clear to him that another person’s view carries greater weight, he is praiseworthy and will be rewarded; he is neither blamed nor punished for this.

If, however, he can examine the evidence and determine which view is stronger, yet shies away from certain questions and instead resorts to following an authority, there is disagreement within Ahmad’s school concerning his case. Ahmad’s explicitly stated position, upheld by his followers, is that such a person is also sinful. This is also the position of al-Shāfiʿī and his followers. It is reported from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan and others that such a person may follow an authority without restriction. Another view permits him to follow someone more learned than himself.

Some have attributed this latter view to Ahmad, as Abū Ishāq mentions in al-Lumaʿ. This attribution to Ahmad is mistaken, however, for Ahmad says this only concerning his companions

translated_text:
He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked to explain what Najm al-Dīn ibn Hamdān stated at the end of Kitāb al-Riʿāyah:

“Whoever commits himself to a school of law is to be censured for departing from it without evidence, reliance on scholarly authority, or another excuse.”

He was also asked to clarify something that had left us puzzled: on certain questions, al-Kāfī, al-Muharrar, al-Muqniʿ, al-Riʿāyah, al-Khulāsah, and al-Hidāyah mention two reported positions or two juristic views without identifying which is more correct or carries greater weight. We therefore do not know which to follow, and if we are asked about the matter, we are at a loss.

Answer

He replied:

Praise be to Allah.

As for these books that mention two reported positions or two juristic views without identifying the correct one, a student of knowledge can ascertain this from other works, such as al-Taʿlīq by Judge Abū Yaʿlā, al-Intisār by Abū al-Khattāb, ʿUmad al-Adillah by Ibn ʿAqīl, the commentaries of Judge Yaʿqūb al-Barzabīnī and Abū al-Hasan ibn al-Zāghūnī, and other extensive works that discuss disputed questions and identify the stronger position. I have abridged the principal questions treated in these works in concise books

such as Ruʾūs al-Masāʾil by Judge Abū al-Husayn. It is reported that Shaykh Abū al-Barakāt, the author of al-Muharrar, used to tell those who asked him about the apparent position of Ahmad’s school that it was the position preferred by Abū al-Khattāb in his Ruʾūs al-Masāʾil.

Other works from which this may be ascertained include al-Mughnī by Shaykh Abū Muhammad and Sharh al-Hidāyah by our grandfather Abū al-Barakāt. Several scholars wrote commentaries on al-Hidāyah, including Abū Halīm al-Nahrawānī; Abū ʿAbd Allāh ibn Taymiyyah, the preacher and author of the Quran commentary, who was Abū al-Barakāt’s uncle; Abū al-Maʿālī ibn al-Munajjā; and Abū al-Baqāʾ the grammarian, though the latter did not complete his commentary.

The scholars of the school have differed over which positions they consider correct: one may consider one reported position correct, while another considers a different reported position correct. Whoever knows these differences reports them, and whoever finds one position stronger than another follows the stronger position. Whoever aims to transmit Ahmad’s school reports the differences they have mentioned concerning reported positions, juristic views, and lines of transmission, just as the followers of al-Shāfiʿī, Abū Hanīfah, and Mālik transmit the schools of their imams. For every school contains well-known differences in the positions reported from its imams, as well as disagreements among their followers over identifying their school’s position and determining which position carries greater weight according to Islamic law.

translated_text:
Islamic law. Ahmad was more knowledgeable than others about the Quran, the Sunnah, and the statements of the Companions and those who followed them in righteousness. Thus, scarcely any position of his contradicts an explicit scriptural text, as occurs with others. Generally, whenever he holds a weak position, another position within his school agrees with the stronger view. Most of his distinctive positions on which his school has not differed are the stronger views.

Examples include his view permitting a change from hajj alone, or hajj combined with ‘umrah, to ‘umrah followed by hajj with release from ihram between them; his acceptance, when necessary, of testimony from non-Muslims under Muslim protection concerning Muslims, as in the case of a bequest made while travelling; his view that marrying a woman who has committed fornication is forbidden until she repents; his acceptance of a slave’s testimony; and his view that the Sunnah in dry ablution is to wipe the hands up to the wrists after striking the ground once.

Another example is his view that a woman experiencing non-menstrual bleeding should, in some circumstances, refer to her usual menstrual pattern; in others, distinguish between the types of blood; and in others, follow the usual menstrual patterns of most women. Three rulings concerning her have been reported from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and Ahmad applied all three, unlike the others.

Further examples are his permission of fruit-sharing and crop-sharing agreements on land without trees as well as land planted with trees, whether the seed is supplied by both parties or by either one of them, and his permission of similar arrangements, even though these fall under partnership rather than hire and are not contrary to analogical reasoning. There are many comparable examples.

As for what some people call a position unique to him because he differs on it from Abū Hanīfah and al-Shāfi‘ī, even though Mālik’s position agrees with Ahmad’s or is close to it

translated_text:
—and these are the positions against which al-Harrāsī wrote a refutation and which were defended by several scholars, including Ibn ‘Aqīl, Judge Abū Ya‘lā the Younger, Abū al-Faraj Ibn al-Jawzī, and Abū Muhammad ibn al-Muthannā—in most such cases, the position of Mālik and Ahmad is stronger than the opposing view. Where the opposing view is stronger, Ahmad is reported to have held differing positions on the matter.

Examples include invalidating legal stratagems that evade zakat, defeat the right of pre-emption, and the like, as well as stratagems that render usury, indecent acts, and similar things permissible; taking purposes and intentions into account in contracts; and interpreting oaths by reference to their occasion and what prompted them, together with the oath-taker’s intention.

Another example is imposing the prescribed punishments on offenders as the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and his rightly guided caliphs did, as when they imposed the prescribed punishment for drinking intoxicants on the evidence of smell, vomit, and the like.

Further examples include taking customary practice into account in contractual conditions, treating a customary condition like an expressly stated condition, and accepting common usage as sufficient in contracts expressed in general terms. Whatever people regard as a sale is a sale; whatever they regard as a lease is a lease; whatever they regard as a gift is a gift; and whatever they regard as an endowment is an endowment. No particular wording is required for any of these. There are many similar examples.

وَقَالَ شَيْخُ الْإِسْلَامِ أَحْمَد بْنُ تَيْمِيَّة رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ الْحَبْرُ الْكَامِلُ الْعَلَّامَةُ الْأَوْحَدُ الْحَافِظُ الزَّاهِدُ؛ الْعَابِدُ الْوَرِعُ؛ الرَّبَّانِيُّ الْمَقْذُوفُ فِي قَلْبِهِ النُّورُ الْإِلَهِيُّ وَالْعُلُومُ الرَّفِيعَةُ وَالْفُنُونُ الْبَدِيعَةُ الْآخِذُ بِأَزْمَةِ الشَّرِيعَةِ النَّاكِصُ عَنْ الْآرَاءِ الْمُزِلَّةِ وَالْأَهْوَاءِ الْمُضِلَّةِ الْمُقْتَفِي لِآثَارِ السَّلَفِ عِلْمًا وَعَمَلًا مُفْتِي الْفِرَقِ مُجْتَهِدُ الْعَصْرِ أَوْحَدُ الدَّهْرِ تَقِيُّ الدِّينِ أَبُو الْعَبَّاسِ أَحْمَد بْنُ عَبْدِ الْحَلِيمِ بْنِ عَبْدِ السَّلَامِ بْنِ تَيْمِيَّة - أَدَامَ اللَّهُ بَرَكَتَهُ وَرَفَعَ فِي الدُّنْيَا وَالْآخِرَةِ مَحَلَّهُ وَدَرَجَتَهُ -:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ عَلَى آلَائِهِ، وَأَشْهَدُ أَنْ لَا إلَهَ إلَّا اللَّهُ وَحْدَهُ لَا شَرِيكَ لَهُ فِي أَرْضِهِ وَسَمَائِهِ. وَأَشْهَدُ أَنَّ مُحَمَّدًا عَبْدُهُ وَرَسُولُهُ وَخَاتَمُ أَنْبِيَائِهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَعَلَى آلِهِ وَأَصْحَابِهِ صَلَاةً دَائِمَةً إلَى يَوْمِ لِقَائِهِ وَسَلَّمَ تَسْلِيمًا.
وَبَعْدُ:
 فَيَجِبُ عَلَى الْمُسْلِمِينَ بَعْدَ مُوَالَاةِ اللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِ مُوَالَاةُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ كَمَا نَطَقَ بِهِ الْقُرْآنُ خُصُوصًا الْعُلَمَاءُ الَّذِينَ هُمْ وَرَثَةُ الْأَنْبِيَاءِ، الَّذِينَ
translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islām Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah have mercy on him—also said: the consummate scholar, the unrivalled authority, the hadith master, the ascetic, the devout worshipper, the scrupulously pious and godly scholar into whose heart divine light, exalted knowledge, and wondrous branches of learning had been cast; who held the reins of the Sacred Law, shunned opinions that cause one to stumble and desires that lead astray, and followed in the footsteps of the early generations in knowledge and practice; the mufti to the various groups, the independent jurist of his age, peerless in his time, Taqī al-Dīn Abū al-‘Abbās Ahmad ibn ‘Abd al-Halīm ibn ‘Abd al-Salām ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah perpetuate his blessings and elevate his standing and rank in this world and the Hereafter:

All praise is due to Allah for His blessings. I bear witness that none has the right to be worshipped but Allah alone, without partner in His earth or His heaven. And I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant, His Messenger, and the last of His prophets. May Allah bestow blessings and peace upon him, his family, and his Companions, blessings enduring until the Day of meeting Him.

To proceed:

After loyalty to Allah and His Messenger, Muslims are obliged to show loyalty to the believers, as the Quran declares, especially the scholars, who are the heirs of the prophets, whom

original_text:
جَعَلَهُمْ اللَّهُ بِمَنْزِلَةِ النُّجُومِ يُهْتَدَى بِهِمْ فِي ظُلُمَاتِ الْبَرِّ وَالْبَحْرِ وَقَدْ أَجْمَعَ الْمُسْلِمُونَ عَلَى هِدَايَتِهِمْ وَدِرَايَتِهِمْ إذْ كَلُّ أُمَّةٍ قَبْلَ مَبْعَثِ مُحَمَّدٍ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فَعُلَمَاؤُهَا شِرَارُهَا إلَّا الْمُسْلِمِينَ فَإِنَّ عُلَمَاءَهُمْ خِيَارُهُمْ؛ فَإِنَّهُمْ خُلَفَاءُ الرَّسُولِ فِي أُمَّتِهِ والمحيون لِمَا مَاتَ مِنْ سُنَّتِهِ بِهِمْ قَامَ الْكِتَابُ وَبِهِ قَامُوا وَبِهِمْ نَطَقَ الْكِتَابُ وَبِهِ نَطَقُوا. وَلِيُعْلَمَ أَنَّهُ لَيْسَ أَحَدٌ مِنْ الْأَئِمَّةِ الْمَقْبُولِينَ عِنْدَ الْأُمَّةِ قَبُولًا عَامًّا يَتَعَمَّدُ مُخَالَفَةَ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فِي شَيْءٍ مِنْ سُنَّتِهِ؛ دَقِيقٍ وَلَا جَلِيلٍ؛ فَإِنَّهُمْ مُتَّفِقُونَ اتِّفَاقًا يَقِينِيًّا عَلَى وُجُوبِ اتِّبَاعِ الرَّسُولِ وَعَلَى أَنَّ كُلَّ أَحَدٍ مِنْ النَّاسِ يُؤْخَذُ مِنْ قَوْلِهِ وَيُتْرَكُ إلَّا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَلَكِنْ إذَا وُجِدَ لِوَاحِدِ مِنْهُمْ قَوْلٌ قَدْ جَاءَ حَدِيثٌ صَحِيحٌ بِخِلَافِهِ فَلَا بُدَّ لَهُ مِنْ عُذْرٍ فِي تَرْكِهِ.
 وَجَمِيعُ الْأَعْذَارِ ثَلَاثَةُ أَصْنَافٍ:
 أَحَدُهَا: عَدَمُ اعْتِقَادِهِ أَنَّ النَّبِيَّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ قَالَهُ.
 وَالثَّانِي:
 عَدَمُ اعْتِقَادِهِ إرَادَةَ تِلْكَ الْمَسْأَلَةِ بِذَلِكَ الْقَوْلِ.
 وَالثَّالِثُ:
 اعْتِقَادُهُ أَنَّ ذَلِكَ الْحُكْمَ مَنْسُوخٌ.
translated_text:
Allah has made like stars by which people find their way through the darkness of land and sea. Muslims unanimously acknowledge their guidance and learning. For in every community before the advent of Muhammad—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—its scholars were its worst members, except for the Muslims, whose scholars are their best. They are the Messenger’s successors among his community, reviving what has fallen into neglect of his sunnah. Through them the Book is upheld, and through it they are upheld; through them the Book speaks, and through it they speak.

Let it be known that none of the imams generally accepted by the Muslim community deliberately opposes the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—in any aspect of his sunnah, minor or major. They are unequivocally agreed that following the Messenger is obligatory and that anyone’s statements may be accepted or rejected, except those of the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace. If, however, one of them holds a view contrary to an authentic hadith, he must have an excuse for not following it.

All such excuses fall into three categories:

First: He does not believe that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said it.

Second: He does not believe that the statement was intended to apply to the issue in question.

Third: He believes that the ruling has been abrogated.

original_text:
وَهَذِهِ الْأَصْنَافُ الثَّلَاثَةُ تَتَفَرَّعُ إلَى أَسْبَابٍ مُتَعَدِّدَةٍ.
 السَّبَبُ الْأَوَّلُ:
 أَلَّا يَكُونَ الْحَدِيثُ قَدْ بَلَغَهُ. وَمَنْ لَمْ يَبْلُغْهُ الْحَدِيثُ لَمْ يُكَلَّفْ أَنْ يَكُونَ عَالِمًا بِمُوجَبِهِ وَإِذَا لَمْ يَكُنْ قَدْ بَلَغَهُ وَقَدْ قَالَ فِي تِلْكَ الْقَضِيَّةِ بِمُوجَبِ ظَاهِرِ آيَةٍ أَوْ حَدِيثٍ آخَرَ؛ أَوْ بِمُوجَبِ قِيَاسٍ؛
 أَوْ مُوجَبِ اسْتِصْحَابٍ:
 فَقَدْ يُوَافِقُ ذَلِكَ الْحَدِيثَ تَارَةً وَيُخَالِفُهُ أُخْرَى. وَهَذَا السَّبَبُ هُوَ الْغَالِبُ عَلَى أَكْثَرِ مَا يُوجَدُ مِنْ أَقْوَالِ السَّلَفِ مُخَالِفًا لِبَعْضِ الْأَحَادِيثِ؛ فَإِنَّ الْإِحَاطَةَ بِحَدِيثِ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ لَمْ تَكُنْ لِأَحَدِ مِنْ الْأُمَّةِ. وَقَدْ كَانَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ يُحَدِّثُ؛ أَوْ يُفْتِي؛ أَوْ يَقْضِي؛ أَوْ يَفْعَلُ الشَّيْءَ فَيَسْمَعُهُ أَوْ يَرَاهُ مَنْ يَكُونُ حَاضِرًا وَيُبَلِّغُهُ أُولَئِكَ أَوْ بَعْضُهُمْ لِمَنْ يُبَلِّغُونَهُ فَيَنْتَهِي عِلْمُ ذَلِكَ إلَى مَنْ يَشَاءُ اللَّهُ مِنْ الْعُلَمَاءِ مِنْ الصَّحَابَةِ وَالتَّابِعِينَ وَمَنْ بَعْدَهُمْ ثُمَّ فِي مَجْلِسٍ آخَرَ قَدْ يُحَدِّثُ أَوْ يُفْتِي أَوْ يَقْضِي أَوْ يَفْعَلُ شَيْئًا وَيَشْهَدُهُ بَعْضُ مَنْ كَانَ غَائِبًا عَنْ ذَلِكَ الْمَجْلِسِ وَيُبَلِّغُونَهُ لِمَنْ أَمْكَنَهُمْ فَيَكُونُ عِنْدَ هَؤُلَاءِ مِنْ الْعِلْمِ مَا لَيْسَ عِنْدَ هَؤُلَاءِ وَعِنْدَ هَؤُلَاءِ مَا لَيْسَ عِنْدَ هَؤُلَاءِ وَإِنَّمَا يَتَفَاضَلُ الْعُلَمَاءُ مِنْ الصَّحَابَةِ وَمَنْ بَعْدَهُمْ بِكَثْرَةِ الْعِلْمِ أَوْ جَوْدَتِهِ. وَأَمَّا إحَاطَةُ وَاحِدٍ بِجَمِيعِ حَدِيثِ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ
translated_text:
These three categories can be subdivided into a number of specific reasons.

The first reason:

The hadith may not have reached him. Someone whom a hadith has not reached is not required to know the ruling it entails. If it has not reached him and he has ruled on the matter according to the apparent meaning of a Quranic verse or another hadith, or on the basis of analogy or the presumption of continuity, his ruling may sometimes agree with that hadith and sometimes differ from it.

This is the predominant reason why statements of the early generations are found to conflict with certain hadiths, for no one in this community has had comprehensive knowledge of all the hadiths of the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace. The Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—would speak, give a legal opinion, pass judgment, or do something, and those present would hear or see him. They, or some of them, would convey it to others, so that knowledge of it would reach whichever scholars Allah willed among the Companions, the Successors, and those who came after them.

Then, on another occasion, he might speak, give a legal opinion, pass judgment, or do something, witnessed by some who had been absent from the earlier gathering. They would convey it to whomever they could. Thus, one group would possess knowledge that the other did not, and the other would possess knowledge that the first did not. Scholars among the Companions and those who came after them differ in merit according to the breadth or depth of their knowledge. As for any one person having comprehensive knowledge of all the hadiths of the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—

original_text:
فَهَذَا لَا يُمْكِنُ ادِّعَاؤُهُ قَطُّ وَاعْتُبِرَ ذَلِكَ بِالْخُلَفَاءِ الرَّاشِدِينَ الَّذِينَ هُمْ أَعْلَمُ الْأُمَّةِ بِأُمُورِ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَسُنَّتِهِ وَأَحْوَالِهِ خُصُوصًا الصِّدِّيقُ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ الَّذِي لَمْ يَكُنْ يُفَارِقُهُ حَضَرًا وَلَا سَفَرًا بَلْ كَانَ يَكُونُ مَعَهُ فِي غَالِبِ الْأَوْقَاتِ حَتَّى إنَّهُ يَسْمَرُ عِنْدَهُ بِاللَّيْلِ فِي أُمُورِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ. وَكَذَلِكَ عُمَرُ بْنُ الْخَطَّابِ - رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ -
 فَإِنَّهُ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ كَثِيرًا مَا يَقُولُ:
 دَخَلْت أَنَا وَأَبُو بَكْرٍ وَعُمَرُ وَخَرَجْت أَنَا وَأَبُو بَكْرٍ وَعُمَرُ ثُمَّ مَعَ ذَلِكَ 
{لَمَّا سُئِلَ أَبُو بَكْرٍ - رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ -
 عَنْ مِيرَاثِ الْجَدَّةِ قَالَ:
 مَا لَك فِي كِتَابِ اللَّهِ مِنْ شَيْءٍ وَمَا عَلِمْت لَك فِي سُنَّةِ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ مِنْ شَيْءٍ وَلَكِنْ اسْأَلْ النَّاسَ فَسَأَلَهُمْ فَقَامَ الْمُغِيرَةُ بْنُ شُعْبَةَ وَمُحَمَّدُ بْنُ مسلمة فَشَهِدَا أَنَّ النَّبِيَّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ أَعْطَاهَا السُّدُسَ}
 وَقَدْ بَلَّغَ هَذِهِ السُّنَّةَ عِمْرَانُ بْنُ حُصَيْنٍ أَيْضًا وَلَيْسَ هَؤُلَاءِ الثَّلَاثَةُ مِثْلَ أَبِي بَكْرٍ وَغَيْرِهِ مِنْ الْخُلَفَاءِ ثُمَّ قَدْ اخْتَصُّوا بِعِلْمِ هَذِهِ السُّنَّةِ الَّتِي قَدْ اتَّفَقَتْ الْأُمَّةُ عَلَى الْعَمَلِ بِهَا. وَكَذَلِكَ عُمَرُ بْنُ الْخَطَّابِ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ لَمْ يَكُنْ يَعْلَمُ سُنَّةَ الِاسْتِئْذَانِ حَتَّى أَخْبَرَهُ بِهَا أَبُو مُوسَى وَاسْتَشْهَدَ بِالْأَنْصَارِ وَعُمَرُ أَعْلَمُ مِمَّنْ حَدَّثَهُ بِهَذِهِ السُّنَّةِ. وَلَمْ يَكُنْ عُمَرُ أَيْضًا يَعْلَمُ أَنَّ الْمَرْأَةَ تَرِثُ مِنْ دِيَةِ زَوْجِهَا بَلْ يَرَى
translated_text:
that can never be claimed. This is illustrated by the Rightly Guided Caliphs, who were the most knowledgeable members of this community concerning the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—his Sunnah, and his circumstances. This was especially true of al-Siddīq—may Allah be pleased with him—who never left his side, whether at home or travelling. Indeed, he was with him most of the time, even staying up with him at night to discuss the affairs of the Muslims. The same was true of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb—may Allah be pleased with him—for the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—would often say:

“I went in with Abū Bakr and ʿUmar, and I went out with Abū Bakr and ʿUmar.”

Yet despite this:

“When Abū Bakr—may Allah be pleased with him—was asked about a grandmother’s share of inheritance, he said: ‘There is no share prescribed for you in the Book of Allah, and I know of none for you in the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace. But ask the people.’ He then asked them, and al-Mughīrah ibn Shuʿbah and Muhammad ibn Maslamah stood up and testified that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—had awarded her one-sixth.”

ʿImrān ibn Husayn also conveyed this Sunnah. These three were not on a par with Abū Bakr and the other caliphs, yet they possessed knowledge that the caliphs lacked concerning this Sunnah, which the community has unanimously agreed to follow.

Likewise, ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb—may Allah be pleased with him—did not know the Sunnah concerning seeking permission to enter until Abū Mūsā informed him of it and corroborating testimony was sought from the Ansār. Yet ʿUmar was more knowledgeable than those who related this Sunnah to him. Nor did ʿUmar know that a woman inherits a share of the blood money paid for her husband’s death; rather, he held

that the blood money belonged to the ʿāqilah (those collectively liable for blood money), until al-Dahhāk ibn Sufyān—whom the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—had appointed over some desert communities—wrote to inform him:

“The Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—awarded Ashyam al-Dibābī’s wife a share of the blood money paid for her husband’s death.”

He therefore abandoned his earlier view, saying: “Had we not heard this, we would have ruled otherwise.”

Nor did he know the ruling concerning the Magians with regard to the jizyah until ʿAbd al-Rahmān ibn ʿAwf—may Allah be pleased with him—informed him that the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—had said:

“Treat them as you treat the People of the Book.”

When he arrived at Sargh and learned that plague had broken out in Syria, he consulted the early Emigrants who were with him, then the Ansār, and then those who had embraced Islam at the conquest of Mecca. Each offered the advice he thought best, but none informed him of any Sunnah on the matter until ʿAbd al-Rahmān ibn ʿAwf arrived and told him of the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—concerning plague, and that he had said:

“If it breaks out in a land where you are, do not leave to flee from it; and if you hear of it in a land, do not go there.”

He and Ibn ʿAbbās also discussed the case of someone who experiences doubt during his prayer. The Sunnah concerning this had not reached him until ʿAbd al-Rahmān ibn ʿAwf related from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—that:

“He should disregard the doubt and proceed on the basis of what he is certain of.”

Abū Hurayrah said:

“Word of this reached me while I was at the rear of the company, so I urged my mount on until I caught up with him and told him what the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—had instructed people to do when the wind blows.”

These were matters he did not know until they were conveyed to him by people who were not his equals. In other matters, the relevant Sunnah never reached him, and he passed judgments or gave legal opinions at variance with it. For example, he ruled that the blood money payable for fingers varied according to their usefulness. Yet Abū Mūsā and Ibn ʿAbbās—both far below him in knowledge—knew that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—had said:

“This one and this one are equal,” meaning the thumb and the little finger.

This Sunnah reached Muʿāwiyah—may Allah be pleased with him—during his rule, and he judged accordingly. The Muslims had no choice but to follow it. This was no fault in ʿUmar—may Allah be pleased with him—since the hadith had not reached him.

Likewise, he, his son ʿAbd Allāh—may Allah be pleased with them both—and other people of virtue used to forbid pilgrims from applying perfume before entering the state of consecration, and before proceeding to Mecca after stoning the pillar at al-ʿAqabah. They had not received the hadith of ʿĀ’ishah—may Allah be pleased with her:

“I applied perfume to the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—for his consecration, before he entered that state, and for his release from it, before he performed circumambulation.”

He also used to instruct anyone wearing a leather sock to wipe over it until he took it off, without

setting a time limit. A group of the early Muslims followed him in this. The hadiths prescribing a time limit had not reached them, although their authenticity had been established by some who were not their equals in knowledge. This had indeed been reported from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—through several authentic chains of transmission.

Likewise, ʿUthmān—may Allah be pleased with him—did not know that a widow should observe her waiting period in the home she occupied at the time of her husband’s death, until al-Furayʿah bint Mālik, the sister of Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, told him about her circumstances when her husband died, and that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—had said to her:

“Remain in your home until the prescribed term comes to an end.”

ʿUthmān then acted accordingly. On another occasion, he was given some game that had been hunted specifically for him. He was about to eat it when ʿAlī—may Allah be pleased with him—told him that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—had declined meat given to him as a gift.

Likewise, ʿAlī—may Allah be pleased with him—said:

“Whenever I heard a hadith from the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—Allah enabled me to benefit from it as He willed. These Companions were the most knowledgeable members of this community, the most learned in religion, the most God-fearing, and the most virtuous. Those who came after them fall short of them, so it is all the more likely that some of the sunnah remained unknown to them. This needs no further explanation. Anyone who believes that every authentic hadith reached every imam, or any particular imam, is making a gross and grievous error.

Even supposing that all his hadiths were contained in such collections, a scholar does not know everything in the books; scarcely anyone could achieve that. Indeed, a man may possess numerous collections without knowing all their contents. Moreover, those who lived before these collections were compiled knew far more of the sunnah than later scholars, because much of what reached them and was established as authentic in their estimation may reach us only through an unknown narrator, or through a disconnected chain of transmission, or may never reach us at all. Their memories were their collections, containing many times what the written collections contain. No one acquainted with the matter doubts this.

Let no one say:

“Anyone who does not know all the hadiths is not qualified to exercise independent legal judgment.”

For if such qualification required knowledge of everything the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said and did concerning legal rulings, there would be no one in this community qualified to exercise independent legal judgment. The most a scholar can attain is knowledge of the greater part of that material, such that only a few details remain unknown to him. Yet he may take a position contrary to those few details that reach him.

The second reason:

The hadith may have reached him, but its authenticity was not established in his estimation. This may be because the person who related it to him, that person’s source, or another narrator in the chain was unknown to him, suspect, or had a poor memory. Alternatively, it may not have reached him with a complete chain, but rather with a disconnected one; or he may not have accurately retained its wording.  اعْتِقَادُ ضَعْفِ الْحَدِيثِ بِاجْتِهَادِ قَدْ خَالَفَهُ فِيهِ غَيْرُهُ مَعَ قَطْعِ النَّظَرِ عَنْ طَرِيقٍ آخَرَ سَوَاءٌ كَانَ الصَّوَابُ مَعَهُ أَوْ مَعَ غَيْرِهِ أَوْ مَعَهُمَا عِنْدَ مَنْ يَقُولُ: كُلُّ مُجْتَهِدٍ مُصِيبٌ؛
 وَلِذَلِكَ أَسْبَابٌ:
 مِنْهَا: أَنْ يَكُونَ الْمُحَدِّثُ بِالْحَدِيثِ يَعْتَقِدُهُ أَحَدُهُمَا ضَعِيفًا؛ وَيَعْتَقِدُهُ الْآخَرُ ثِقَةً. وَمَعْرِفَةُ الرِّجَالِ عِلْمٌ وَاسِعٌ؛ ثُمَّ قَدْ يَكُونُ الْمُصِيبُ مَنْ
translated_text:
transmitted by narrators other than those he considered unreliable; or it may have been transmitted through a connected chain other than the disconnected one, with its wording accurately preserved by some of the hadith masters; or the report may have corroborating reports and supporting chains that establish its authenticity. This, too, is very common.

Among the Successors and their followers, down to the renowned imams who came after them, this was more prevalent than in the earliest generation—or was common within the first category. Hadiths had spread and become widely known, but they reached many scholars through weak chains, while reaching others through different, authentic chains. A hadith would thus constitute authoritative evidence through a chain by which it had not reached the scholar whose position differed from it. Hence, more than one imam made acceptance of what a hadith entailed conditional upon its authenticity, saying:

“My position on this issue is such-and-such. A hadith stating otherwise has been reported concerning it; if it is authentic, then that is my position.”

The third reason:

A scholar may consider a hadith weak on the basis of an independent assessment in which another scholar disagrees with him, even without considering any other chain of transmission. This applies whether he is correct, the other scholar is correct, or both are correct according to those who say, “Everyone who exercises independent legal judgment is correct.”

There are several reasons for this.

One is that one scholar may consider the narrator of a hadith weak, while another considers him trustworthy. Knowledge of narrators is a vast field. Yet the scholar who is correct may be the one who

 أَلَّا يَعْتَقِدَ أَنَّ الْمُحَدِّثَ سَمِعَ الْحَدِيثَ مِمَّنْ حَدَّثَ عَنْهُ وَغَيْرُهُ يَعْتَقِدُ أَنَّهُ سَمِعَهُ لِأَسْبَابِ تُوجِبُ ذَلِكَ مَعْرُوفَةٍ.
 وَمِنْهَا:
 أَنْ يَكُونَ لِلْمُحَدِّثِ حَالَانِ: حَالُ اسْتِقَامَةٍ وَحَالُ اضْطِرَابٍ مِثْلَ أَنْ يَخْتَلِطَ أَوْ تَحْتَرِقَ كُتُبُهُ فَمَا حَدَّثَ بِهِ فِي حَالِ الِاسْتِقَامَةِ صَحِيحٌ وَمَا حَدَّثَ بِهِ فِي حَالِ الِاضْطِرَابِ ضَعِيفٌ فَلَا يَدْرِي ذَلِكَ الْحَدِيثَ مِنْ أَيِّ النَّوْعَيْنِ؟ وَقَدْ عَلِمَ غَيْرُهُ أَنَّهُ مِمَّا حَدَّثَ بِهِ فِي حَالِ الِاسْتِقَامَةِ.
 وَمِنْهَا:
 أَنْ يَكُونَ الْمُحَدِّثُ قَدْ نَسِيَ ذَلِكَ الْحَدِيثَ فَلَمْ يَذْكُرْهُ فِيمَا بَعْدُ أَوْ أَنْكَرَ أَنْ يَكُونَ حَدَّثَهُ مُعْتَقِدًا أَنَّ هَذَا عِلَّةٌ تُوجِبُ تَرْكَ الْحَدِيثِ. وَيَرَى غَيْرُهُ أَنَّ هَذَا مِمَّا يَصِحُّ الِاسْتِدْلَالُ بِهِ. وَالْمَسْأَلَةُ مَعْرُوفَةٌ.
 وَمِنْهَا:
 أَنَّ كَثِيرًا مِنْ الْحِجَازِيِّينَ يَرَوْنَ أَلَّا يُحْتَجَّ بِحَدِيثِ عِرَاقِيٍّ أَوْ شَامِيٍّ إنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ لَهُ أَصْلٌ بِالْحِجَازِ حَتَّى قَالَ قَائِلُهُمْ: نَزِّلُوا أَحَادِيثَ
translated_text:
considers him weak because he knows of grounds for impugning his reliability. Yet the other scholar may be correct because he knows that those grounds do not warrant such criticism—either because they are not inherently discrediting, or because the narrator had an excuse that precludes criticism in that instance. This is a vast field. Scholars of narrators and their circumstances have areas of agreement and disagreement, just as other scholars do within their respective disciplines.

Another reason is that one scholar may not believe that a narrator heard the hadith from the person on whose authority he relates it, while another believes that he did, on well-known grounds that establish this.

Another reason is that a narrator may have experienced two periods: one of sound transmission and another of unreliable transmission, as when his memory becomes confused or his books are destroyed by fire. What he transmitted during the period of sound transmission is authentic, while what he transmitted during the period of unreliable transmission is weak. One scholar may not know to which category a particular hadith belongs, while another knows that it was transmitted during the period of sound transmission.

Another reason is that a narrator may have forgotten the hadith and been unable to recall it later, or denied having transmitted it. One scholar considers this a defect requiring that the hadith be rejected, whereas another holds that it may validly be cited as evidence. This is a well-known issue.

Another reason is that many scholars of the Hijaz hold that a hadith transmitted by an Iraqi or Syrian narrator should not be accepted as authoritative evidence unless it has a basis in the Hijaz. Indeed, one of them went so far as to say: “Treat the hadiths

السَّبَبُ الرَّابِعُ:

translated_text:
of the people of Iraq as you would the reports of the People of the Book: neither affirm nor deny what they say.” Another was asked: “Is a report transmitted by Sufyān, from Mansūr, from Ibrāhīm, from ‘Alqamah, from ‘Abd Allāh authoritative evidence?” He replied: “Not if it has no basis in the Hijaz.”

This was because they believed that the people of the Hijaz had accurately preserved the Sunnah, so that none of it had escaped them, whereas inconsistencies had arisen in the hadiths transmitted by the Iraqis that warranted withholding judgment. Some Iraqi scholars likewise held that hadiths transmitted by Syrian narrators should not be accepted as authoritative evidence. Most scholars, however, do not consider this a basis for declaring a hadith weak. Whenever its chain of transmission is sound, the hadith constitutes authoritative evidence, whether it comes from the Hijaz, Iraq, Syria, or elsewhere.

Abū Dāwūd al-Sijistānī compiled a book on Sunnah reports transmitted uniquely by the people of particular cities. In it, he identifies the Sunnah reports peculiar to each city that are not transmitted with chains of transmission by people elsewhere, including Medina, Mecca, Taif, Damascus, Homs, Kufa, Basra, and others. There are further reasons besides these.

The fourth reason:

A scholar may stipulate conditions for accepting a solitary report from a trustworthy narrator with an accurate memory, while other scholars disagree with those conditions. For example, some stipulate that the hadith be checked against the Quran

and the Sunnah. Others stipulate that the narrator must be a jurist if the hadith conflicts with analogical reasoning based on established principles. Still others require that the hadith be widely transmitted and well known if it concerns matters commonly encountered. There are further conditions of this kind, discussed in their respective places.

The fifth reason:

The hadith may have reached a scholar, and its authenticity may have been established to his satisfaction, but he then forgot it. This can happen with both the Quran and the Sunnah, as in the well-known hadith:

“It is related of ‘Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) that he was asked about a man who enters a state of major ritual impurity while travelling but cannot find water. He replied, ‘He should not pray until he finds water.’ ‘Ammār said to him, ‘O Commander of the Faithful, do you not remember when you and I were with the camels and both entered a state of major ritual impurity? I rolled on the ground as an animal does, whereas you did not pray. I mentioned this to the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace), and he said, “It would have been enough for you to do this,” striking the ground with his hands and wiping his face and hands with them?’”

‘Umar said to him, “Fear Allah, ‘Ammār.” He replied, “If you wish, I will not relate it.” ‘Umar said, “Rather, we leave you to bear responsibility for what you have related.”

Here was a Sunnah that ‘Umar had witnessed but then forgotten, to the point that he issued a ruling contrary to it. ‘Ammār reminded him, but he did not remember. Yet he did not accuse ‘Ammār of lying; rather, he told him to relate it.

An even more striking example is that he addressed the people, saying, “If any man exceeds the dowers given to the wives and daughters of the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace), I shall have it returned.”

A woman said, “O Commander of the Faithful, why do you deprive us of something Allah has granted us?” Then she recited:

{لَا طَلَاقَ وَلَا عَتَاقَ فِي إغْلَاقٍ}
 فَإِنَّهُمْ قَدْ فَسَّرُوا الْإِغْلَاقَ بِالْإِكْرَاهِ وَمَنْ يُخَالِفُهُ لَا يَعْرِفُ هَذَا التَّفْسِيرَ. وَتَارَةً لِكَوْنِ مَعْنَاهُ فِي لُغَتِهِ وَعُرْفِهِ غَيْرَ مَعْنَاهُ فِي لُغَةِ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَهُوَ يَحْمِلُهُ عَلَى مَا يَفْهَمُهُ فِي لُغَتِهِ بِنَاءً عَلَى أَنَّ الْأَصْلَ بَقَاءُ اللُّغَةِ كَمَا سَمِعَ بَعْضُهُمْ آثَارًا فِي الرُّخْصَةِ فِي النَّبِيذِ فَظَنُّوهُ بَعْضَ أَنْوَاعِ الْمُسْكِرِ؛ لِأَنَّهُ لُغَتُهُمْ وَإِنَّمَا هُوَ مَا يُنْبَذُ لِتَحْلِيَةِ الْمَاءِ قَبْلَ أَنْ يَشْتَدَّ؛ فَإِنَّهُ جَاءَ مُفَسَّرًا فِي أَحَادِيثَ كَثِيرَةٍ صَحِيحَةٍ. وَسَمِعُوا لَفْظَ الْخَمْرِ فِي الْكِتَابِ وَالسُّنَّةِ فَاعْتَقَدُوهُ عَصِيرَ الْعِنَبِ الْمُشْتَدِّ خَاصَّةً بِنَاءً عَلَى أَنَّهُ كَذَلِكَ فِي
translated_text:
“And you have given one of them a great amount.”

‘Umar then accepted her point. He had memorized the verse but had forgotten it. Likewise, it is related that, on the day of the Battle of the Camel, ‘Alī reminded al-Zubayr of something the Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) had entrusted to them both. Al-Zubayr remembered it and withdrew from the fighting. Such instances are frequent among earlier and later generations.

The sixth reason:

The scholar may not understand what the hadith means. Sometimes this is because a word in it is unfamiliar to him, such as muzābana, muhāqala, mukhābara, mulāmasa, munābadha, gharar, and other unfamiliar terms whose interpretation scholars may dispute. Another example is the hadith traced back to the Prophet:

“Neither divorce nor emancipation is valid in a state of ighlāq.”

Some scholars have interpreted ighlāq as coercion, while someone who disagrees with them may be unaware of this interpretation.

At other times, a word’s meaning in the scholar’s own language and customary usage differs from its meaning in the language of the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace). He understands it according to his own usage, on the presumption that linguistic meanings remain unchanged. For example, some heard reports permitting nabīdh and thought it meant certain kinds of intoxicating drink, because that was its meaning in their usage. Yet what was intended was simply a drink made by steeping ingredients in water to sweeten it, before it becomes intoxicating, as explained in many authentic hadiths.

They also heard the word khamr in the Quran and the Sunnah and believed that it referred exclusively to intoxicating grape juice, on the assumption that this was its meaning in

اللُّغَةِ وَإِنْ كَانَ قَدْ جَاءَ مِنْ الْأَحَادِيثِ أَحَادِيثُ صَحِيحَةٌ تُبَيِّنُ أَنَّ الْخَمْرَ اسْمٌ لِكُلِّ شَرَابٍ مُسْكِرٍ. وَتَارَةً لِكَوْنِ اللَّفْظِ مُشْتَرِكًا أَوْ مُجْمَلًا؛ أَوْ مُتَرَدِّدًا بَيْنَ حَقِيقَةٍ وَمَجَازٍ؛

 عَلَى الْيَدِ إلَى الْإِبِطِ. وَتَارَةً لِكَوْنِ الدَّلَالَةِ مِنْ النَّصِّ خَفِيَّةً؛ فَإِنَّ جِهَاتِ دَلَالَاتِ الْأَقْوَالِ مُتَّسِعَةٌ جِدًّا يَتَفَاوَتُ النَّاسُ فِي إدْرَاكِهَا وَفَهْمِ وُجُوهِ الْكَلَامِ بِحَسَبِ مِنَحِ الْحَقِّ سُبْحَانَهُ وَمَوَاهِبِهِ ثُمَّ قَدْ يَعْرِفُهَا الرَّجُلُ مِنْ حَيْثُ الْعُمُومُ وَلَا يَتَفَطَّنُ لِكَوْنِ هَذَا الْمَعْنَى دَاخِلًا فِي ذَلِكَ الْعَامِّ ثُمَّ قَدْ يَتَفَطَّنُ لَهُ تَارَةً ثُمَّ يَنْسَاهُ بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ. وَهَذَا بَابٌ وَاسِعٌ جِدًّا لَا يُحِيطُ بِهِ إلَّا اللَّهُ وَقَدْ يَغْلَطُ الرَّجُلُ فَيَفْهَمُ مِنْ الْكَلَامِ مَا لَا تَحْتَمِلُهُ اللُّغَةُ الْعَرَبِيَّةُ الَّتِي بُعِثَ الرَّسُولُ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ بِهَا.
السَّبَبُ السَّابِعُ:
 اعْتِقَادُهُ أَنْ لَا دَلَالَةَ فِي الْحَدِيثِ. وَالْفَرْقُ بَيْنَ هَذَا وَبَيْنَ الَّذِي قَبْلَهُ أَنَّ الْأَوَّلَ لَمْ يَعْرِفْ جِهَةَ الدَّلَالَةِ وَالثَّانِي عَرَفَ
translated_text:
the language, even though authentic hadiths make clear that khamr is a name for every intoxicating drink.

At other times, a word has several meanings, is indeterminate, or admits both a literal and a figurative interpretation. The scholar adopts whichever meaning seems more likely to him, although the other is intended. Thus, some Companions initially understood the white thread and the black thread to mean actual cords. Others understood His words:

“Wipe your faces and hands”

to include the arms up to the armpits.

At other times, the way the text conveys its meaning is subtle. Statements can convey meaning in a great many ways, and people differ in their ability to perceive these and understand the various aspects of speech, according to the gifts and endowments bestowed by the True One—glorified is He. A person may understand a general indication without realizing that a particular meaning falls within its scope. He may also recognize this at one time, only to forget it later. This is an exceedingly vast subject, which none but Allah fully encompasses. A person may also err by understanding words in a sense that cannot be borne by the Arabic language with which the Messenger (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) was sent.

The seventh reason:

The scholar believes that the hadith does not indicate the ruling. The difference between this reason and the preceding one is that, in the former case, he did not recognize how the hadith indicated the ruling, whereas in the latter he has recognized

جِهَةَ الدَّلَالَةِ لَكِنْ اعْتَقَدَ أَنَّهَا لَيْسَتْ دَلَالَةً صَحِيحَةً بِأَنْ يَكُونَ لَهُ مِنْ الْأُصُولِ مَا يَرُدُّ تِلْكَ الدَّلَالَةَ سَوَاءٌ كَانَتْ فِي نَفْسِ الْأَمْرِ صَوَابًا أَوْ خَطَأً مِثْلَ أَنْ يَعْتَقِدَ أَنَّ الْعَامَّ الْمَخْصُوصَ لَيْسَ بِحُجَّةِ وَأَنَّ الْمَفْهُومَ لَيْسَ بِحُجَّةِ وَأَنَّ الْعُمُومَ الْوَارِدَ عَلَى سَبَبٍ مَقْصُورٍ عَلَى سَبَبِهِ أَوْ أَنَّ الْأَمْرَ الْمُجَرَّدَ لَا يَقْتَضِي الْوُجُوبَ؛ أَوْ لَا يَقْتَضِي الْفَوْرَ أَوْ أَنَّ الْمُعَرَّفَ بِاللَّامِ لَا عُمُومَ لَهُ أَوْ أَنَّ الْأَفْعَالَ الْمَنْفِيَّةَ لَا تَنْفِي ذَوَاتِهَا وَلَا جَمِيعَ أَحْكَامِهَا أَوْ أَنَّ الْمُقْتَضِي لَا عُمُومَ لَهُ؛

 هَلْ هِيَ مِنْ ذَلِكَ الْجِنْسِ أَمْ لَا؟ مِثْلَ أَنْ يَعْتَقِدَ أَنَّ هَذَا اللَّفْظَ الْمُعَيَّنَ مُجْمَلٌ بِأَنْ يَكُونَ مُشْتَرَكًا لَا دَلَالَةَ تُعَيِّنُ أَحَدَ مَعْنَيَيْهِ أَوْ غَيْرَ ذَلِكَ.
السَّبَبُ الثَّامِنُ:
 اعْتِقَادُهُ أَنَّ تِلْكَ الدَّلَالَةَ قَدْ عَارَضَهَا مَا دَلَّ عَلَى أَنَّهَا لَيْسَتْ مُرَادَةً مِثْلَ مُعَارَضَةِ الْعَامِّ بِخَاصِّ أَوْ الْمُطْلَقِ بِمُقَيَّدِ أَوْ الْأَمْرِ الْمُطْلَقِ بِمَا يَنْفِي الْوُجُوبَ أَوْ الْحَقِيقَةَ بِمَا يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْمَجَازِ إلَى أَنْوَاعِ الْمُعَارَضَاتِ. وَهُوَ بَابٌ وَاسِعٌ أَيْضًا؛ فَإِنَّ تَعَارُضَ دَلَالَاتِ الْأَقْوَالِ وَتَرْجِيحَ بَعْضِهَا عَلَى بَعْضٍ بَحْرٌ خِضَمٌّ.
translated_text:
how the hadith indicates the ruling, but believes that this indication is invalid because he holds principles that rule it out, whether those principles are in fact correct or mistaken. For example, he may believe that a general expression whose scope has been partially restricted has no probative force; that an implied meaning has no probative force; that a general expression occasioned by a particular circumstance applies only to that circumstance; that an unqualified command does not entail obligation, or does not require immediate compliance; that an expression made definite by the definite article does not have general scope; that statements negating acts negate neither the acts themselves nor all their legal effects; or that textual implication does not establish generality, so that no general scope is claimed for unstated elements and implied meanings. There are many other matters of this kind that could be discussed at length.

Indeed, disputed questions making up half of legal theory fall under this heading, although abstract principles do not encompass all the disputed forms of indication. This heading also includes particular instances of the various classes of indication: does a given instance belong to that class or not? For example, a scholar may believe that a particular expression is indeterminate because it has two meanings and there is no indication specifying which is intended, or for some other reason.

The eighth reason:

The scholar believes that this indication is countered by evidence showing that it is not intended. Examples include countering a general expression with a specific one, an unrestricted expression with a qualified one, an unqualified command with evidence negating obligation, or a literal meaning with evidence indicating a figurative meaning, along with other forms of conflicting evidence. This, too, is a vast subject: conflicts between the meanings conveyed by statements, and the grounds for giving some precedence over others, constitute a vast, deep ocean.

السَّبَبُ التَّاسِعُ:
 اعْتِقَادُهُ أَنَّ الْحَدِيثَ مُعَارَضٌ بِمَا يَدُلُّ عَلَى ضَعْفِهِ؛ أَوْ نَسْخِهِ؛

 مَعَ عِلْمِهِ بِأَنَّ النَّاسَ قَدْ قَالُوا خِلَافَهُ حَتَّى إنَّ مِنْهُمْ مَنْ يُعَلِّقُ الْقَوْلَ فَيَقُولُ:
 إنْ كَانَ فِي الْمَسْأَلَةِ إجْمَاعٌ فَهُوَ أَحَقُّ مَا يَتْبَعُ وَإِلَّا فَالْقَوْلُ عِنْدِي كَذَا وَكَذَا
translated_text:
The ninth reason:

The scholar believes that the hadith is countered by evidence indicating its weakness, its abrogation, or—if it admits of interpretation—the need to interpret it differently. This opposing evidence is of a kind unanimously accepted as admissible, such as a Quranic verse, another hadith, or consensus. This takes two forms:

The first: He believes that the opposing evidence outweighs the hadith overall, so that one of these three explanations must apply, without specifying which. Sometimes he identifies one of them, believing that the hadith has been abrogated or must be interpreted differently. He may, however, be mistaken about abrogation, taking what came later to have come earlier. He may also err in interpretation by assigning the hadith a meaning its wording cannot bear, or one that other evidence rules out.

When he counters the hadith on general grounds, the opposing evidence may not actually support his contention. The opposing hadith may also fall short of the first in the strength of its chain of transmission or its text. The reasons mentioned earlier, along with others, come into play here with regard to the first hadith. Moreover, the claimed consensus usually amounts merely to not knowing of anyone who disagrees.

We have found eminent scholars adopting positions on the grounds that they knew of no dissenting view, even though, in their own judgment, the apparent meaning of the evidence entailed the opposite. Yet a scholar cannot introduce a position that he knows of no one having held, while knowing that others have held the contrary. Some even make their position conditional, saying: “If there is consensus on the matter, it has the strongest claim to be followed; otherwise, my view is such and such.”

 وَقَبُولُهَا مَحْفُوظٌ عَنْ عَلِيٍّ وَأَنَسٍ وشريح وَغَيْرِهِمْ وَيَقُولُ:

translated_text:
An example is someone who says: “I know of no one who has allowed a slave’s testimony.” Yet its acceptance is reliably reported from ʿAlī, Anas, Shurayh, and others. He also says: “They unanimously agree that a partially emancipated slave does not inherit.” Yet allowing such a person to inherit is reliably reported from ʿAlī and Ibn Masʿūd, and there is a hadith graded good on this matter from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

Another says: “I know of no one who has made invoking blessings upon the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, obligatory during prayer.” Yet this obligation is reliably reported from Abū Jaʿfar al-Bāqir.

This is because many scholars’ knowledge extends no further than the views of the scholars they encountered in their own lands and those of certain other groups. Thus, many earlier scholars knew only the views of the scholars of Medina and Kufa, while many later scholars know only the views of two or three of the imams whose teachings are followed. Whatever falls outside those views is, in their judgment, contrary to consensus: they know of no one who holds it, and they have continually heard the opposite. Such a scholar cannot bring himself to follow a hadith that conflicts with these views, either because he fears that doing so might violate consensus or because he believes that it does—and consensus is the strongest proof.

This is the excuse of many people for much of what they leave aside. Some are genuinely excused in this regard; others are excused in it, yet are not, in reality, excused. The same applies to many of the reasons discussed before and after this one.

The tenth reason:

He counters the hadith with evidence indicating its weakness, its abrogation, or the need to interpret it differently

translated_text:
which others do not regard as counterevidence, either in itself or as a category, or which does not in fact constitute stronger counterevidence. An example is the way many Kufan scholars counter an authentic hadith with the apparent meaning of the Quran, believing that the Quran’s apparent meaning—such as the general scope of its wording—takes precedence over the explicit wording of the hadith. A scholar may also regard a meaning as apparent when it is not, given the many ways in which statements convey meaning.

For this reason, they rejected the hadith concerning one witness together with an oath, although other scholars know that nothing in the Quran’s apparent meaning precludes issuing a judgment on the basis of one witness and an oath. Even if it did, these other scholars hold that the Sunnah explains the Quran. Al-Shāfi'ī has a well-known discussion of this principle, and Ahmad has his celebrated treatise refuting those who claim that the Quran’s apparent meaning suffices without the explanation provided by the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. In it, he presents more evidence than there is room to recount here.

Another instance is rejecting a report that restricts the general scope of the Book, qualifies its unrestricted wording, or adds to it. Those who take this position believe that an addition to a text, like the qualification of unrestricted wording, constitutes abrogation, and that restricting the scope of general wording also constitutes abrogation.

Another example is the way a group of Medinan scholars counter an authentic hadith with the practice of the people of Medina, on the premise that they unanimously agree on a position contrary to the report, and that their consensus constitutes evidence taking precedence over it. This includes departing from the hadiths concerning the right to cancel a sale before the parties separate, on the basis of this principle, even though most scholars may well demonstrate

that the Medinan scholars differed on that issue, and that even if they had reached a consensus while others disagreed with them, the authoritative proof would lie in the report.

Another example is the way some scholars from both cities counter certain hadiths with clear analogical reasoning, on the premise that universal principles cannot be overturned by a report of this kind. There are other forms of counterargument as well, whether those advancing them are right or mistaken.

These ten reasons are evident. In the case of many hadiths, a scholar may have grounds for not acting upon a hadith of which we are unaware. The avenues to knowledge are vast, and we have not discovered everything within the minds of scholars. A scholar may or may not disclose his evidence; if he does, it may or may not reach us; and if it reaches us, we may or may not understand how it supports his argument, whether or not that evidence is actually sound.

Yet, although we acknowledge this possibility, we may not abandon a position whose evidence has become clear through an authentic hadith, and which a group of scholars has adopted, in favor of another position held by a scholar who might possess something that counters this evidence—even if he is more learned. For scholars’ opinions are more susceptible to error than the revealed proofs: the revealed proofs constitute Allah’s binding evidence against all His servants, unlike a scholar’s opinion.

and a revealed proof cannot be erroneous when no other proof opposes it, whereas a scholar’s opinion is not so. If it were permissible to act on this possibility, we would be left with none of the proofs to which such a possibility could apply. The point, however, is that the scholar himself may be excused for not acting upon it, while we are excused for declining to follow him in that omission. Allah, Exalted is He, says:

“That was a nation that has passed away; theirs is what they earned”—and so on to the end of the verse.

He, Exalted is He, also says:

“If you disagree over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger.”

No one may counter a hadith from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, with anyone else’s statement. Thus, when a man asked Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, about an issue, he answered him with a hadith. The man replied, “But Abū Bakr and ʿUmar said…” Ibn ʿAbbās responded, “Stones may soon rain down upon you from heaven! I say, ‘The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said,’ and you say, ‘Abū Bakr and ʿUmar said’?”

Since a scholar may refrain from acting upon a hadith for some of these reasons, then, when an authentic hadith establishes that something is lawful or unlawful, or lays down a ruling, it is not permissible to believe that a scholar who does not act upon it—one of those whose reasons we have described—will be punished for declaring the unlawful lawful, declaring the lawful unlawful, or judging by something other than what Allah has revealed.

We know of no disagreement within the Muslim community concerning this, apart from a view attributed to certain Muʿtazilites of Baghdad, such as al-Marīsī and his like: they claimed that a scholar who errs in exercising independent legal judgment is punished for his error.

This is because the application of the threatened punishment to someone who commits a forbidden act is conditional upon his knowing that it is forbidden, or being able to acquire that knowledge. Someone who grew up in the desert or recently embraced Islam, and committed a forbidden act without knowing that it was forbidden, incurs no sin and is not subjected to a prescribed punishment—even if he did not base his belief in its permissibility on any scriptural evidence. Someone whom the hadith prohibiting the act has not reached, and who relies on scriptural evidence for its permissibility, is therefore all the more deserving of being excused.

Indeed, such a scholar is rewarded and praised for his exercise of independent judgment. Allah, Glorified is He, says:

“And David and Solomon”—through to His words—“and knowledge.”

He thus singled out Solomon for understanding, while praising both for judgment and knowledge.

In the two Sahīh collections, ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀs, may Allah be pleased with him, relates that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When a judge exercises independent judgment and is correct, he receives two rewards; when he exercises independent judgment and errs, he receives one reward.”

It is thus clear that a scholar who exercises independent judgment receives a reward despite his error. He is rewarded for his effort, and his error is forgiven, because reaching the correct conclusion in every individual ruling is either impossible or exceedingly difficult. Allah, Exalted is He, says:

“He has placed no hardship upon you in religion.”

He, Exalted is He, also says:

“Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you.”

Likewise, “he did not impose retaliation, blood money, or expiation upon Usāmah ibn Zayd when he killed the man who said, ‘There is no god but Allah,’ during the al-Hariqāt expedition.” Usāmah believed that killing him was permissible because he considered the man’s acceptance of Islam invalid, even though killing him was forbidden.

The early generations and the majority of jurists applied this principle: when rebels shed the blood of those on the just side, believing it permissible on the basis of a tenable interpretation, they incur no liability for retaliation, blood money, or expiation, even though killing and fighting those people is forbidden.

This condition we have mentioned for a threatened punishment to apply need not be stated in every address, since knowledge of it is firmly established in people’s hearts. Likewise, the promise of reward for a deed is conditional upon its being performed sincerely for Allah and not being nullified by apostasy; yet this condition is not mentioned in every hadith containing a promise.

Furthermore, even when the grounds for a threatened punishment are assumed to be present, an impediment may prevent its application. translated_text:
an intercessor whose intercession is accepted, and the mercy of the Most Merciful. If all these means are absent—and they will be absent only in the case of someone who defiantly rebels and strays from Allah as a camel bolts from its owners—then the threatened punishment will befall him. For a threat of punishment essentially states that a particular deed is a cause of a particular punishment. This establishes that the deed is forbidden and reprehensible. But the claim that everyone in whom that cause is present must necessarily suffer its consequence is certainly false, since that consequence depends upon the requisite condition being fulfilled and all impediments being removed.

To clarify this, anyone who does not act upon a hadith falls into one of three categories:

First, his not acting upon it may be permissible by the agreement of the Muslims. This applies, for example, to someone whom the hadith has not reached and who has not been negligent in seeking it when needing to issue a fatwa or a judgment, as we have mentioned concerning the Rightly Guided Caliphs and others. No Muslim doubts that such a person incurs no blame for not acting upon it.

Second, his not acting upon it may be impermissible. This scarcely ever occurs among the leading scholars, Allah willing. Yet there may be grounds to fear that some scholars have an inadequate grasp of a particular issue: a scholar may express an opinion without sufficient grounds, even though he has examined the issue and exercised scholarly judgment; or he may fall short in examining the evidence and express an opinion before his inquiry has run its full course, although he is relying on an argument; or a habit or personal motive may prevail over him, preventing him from examining the matter fully and considering what conflicts with the evidence he has, even if he has spoken only

on the basis of scholarly judgment and reasoning from evidence. For the extent to which scholarly inquiry must be pursued may not be clear to the scholar exercising judgment. This is why scholars feared such shortcomings, lest the requisite scholarly effort had not been made in that particular issue. These are sins. Yet punishment for a sin overtakes only someone who has not repented, and it may be averted through seeking forgiveness, doing good, affliction, intercession, and mercy.

This discussion does not include someone so overcome and overpowered by desire that he champions what he knows to be false, or someone who declares an opinion definitively right or wrong without knowing the evidence for or against it. Both such people are in the Fire, as the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Judges are of three kinds: two are in the Fire and one is in Paradise. The one in Paradise is a man who knew the truth and judged accordingly. As for the two in the Fire, one is a man who judged between people in ignorance, and the other is a man who knew the truth but judged contrary to it.”

The same applies to those who issue fatwas. Nevertheless, as we have explained, there are also impediments that prevent the threatened punishment from befalling a particular individual. Thus, if we suppose that some such conduct occurred on the part of certain individual scholars whom the Muslim community holds in high esteem—although this is unlikely or has not occurred—none of them would lack at least one of these grounds for averting punishment. Even if it occurred, it would not undermine their overall standing as leading scholars. For we do not regard these scholars as infallible; rather, they may commit sins. Even so, we hope that they will attain the highest ranks, because of the righteous deeds and noble qualities with which Allah has distinguished them

The same applies to the Companions regarding the scholarly judgments they exercised in issuing fatwas, deciding cases, the bloodshed that occurred between them, and other matters.

Nevertheless, knowing that someone who refrains from acting upon a hadith in the circumstances described is excused—indeed, rewarded—does not prevent us from following authentic hadiths for which we know of no countervailing evidence that would override them, or from believing that the Muslim community is obliged to act upon them and that they must be conveyed. This is something about which scholars do not disagree.

These hadiths fall into two categories: those whose import is definitive, being certain in both transmission and meaning—that is, we know with certainty that the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said it, and that he intended it to apply to the case in question—and those whose import is apparent but not definitive.

As for the first category, one must accept what it establishes as knowledge and act accordingly. There is no disagreement among scholars about this as a general principle. They may, however, disagree over particular reports: Is their transmission certain or not? Is their meaning definitive or not? An example is their disagreement concerning a non-mass-transmitted report that the Muslim community has accepted and affirmed as true, or upon which it has agreed to act. Jurists generally, and most speculative theologians, hold that such a report yields certain knowledge, whereas some groups of speculative theologians hold that it does not. This rests on the principle that a report yielding certain knowledge may do so because of the number of transmitters, their qualities, the act of reporting itself, the transmitter’s own perception of the matter, or the subject matter reported. A small number of people may convey a report that yields certain knowledge because their religious integrity and accurate retention make them secure against lying or error, whereas a report conveyed by several times that number of other people may not yield certain knowledge. This is undoubtedly the truth, and it is the position of the majority of jurists and hadith scholars, as well as some groups of speculative theologians.

Other groups of speculative theologians and some jurists hold that whenever a report conveyed by a given number of people yields certain knowledge about one matter, a report conveyed by the same number yields certain knowledge about every matter. This is unquestionably false, but this is not the place to explain why.

Rather, each may lead sometimes to certain knowledge and sometimes to probable belief, even when grounds for certain knowledge from both happen to coincide, or grounds for certain knowledge from one coincide with grounds for probable belief from the other. Those with greater knowledge of reports may be certain of the truth of reports whose truth others less knowledgeable cannot establish with certainty.

Sometimes scholars differ over whether a hadith’s meaning is conclusive because they disagree over whether its meaning is unequivocal or merely presumptive. If it is presumptive, does it contain anything that rules out the less likely interpretation? This too is a vast subject. Some scholars may be certain of what particular hadiths signify, while others are not: either because they know that the hadith admits only that meaning, because they know that interpreting it in the alternative sense is precluded, or because of other evidence that establishes certainty.

As for the second category, that which is presumptive, it must be acted upon in matters of Islamic law, according to the agreement of scholars of recognized authority. A similar example is the practice of most scholars in citing as evidence Quranic readings authentically transmitted from some of the Companions, even though they are not found in the codex of ‘Uthmān, may Allah be pleased with him. These readings concern both practice and belief, and constitute authentic solitary reports. The scholars therefore cited them to establish practical rulings, but did not establish them as Quran, since their status as Quran is a matter that can only be established with certainty.

Most jurists, however—and this is the position of the early generations generally—hold that these hadiths are authoritative evidence for all the threats of punishment they contain. The Companions of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the Successors after them consistently affirmed the threatened punishment on the basis of these hadiths, just as they established practical rulings on their basis. On the strength of this argument, most scholars have given precedence to evidence indicating prohibition over evidence indicating permissibility. On this same basis, many jurists have relied on the argument from precaution in numerous rulings. As for exercising precaution in one’s actions, rational people virtually agree that it is generally commendable. Thus, if his fear of error in rejecting belief in the threatened punishment is balanced by his fear of error in not holding this belief, two unopposed arguments remain: the evidence requiring belief in it, and the deliverance attained through such belief.

No one may say: “The absence of conclusive evidence for the threatened punishment is evidence of its nonexistence, just as with the absence of mass-transmitted reports establishing readings beyond those contained in the Quranic codex.” For the absence of evidence does not establish the nonexistence of what it would indicate. Whoever categorically denies any matter of knowledge merely because there is no conclusive evidence for its existence—as is the approach of a group of speculative theologians—is plainly mistaken.

However, if we know that the existence of something necessarily entails the existence of evidence for it, and we know that this evidence is absent, we can categorically conclude that the thing entailing it does not exist. For the absence of a necessary consequence establishes the absence of that which entails it. We know that there are abundant motives for transmitting Allah’s Book and His religion, and that the Muslim community cannot collectively conceal what needs to be transmitted as universally binding proof. Thus, since neither a sixth prayer nor an additional surah has been transmitted on a widespread basis, we know with certainty that neither exists.

translated_text:
Threats of punishment, however, do not fall into this category. Not every threat attached to an act must be conveyed through mass-transmitted reports, just as mass transmission is not required for the ruling concerning that act. Thus, hadiths containing threats must be acted upon according to their import: one must believe that whoever commits the act is threatened with that punishment. Its actual infliction, however, depends upon certain conditions, and there are impediments that may prevent it.

This principle becomes clear through examples. It is authentically reported that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Allah has cursed the one who consumes ribā (usury), the one who pays it, its two witnesses, and its scribe.”

It is also authentically reported through several chains that he said to someone who exchanged two sāʿ for one, hand to hand:

“Alas! That is ribā itself!”

He also said:

“Wheat for wheat is ribā unless exchanged on the spot”—and the hadith continues.

This entails that both kinds of ribā—that involving an excess and that involving deferment—are included in the hadith.

Yet some people received the Prophet’s statement, peace and blessings be upon him:

“Ribā is only in deferment,”

and consequently regarded exchanging two sāʿ for one, hand to hand, as permissible. These included Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him, and his companions: Abū al-Shaʿthāʾ, ʿAtāʾ, Tāwūs, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, ʿIkrimah, and other eminent Meccans who were among the finest of this community in knowledge and practice. No Muslim may believe that the curse upon those who consume ribā befalls any one of them individually, or anyone who followed their opinion where such following was permissible. For they acted on an interpretation that was, in general, defensible.

translated_text:
The same applies to reports that a group of eminent Medinans engaged in anal intercourse, despite the report narrated by Abū Dāwūd that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Whoever has intercourse with a woman in her anus has disbelieved in what was revealed to Muhammad.”

Would any Muslim consider it permissible to say that so-and-so and so-and-so disbelieved in what was revealed to Muhammad?

Likewise, it is authentically reported from him, peace and blessings be upon him, that “he cursed ten people in connection with khamr (intoxicating drink): the one who presses it, the one who has it pressed, and the one who drinks it.”

It is also authentically reported through several chains that he said:

“Every drink that intoxicates is khamr.”

And he said:

“Every intoxicant is khamr.”

ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, addressed the Emigrants and the Helpers from the Prophet’s pulpit, peace and blessings be upon him, saying: “Khamr is whatever clouds the mind.” Allah revealed the prohibition of khamr, and the occasion for that revelation was what they used to drink in Medina. Their only drink was fadīkh, a drink made from crushed unripe dates; they had no grape wine at all.

Yet some Kufans, among the finest of this community in knowledge and practice, believed that only drink made from grapes was khamr, and that, for infused drinks made from anything other than grapes and dates, only the quantity that caused intoxication was forbidden. They would drink what they believed to be lawful.

It is therefore impermissible to say that these men fall under the threat of punishment, because of the excuse underlying their interpretation or because of other impediments. Nor may it be said that the drink they consumed was not among the khamr whose drinker is cursed. For the particular circumstance that occasioned a general statement must necessarily fall within its scope, and there was no grape wine in Medina. Furthermore, “the Prophet

peace and blessings be upon him, cursed the seller of khamr.” One of the Companions sold khamr, and when news of this reached ʿUmar, he said:

“May Allah confound so-and-so! Did he not know that the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said: ‘Allah cursed the Jews: animal fats were forbidden to them, yet they sold them and consumed the proceeds’?”

That Companion did not know that selling it was forbidden. Yet ʿUmar’s knowledge of his ignorance did not prevent him from explaining the punishment for this sin, so that he and others would refrain from it once they learned of its prohibition.

The Prophet also cursed the one who presses it and the one who has it pressed. Yet many jurists permit a man to press grapes for another person even when he knows that the latter intends to make khamr from them. This is an explicit text cursing the one who presses it, although we know that the ruling does not apply to an excused person because an impediment prevents its application.

Likewise, in several authentic hadiths, he cursed the woman who attaches hair extensions and the woman who has them attached. Yet some jurists merely regard this as disliked.

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Whoever drinks from silver vessels is only gulping the fire of Hell into his belly.”

Yet some jurists regard this as disliked rather than forbidden.

Likewise, he said, peace and blessings be upon him:

“When two Muslims confront one another with their swords, both the killer and the one killed are in the Fire.”

This hadith must be applied in establishing the prohibition of fighting believers

without right. Yet we know that those who fought at the Camel and Siffīn are not in the Fire, for both sides had excuses and an interpretive basis for fighting, as well as good deeds that prevented the grounds for punishment from taking effect.

He said, peace and blessings be upon him, in an authentic hadith:

“There are three whom Allah will neither speak to nor look at on the Day of Resurrection, nor will He purify them, and theirs will be a painful punishment: a man who has surplus water but withholds it from a wayfarer—Allah will say to him, ‘Today I withhold My bounty from you, just as you withheld the surplus of what your hands did not produce’; a man who pledges allegiance to a ruler solely for worldly gain—if he is given something, he is pleased, but if he is not, he is displeased; and a man who, after the afternoon prayer, swears falsely concerning a commodity that he had been offered more for it than he actually had.”

This is a grave warning against anyone who withholds his surplus water, although some scholars permit a man to do so. This disagreement does not prevent us from believing that it is forbidden, citing the hadith as evidence. Nor does the existence of the hadith prevent us from believing that someone who adopts a different interpretation is excused in this matter and is not subject to this warning.

He also said, peace and blessings be upon him:

“May Allah curse the man who marries a woman to make her lawful again for her former husband, and the man for whom this is done.”

This is an authentic hadith transmitted from him through several routes, and also from his Companions. Nevertheless, some scholars have held such a marriage to be valid without qualification. Others have held it to be valid if this purpose is not stipulated in the contract. They have well-known grounds for being excused in this matter. According to the first group, analogy with established principles dictates that a marriage is not invalidated by stipulations, just as it is not invalidated by either of the two considerations being unknown.
