He may be answered as follows:

When you say, “If the expression were literal in the applications mentioned, it would be equivocal,” what do you mean by “equivocal”? If you mean equivocation in the strict sense—that an expression signifies two meanings without signifying any meaning common to them—some people dispute that this exists within a single language based on a single assignment of meanings. They say that it occurs only in two separate settings, as when one man gives his son a name and another gives his son that same name.

They do not say that giving heavenly bodies such names as Suhayl, al-Mushtarī, the Lion’s Heart, the Eagle, and the like involves a second assignment, whereby the Arabs and others who named them gave them transferred names, like transferred proper names—as when a man names his son Kalb (“dog”), Asad (“lion”), Namir (“leopard”), Bahr (“sea”), and so forth.

No reasonable person disputes equivocation in this sense. Yet it is clear that this is a second assignment. This is not altered by the way assigned proper names signify their referents, or by the distinguishing mark in figurative usage. In giving a name, one may intend the bearer to possess the quality it signifies: one may take its meaning as a good omen, seek to ward off the evil eye, name him after someone dear to oneself—a father, a teacher, or someone distinguished—or choose a name with a praiseworthy meaning, such as ‘Abd Allāh, ‘Abd al-Rahmān, Muhammad, or Ahmad.

In any event, this is a second assignment of the name to this bearer, and in this respect the expression becomes equivocal. Hence, with proper names, it is necessary to distinguish a person by his father’s name, or by his grandfather’s name together with his father’s if his own name and his father’s do not suffice to distinguish him. When these suffice, one confines oneself to them, as the Prophet did

translated_text:
—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—when drawing up the peace treaty between himself and Quraysh, in which he wrote:

“This is what Muhammad ibn ‘Abd Allāh has agreed upon with Suhayl ibn ‘Amr.”

This was after the polytheists had refused to write “Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah.” He—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—is distinguished before Allah by his status as Messenger and Prophet. When he changed from being identified by the description that requires people to accept his truthfulness and believe in him, he agreed to their identifying him by his father’s name.

The point is that some people say that whenever an expression has two meanings within a single language, those meanings necessarily share something in common. Indeed, they maintain this even regarding letters, holding that there is a correspondence between them and their meanings which motivates the speaker to assign a particular expression to a particular meaning.

No reasonable person has ever said that an expression signifies its meaning by itself, without anyone intending it to do so, and that this signification is an inseparable attribute of the expression. There is therefore no basis for the objection: “If an expression bore a correspondence to its meaning, it would not differ from one nation to another.” For matters involving choice, such as expressions and customary actions, do possess correspondences that motivate an agent acting by choice, even though they vary according to place, time, and circumstances.

Natural phenomena that do not result from a creature’s choice also vary. Heat and cold, blackness and whiteness, and similar natural phenomena vary according to the natural characteristics of different lands. Matters involving choice—food, drink, clothing, housing, mounts, marriage, and so forth—vary according to people’s customs

الِاشْتِقَاقُ الْأَصْغَرُ:

وَالثَّانِي الِاشْتِقَاقُ الْأَوْسَطُ:

translated_text:
, even though these are matters of choice and have their own correspondences. Thus, some of these things suit people in one place and time but do not suit people in another time. People choose things in winter and in cold countries that they do not choose in summer and in hot countries, yet in each case there is a correspondence motivating their choice. In hot weather, they choose light foods and fruit that are easy to digest, because their insides are cold and their digestive faculties weak. In winter and in cold countries, they choose heavier foods instead, because the digestive heat within them is strong; or because winter is a time when the interiors of inanimate things, animals, trees, and other things grow warm while their exteriors grow cold. This is because the air grows cold in winter, and like is drawn to like: cold is drawn towards the air, leaving the interiors warm. In hot weather, the air grows warm, drawing heat towards it and leaving the interiors cold. Springs are therefore cold in summer because the earth’s interior is cold, and grow warm in winter because the earth’s interior is warm.

The point here is that it is not ‘Abbād ibn Sulaymān alone, but many people—indeed, most discerning scholars of Arabic and rhetoric—who affirm a correspondence between expressions and meanings. They divide derivation into three types:

Minor derivation: two words share the same root letters in the same order, as in ‘ilm (knowledge), ‘ālim (one who knows), and ‘alīm (very knowledgeable).

The second is intermediate derivation: the two words share the same root letters, but not in the same order

translated_text:
, as in summiya (was named) and wusima (was marked).

The Kufans’ statement that ism (name) is derived from sima (mark) is correct if this kind of derivation is intended. If, however, what is intended is correspondence in both the letters and their order, then the Basrans’ view—that it is derived from sumuww (elevation)—is correct. For the verb is sammāhu (he named him), not wasamahu (he marked him); its diminutive is sumayy, not wusaym; and its plural is asmā’, not awsām.

The third kind of derivation involves correspondence in some letters but not others. More specifically, the remaining letters may belong to the same class—for example, they may be letters articulated in the throat, as in hazara, ‘azara, and azara. The root material conveys strength, while hā’, ‘ayn, and hamza belong to the same class insofar as they are throat letters.

This also includes alternation between a weak radical and a doubled consonant, as in taqaddā al-bāzī (the hawk swooped) and taqaddada. Another example is the statement that surriyya (concubine) is derived from sirr, meaning sexual intercourse. Likewise, Abū Ja‘far al-Bāqir said: “Al-‘āmma (the common people) is derived from al-‘amā (blindness).” Another example is their statement that damān (guarantee) is derived from damm (joining), meaning joining one party’s legal liability to another’s.

translated_text:
whether one is the original and the other its derivative. In this case, derivation denotes a different kind of relationship between the two expressions. Derivation may also mean that one precedes the other and is its source, just as a father is the source of his child.

According to the first meaning, whether one says that the verb is derived from the verbal noun or that the verbal noun is derived from the verb, both positions—that of the Basrans and that of the Kufans—are correct. According to the second meaning, however, if logical order is intended, the Basrans’ position is more correct, since the verbal noun denotes only the action, whereas the verb denotes both the action and time. If the order of actual existence is intended—meaning that one came into existence before the other—there is no fixed rule: speakers may have used the verb before the verbal noun, or the verbal noun before the verb. They have also used verbs without verbal nouns, such as budd, and verbal nouns without verbs, such as “wayh” (alas) and “wayl” (woe).

They may also predominantly use a verb together with the verbal noun belonging to another verb, as in the case of hubb (love). Its usual verb is the four-letter form: ahabba, yuhibbu (he loved, he loves), while its usual verbal noun is hubb rather than ihbāb. For the active participle, they say muhibb (one who loves), not hābb. For the passive participle, they say mahbūb (beloved), and they use muhibb only as the active participle. By morphological analogy, one would expect ahabbahu ihbāban (he loved him), just as one says a‘lamahu i‘lāman (he informed him).

 إمَّا كَثْرَةُ الِاسْتِعْمَالِ: وَإِمَّا نَقْلُ بَعْضِ الْأَلْفَاظِ؛ وَإِمَّا غَيْرُ ذَلِكَ كَمَا يَعْرِفُ ذَلِكَ أَهْلُ النَّحْوِ وَالتَّصْرِيفِ؛ إذْ كَانَتْ أَقْوَى الْحَرَكَاتِ هِيَ الضَّمَّةَ؛ وَأَخَفُّهَا الْفَتْحَةَ؛ وَالْكَسْرَةُ مُتَوَسِّطَةٌ بَيْنَهُمَا؛
 فَجَاءَتْ اللُّغَةُ عَلَى ذَلِكَ مِنْ الْأَلْفَاظِ الْمُعْرَبَةِ وَالْمَبْنِيَّةِ فَمَا كَانَ مِنْ الْمُعْرَبَاتِ عُمْدَةٌ فِي الْكَلَامِ لَا بُدَّ لَهُ مِنْهُ:
 كَانَ لَهُ الْمَرْفُوعُ؛ كَالْمُبْتَدَأِ وَالْخَبَرِ وَالْفَاعِلِ وَالْمَفْعُولِ الْقَائِمِ مَقَامَهُ وَمَا كَانَ فَضْلَةً كَانَ لَهُ النَّصْبُ؛ كَالْمَفْعُولِ وَالْحَالِ وَالتَّمْيِيز.
 وَمَا كَانَ مُتَوَسِّطًا بَيْنَهُمَا لِكَوْنِهِ يُضَافُ إلَيْهِ الْعُمْدَةُ تَارَةً وَالْفَضْلَةُ تَارَةً:
 كَانَ لَهُ الْجَرُّ وَهُوَ الْمُضَافُ إلَيْهِ. وَكَذَلِكَ فِي الْمَبْنِيَّاتِ؛
 مِثْلَ مَا يَقُولُونَ فِي أَيْنَ وَكَيْفَ:
 بُنِيَتْ عَلَى الْفَتْحِ طَلَبًا لِلتَّخْفِيفِ لِأَجْلِ الْيَاءِ. وَكَذَلِكَ فِي حَرَكَاتِ الْأَلْفَاظِ الْمَبْنِيَّةِ الْأَقْوَى لَهُ الضَّمُّ وَمَا دُونَهُ لَهُ الْفَتْحُ؛
 فَيَقُولُونَ:
 كَرِهَ الشَّيْءَ وَالْكَرَاهِيَةُ يَقُولُونَ فِيهَا: كَرْهًا بِالْفَتْحِ كَمَا قَالَ تَعَالَى: 
{وَلَهُ أَسْلَمَ مَنْ فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ طَوْعًا وَكَرْهًا}
 وَقَالَ: 
{ائْتِيَا طَوْعًا أَوْ كَرْهًا}
 .
 وَكَذَلِكَ الْكَسْرُ مَعَ الْفَتْحِ فَيَقُولُونَ فِي الشَّيْءِ الْمَذْبُوحِ وَالْمَنْهُوبِ:
 ذِبْحٌ ونهب بِالْكَسْرِ كَمَا قَالَ تَعَالَى: 
{وَفَدَيْنَاهُ بِذِبْحٍ عَظِيمٍ}
 وَكَمَا فِي الْحَدِيثِ 
{أُتِيَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ بنهب إبِلٍ}
 وَفِي الْمَثَلِ السَّائِرِ: 
" أَسْمَعُ جَعْجَعَةً وَلَا أَرَى طِحْنًا "
 بِالْكَسْرِ؛
 أَيْ:
 وَلَا أَرَى
translated_text:
And this too has causes known to grammarians and morphologists: frequent usage, the transfer of certain word forms, or other factors. As specialists in grammar and morphology know, the strongest vowel is damma (u), the lightest is fatha (a), and kasra (i) lies between them.

The language follows this pattern in both inflected and uninflected words. An inflected word that constitutes an indispensable core element of the sentence takes the nominative, as with the subject and predicate of a nominal sentence, the subject of a verb, and the object that takes its place in a passive construction. A supplementary element takes the accusative, as with the object, the circumstantial qualifier, and the accusative of specification. What occupies an intermediate position—because either a core element or a supplementary element may be annexed to it—takes the genitive: this is the second term of a possessive construction.

The same applies to uninflected words. Thus, they say of ayna (where) and kayfa (how) that their endings are fixed with fatha to ease pronunciation because of the yā’. Likewise, in the vocalization of fixed forms, the stronger takes damma and the weaker takes fatha. They say kariha al-shay’a (he disliked the thing), and for dislike they use karhan, with fatha, as Allah Most High says:

“To Him submits whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly.”

And He says:

“Come, willingly or unwillingly.”

The same applies to the contrast between kasra and fatha. For something slaughtered or taken as booty, they say dibh and nihb, with kasra, as Allah Most High says:

“And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice.”

And as it occurs in the hadith:

“Camels taken as booty were brought to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.”

And in the familiar proverb:

“I hear the millstones clattering, but see no flour.”

Here tihn is pronounced with kasra; that is: I see no

flour. Whoever pronounces it with fatha means the act of grinding, just as dhabh (slaughtering) and nahb (plundering) denote actions. Some consider the person who uses this pronunciation mistaken.

These and similar features of Arabic are familiar to those acquainted with the language. They are known sometimes through induction and experience, and at other times through analogy, just as physicians investigate the natural properties of bodies, and as ordinary phenomena are known through experience combining sensory perception and reason. As has been said:

“Through analogy you know what you have not experienced.”

It is well known that, according to the vast majority of rational people, Muslims and others alike, these things have causes and fitting connections. As for any speculative thinker who denies this, there is no point discussing these particular connections with him, for he holds that created things possess no power through which an action occurs, nor any cause that singles out one of two like things. Rather, his fundamental principle is that the Creator’s sheer will singles out one of two like things without any cause or wise purpose.

Such a person therefore says: if a word’s signifying a meaning comes about through Allah’s speech, this is merely a matter of customary association. In his view, the Lord does not single anything out for a cause or a wise purpose; rather, will itself singles out one of two like things without wisdom or cause. If, however, it comes about through a servant’s choice, the cause may be that this particular word, rather than another, occurred to the person assigning it its meaning.

translated_text:
he adduced to establish figurative usage—namely, his statement, “If these expressions are literal, they must be homonymous”—rests on two premises: first, that homonymy necessarily follows; and second, that it is invalid. This argument is weak, for the first premise may be challenged, the second may be challenged, or both may be challenged together.

His assertion that “homonymy necessarily follows” holds only if he is granted that, within a single language and under a single linguistic convention, there are expressions denoting disparate meanings with no shared element. This is a matter of well-known dispute. Even if it is conceded, those who accept homonymy agree that language contains expressions whose meanings have both a shared element and a distinguishing element. This occurs sometimes with identical word forms and sometimes with different ones. Just as a single expression may have multiple meanings, multiple expressions may have a single meaning, as in the case of synonyms.

Although some people deny absolute synonymy, the point is that two expressions may agree in denoting a meaning, while one conveys something additional. For example, a sword may be called sayf (sword), sārim (cutter), and muhannad (Indian blade). The word sayf denotes it without qualification; sārim originally denotes its quality of cutting; and muhannad denotes its association with India.  .
translated_text:
the object itself, without regard to this association. When this association is taken into account, however, some say that these names are not synonymous, because some convey an additional meaning.

Others regard them as synonymous because they all denote the same entity. The former say, “They are disparate terms, like ‘man’ and ‘lion’,” while the latter reply, “They are not like disparate terms.”

The fair assessment is that they agree in denoting the same entity but differ in the attributes they denote. They therefore constitute another category, which may be called “equivalent terms.” Allah’s most beautiful names, and the names of His Messenger and His Book, belong to this category.

For when you say that Allah is Almighty, All-Wise, All-Forgiving, Most Merciful, All-Knowing and All-Powerful, all these names denote the One possessed of these attributes—glorified and exalted is He. Each name also denotes an attribute particular to it: one denotes might, another wisdom, another forgiveness, another mercy, another knowledge, and another power.

Likewise, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“I have five names: I am Muhammad; I am Ahmad; I am al-Māhī, through whom Allah effaces disbelief; I am al-Hāshir, in whose wake people will be gathered; and I am al-Āqib, after whom there is no prophet.”

The names for which Allah rebuked the polytheists when they applied them to their idols also belong to this category. He said:

“They are nothing but names you and your forefathers have named, for which Allah has sent down no authority.”

They called them gods, thereby attributing to them the divinity that would entitle them to be worshipped. This meaning cannot be affirmed without authority—that is, proof. To say that something is an object of worship may mean that Allah has commanded its worship; this can only be established through a revealed scripture. Or it may mean that it possesses lordship and the power of creation, which would entitle it to worship; whether it possesses these attributes or not can be established through reason.

For this reason, the Exalted said:

“Say, ‘Have you considered those you invoke besides Allah? Show me what they have created of the earth. Or do they have a share in the heavens? Bring me a scripture predating this, or some remnant of knowledge, if you are truthful.’”

And He said in Sūrah Fātir:

“Say, ‘Have you considered those partners of yours whom you invoke besides Allah? Show me what they have created of the earth. Or do they have a share in the heavens? Or have We given them a scripture, so that they stand on clear evidence from it?’ Rather, the wrongdoers promise one another nothing but delusion.”

Thus, He demanded of them proof grounded in reason and direct observation, as well as proof grounded in revelation and divine law. He said:

“Show me what they have created of the earth. Or do they have a share in the heavens?”

Then He said:

“Or have We given them a scripture, so that they stand on clear evidence from it?”

Likewise, He said in the other passage:

“Show me what they have created of the earth. Or do they have a share in the heavens?”

Then He said: “Bring me a scripture

predating this, or some remnant of knowledge.” Here, “scripture” means a revealed scripture, while “remnant” means what is transmitted from the prophets through narration and chains of transmission. This may also be recorded in books; hence it has been interpreted as both narration and writing. This is a demand for evidence from revelation that Allah has prescribed worshipping another besides Him, taking that being as an intercessor or seeking nearness to Allah through worshipping it. It also makes clear that no worship is legitimate without a command from Allah.

For this reason, the Exalted said:

“Whoever invokes another god alongside Allah, for whom he has no proof, his reckoning rests only with his Lord.”

As He said elsewhere:

“So direct your face toward the religion, inclining to truth—the natural disposition with which Allah created mankind. There is no altering Allah’s creation. That is the upright religion, but most people do not know. Turn to Him in repentance, fear Him, establish prayer, and do not be among the polytheists—those who divided their religion and became sects, each faction rejoicing in what it has. When hardship touches people, they call upon their Lord, turning to Him in repentance. Then, when He lets them taste mercy from Him, some of them associate partners with their Lord, showing ingratitude for what We have given them. So enjoy yourselves; you will soon know. Or have We sent down to them an authority that speaks in support of the partners they associate with Him?”

The authority that speaks in support of this would be a revealed scripture, as He said:

“Or do you have a clear authority? Then bring your scripture, if you are truthful.”

And He said:

“Those who dispute concerning Allah’s signs without any authority having come to them have nothing in their hearts but an ambition for greatness that they will never attain.”

translated_text:
And the point here is that expressions with different wordings may have the same meaning, such as julūs and quʿūd (both meaning “sitting”); these are synonyms. Others have distinct meanings, such as “heaven” and “earth.” Still others agree in one respect and differ in another, such as sārim (“a sharp sword”) and muhannad (“a sword made of Indian iron”). This is a third category: the meaning of one is neither distinct from that of the other as heaven is distinct from earth, nor identical to it as the meaning of julūs is identical to that of quʿūd.

Likewise, expressions identical in wording may have the same meaning; these are univocal terms. Or they may have distinct meanings; these are lexically equivocal terms, such as “Suhayl,” used for both the star and a man. Or their meanings may agree in one respect and differ in another. This is a third category, unlike either lexical equivocation or univocal agreement. They thus share an element of meaning in one respect and differ in meaning in another. This, however, occurs only when each expression is qualified by something indicating its particular meaning.

Such expressions are frequent in connected discourse; indeed, they constitute most of the expressions found in the connected discourse of any speaker. For expressions described as univocal—generic nouns such as “messenger,” “governor,” “judge,” “man,” “woman,” “leader,” “house,” and the like—may convey their general meaning, or they may convey a more specific meaning when made definite by a genitive construction or the definite article, as in His words:

“Indeed, We have sent to you a messenger

as a witness over you, just as We sent to Pharaoh a messenger.”

“But Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger.”

He says elsewhere:

“Do not treat the Messenger’s call among you like your calls to one another.”

The expression “the messenger” is identical in both passages and includes the definite article. In each passage, however, it refers to the messenger known to those being addressed in that context. Thus, when He says here:

“Just as We sent to Pharaoh a messenger.”

“But Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger.”

the definite article identifies the messenger sent to Pharaoh: Moses, son of ʿImrān, peace be upon him.

When He says to the community of Muhammad:

“Do not treat the Messenger’s call among you like your calls to one another,”

the definite article identifies the Messenger known to those addressed by the Quran, who are commanded to obey his commands and refrain from what he forbids: the community of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

It is well known, by common agreement, that an expression of this kind cannot be said to be figurative in either instance. Nor can it be described as purely lexically equivocal, like al-mushtarī, which denotes both a buyer and the planet Jupiter, or Suhayl, which denotes both a star and a man.

Nor can it be described as a univocal term indicating only the shared meaning in both passages. For it is known that in one passage it refers to Muhammad and in the other to Moses, although the expression “the messenger” is identical. Rather, this expression was uttered within a context whose import is conveyed by the definite article. The same applies to all definite nouns, for nouns are of two kinds: definite and indefinite.

“O my father, hire him.”

The word “father” in the former passage refers to Jacob, while in the latter it refers to the man of Midian whose daughter Moses married. He was not Shuayb, as some mistakenly suppose. Rather, Muslim scholars of the early generations and the People of the Book know that he was not Shuayb, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

translated_text:
category has a single verbal form, as with “I” and “you,” or “this” and “that.” Yet in each instance it denotes a particular speaker, addressee, or person spoken of. These expressions cannot be called equivocal, like the name “Suhayl,” nor univocal, like the word “human.” Rather, they have both a shared element and a distinguishing element. In respect of the shared element, they resemble univocal terms; in respect of the distinguishing element, they resemble terms that share only their wording. They are never used without accompanying indications that identify the referent of the pronoun, the object pointed to, and so forth. Their meaning thus derives jointly from their wording and an accompanying contextual indication that identifies the referent. Everyone agrees that this is literal usage. No rational person calls it figurative, even though these expressions never convey their meaning without a contextual indication specifying the intended referent.

If one asks about the expression “I,” the answer is that it denotes the speaker in general. Yet no one has ever uttered it in the abstract, for there is no abstract, universal speaker common to many individuals. Rather, every speaker is a particular individual distinct from others. Thus, when one seeks to understand what these expressions denote and mean, one asks: Who is speaking these words? Who is being addressed by “you,” whether as subject or object, and by similar expressions?

If the one speaking is Allah, as in His words to Moses:

“Indeed, I am Allah. There is no deity except Me,”

and similar passages, then this expression in this context is a designation for Allah Most High and can refer to no other. No created being can say:

“Indeed, I am Allah. There is no deity except Me, so worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance.”

إذَا تَبَيَّنَ هَذَا فَيُقَالُ لَهُ:

translated_text:
He, glorified be He, also relates that the man who disputed with Abraham about his Lord said:

“I give life and cause death.”

He relates that Joseph’s companion said:

“I will inform you of its interpretation, so send me.”

He tells us that a mighty one among the jinn said:

“I will bring it to you before you rise from your place,”

and that the one who had knowledge of the Scripture said:

“I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you.”

Thus, in each particular context, the expression “I” denotes someone different from the one it denotes in another context, although the expression itself is identical in both. No rational person has ever called this expression equivocal or figurative, even though it conveys its meaning only with a contextual indication that makes the intended referent clear.

Section

If this is understood, he may be told:

These nouns you have mentioned—such as zahr (back), matn (back), sāq (leg), and kabid (liver)—can only be used in the language with an accompanying indication of the thing to which they are attributed. This makes the intended meaning clear.

Thus, saying “the zahr and matn of a road” is not like saying “the zahr and matn of a person,” nor even “the zahr and matn of a horse,” nor “the zahr of a mountain.”

Likewise, the expression “the kabid (centre) of the sky” is not like “the kabid (middle) of a bow,” and neither is like “the kabid (liver) of a human being.”

Similarly, the word “sword” in the Prophet’s statement, peace and blessings be upon him:

“Indeed, Khālid is a sword that Allah has drawn against the polytheists,”

is not like the word “sword” in his statement:

“If anyone comes to you while you are united under one man, seeking to divide your community, strike his neck with the sword, whoever he may be.”

In each instance, the word “sword” is accompanied by something that clarifies its meaning.

Admittedly, one might say: “The meanings of ‘messenger’ in its two uses resemble each other more closely than do those of ‘kabid’ or ‘sword’ in their respective uses.”

The reply is that this distinguishing element is indicated by the particular wording, as in His words:

“Indeed, the frailest of houses is the spider’s house,”

and His words:

“And purify My House for those who circle it,”

and His words:

“Do not enter the Prophet’s houses,”

and the Prophet’s statement, peace and blessings be upon him:

“Whoever builds a mosque for Allah, Allah will build for him a house in Paradise.”

It is well known that the spider’s house is not identical in its actual nature to His House, the Prophet’s house, peace and blessings be upon him, or a house in Paradise. Yet the word “house” is indisputably used literally in every instance, since it is the possessive construction that specifies the meaning. In “the spider’s house” and “the Prophet’s house,” it indicates that the house’s occupant lives there. “Allah’s House,” however, does not indicate that Allah dwells there. Rather, each attribution is understood according to what is being attributed. His House is the one He has designated for remembering Him, worshipping Him, and calling upon Him. This is like knowing Him in the heart and mentioning Him with the tongue.

Every existing thing has an existence in external reality, in knowledge, in speech, and in writing. The name “Allah” is used to refer to each of these four in the speech of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and in Allah’s speech.

You are then answered:

The expressions at issue are ‘the back of the road,’ ‘its ridge,’ ‘the wing of a journey,’ and the like. Each such expression has only one meaning, not several different meanings. If you say, ‘But the words “back,” “ridge,” and “wing” have meanings other than these,’ the reply is:

‘The expression “the back of the road” or “its wing” is not the expression “the back of a human being,” “the wing of a bird,” or “the wings of the angels.” The words “the back” and “the road” are made definite by the definite article, which indicates a known referent denoted by the expression—the human back, for example. This is not like the expression “the back of the road”; rather, the two expressions differ.’

Thus one cannot say, ‘The expression occurs in a single context.’ More telling still, it is unanimously agreed that the word ‘back’ is used literally of all animals. Nevertheless, for many people, only the human back may immediately come to mind. They do not think of the back of a dog, a fox, a wolf, a weasel, an ant, or a louse. This is because the human back is what they picture and frequently refer to in their ordinary speech. When used with the definite article, the word refers to the familiar back.

translated_text:
For this reason, jurists interpret oaths according to what the person addressed understands in his own language, even if the expression is also used literally of other things. Thus, if someone swears not to eat heads, this may mean the heads of livestock, the heads of sheep and goats, or the kinds of heads customarily eaten. Likewise, the word “eggs” means the eggs familiar to them. The heads of ants, fleas, and the like do not fall within the expression, nor do fish eggs fall within the oath, even though “ants’ eggs” and “fish eggs” are literal expressions when used in these possessive constructions.

Similarly, if someone says, “I have sold it to you for ten dirhams or dinars,” the unqualified wording refers to what people understand that expression to denote in such a transaction in that locality. Indeed, even within a single locality, “dinar” may mean pure gold when pricing certain goods, debased gold when pricing others, and a particular sum of dirhams when pricing still others. By the unanimous agreement of the jurists, an unqualified contract is therefore interpreted according to the shared understanding of buyer and seller, even though the expression is used in other senses only with something that clarifies its meaning.

How much more so, then, when the expressions themselves differ, as with “the back of a human being” and “the back of the road”; “the head of a human being,” “the head of a lane,” “the head of wealth” (capital), or “the head of a spring” (its source)? Or when one expression is qualified by the definite article, as in “the back,” while the other is qualified by a possessive construction? The definite article indicates what is familiar to the person addressed, whereas the possessive construction specifies the referent through its relation to the noun that follows. Thus, an expression made definite by the definite article is not the same as one made definite by a possessive construction, either in wording or in meaning.

 فِي مَسَائِلِهِ
translated_text:
The definite article may be used in both instances, yet the meaning may still differ, as with the expression “the messenger.” This is because the addressee’s knowledge forms part of what determines the meaning, while the expression is literal in both instances. How much more, then, when definiteness through a possessive construction is compared with definiteness through the definite article?

It is thus clear that the expression denoting a human being’s back is not the same expression as that denoting the back of a road. Accordingly, the difference in meaning between the two expressions does not entail homonymy, because homonymy does not occur in a single expression whose meaning differs; and that is not the case here.

If it is objected, “This would entail that there are no homonymous expressions in the language, since a homonymous expression is used only alongside something that clarifies which of its two meanings is intended,” the reply is: Either this conclusion necessarily follows or it does not. If it does not, the objection falls away. If it does, we accept the position of those who deny homonymy, provided that this is indeed the case, just as one accepts the position of those who deny figurative usage.

If it is asked, “How can you deny the existence of homonymy when evidence has established it?” the reply is: We do not concede that evidence has established its existence in the manner they claim. The author of the book, Abū al-Hasan al-Āmidī, himself acknowledges the weakness of the arguments advanced by those who affirm it. He has offered an argument of his own that is weaker still than those advanced by others. For, in his discussion of these questions, he says:

 وَهُوَ مُمْتَنِعٌ قَالَ:
 وَهُوَ غَيْرُ سَدِيدٍ مِنْ حَيْثُ إنَّ الْأَسْمَاءَ إنْ كَانَتْ مُرَكَّبَةً مِنْ الْحُرُوفِ الْمُتَنَاهِيَةِ فَلَا يَلْزَمُ أَنْ يَكُونَ مُتَنَاهِيَةً إلَّا أَنْ يَكُونَ مَا يَحْصُلُ مِنْ تَضَاعُفِ التَّرْكِيبَاتِ مُتَنَاهِيَةً فَلَا نُسَلِّمُ أَنَّ الْمُسَمَّيَاتِ الْمُتَضَادَّةَ وَالْمُخْتَلِفَةَ - وَهِيَ الَّتِي يَكُونُ اللَّفْظُ مُشْتَرِكًا بِالنِّسْبَةِ إلَيْهَا -: غَيْرُ مُتَنَاهِيَةٍ وَإِنْ كَانَتْ غَيْرَ مُتَنَاهِيَةٍ غَيْرَ أَنَّ وَضْعَ الْأَسْمَاءِ عَلَى مُسَمَّيَاتِهَا مَشْرُوطٌ بِكَوْنِ كُلِّ وَاحِدٍ مِنْ الْمُسَمَّيَاتِ مَقْصُودًا بِالْوَضْعِ وَمَا لَا نِهَايَةَ لَهُ مِمَّا يَسْتَحِيلُ فِيهِ ذَلِكَ وَإِنْ سَلَّمْنَا أَنَّهُ غَيْرُ مُمْتَنِعٍ؛ وَلَكِنْ لَا يَلْزَمُ مِنْ ذَلِكَ الْوَضْعُ. وَلِهَذَا يَأْتِي كَثِيرٌ مِنْ الْمَعَانِي لَمْ تَضَعْ الْعَرَبُ بِإِزَائِهَا أَلْفَاظًا تَدُلُّ عَلَيْهَا بِطَرِيقِ الِاشْتِرَاكِ وَلَا التَّفْضِيلِ كَأَنْوَاعِ الرَّوَائِحِ وَكَثِيرٍ مِنْ الصِّفَاتِ.
translated_text:
“The First Question”: People have differed over whether homonymous expressions exist in the language. Some affirm their existence, while others deny it.

He says:

“The preferred position is that their occurrence is possible. As for rational discourse, nothing precludes a single person from assigning an expression more than one meaning. Nor is it impossible for one tribe to assign a name to one meaning and another tribe to assign it to a different meaning, neither knowing what the other has assigned it to. Both usages then become widespread, while their origin remains obscure.”

He says: “This is the more likely explanation.”

He says:

“As for establishing their actual occurrence, the argument is that, if homonymous expressions did not occur in the language, most things named would lack names denoting them, despite the need for such names. This is because effects are infinite, whereas names are finite, since they are necessarily composed of a finite set of letters. Such a lack is impossible.”

He says:

“This argument is unsound. Although names are composed of a finite set of letters, it does not follow that the names themselves are finite unless the combinations produced by repeated compounding are also finite. Nor do we concede that mutually opposed and distinct things named—those in relation to which an expression would be homonymous—are infinite.

“Even if they are infinite, assigning names to their referents requires each referent to be individually intended in the act of naming, which is impossible with an infinite number of things. Even if we concede that this is not impossible, it still does not follow that such names have actually been assigned. Thus, many meanings arise for which the Arabs have assigned no expressions to denote them, whether through homonymy or preference, such as kinds of smells and many qualities.”

translated_text:
He says:

“Abū al-Husayn al-Basrī said: ‘Speakers of the language apply the term qur’ to both menstruation and purity, which are opposites. This demonstrates that homonymous expressions occur in the language.’”

He says:

“One may object: Those who originally assigned the term have not been reported as declaring it homonymous. All that is established is that a single term has multiple referents. Perhaps it was applied to both on account of a single meaning common to them, rather than their differing realities. Alternatively, it may be literal in one case and figurative in the other, even though we do not know which usage is literal and which is figurative. These explanations are preferable: the first avoids both figurative usage and homonymy, while the second rests on the principle that figurative usage is preferable to homonymy, as will be explained in its proper place.”

He says:

“A stronger argument is the universal agreement that the term ‘existence’ applies literally to both the eternal and the temporally originated. Were its application figurative in either case, it could validly be denied, since this is a sign of figurative usage; yet such denial is impossible. Accordingly, the term ‘existence’ must denote either the Lord’s essence or a reality additional to His essence.

“If the former, it is evident that the Lord’s essence is intrinsically different from all other, temporally originated beings. Otherwise, it and whatever shared its meaning would necessarily share necessary existence, since they would be equal in what is meant by ‘essence’; but this is impossible. If, however, the term ‘existence’ denotes an attribute additional to the essence of the Lord—exalted is He—

The former entails that what ‘existence’ denotes is intrinsically necessary in reality, since the Creator’s existence is intrinsically necessary; or else that the Lord’s existence is contingent, since the existence of everything other than Allah is contingent. This, then, is his argument, and it is extremely weak, for it rests on two premises: that the term ‘existence’ applies literally to both the necessary and the contingent, and that this entails homonymy. The second premise is unquestionably false. The first is disputed, contrary to his claim of consensus.

Some have said:

“Every name used to designate a created being can be applied to the Creator only figuratively—even the word ‘thing.’”

This is the position of Jahm and those among the Bātiniyyah (esotericists) who agree with him. These people do not call Him ‘existent’ or ‘a thing,’ nor do they apply any other names to Him.

Others have taken the opposite position, saying:

“Rather, every name applied to the Lord is literal when applied to Him and figurative when applied to anyone else.”

This is the position of Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Nāshī of the Muʿtazilah.

translated_text:
The majority held that the term applies literally to both. Most of them, however, considered it univocal in the broad sense—or graded in its application, if graded terms are treated as a separate category. This differs from strict univocity, in which a term’s meanings are identical across its applications. Only a small handful of later thinkers considered it homonymous; this view is not known to have been held by any major school or prominent speculative thinkers. Whoever attributes it to al-Ashʿarī, as al-Rāzī did, is mistaken.

For his position, and that of most of his followers, is that ‘existence’ is a general term divided into eternal and temporally originated existence. His position, however, is that the existence of each thing is identical with its quiddity. This is the position of the vast majority of rational thinkers, Muslims and others alike. Some supposed that this necessarily makes the term homonymous, as al-Āmidī argued. This is mistaken, as we have explained at length elsewhere, and as will become clear through our discussion of his argument.

As for his statement:

“The term ‘existence’ must denote either the essence or an attribute additional to the essence.”

He should be asked: Do you mean the general term ‘existence,’ which is divided into necessary and contingent existence, or existence in a particular sense, as when one says ‘the existence of the necessary’ and ‘the existence of the contingent’? For it is well known that names used to designate the Lord and others—indeed, any

 إذَا كَانَ عَامًّا يَتَنَاوَلُ الْوَاجِبَ وَإِذَا قِيلَ: 
{وَتَوَكَّلْ عَلَى الْحَيِّ الَّذِي لَا يَمُوتُ}
 
{اللَّهُ لَا إلَهَ إلَّا هُوَ الْحَيُّ الْقَيُّومُ}
 
{وَهُوَ الْعَلِيمُ الْحَكِيمُ}
 وَنَحْوُ ذَلِكَ مِمَّا يَخْتَصُّ بِالرَّبِّ: لَمْ يَتَنَاوَلْ ذَلِكَ الْمَخْلُوقَ كَمَا إذَا قِيلَ: 
{يُخْرِجُ الْحَيَّ مِنَ الْمَيِّتِ}
 لَمْ يَدْخُلْ الْخَالِقُ فِي اسْمِ هَذَا الْحَيِّ.
 وَكَذَلِكَ إذَا قِيلَ:
 الْعِلْمُ وَالْقُدْرَةُ؛ وَالْكَلَامُ؛ وَالِاسْتِوَاءُ؛
 وَالنُّزُولُ وَنَحْوُ ذَلِكَ:
 تَارَةً يُذْكَرُ مُطْلَقًا عَامًّا: وَتَارَةً يُقَالُ: عِلْمُ اللَّهِ وَقُدْرَتُهُ؛ وَكَلَامُهُ؛ وَنُزُولُهُ؛
 وَاسْتِوَاؤُهُ:
 فَهَذَا يَخْتَصُّ بِالْخَالِقِ؛ لَا يَشْرَكُهُ فِيهِ الْمَخْلُوقُ.
 كَمَا إذَا قِيلَ:
 عِلْمُ الْمَخْلُوقِ وَقُدْرَتُهُ: وَكَلَامُهُ؛ وَنُزُولُهُ؛ وَاسْتِوَاؤُهُ فَهَذَا يَخْتَصُّ بِالْمَخْلُوقِ وَلَا يَشْرَكُهُ فِيهِ الْخَالِقُ. فَالْإِضَافَةُ أَوْ التَّعْرِيفُ خَصَّصَ وَمَيَّزَ وَقَطَعَ الِاشْتِرَاكَ بَيْنَ الْخَالِقِ وَالْمَخْلُوقِ.
 وَكَذَلِكَ إذَا قِيلَ لَفْظُ الْوُجُودِ مُطْلَقًا وَقِيلَ:
 وُجُودُ الْوَاجِبِ وَوُجُودُ الْمُمْكِنِ فَهَذِهِ ثَلَاثَةُ مَعَانٍ.
 فَإِذَا قِيلَ:
 وُجُودُ الْعَبْدِ وَذَاتُهُ وَمَاهِيَّتُه وَحَقِيقَتُهُ كَانَ ذَلِكَ مُخْتَصًّا بِهِ دَالًّا عَلَى ذَاتِهِ الْمُخْتَصَّةِ بِهِ الْمُتَّصِفَةِ بِصِفَاتِهِ.
translated_text:
two entities—are sometimes understood in an unrestricted, general sense encompassing both kinds, and sometimes as restricted to a particular entity. When terms such as ‘living,’ ‘knowing,’ ‘powerful,’ ‘hearing,’ ‘seeing,’ ‘existent,’ ‘thing,’ and ‘essence’ are used generally, they encompass the necessary existent. But when it is said:

“And rely upon the Ever-Living who does not die,”

“Allah—there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all existence,”

“And He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise,”

or similar expressions referring specifically to the Lord, these do not encompass the creature. Likewise, when it is said:

“He brings the living out of the dead,”

the Creator is not included in the designation ‘the living’ here.

Similarly, terms such as knowledge, power, speech, rising, and descent are sometimes used in an unrestricted, general sense. At other times, one speaks of Allah’s knowledge, power, speech, descent, and rising. These are specific to the Creator; the creature has no share in them. Likewise, when one speaks of the creature’s knowledge, power, speech, descent, and rising, these are specific to the creature; the Creator has no share in them. Thus, a possessive construction or definite designation specifies and distinguishes the referent, eliminating the shared application between Creator and creature.

Likewise, when the term ‘existence’ is used without qualification, and when one speaks of ‘the existence of the necessary’ and ‘the existence of the contingent,’ these are three meanings.

When one speaks of the servant’s existence, essence, quiddity, and reality, these expressions refer specifically to him, denoting his own particular essence, characterized by its attributes.

translated_text:
Likewise, when one speaks of the Lord’s existence, His self, His essence, His quiddity, and His reality, these expressions denote what is specific to the Lord: His very self, characterized by His attributes.

As for his statement, “The term ‘existence’ denotes either the Lord’s essence or an additional attribute,” he is told: If you mean the unrestricted, general term ‘existence,’ which encompasses both the necessary and the contingent, it denotes neither what is specific to the necessary nor what is specific to the contingent. Rather, it denotes the shared universal. Yet the shared universal is shared and universal only in the mind and in language; nothing that exists in external reality is itself a universal.

This is like using the terms ‘essence’ and ‘self’ in a sense encompassing both the necessary and the contingent: they denote only the general, universal meaning, not what is specific to either one. Examples include saying, “Existence is divided into necessary and contingent,” or “Essence is divided into necessary and contingent,” and similar expressions.

If, however, ‘existence’ is intended to encompass both together—as when one says, “All existence, both necessary and contingent,” or “Necessary and contingent existence”—then it denotes what is specific to each, just as when one says, “The existence of the necessary and the existence of the contingent.”

In sum, a term may denote only what is shared, as with existence considered as divisible into categories, or only what is distinctive, as in the expressions ‘the existence of the necessary’ and ‘the existence of the contingent’

or both, as when you say, “All existence, both necessary and contingent,” or “Necessary and contingent existence.” In every case, equivocation does not necessarily follow.

As for his statement, “If it denotes the Lord’s essence, then His essence differs from all other existent things,” the response is: The unrestricted term ‘existence,’ considered as divisible into categories, does not denote what is specific to the Lord. But when ‘existence’ is used specifically for the Lord’s existence, or inclusively, as when we say, “Necessary and contingent existence,” and similar expressions, it does denote what is specific to the Lord’s essence, even though His essence differs from that of others. Likewise, the expressions ‘the Lord’s essence’ and ‘the servant’s essence’ denote what is specific to the Lord and to the servant, even though the reality of the one differs from that of the other. Similarly, the term ‘existence’ denotes both, despite the difference between the realities of the two existent beings.

If it is said, “If the reality of this existence differs from the reality of that existence, then the term is equivocal,” the response is:

This is a mistake from which the error of this man and others like him has arisen. All differing realities share general names that encompass them through univocal and graded predication. For example, the term ‘color’ encompasses blackness, whiteness, and redness, despite the differences between the realities of these colors. Likewise, the terms ‘attribute,’ ‘accident,’ and ‘meaning’ encompass knowledge, power, life, taste, color, and smell, despite the differences between the realities of colors.

translated_text:
Likewise, the term ‘animal’ encompasses both humans and beasts, despite the difference between their realities. This applies all the more to the term ‘existence’. These differing realities may share a general meaning that encompasses them, with the term denoting that meaning, as with the term ‘color’. Then, when qualified, it encompasses what is specific to each, as when one says, ‘the color of a black thing’ and ‘the color of a white thing’, or ‘the Lord’s existence’ and ‘the servant’s existence’.

If one uses a general term encompassing its individual instances, such as ‘color’, ‘colors’, ‘animal’, ‘accident’, or ‘existence’, it encompasses everything falling within its scope, even if these have differing realities. This is because the term encompasses them, just like other general terms, even though their individual instances differ in a respect other than that denoted by the general term.

Furthermore, regarding his statement, ‘If what the term “existence” denotes is an attribute, then, if the concept is the same for the necessary and the contingent, it follows that the necessary is contingent and the contingent necessary; otherwise, equivocation follows,’ the response is:

Do you mean that the term denotes unrestricted existence, or existence qualified by attribution, as when one says, ‘the existence of the necessary’ and ‘the existence of the contingent’? If you mean the former, then the concept is one and the same, but this does not entail that the two instances are alike. Even if the meaning of existence in the mind is alike in both cases, it does not follow that its instances in external reality are alike.

and it need only apply to both and encompass them, like other univocal terms that admit differences of degree. Thus, “blackness” applies to the blackness of pitch and ink, although the two are not alike. Likewise, “white,” “red,” and similar terms encompass both perfect and imperfect instances. The term “living” likewise encompasses the life of angels, the inhabitants of Paradise, flies, and mosquitoes, although their lives are not alike. How, then, could the Lord’s existence, knowledge, or power be considered like the creature’s existence, knowledge, or power merely because they fall under the unrestricted terms “existence,” “knowledge,” or “power”?

If he says, “Rather, I mean qualified existence, as when we say ‘the existence of the necessary’ and ‘the existence of the contingent,’” the reply is:

Here the concepts differ, because each has a distinct expression qualifying “existence,” namely, the attribution. This qualifying attribution precludes their being alike, but it does not entail equivocation. For the difference here arises in the very term “existence”—rather, in the attribution added to the term, and in attribution or definiteness, as when we say “the Lord’s existence” or “necessary existence,” and “the creature’s existence” or “contingent existence,” and the like.

 أَنَّ كُلَّ وَاحِدٍ لَهُ مِنْهُ نَصِيبٌ كَالْمُشْتَرَكِينَ فِي الْعَقَارِ وَنَحْوِ ذَلِكَ.
translated_text:
he used to argue for figurative usage when he said:

“If the word is used literally in both instances, equivocation necessarily follows.”

This is mistaken. For what indicates the specific meaning in one instance is not what indicates the specific meaning in the other; rather, it is what is added to the word.

Thus, saying “the Lord’s existence” and “the servant’s existence” is comparable to saying “a man’s back” and “a horse’s back,” just as one speaks of a man’s back and the surface of a road. In all these instances, what indicates the distinction between one and another is the wording specific to each instance, not merely the shared word. Rather, the shared wording indicates what is shared, and the distinctive wording indicates what is distinctive. This entails that the two backs have an aspect in common and an aspect in which they differ. Likewise, the two instances of existence have an aspect in common and an aspect in which they differ. This is what is meant by commonality and distinction.

Some people, however, imagine that what the two have in common exists in external reality as something shared between them. This is mistaken. Rather, each is distinct in external reality, while the mind abstracts from them a common universal element. Thus, one says, “They share in existence, animal nature, and human nature.” As Allah Most High says:

“Since you did wrong, it will not benefit you today that you share in the punishment.”

And He says:

“Indeed, on that Day they will share in the punishment.”

Thus, the punishment that befalls one corresponds to that which befalls the other and is of the same kind: they share in the kind of punishment. There is no single, particular thing in external reality that they both share. Rather, they share in the particular punishment in the sense that each has a portion of it, like those who share ownership of a property and the like.

translated_text:
The sixth response:

One may contest the second premise, namely his statement:

“If the term were equivocal, one meaning rather than another would not come first to mind when these words are used without qualification, since they necessarily signify their literal meanings equally. Yet there is no doubt that what first comes to mind when ‘lion’ is used without qualification is the beast of prey, and when ‘donkey’ is used without qualification, it is the animal. The same is necessarily true in similar cases.”

The reply is:

When ‘lion’ and ‘donkey’ are used with the definite article al-, they refer to what is known to the speaker or the addressee. If the identified referent is the animal, the word refers to it. This is indeed the familiar referent for most people most of the time. But it does not follow that, when the definite form directs the reference to a dullard or a brave man, the usage cannot also be literal. An example is Abū Bakr’s statement:

“No, by Allah! He would not single out one of Allah’s lions, who fights for Allah and His Messenger, and give you his spoils.”

Likewise, someone may point to a person and say, “This lion,” or to a dullard and say, “This donkey.” Here, definiteness identifies the referent and rules out any other intended meaning. Similarly, when words such as ‘heads,’ ‘eggs,’ and ‘houses’ are used without qualification, ‘heads’ and ‘eggs’ refer to those customarily eaten, while ‘houses’ refers to people’s dwellings. Yet when one says ‘a spider’s house,’ ‘ants’ eggs,’ or ‘locusts’ heads,’ these usages are also literal, by common agreement.

The seventh response:

One may say: You have made the criterion of literal usage that its meaning should come first to mind when the word is used without qualification. Thus, on the listener’s side, you have taken into account what first comes to his mind;

translated_text:
and, on the speaker’s side, his use of the expression without qualification. Yet there is no fixed criterion for this: in each instance, what first comes to the listener’s mind is whatever the evidence in that context indicates. If someone speaks of “the back of the road” or “its spine,” the back of an animal never comes to the listener’s mind; indeed, he considers it impossible that this could be intended.

The eighth response:

Your phrase, “from the unqualified use of the entire expression,” is ambiguous. If you mean that the expression is free of all qualifications, this never occurs.

For the inquiry concerns nouns as they occur in the speech of any speaker: Allah, His angels, His prophets, the jinn, and all other human beings and nations. An expression occurs only in conjunction with other words, within either a nominal or a verbal sentence. It necessarily comes from a speaker, and it can serve as evidence only when that speaker’s customary use of such an expression is known. Thus, we have a qualified expression conjoined with other words, a speaker whose customary usage is known, and a listener who knows the speaker’s customary use of that expression. These qualifications are indispensable to speech whose meaning can be understood; the expression cannot, therefore, be free of them. If he means that it is free of one qualification but not another, what he has said does not establish that.

It is thus clear that his statement comes down to what is understood when the expression is used without qualification.

The ninth response:

One may say to him: Mention whatever qualification you wish, and distinguish between a qualifier and what it qualifies. Whatever he mentions will be open to refutation. I shall show you, from the definitions you cite to distinguish literal from figurative usage, that what you classify as literal you also classify as figurative, and what

translated_text:
you classify as figurative you also classify as literal, and that anyone who distinguishes between the two on the basis of unqualified and qualified usage speaks like someone who has no clear conception of what he is saying, much less the ability to express it. Expression depends upon conception; whoever has no conception of what he is saying says nothing that is not mistaken.

Section

As for his second argument, he says:

“How can that be, when people throughout the ages have continually transmitted, in their speech and writings, from those who established linguistic conventions, the designation of this as literal and that as figurative?”

The response is that this is known with certainty to be false. No one has ever transmitted from those who established linguistic conventions that they said, “This is literal and that is figurative.” It is self-evident that they never did this, nor did anyone who transmitted their language report it from them. Indeed, no one has even reported this from the Companions who explained the Quran, clarified its meanings, and explained what it indicates in each passage. None of them said, “This expression is literal and that is figurative,” or anything resembling it: neither Ibn Mas'ūd and his companions, nor Ibn 'Abbās and his companions, nor Zayd ibn Thābit and his companions, nor those who came after them; neither Mujāhid, Sa'īd ibn Jubayr, 'Ikrimah, al-Dahhāk, Tāwūs, al-Suddī, Qatādah, nor anyone else among them; nor any of the imams of jurisprudence, such as the imams

translated_text:
of the four schools and others, nor al-Thawrī, al-Awzā'ī, al-Layth ibn Sa'd, or anyone else. The term does occur in the words of Ahmad ibn Hanbal, but with a different meaning, just as it occurs in the words of Abū 'Ubaydah Ma'mar ibn al-Muthannā with a different meaning. Nor is the division of speech into literal and figurative found in the writings of the leading authorities on grammar and language, such as Abū 'Amr ibn al-'Alā', Abū 'Amr al-Shaybānī, Abū Zayd, al-Asma'ī, al-Khalīl, Sībawayh, al-Kisā'ī, and al-Farrā'. None of them knew of this distinction as something received from the Arabs.

Anyone who investigates this matter knows it with certainty, just as it is known with certainty that the Arabs did not speak using the terminology of the grammarians, who classified one expression as a subject, another as an object, and a third as a verbal noun, and classified some words as declinable and others as indeclinable. This is known to be the grammarians’ terminology, but it is terminology whose meaning is sound, unlike the terminology adopted by those who use the terms “literal” and “figurative.”

The latter is a later convention, and its meaning is unsound in this respect: there is no actual distinction between the two that would warrant assigning one term to this and another to that. Rather, whatever meaning they assign exclusively to the term “literal” is also found in what they call figurative, and whatever meaning they assign exclusively to the term “figurative” is also found in what they call literal. They cannot provide anything that distinguishes the two categories.

Nor are they being required to supply what is said to constitute a real definition, composed of genus

translated_text:
and differentia; for even if this were true, they would not be required to provide it—how much less so when it is false? Rather, what is required is a distinction between what the two terms denote. This is what a nominal definition amounts to, just as one distinguishes between what is denoted by “declinable noun,” “indeclinable noun,” “subject,” and “object,” and between the things denoted by all other terms. They are therefore required to provide a means of distinguishing what they call literal from what they call figurative. Yet no such distinction actually exists, for there are not, in reality, two distinct categories such that one may be called literal and the other figurative.

This is a rational inquiry, distinct from the terminological inquiry, for they acknowledge that the dispute over this question is terminological. They have supposed that this terminology and distinction were transmitted from the Arabs, and in this they are mistaken. Equally mistaken is anyone who supposes that this terminology and distinction occur in the words of the Companions, the Successors, and the leading scholars; that al-Shāfi‘ī or another scholar mentioned them; or that any of these authorities spoke in these terms. This error resembles that of someone brought up with terminology devised by a particular group, who then supposes that the earlier scholars used the same terminology.

Still more plainly mistaken is anyone who supposes that the Arabs themselves made this classification, or that it was received from them through direct transmission, as is found in the writings of some authors on the principles of jurisprudence. Such a claim occurs in the writings of a number of authors, including Abū al-Husayn al-Basrī, al-Qādī Abū al-Tayyib, al-Qādī Abū Ya‘lā, and others.

As for the argument he mentioned of those who deny figurative usage, he said:

“If it is objected: ‘Were there a figurative expression in the Arabic language, its meaning would either be delimited by a contextual indication or not. In the first case, the expression, together with the indication, would admit of no other meaning; thus, together with that indication, it would be literal in that meaning. In the second case, it would likewise be literal, since a literal expression means nothing other than one that conveys its meaning independently, without a contextual indication.’”

He then said:

“We reply: Our answer to the first case is that, unless a figurative usage is widely familiar, it conveys its meaning only through a contextual indication. This is all that is meant by figurative usage, and the dispute over this is terminological. Moreover, are not figurativeness and literalness attributes of expressions rather than of nonverbal contextual indications? Literalness therefore cannot be an attribute of the combination.”

The response is:

He has conceded that the dispute is terminological. We reply: ‘We do not concede any change in linguistic convention. At most, a contextual indicator diverts the expression from what it would signify when unqualified to another meaning.’”

Thus, if “There is no god except Allah” falls within the matter under dispute, he has passed judgment on it: he claims that every general expression whose scope is restricted, even by an exception, is figurative. Accordingly, “There is no god except Allah” would, in his view, be figurative. It is well known that this statement is among the gravest enormities in the Sharia. Its proponent is more deserving of being called upon to repent—if he repents, so be it; otherwise, he is to be executed—than of being counted among Muslim scholars.

Moreover, the person making this claim misrepresents language, the Sharia, and reason. The Arabs did not use the expression “There is no god” on its own, nor did they deny the Creator such that they would say, “There is no god.” Rather, they set up other gods alongside Allah. Allah Most High says:

“Do you truly testify that there are other gods besides Allah? Say, ‘I do not so testify.’”

This is why they said:

“Has he made the gods into one God? This is truly an astonishing thing!”

The entire Quran affirms that Allah alone is worthy of worship and censures them for associating partners with Him. Mass-transmitted reports establish that the first thing he—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—called people to was the testimony that there is no god except Allah. He said:

“I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god except Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah.”

As for the assertion:

The reply is: This is a fallacy. When qualified, the expression is not unrestricted. It does not entail universal negation when it is unrestricted and unqualified. With qualification, however, the statement is: “There is no god except Allah.” As for the expression without qualification, how can it be said that it has been diverted from what it would have entailed had it been unrestricted? Had it been unrestricted, it would have entailed universal negation. Qualification therefore removes the unrestrictedness that would entail this. This is what a change in signification means: if the expression had a particular signification when unrestricted, that signification would cease, and it would acquire another when qualified and accompanied by an exception.

According to the majority, who affirm general applicability, the exception excludes from the expression something that would otherwise have fallen within its scope. According to those who suspend judgment, it excludes something that could otherwise have fallen within its scope. It may then be said: These people have no consistent criterion. Some regard using an expression for part of its meaning as literal; others regard it as figurative; and still others regard it as both literal and figurative, as he has mentioned in discussing generality and a command intended to convey recommendation. This demonstrates the inconsistency of this principle.

It may further be said: Granted that this is a property of expressions, it is nevertheless a property of an expression as actually used to convey its intended meaning. Your statement, “It is an attribute of expressions, not of contextual indicators relating to meaning, so being literal cannot be an attribute of the combination,” is therefore false for several reasons.

First, an expression has never conveyed meaning without contextual indicators relating to meaning: the speaker is rational, habitually uses that expression in that sense, and is speaking in accordance with his customary usage, while the listener knows this. All these are contextual indicators relating to meaning, apprehended through reason, and the expression conveys meaning only in conjunction with them. The claim that an expression conveys meaning while stripped of all rational contextual indicators is therefore mistaken.

This is clarified by the sixth point: Your claim, “How could that be, when ‘figurative’ and ‘literal’ are attributes of expressions, not of contextual indicators relating to meaning, so that ‘literal’ cannot be an attribute of the combination?” merely restates the terminology you have devised. If your opponent replies, “Rather, ‘literal’ designates the whole that conveys meaning—the expression together with the contextual indicator relating to meaning,” he has countered your terminology with his own. His terminology is better than yours, since he calls all the forms of expression Allah has taught His servants literal, whereas you classify much or most of them as figurative.

If you say, “Then this dispute is merely verbal,” you will be told: That is your first answer—your statement that the dispute over this is merely verbal.

The statement, “I have another answer beyond this”—namely, your claim, “How could that be, when ‘figurative’ and ‘literal’ are attributes of expressions, not of contextual indicators relating to meaning, so that ‘literal’ cannot be an attribute of the combination?”—implies that you have offered a second answer distinct from the first. Yet it merely restates what that terminology means: we have agreed to call the expression ‘literal,’ excluding the contextual indicators relating to meaning.

It is therefore clear that you have nothing beyond your acknowledgment that the dispute is merely verbal. Thus, even if this terminology were sound, those who deny figurative usage and call all speech literal, provided that it makes the intended meaning clear, would not have been any worse

 مَجَازًا وَجَعَلَهُ فَرْعًا فِي اللُّغَةِ لَا أَصْلًا؛ وَوَضْعًا حَادِثًا غَيَّرَ بِهِ الْوَضْعَ الْمُتَقَدِّمَ؛ وَجَعَلَهُ تَابِعًا لِغَيْرِهِ لَا مَتْبُوعًا.
فَصْلٌ:
وَقَدْ ذَكَرَ نُفَاةِ الْمَجَازِ حُجَّةً ضَعِيفَةً وَهِيَ قَوْلُهُمْ:
 وَأَيْضًا مَا مِنْ صُورَةٍ مِنْ الصُّوَرِ إلَّا وَيُمْكِنُ أَنْ يُعَبَّرَ عَنْهَا بِاللَّفْظِ الْحَقِيقِيِّ الْخَاصِّ بِهَا فَاسْتِعْمَالُ اللَّفْظِ الْمَجَازِيِّ فِيهَا مَعَ افْتِقَارِهِ إلَى الْقَرِينَةِ مِنْ غَيْرِ حَاجَةٍ بَعِيدٌ عَنْ أَهْلِ الْحِكْمَةِ وَالْبَلَاغَةِ فِي وَضْعِهِمْ.
 وَقَدْ أَجَابَ عَنْ هَذَا بِقَوْلِهِ:
 وَجَوَابُ الثَّانِي: أَنَّ الْفَائِدَةَ فِي اسْتِعْمَالِ اللَّفْظِ الْمَجَازِيِّ دُونَ الْحَقِيقَةِ قَدْ يَكُونُ لِاخْتِصَاصِهِ بِالْخِفَّةِ عَلَى اللِّسَانِ؛ أَوْ لِمُسَاغَتِهِ فِي وَزْنِ الْكَلَامِ لَفْظًا وَنَثْرًا وَالْمُطَابَقَةِ؛ وَالْمُجَانَسَةِ؛ وَالسَّجْعِ وَقَصْدِ التَّعْظِيمِ وَالْعُدُولِ عَنْ الْحَقِيقِيِّ لِلتَّحْقِيقِ إلَى غَيْرِ ذَلِكَ مِنْ الْمَقَاصِدِ الْمَطْلُوبَةِ مِنْ الْكَلَامِ.
 فَيُقَالُ:
 هَذِهِ الْحُجَّةُ ضَعِيفَةٌ وَالْمُحْتَجُّ بِهَا يَلْزَمُهُ أَنْ يُسَلِّمَ لَهَا انْقِسَامَ الْكَلَامِ إلَى حَقِيقَةٍ وَمَجَازٍ لَكِنَّهُ يُوجِبُ اسْتِعْمَالَ الْحَقِيقَةِ دُونَ الْمَجَازِ وَهَذَا يُنَاقِضُ قَوْلَهُ: لَيْسَ فِي اللُّغَةِ مَجَازٌ؛ بَلْ الْمَوَاضِعُ الَّتِي سَمَّوْهَا
translated_text:
off than those who call some of the finest, most beautiful, and most fully expressive speech figurative, treating it as derivative rather than foundational in language, as a later assignment of meaning that altered an earlier one, and as dependent on other usage rather than something other usage follows.

Section

Those who deny figurative usage have advanced a weak argument, saying:

“Furthermore, there is no situation that cannot be expressed by a literal expression specific to it. Using a figurative expression instead, when it requires a contextual indicator and serves no need, is far removed from the practice of wise and eloquent people in establishing linguistic conventions.”

He answered this by saying:

“The answer to the second argument is that using a figurative expression rather than a literal one may offer the advantage of being easier on the tongue; fitting the cadence of speech, in wording and prose; achieving correspondence, similarity of sound, or rhymed prose; conveying magnification; or departing from the literal expression for emphasis—among other purposes sought through speech.”

The response is:

This argument is weak. Whoever advances it must concede the division of speech into literal and figurative usage, but then insists that literal rather than figurative expressions must be used. This contradicts his statement, “There is no figurative usage in language.” Rather, the instances they have called

figurative—if their use in the language is established—are all literal according to this view. Some literal expressions are finer and more eloquent than others, and clarity and eloquence vary in degree. All these meanings are conveyed literally by the wording, and wording conveys meaning only alongside a contextual indicator. Whoever thinks that the literal meaning of His words,

“And ask the town,”

is to question the walls is ignorant.

This line of argument resembles that of these people: they all deny that a word can be used in one situation with one meaning and in another situation with another meaning, as the word “town” is sometimes used for the inhabitants and sometimes for the dwellings. They claim that it means only the dwellings. In this error they agree with the other group, but that group says, “Something has been omitted here; the full wording is: ‘And ask the people of the town.’” The former group, however, says, “Rather, what is meant is: ‘And ask the walls.’”

The correct view is that “town” refers to the people themselves who live together in that place. Here, the word “town” is intended to refer to these people, as in the words of Allah Most High:

“How many a town, mightier than your town which drove you out, We destroyed! They had none to help them.”

Likewise, Allah Most High says:

“Such is your Lord’s seizure when He seizes towns while they are doing wrong.”

And He says:

“How many a town rebelled against the command of its Lord and His messengers! So We called it to a severe account and punished it with a terrible punishment.”

There are many similar examples.

Section

To complete this discussion, we must address what he mentioned concerning figurative language in the Quran. He said: “An explanation must be offered for His words,

‘Beneath which rivers flow,’

although rivers themselves do not flow.”

The answer is that “river,” like “town,” “waterspout,” and similar terms, may refer either to what occupies a place or to the place itself. Thus, when one says, “He dug the river,” the place is meant; when one says, “The river flowed,” what occupies it is meant.

As for His words,

“And my head has blazed with grey hair,”

the claim that the head does not blaze as fire blazes is conceded. But the answer is that the word “blazing” is not used here in that sense. Rather, it is used for the whiteness that emerged and spread from the blackness, as a flame spreads from fire. This is a comparison and a metaphor. Yet in His words,

“And my head has blazed,”

the word “blazed” is qualified by its reference to the head, so the wording does not admit the meaning of firewood burning. This expression—namely, His words,

“And my head has blazed with grey hair”—

has never been used outside its proper setting; indeed, it has only ever been used with this meaning. Even if this usage brings a change after the establishment of “the fire blazed,” that poses no difficulty. Nor does it pose any difficulty if the intention is to liken that meaning to this one. Rather, this is the nature of general terms: it is necessary that

the two meanings have something in common by virtue of which their individual instances resemble one another. As for calling it a metaphor, it is well known that they did not borrow the word itself. Rather, they combined the word “blazed” with “head” in a construction they have never used, or intended, in any other sense.

For this reason, one cannot say in such a case, “The head has not blazed with grey hair.” Rather, one says, “The blazing of the head is not like the blazing of firewood, even though it resembles it in certain respects.”

He said: “And what of His words,

‘And lower to them the wing of humility,’

when humility has no wing?”

The answer is: There is no doubt that humility has no wing like a bird’s wing, just as a bird has no wing like the wings of the angels. Nor is the wing of humility like the wing of travel. Yet a person’s wing is his side, just as a bird’s wing is its side. A child is commanded to lower his side before his parents, doing so in humble submission to them, not merely lowering it without humility. He also said to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“And lower your wing to those of the believers who follow you.”

He did not say, “the wing of humility.” Thus, the Messenger was commanded to lower his wing, which is his side, whereas the child was commanded to lower his wing in humility. Along with lowering his wing, he must therefore humble himself before his parents, unlike the Messenger, who was not commanded to humble himself. Thus, the way the words of the Quran are combined indicates how their meanings are combined, with each meaning given its due.

translated_text:
Then He, glorified is He, completed this with His words:

“Out of mercy.”

Thus, it is a wing of humility born of mercy, not a wing of humility born of helplessness and weakness: the former is praiseworthy, whereas the latter is blameworthy.

He said: “And what of His words, ‘well-known months,’ when the months are not Hajj itself?”

The answer is: It is understood that the times for Hajj are well-known months. The meaning is not that the acts themselves are a period of time, nor does anyone understand this from the wording. One may, however, say that something has been omitted, and that the full expression is: “The time for Hajj is well-known months.” It is an admirable feature of Arab discourse that, for brevity, they omit what the stated words indicate, just as they sometimes add words to reinforce and emphasize the meaning.

An example of the former is His saying:

“Strike the sea with your staff, and it split apart.”

It is understood that the meaning is: “He struck it, and it split apart.” Yet there was no need to state this explicitly, since the wording, “We said, ‘Strike,’” followed by “and it split apart,” indicates that he struck it and it split apart.

Likewise, His words, “whoever believes,” are understood as “the righteousness of whoever believes,” or “befriend whoever believes.”

Similarly, His words, “Hajj is months,” mean: “The times for Hajj are months.” The meaning is therefore agreed upon; the dispute concerns calling this a metaphor. The objection, “Hajj itself is not months,” would be pertinent only if that were what the statement signified. But it is not. Rather, what it signifies to both its speaker and its hearer is that the times for Hajj are well-known months.
