قَالَ:
 وَقَوْلُهُ: 
{لَهُدِّمَتْ صَوَامِعُ وَبِيَعٌ وَصَلَوَاتٌ وَمَسَاجِدُ}
 وَالصَّلَوَاتُ لَا تَنْهَدِمُ؟
 فَيُقَالُ:
 قَدْ قِيلَ: إنَّ الصَّلَوَاتِ اسْمٌ لِمَعَابِدِ الْيَهُودِ يُسَمُّونَهَا صَلَوَاتٍ بِاسْمِ مَا يُفْعَلُ فِيهَا كَنَظَائِرِهِ؛
 وَهُوَ إنَّمَا اسْتَعْمَلَ لَفْظَ الصَّلَوَاتِ فِي الْمَكَانِ مَقْرُونًا بِقَوْلِهِ:
 
{لَهُدِّمَتْ}
 وَالْهَدْمُ إنَّمَا يَكُونُ لِلْمَكَانِ فَاسْتَعْمَلَهُ مَعَ هَذَا اللَّفْظِ فِي الْمَكَانِ.
قَالَ:
 وَقَوْلُهُ: 
{أَوْ جَاءَ أَحَدٌ مِنْكُمْ مِنَ الْغَائِطِ}
 ؟
 فَنَقُولُ:
 لَفْظُ الْغَائِطِ فِي الْقُرْآنِ يُسْتَعْمَلُ فِي مَعْنَاهُ اللُّغَوِيِّ وَهُوَ: الْمَكَانُ الْمُطْمَئِنُّ مِنْ الْأَرْضِ؛ وَكَانُوا يَنْتَابُونَ الْأَمَاكِنَ الْمُنْخَفِضَةَ لِذَلِكَ وَهُوَ الْغَائِطُ كَمَا يُسَمَّى خَلَاءٌ لِقَصْدِ قَاضِي الْحَاجَةِ الْمَوْضِعَ الْخَالِيَ وَيُسَمَّى مِرْحَاضًا لِأَجْلِ الرَّحْضِ بِالْمَاءِ وَنَحْوِ ذَلِكَ وَالْمَجِيءُ مِنْ الْغَائِطِ اسْمٌ لِقَضَاءِ الْحَاجَةِ؛
 لِأَنَّ الْإِنْسَانَ فِي الْعَادَةِ إنَّمَا يَجِيءُ مِنْ الْغَائِطِ إذَا قَضَى حَاجَتَهُ فَصَارَ اللَّفْظُ حَقِيقَةً عُرْفِيَّةً يُفْهَمُ مِنْهَا عِنْدَ الْإِطْلَاقِ التَّغَوُّطُ فَقَدْ يُسَمُّونَ مَا يَخْرُجُ مِنْ الْإِنْسَانِ غَائِطًا تَسْمِيَةً لِلْحَالِّ بِاسْمِ مَحَلِّهِ كَمَا فِي قَوْلِهِ:
 جَرَى الْمِيزَابُ.
 وَمِنْهُ قَوْلُ عَائِشَةَ:
 مُرْنَ أَزْوَاجَكُمْ يَغْسِلْنَ عَنْهُنَّ أَثَرَ الْغَائِطِ.
 وَلَيْسَ فِي قَوْلِهِ:
 
{أَوْ جَاءَ أَحَدٌ مِنْكُمْ مِنَ الْغَائِطِ}
 اسْتِعْمَالُ اللَّفْظِ فِي غَيْرِ مَعْنَاهُ؛ بَلْ الْمَجِيءُ مِنْ الْغَائِطِ يَتَضَمَّنُ التَّغَوُّطَ فَكَنَّى عَنْ ذَلِكَ الْمَعْنَى بِاللَّفْظِ الدَّالِّ عَلَى الْعَمَلِ
translated_text:
He said: “And what of His words, ‘Monasteries, churches, salawāt (prayers), and mosques would have been demolished’—when prayers cannot be demolished?”

The answer is: It has been said that salawāt is a name for Jewish houses of worship. They call them salawāt after what is performed in them, as in similar instances. He used the word salawāt to designate places only in conjunction with His words, “would have been demolished.” Demolition applies only to places, so it is in conjunction with this wording that He used it to designate places.

He said: “And what of His words, ‘or one of you comes from al-ghā’it (the low ground)’?”

We answer: In the Quran, the word al-ghā’it is used in its linguistic sense: a low-lying piece of ground. People used to frequent low-lying places for that purpose; this is al-ghā’it. Likewise, a privy is called khalā’ (an empty place) because someone relieving himself seeks out an unoccupied spot, and mirhād (a place for washing) because of rahd (washing) with water, and so forth. Coming from the low ground is an expression for relieving oneself, since a person ordinarily comes from such a place only after relieving himself. The expression thus acquired a literal meaning through customary usage and, when used without qualification, is understood to mean defecation. They may also call what comes out of a person ghā’it, naming what occupies a place after the place itself, as in the expression, “The gutter ran.” Another example is the statement of Ā’ishah: “Tell your spouses to wash the traces of excrement off themselves.”

His words, “or one of you comes from the low ground,” do not use the expression in a sense other than its own. Rather, coming from the low ground implies defecation, so He alluded to that meaning through an expression denoting the act

الظَّاهِرِ الْمُسْتَلْزِمِ الْأَمْرَ الْمَسْتُورَ وَكِلَاهُمَا مُرَادٌ. وَهَذَا كَثِيرٌ فِي الْكَلَامِ يُذْكَرُ الْمَلْزُومُ لِيُفْهَمَ مِنْهُ لَازِمُهُ الْمَدْلُولُ.
 وَكِلَاهُمَا دَلَّ عَلَيْهِ اللَّفْظُ لَكِنَّ أَحَدَهُمَا وَسِيلَةٌ إلَى الْآخَرِ كَقَوْلِ إحْدَى النِّسْوَةِ فِي حَدِيثِ أُمِّ زَرْعٍ:
 
{زَوْجِي عَظِيمُ الرَّمَادِ طَوِيلُ النِّجَادِ قَرِيبُ الْبَيْتِ مِنْ الناد}
 . فَإِنَّ عِظَمَ الرَّمَادِ يَسْتَلْزِمُ كَثْرَةَ الطَّبْخِ الْمُسْتَلْزِمَ فِي عَادَتِهِمْ لِكَثْرَةِ الضَّيْفِ؛ الْمُسْتَلْزِمِ لِلْكَرَمِ. وَطُولَ النِّجَادِ يَسْتَلْزِمُ طُولَ الْقَامَةِ وَقُرْبَ الْبَيْتِ مِنْ النَّادِّ يَسْتَلْزِمُ قَصْدَهُ بِحُجَّةِ النَّادِّ إلَى بَيْتِهِ وَالنَّادُّ اسْمٌ لِلْحَالِّ وَالْمَحَلِّ أَيْضًا.
 وَمِنْهُ قَوْلُهُ:
 
{فَلْيَدْعُ نَادِيَهُ}
 وَقَوْلُهُ: 
{وَتَأْتُونَ فِي نَادِيكُمُ الْمُنْكَرَ}
 فَهُنَا هُوَ الْمَحَلُّ وَفِي تِلْكَ هُوَ الْحَالُّ وَهُمْ الْقَوْمُ الَّذِينَ يَنْتَدُونَ وَمِنْهُ 
" دَارُ النَّدْوَةِ "
.
 وَأَصْلُهُ مِنْ مُنَادَاةِ بَعْضِهِمْ لِبَعْضِ بِخِلَافِ النِّجَاءِ فَإِنَّهُمْ الَّذِينَ يَتَنَاجَوْنَ قَالَ الشَّعْبِيُّ:
 إذَا كَثُرَتْ الْحَلَقَةُ فَهِيَ إمَّا نِدَاءٌ وَإِمَّا نِجَاءٌ قَالَ تَعَالَى: 
{وَنَادَيْنَاهُ مِنْ جَانِبِ الطُّورِ الْأَيْمَنِ وَقَرَّبْنَاهُ نَجِيًّا}
 فَنَادَاهُ. وَنَاجَاهُ.
وَقَالَ:
 قَوْلُهُ: 
{اللَّهُ نُورُ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ}
 ؟
 فَيُقَالُ:
 قَدْ ثَبَتَ فِي الصَّحِيحِ أَنَّ {النَّبِيَّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ كَانَ يَقُولُ فِي دُعَائِهِ: اللَّهُمَّ لَك الْحَمْدُ أَنْتَ قَيِّمُ السَّمَوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ
translated_text:
that is outwardly apparent and entails the concealed matter; both are intended. This is common in speech: something is mentioned so that what it necessarily entails may be understood from it. Both are indicated by the wording, but one serves as a means to the other. An example is what one of the women said in the account of Umm Zarʿ:

“My husband has a great heap of ashes, a long sword-belt, and a house near the gathering place.”

A great heap of ashes implies much cooking, which, according to their custom, implies many guests, which in turn implies generosity. A long sword-belt implies tall stature, while the nearness of his house to the gathering place implies that people seek him out at home on account of the gathering. The word nād denotes both those present and the place itself.

Examples include His words:

“Then let him summon his assembly,”

and His words:

“And you commit evil in your gatherings.”

Here it denotes the place, whereas in the former verse it denotes those present—the people who assemble. The name Dār al-Nadwah (Assembly House) derives from the same usage.

Its root sense is that of people calling out to one another, in contrast to private conversation, in which people speak confidentially to one another. Al-Shaʿbī said: “When a gathering grows large, there is either calling aloud or private conversation.” Allah Most High said:

“We called to him from the right side of the Mount and brought him near for intimate conversation.”

Thus, He both called to him and spoke privately with him.

He said: “And what of His words, ‘Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth’?”

The answer is: It is established in the Sahīh that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to say in his supplication: “O Allah, to You belongs all praise. You are the Sustainer of the heavens and the earth

original_text:
وَمَنْ فِيهِنَّ وَلَك الْحَمْدُ أَنْتَ نُورُ السَّمَوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ وَمَنْ فِيهِنَّ} فَلَيْسَ مَفْهُومُ اللَّفْظِ أَنَّهُ شُعَاعُ الشَّمْسِ وَالنَّارِ؛
 فَإِنَّ هَذَا لَيْسَ هُوَ نُورُ السَّمَوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ كَمَا ظَنَّ بَعْضُ الغالطين أَنَّ هَذَا مَدْلُولُ اللَّفْظِ وَالنُّورُ يُرَادُ بِهِ الْمُسْتَنِيرُ الْمُنِيرُ لِغَيْرِهِ بِهَدْيِهِ فَيَدْخُلُ فِي هَذَا أَنْتَ الْهَادِي لِأَهْلِ السَّمَوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ وَقَدْ قَالَ ابْنُ مَسْعُودٍ:
 إنَّ رَبَّكُمْ لَيْسَ عِنْدَهُ لَيْلٌ وَلَا نَهَارٌ نُورُ السَّمَوَاتِ مِنْ نُورِ وَجْهِهِ وَإِذَا كَانَ كَوْنُهُ رَبَّ السَّمَوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ وَقَيِّمَهَا لَا يُنَاقِضُ أَنْ يَكُونَ قَدْ جَعَلَ بَعْضَ عِبَادِهِ يَرُبُّ بَعْضًا مِنْ بَعْضِ الْوُجُوهِ وَيَفْهَمُهُ؛ فَكَذَلِكَ كَوْنُهُ 
{اللَّهُ نُورُ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ}
 مُنِيرُهَا لَا يُنَاقِضُ أَنْ يَجْعَلَ بَعْضَ مَخْلُوقَاتِهِ مُنِيرًا لِبَعْضِ. وَاسْمُ النُّورِ إذَا تَضَمَّنَ صِفَتَهُ وَفِعْلَهُ كَانَ ذَلِكَ دَاخِلًا فِي مُسَمَّى النُّورِ؛ فَإِنَّهُ لَمَّا جَعَلَ الْقَمَرَ نُورًا كَانَ مُتَّصِفًا بِالنُّورِ وَكَانَ مُنِيرًا عَلَى غَيْرِهِ وَهُوَ مَخْلُوقٌ مِنْ مَخْلُوقَاتِهِ وَالْخَالِقُ أَوْلَى بِصِفَةِ الْكَمَالِ الَّذِي لَا نَقْصَ فِيهِ مِنْ كُلِّ مَا سِوَاهُ.
قَالَ:
 وَقَوْلُهُ: 
{فَاعْتَدُوا عَلَيْهِ بِمِثْلِ مَا اعْتَدَى عَلَيْكُمْ}
 قَالَ: وَالْقِصَاصُ لَيْسَ بِعُدْوَانِ؟
 فَيُقَالُ:
 الْعُدْوَانُ مُجَاوَزَةُ الْحَدِّ لَكِنْ إنْ كَانَ بِطَرِيقِ الظُّلْمِ كَانَ مُحَرَّمًا وَإِنْ كَانَ بِطَرِيقِ الْقِصَاصِ كَانَ عَدْلًا مُبَاحًا فَلَفْظُ الْعُدْوَانِ فِي
translated_text:
and all who are in them. To You belongs all praise. You are the Light of the heavens and the earth and all who are in them.” The wording does not mean that He is the radiance of the sun and fire, for that is not the light of the heavens and the earth, as some have mistakenly supposed the wording to mean.

The term “light” denotes One who is luminous and illuminates others through His guidance. This includes the meaning: “You are the Guide of the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth.” Ibn Masʿūd said: “With your Lord there is neither night nor day; the light of the heavens comes from the light of His Face.”

His being the Lord and Sustainer of the heavens and the earth does not contradict His having some of His servants nurture others in certain respects and impart understanding to them. Likewise, the fact that “Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth”—the One who illuminates them—does not contradict His making some of His creatures illuminate others.

When the name “Light” encompasses His attribute and His action, both fall within what that name denotes. When He made the moon a light, it possessed light and illuminated other things, yet it is merely one of His creatures. The Creator is more worthy than anything besides Him of the attribute of perfection that is free of all deficiency.

He said: “And His words:

‘Then transgress against him in the same way that he has transgressed against you.’”

He said: “But just retribution is not aggression?”

The answer is: Aggression means overstepping a limit. If done unjustly, it is forbidden; if done as retribution, it is just and permissible. Thus, the term “aggression” in

such a case means crossing the boundary separating the two parties. Yet once one party has transgressed, it becomes permissible to transgress against him. The first transgression is unjust, whereas the second is permissible. The term “just” is permissible.

Here, “transgression” is qualified by wording that makes clear that it is an act of retribution, unlike initiating aggression, which is unjust. When the term is not qualified as retribution, it is understood to mean initiating aggression, since the default assumption is that no corresponding act preceded it.

He said: “And what of His words, ‘The recompense of an evil is an evil like it,’ and His words, ‘Allah mocks them,’ and ‘They plot, and Allah plots’?”

The answer is: An evil is a name for something that precedes the person concerned. If it is inflicted upon him justly, as retribution, then he deserves the evil inflicted upon him. It is not meant that it precedes the doer, such that he should be forbidden to do it; rather, it precedes the person being requited with it. The terms “evil” and “good” can refer to disobedience and obedience, or to misfortune and blessing, as in His words:

“Whatever good befalls you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself.”

And His words:

“If good touches you, it distresses them; but if evil befalls you, they rejoice at it.”

His words, “The recompense of an evil,” do not refer to everyone who commits a sin. Rather, they refer to requiting someone who has wrongfully harmed another. That harm is among the misfortunes suffered by the injured party, and its recompense is for the wrongdoer to suffer a similar misfortune. It is as though He said: The recompense of someone who harms you is that you harm him just as he harmed you. This is an evil in the literal sense.

As for mockery and plotting—whereby a person outwardly displays good while intending evil—if this involves denying the truth and wronging others, it is a forbidden sin. If, however, it requites someone who has acted in this way with the like of his own deed, it is good and just. Allah Most High says:

“When they meet those who believe, they say, ‘We believe.’ But when alone with their devils, they say, ‘We are with you; we were only mocking.’”

“Allah mocks them.”

For recompense corresponds to the deed. He Most High also says:

“They plotted, and We too plotted.”

Likewise, He says:

“They are surely plotting,”

“And I too am plotting.”

And He says:

“Thus did We plan for Joseph.”

The same applies to requiting an aggressor with the like of his own deed: recompense corresponds to the deed, and this is good and just. It constitutes plotting and scheming when one outwardly shows him something contrary to what one conceals.

He said:

“Whenever they kindle a fire for war, Allah extinguishes it.”

This expression originally refers to combatants kindling a fire around which their supporters gather to help their ally against their enemy. Their war effort cannot be fully mounted without it; when it is extinguished, they cannot unite their forces. The expression then came to be used proverbially of any combatant whose scheme is thwarted. It is like the saying, “Your own hands tied the skin, and your own mouth inflated it,” meaning: you brought this upon yourself.

Likewise, people say, “In summer you squandered the milk,” meaning: you neglected the opportunity when it was available. These expressions originally had a specific meaning, but customary usage transferred them to a meaning

أَعَمَّ مِنْ ذَلِكَ وَصَارَ يُفْهَمُ مِنْهَا ذَلِكَ عِنْدَ الْإِطْلَاقِ لِغَلَبَةِ الِاسْتِعْمَالِ وَلَا يُفْهَمُ مِنْهَا خُصُوصُ مَعْنَاهَا الْأَوَّلِ كَسَائِرِ الْأَلْفَاظِ الَّتِي نَقَلَهَا أَهْلُ الْعُرْفِ إلَى أَعَمَّ مِنْ مَعْنَاهَا مِثْلَ لَفْظِ الرَّقَبَةِ وَالرَّأْسِ فِي قَوْلِهِ:
 
{فَتَحْرِيرُ رَقَبَةٍ}
 وَقَدْ يُقَالُ: إنَّ هَذَا مِنْ بَابِ دَلَالَةِ اللُّزُومِ فَإِنَّ تَحْرِيرَ الْعُنُقِ يَسْتَلْزِمُ تَحْرِيرَ سَائِر الْبَدَنِ؛
 وَلِهَذَا تَنَازَعَ الْفُقَهَاءُ إذَا قَالَ:
 يَدُك حُرٌّ إنْ دَخَلْت الدَّارَ؛
 فَقُطِعَتْ يَدُهُ ثُمَّ دَخَلَ الدَّارَ:
 هَلْ يُعْتَقُ؟ عَلَى وَجْهَيْنِ بِنَاءً عَلَى أَنَّهُ مِنْ بَابِ السِّرَايَةِ أَوْ مِنْ بَابِ الْعِبَادَةِ.
 وَالصَّحِيحُ أَنَّهُ مِنْ بَابِ الْعِبَادَةِ وَمَعْنَاهُ:
 أَنْتَ حُرٌّ إنْ فَعَلْت كَذَا وَالْحَقِيقَةُ الْحَرْفِيَّةُ وَالشَّرْعِيَّةُ مَعْلُومَةٌ فِي اللُّغَةِ.
 قَالَ:
 إلَى مَا لَا يُحْصَى ذِكْرُهُ مِنْ الْمَجَازَاتِ؟

{يَا أَرْضُ ابْلَعِي مَاءَكِ وَيَا سَمَاءُ أَقْلِعِي وَغِيضَ الْمَاءُ}

translated_text:
broader than that. Through predominant usage, this broader meaning came to be understood whenever these expressions were used without qualification, rather than their original, specific meaning. This is like other expressions that customary usage has extended beyond their original scope, such as “neck” and “head,” as in His saying:

“Then the freeing of a slave.”

It may be said that this is a case of implication, since freeing the neck necessarily entails freeing the rest of the body. Hence the jurists disagreed concerning someone who says, “Your hand is free if you enter the house,” whereupon the slave’s hand is cut off and he subsequently enters the house: is he emancipated? There are two views, depending on whether this is a case of emancipation extending from a part to the whole or a case of 'ibāda (worship). The correct view is that it is a case of 'ibāda, meaning: “You are free if you do such-and-such.” Letter-based and Sharīʿah-defined literal usage are recognized in the language.

He said: “And so on, to countless instances of figurative usage?”

They replied: “In the examples cited under this heading, either the meaning is disputed, or the meaning is agreed upon and the dispute concerns calling it figurative. In either case, it provides no evidence for your position.”

An example is His saying:

“O earth, swallow your water, and O sky, withhold! And the water subsided.”

It has been said that “sky” here means rain—that is, “O rain, cease!” But that is not so. Rather, ceasing means withholding: “O sky, withhold your rain.” Those making such claims frequently take expressions with well-known meanings and claim that they are used

in senses other than these, without evidence, and say: “This is figurative.” Such a claim is unacceptable. Those who divide speech into literal and figurative usage agree that the presumption in speech is literal usage. This has two meanings. First, when an expression’s meaning is known and someone says, “This usage is figurative,” the reply is: “Rather, the presumption is literal usage.” Second, when an expression is known to have two senses, one literal and the other figurative, the presumption is that it bears its literal meaning. Thus, sometimes the known meaning is used to establish that the expression denotes it, and sometimes an expression whose signification is known is used to establish the meaning it denotes.

If someone says, concerning the words of the Most High,

“So Allah made it taste the garment of hunger and fear,”

that tasting is originally done with the mouth, the reply is: that is tasting food. Tasting may apply to food, but it may also apply to punishment generally, as He says:

“And We will surely make them taste the lesser punishment before the greater punishment, so that they may return.”

And His words:

“Taste! Indeed, you are the mighty, the noble!”

And His words:

“Taste the touch of Hell!”

His words, “Taste the touch of Hell!” explicitly refer to tasting the touch of punishment and cannot mean tasting food. Moreover, when hunger and fear clothe the body, the pain is greater, unlike a slight degree of either. Thus, when He said:

“So Allah made it taste the garment of hunger and fear,”

it did not indicate that it clothed and encompassed the sufferer. These meanings are conveyed by these expressions, unlike saying, “It became hungry and afraid,” which indicates the general experience, but not its severity or extent. This is an instance of perfect clarity of expression. In all these instances, each expression is used only in its familiar linguistic meaning. For His expression, “tasting the garment of hunger and fear,” is not

Thus, a precise understanding of this subject belongs to the science of rhetoric, through which a person appreciates something of the Quran’s greatness. No expression in the Quran occurs without something accompanying it that clarifies its intended meaning. Whoever misunderstands the Quran does so because of his own limitations or negligence.

If someone claims that the preposition bā’ in “drink of it” is redundant, that reflects his own understanding. A person may drink without having his thirst quenched. Saying “He drinks from it” does not indicate that his thirst is quenched. But when the meaning of quenching thirst is incorporated into the expression “drink of it,” it indicates drinking that quenches thirst. This is a particular kind of drinking, indicated by the preposition bā’.

Likewise, the preposition bā’ in His words,

“Wipe over your faces and hands,”

indicates bringing the substance used for wiping into contact with the bodily part; what is intended is not simply wiping the face. Whoever says that the bā’ is redundant makes the meaning “Wipe your faces.” Yet simply wiping the face does not entail applying the water or earth used for wiping.

As for the reading “and your feet” with the accusative ending, it refers back to the face and hands, as shown by His words, “up to the ankles.” If it were coordinated according to the underlying syntactic position, the meaning would be spoiled: it would amount to saying, “Wipe your heads.”

Moreover, all the reciters read His words concerning dry ablution:

“Wipe over your faces and hands with it.”

The wording of the two verses follows the same pattern. If the expression coordinated with a noun in the genitive were coordinated according to its underlying syntactic position, they would have read “your hands” in the accusative. Since they do not read it that way, it becomes clear that His words:

Ibn Aqīl said:

Section: Their Questions

They have gone to the utmost lengths of strained reasoning and forced interpretation to demonstrate that the wording is literal.

Among their statements is the following:

Qaryah (“village”) means a gathering of people. It is derived from qaraytu al-mā’a fī al-hawd (“I collected water in the basin”), and from mā qara’at al-nāqatu fī rahimihā (“the she-camel has carried nothing in her womb”). Likewise, the hospitality-related terms muqri’ and muqrin refer to guests gathering with their hosts. The Quran and qirā’ah (“recitation”) are so named for the same reason, since they comprise words gathered together. Similarly, gathering properly applies to people, not walls. Thus, He intended only the gathering of people, which is itself the literal meaning of qaryah. This is clarified by His words, Most High:

“And those towns—We destroyed them when they did wrong,”

and His words, Most High:

“And how many a town rebelled against the command of its Lord and His messengers!”

This refers to the gathering—to the people, not the walls. And ‘īr means a caravan.

They said:

If Allah wills buildings and donkeys to speak, He makes them speak. The age of prophethood is a time of extraordinary occurrences. Had he questioned them, they would have answered him about his situation, as a miracle and an honor granted to him.

As for His words, Most High:

“And, because of their disbelief, they were made to drink the calf into their hearts,”

Ibn Aqīl said:

The reply is that qaryah denotes that which gathers people and in which they gather, not the gathered people themselves. Similarly, qur’ and its plural aqrā’ designate the time of menstruation or the time of purity. Likewise, tasriyah (retaining milk), musarrāh (an animal whose milk is retained), and sarāh designate where milk and water collect, not the collected milk and water themselves. A qārī is one who gathers provisions for hospitality, and a muqrī is one who gathers guests—not the guests themselves.

Nor is a caravan called an ‘īr unless it includes particular beasts of burden. Pedestrians and men on foot are not called an ‘īr. If the word merely meant a caravan, it would apply to men on foot just as it applies to those with riding animals. Their claim is therefore disproved.

As for their statement, “Had he asked, the wall would have answered,” such a thing does not happen at one’s choosing, nor can one rely on its occurrence except when presenting it as a miraculous challenge. It does not happen merely because the thought occurs to someone, or at any and every time.

 الْمُرَادُ نَفْسُ ذَاتِ الْعِجْلِ لَمَّا نَسَفَهُ: فَإِذَا نُسِفَ خَرَجَ عَنْ أَنْ يَكُونَ عِجْلًا: بَلْ الْعِجْلُ حَقِيقَةُ الصُّورَةِ الْمَخْصُوصَةِ الَّتِي خَارَتْ وَإِلَّا بُرَادَةُ الذَّهَبِ لَا تَصِلُ إلَّا الْقُلُوبَ وَغَايَةُ مَا تَصِلُ إلَى الْأَجْوَافِ: فَإِمَّا أَنْ يَسْبِقَهَا الطَّبْعُ فَيُحِيلَهَا إلَى أَنْ تَصِلَ إلَى الْقَلْبِ فَلَيْسَ كَذَلِكَ بَلْ سُحَالَةُ الذَّهَبِ إذَا حَصَلَتْ فِي الْمَعِدَةِ رَسَبَتْ بِحَيْثُ لَا تَرْتَقِي إلَى غَيْرِ مَحَلِّهَا فَضْلًا عَنْ أَنْ تَصِلَ إلَى الْقَلْبِ؛
 وَلِأَنَّ قَوْلَ الْعَرَبِ:
 أُشْرِبُوا: لَا يَرْجِعُ إلَى الشُّرْبِ إنَّمَا يَرْجِعُ إلَى الْأَسْبَابِ وَهُوَ: الإيساغ وَذَلِكَ يَرْجِعُ إلَى الْحُبِّ لَا إلَى الذَّوَاتِ الَّتِي هِيَ الْأَجْسَامُ؛
 وَلِهَذَا لَا يُقَالُ:
 أُشْرِبُوا فِي قُلُوبِهِمْ الْمَاءَ إذْ هُوَ مَشْرُوبٌ فَكَيْفَ يُقَالُ فِي الْعِجْلِ عَلَى أَنَّ إضَافَتَهُ نَفْسَهُ إلَى الْقَلْبِ إضَافَةٌ لَهُ إلَى مَحَلِّ الْحُبِّ؟
 وَقَدْ وَرَدَ فِي الْخَبَرِ أَنَّهُمْ كَانُوا يَقُولُونَ فِي سِحَالَتِهِ إذَا تَنَاوَلُوهَا:
 هَذَا أَحَبُّ إلَيْنَا مِنْ مُوسَى وَمِنْ إلَهِ مُوسَى؛ لِمَا نَالَهُمْ مِنْ مَحَبَّتِهِ فِي قُلُوبِهِمْ.
translated_text:
As for His words,

“That is Jesus,”

referring to the name: if they interpret them in this way, they are figurative, because the utterance—which is the name—is not ascribed to him. For this reason we say:

“It is not for Allah to take a son. Glory be to Him!”

The name, which is an utterance, is not the son of Mary. Rather, the son of Mary is the very body and spirit to which the name applies—the one at whose hands miraculous signs appeared, and whom they made a god because those signs appeared.

As for their statement that what is meant is the very substance of the calf when he scattered it: once scattered, it ceased to be a calf. Rather, “the calf” properly denotes the particular form that lowed. Otherwise, gold filings reach only the hearts, and the furthest they reach is the bodily cavities. As for the natural faculty preceding them and transforming them until they reach the heart, that is not the case. Rather, when gold filings enter the stomach, they settle there, unable to rise beyond that location, let alone reach the heart.

Furthermore, the Arabic expression “they were made to imbibe” does not refer to drinking itself, but to its causes—namely, making something be swallowed. This pertains to love, not to entities that are physical bodies. Hence one does not say, “They were made to imbibe water into their hearts,” even though water is something drunk. How, then, could this be said of the calf, especially when its very association with the heart associates it with the seat of love?

It is related in a report that, when they consumed its filings, they would say, “This is dearer to us than Moses and the God of Moses,” because of the love for it that had taken hold of their hearts.

 مَا قَرَأْت النَّاقَةَ سَلًّا جَزُورٌ قَطُّ؛

 مَا أَظْهَرَتْهُ وَأَخْرَجَتْهُ مِنْ رَحِمِهَا وَالْقَارِي: هُوَ الَّذِي يُظْهِرُ الْقُرْآنَ وَيُخْرِجُهُ قَالَ تَعَالَى: 
{إنَّ عَلَيْنَا جَمْعَهُ وَقُرْآنَهُ}
 فَفَرَّقَ بَيْنَ الْجَمْعِ وَالْقُرْآنِ
translated_text:
I say:

As for their discussion of the settlement: “settlement,” “river,” and similar terms designate both a place and what occupies it. Thus, “settlement” encompasses both the dwellings and their inhabitants. A statement about it may concern the inhabitants, the dwellings, or both. This is like the term “human being,” which designates both soul and body, although a statement may concern only one of them. Likewise, “speech” designates both wording and meaning, although a statement may concern only one of them.

As for the derivation of these words, some scholars have erred here by failing to distinguish between qaraʾa, with a hamza, and qarā–yaqrī, with a yā. The verb meaning “to gather” is qarā–yaqrī, without a hamza. From it come qarya (settlement), qirāʾa (reading), and similar words. Another example is qaraytu al-dayfa, aqrīhi: that is, “I brought the guest in and drew him close.” Qaraytu al-māʾa fī al-hawd means “I gathered the water in the basin”; taqarraytu al-miyāh means “I sought out the watering places.” Qarawtu al-bilāda, qaraytuhā, and istaqraytuhā are used when you explore lands, travelling from one to another. From this comes istiqrāʾ: examining something in its entirety. This differs from istaqraʾtuhu al-Qurʾāna, “I asked him to recite the Quran,” for that derives from the root containing a hamza. Thus, a settlement is the place where people gather, and a statement about it sometimes concerns the place and sometimes the people.

As for qaraʾa with a hamza, its meaning is to make manifest and clear. Qurʾ and qirāʾa (recitation) belong to this root. An example is their saying:

“The she-camel—a slaughter camel—has never brought forth a fetal membrane.”

That is, she has not made it manifest and expelled it from her womb. The reciter is the one who brings forth the Quran and makes it manifest. Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation.”

Thus, He distinguishes between collecting and reciting.

{ثَلَاثَةَ قُرُوءٍ}

translated_text:
And qurʾ denotes blood because it becomes manifest and emerges. It likewise denotes a time, since times are determined by something observable. The interval of purity is then included in the term qurʾ by extension, just as the night is included in the term “day.” The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to a woman experiencing non-menstrual bleeding:

“Refrain from prayer during the days of your menstrual periods.”

An interval of purity followed by menstruation constitutes a qurʾ; thus, the term encompasses the whole. An interval of purity alone, however, is not called a qurʾ. Hence, if a woman is divorced during a menstrual period, she does not count that as a qurʾ, because she must observe a waiting period of three qurūʾ. If she is divorced during an interval of purity, the qurʾ consists of the menstrual period together with the preceding interval of purity. This is why the senior Companions—including ʿUmar, ʿUthmān, ʿAlī, Abū Mūsā, and others—held that the qurūʾ are menstrual periods: she is commanded to wait for three qurūʾ. If a qurʾ meant an interval of purity, her waiting period would consist of two qurūʾ and part of a third.

The disagreement between the two groups concerns the third menstrual period. The senior Companions and those who agreed with them say that her husband has the prior right to take her back as long as she has not bathed after her third menstrual period. The younger Companions say that once she enters her third menstrual period, she is free to remarry.

It is established by both scriptural evidence and consensus that the sunnah is to divorce her during an interval of purity in which he has not had intercourse with her. By then, part of that interval of purity has already elapsed. Yet Allah commanded that divorce take place with the waiting period still ahead, not when it is already under way. His words “three qurūʾ” specify a number, unlike the word “months,” which is a plural form, not a number. There must therefore be three qurūʾ, as Allah commanded; part of the third is not sufficient.

As for the words you cite:

“That is Jesus, son of Mary—the word of truth.”

There are two well-known readings: the nominative and the accusative. Under either reading, it has been said that “the word of truth” refers to Jesus, just as he is called the Word of Allah.

It has also been said that the meaning is: “What We have mentioned is the word of truth.” In that case, it is the predicate of an omitted subject. This has parallels, such as His words:

“They will say, ‘Three, their fourth being their dog’”—and the rest of the verse;

and:

“Say, ‘The truth is from your Lord.’”

That is: “This truth is from your Lord.” If Jesus is intended, calling him “the word of truth” is like calling him the Word of Allah. On this interpretation, it functions as a predicate and as an appositive. Either interpretation has parallels, so the question of calling it figurative is the same as with those parallels. The more apparent meaning is that this account We have given of Jesus, son of Mary, is the word of truth—although his being the son of a servant of Allah is included in this.

Some say that “the Truth” means Allah, and that the intended meaning is “the word of Allah.” Although this is a sound meaning, the Quran’s usual practice, when attributing speech to Allah, is to say “the word of Allah.” It does not say “the word of truth” unless a true statement is intended, as in His words:

“His word is the truth”;

“Allah speaks the truth”;

and:

“The truth—and the truth I speak.”

 وَإِذَا ثَبَتَ أَنَّهُ عَرَبِيٌّ فَلُغَةُ الْعَرَبِ مُشْتَمِلَةٌ عَلَى الِاسْتِعَارَةِ وَالْمَجَازِ وَهِيَ بَعْضُ طُرُقِ الْبَيَانِ وَالْفَصَاحَةِ فَلَوْ أَخَلَّ بِذَلِكَ لَمَا تَمَّتْ أَقْسَامُ الْكَلَامِ وَفَصَاحَتُهُ عَلَى التَّمَامِ وَالْكَمَالِ وَإِنَّمَا يَبِينُ تَعْجِيزُ الْقَوْمِ إذَا طَالَ وَجَمَعَ مِنْ اسْتِعَارَتِهِمْ وَأَمْثَالِهِمْ وَصِفَاتِهِمْ وَلَا نَصَّ بِجَوَازِ الْأَلْفَاظِ إلَّا إذَا طَالَتْ؛
 وَلِهَذَا لَا يَحْصُلُ التَّحَدِّي بِمِثْلِ بَيْتٍ وَلَا بِالْآيَةِ وَالْآيَتَيْنِ وَلِهَذَا جَعَلَ حُكْمَ الْقَلِيلِ مِنْهُ غَيْرَ مُحْتَرَمٍ احْتِرَامَ الطَّوِيلِ فَسَوَّغَ الشَّرْعُ لِلْجُنُبِ وَالْحَائِضِ تِلَاوَتَهُ كُلَّ ذَلِكَ لِأَنَّهُ لَا إعْجَازَ فِيهِ فَإِذَا أَتَى بِالْمَجَازِ وَالْحَقِيقَةِ وَسَائِرِ ضُرُوبِ الْكَلَامِ وَأَقْسَامِهِ فَفَاقَ كَلَامُهُ الْجَامِعَ الْمُشْتَمِلَ عَلَى تِلْكَ الْأَقْسَامِ:
 كَانَ الْإِعْجَازُ؛ وَظَهَرَ التَّعْجِيزُ لَهُمْ فَهَذَا يُوجِبُ أَنْ يَكُونَ فِي الْقُرْآنِ مَجَازٌ.
translated_text:
the grammarians of Kufa and others, instances of a noun being joined to its adjective in a genitive construction without any ellipsis. Many grammarians of Basra, however, maintain that the noun governed by the genitive construction has been omitted, the underlying wording being “the prayer of the first hour.” The first view is more correct: nothing in the wording indicates the supposedly omitted noun, nor does it come to mind. The adjectival construction also occurs in several places, as in His words:

“The final abode”;

and:

“His word is the truth.”

In short, parallels to this are numerous in the Quran and in Arabic speech. This provides no argument for those who call it figurative beyond whatever argument they have concerning its parallels. The matter must therefore be referred back to the underlying principle.

Ibn ʿAqīl said:

“Among our proofs are the words of the Most High:

‘In a clear Arabic tongue.’

Since it is established that the Quran is Arabic, and the Arabic language includes metaphor and figurative expression among its means of clarity and eloquence, were the Quran to omit these, it would not fully encompass the forms of speech or attain complete eloquence. The Arabs’ inability to match it becomes apparent only when the discourse is lengthy and brings together their metaphors, comparisons, and descriptions. Nor is there any text authorizing such wording unless it is lengthy.

“For this reason, the challenge cannot be issued through something like a single line of poetry, or through one or two verses. Likewise, a short portion of the Quran was not accorded the same inviolability as a long passage, so the revealed Law permitted a person in a state of major ritual impurity and a menstruating woman to recite it. All this is because such a portion does not possess inimitability.

“Thus, if He employs figurative and literal expression, together with all the other forms and categories of speech, and His speech surpasses discourse encompassing all those categories, its inimitability is established and their inability to match it becomes evident. This requires that the Quran contain figurative expression.”

translated_text:
I say:

Most scholars dispute his statement that a short surah possesses no inimitability. They maintain that even a short surah is inimitable. Indeed, some of our fellow scholars disputed his claim even regarding one or two verses. Abū Bakr Ibn al-‘Imād—the teacher of my grandfather Abū al-Barakāt—said:

“I do not consider his statement correct that a person in a state of major ritual impurity may recite a small portion of the Quran only because it possesses no inimitability. The whole of it is inviolable. Such a person was permitted to recite part of a verse only to afford ease to the legally accountable person, with consideration for attaining reward and for hardship, while its inviolability remains intact. Likewise, he was permitted to pray with a small amount of blood present, despite its impurity.”

I say:

As for his statement that the Quran was revealed in the language of the Arabs, that is true. More specifically, it was revealed in the tongue of Quraysh, as the Most High says:

“We never sent a messenger except in the language of his people.”

‘Umar and ‘Uthmān said: “This Quran was revealed in the language of this tribe, Quraysh.” Thus, anyone who says that the expressions it contains are not figurative, while their counterparts in Arabic speech are figurative, contradicts himself. However, our fellow scholars who said that the Quran contains no figurative expression are not known to have acknowledged that the Arabic language contains figurative expression. They therefore need not be guilty of contradiction.

Moreover, one may say that Arabic contains figurative expression of a kind whose counterpart is not found in the Quran. The speech of created beings contains exaggeration and reckless overstatement—in praise, satire, al-murā’ī, and other forms—from which the speech of a wise person should be kept free, let alone the speech of Allah. If someone applies the designation “figurative” only to speech of this kind, he is not obliged to apply that designation to

translated_text:
what occurs in the Quran. This is because classifying some speech as figurative is merely a matter of convention, not something determined by religious law, linguistic usage, or reason. Thus, some call an expression figurative when it is used for something distinct from what it denotes, but not when it is used for part of what it denotes. They therefore do not regard a general expression used for only part of its scope as figurative, nor a command intended to convey recommendation. This is the convention followed by most jurists.

They may not describe this as using an expression for something other than what it was assigned to denote, on the grounds that part of a whole is not, without qualification, called something other than that whole. Thus, one out of ten is not said to be something other than those ten, nor a person’s hand something other than that person. Moreover, in their view, figurative usage requires a contextual indicator to establish the intended meaning, except where the indicator serves to exclude an unintended meaning. In the case of a command, the contextual indicator excludes part of what the wording signifies while leaving the remainder signified by the wording itself. By contrast, the contextual indicator accompanying “lion” makes clear that the intended referent does not fall within what the word “lion” denotes when used without qualification.

While most jurists conventionally distinguish between literal and figurative usage in this way, others adopt the convention that whenever an expression is not intended to convey its entire meaning, it is figurative. Most of the latter, however, distinguish between a contextual indicator that is separate or independent and one rooted in the wording, forming part of it, or lacking independent standing. They do not regard the latter cases as figurative, lest they be obliged to consider most speech figurative—even the statement:

“There is no god but Allah.”

This would be so despite its being known that the polytheists did not dispute

translated_text:
that Allah is a true God; rather, they set up other gods alongside Him. Thus, the dispute between the Messenger and them concerned denying divinity to anything other than Allah, in the literal sense, since the expression was not used for anything other than what it was assigned to denote. As for the claim that its original assigned meaning is negation—namely, the absolute denial of any deity—no Arab ever held such a belief. Indeed, they had no intention of expressing it, nor did they originally assign any expression to convey it. Expression conveys meanings conceived in the mind, and they conceived of this meaning only to deny it, not to affirm it. Negating a negation is affirmation.

Anyone who claims that the meaning they intended by this expression in their language was that the Messenger should be sent to deny every deity; that this was the meaning for which they originally assigned the expression; and that their statement, “There is no god but Allah,” uses that expression in a sense other than its assigned meaning—such a person plainly misrepresents them even in their state of polytheism, let alone their state of faith.

Undoubtedly, all restrictions of scope contained within the wording itself—such as an adjectival qualification, a condition, a limiting endpoint, apposition, or an exception—stand on the same footing. However, they used most expressions sometimes without these restrictions and sometimes accompanied by them. This is unlike the statement, “There is no god but Allah,” which they have never been known to use without the exception, since they regarded the resulting meaning as false. Whoever regards that as the literal meaning in their language plainly misrepresents them. If he distinguishes one exception from another, he contradicts himself and departs from consensus. This is so

translated_text:
because it is founded on a false, self-contradictory premise. When the proponent of a contradictory position follows it through consistently and is held to its implications, its falsity and objectionable character become apparent in ways that were not evident before. If he does not follow it through, he contradicts himself, and its falsity becomes apparent. Thus, its falsity follows either way.

For this reason, proponents of figurative usage have no coherent position whatsoever. Rather, all their positions are contradictory, and their definitions and the distinguishing signs they mention are unsound. Since the foundation of their position is false, they have invented a division and terminology within the language that have no basis in reality. Indeed, this division is false, so it cannot be accurately conceived or expressed in sound terms. A sound meaning, by contrast, can be expressed in sound words, as Allah Most High says:

“O you who believe, fear Allah and speak words that are right.”

Sound speech is apt and correct, corresponding to the truth without addition or omission; it is just and truthful. This is unlike the speech of someone who seeks to distinguish between two equivalent things and treat them as different—indeed, as opposites. Such speech is not sound. This is discussed at length in its proper place.

The point here is that those who say, “There is no figurative language in the Quran”—if they mean by this that His words,

“Ask the town,”

mean “Ask the walls,” and that “the caravan” means the beasts, and other such things reported from them, then they are mistaken. If they classify an expression used in a particular sense outside the Quran as figurative, but do not classify it as figurative when used in that sense in the Quran, they are also mistaken. If, however, they mean that writings other than the Quran contain exaggerations, reckless assertions, unnecessary expressions, and similar things from which the Quran is free, then they are correct in this.

“We call those things figurative, unlike the expressions used in the Quran and similar Arabic speech,” then their terminology is closer to being correct than that of those who classify most Arabic speech as figurative. Thus, Ibn Jinnī is reported to have said: “The statement ‘Zayd went out’ is figurative, because the verb denotes the verbal noun, and the verbal noun made definite by the definite article encompasses every instance of going out. This would entail that Zayd performed every kind of going out. This is the literal meaning of the expression; if a single instance of going out is intended, it is figurative.”

No one who properly conceives what he is saying would say this. Ibn Jinnī possessed learning and intelligence, and probed subtle meanings in *Sirr al-Sināʿa*, *al-Khasāʾis*, *Iʿrāb al-Qurʾān*, and elsewhere. If he did not say this, that would be more in keeping with his scholarly merit. If he did say it, even a learned man may say something that otherwise only the most ignorant would say.

The verb denotes only what the verbal noun names: the action as such, without any qualification of universality or, indeed, any other qualification. Thus, when one says, “Zayd went out,” “Bakr stood up,” or something similar, the verb indicates that an act of going out or standing up occurred on his part, without the wording indicating its kind or extent. Rather, it can apply to these as alternatives, not collectively, as in His words:

“Then the freeing of a slave.”

He has required the freeing of one slave, not every slave; and the expression encompasses all

translated_text:
slaves as alternatives, so whichever slave he frees suffices. Likewise, saying “He went out” indicates that an act of going out occurred. It may have been brief or prolonged, and he may have been riding or walking. Even so, the alternatives encompassed are only instances of going out possible for Zayd. But to claim that this expression entails the universal inclusion of everything in existence called “going out,” though not collectively—no one would say this unless his understanding were corrupted and he were closer to a beast. We should presume that Ibn Jinnī would not say this.

Moreover, this meaning exists in all other languages. Would any rational person say that the speakers of every language who use verbal sentences—which every nation must use—originally assigned those sentences to encompass every kind of that action existing in the world, and that using them for particular instances departs from the meaning for which the expression was originally assigned?

Rather, this demonstrates the unsoundness of the very basis of the doctrine of figurative usage, if it leads to such nonsense being uttered at all and then made into a disputed question included in works on the principles of jurisprudence.

Thus, whoever among those who deny figurative usage in the Quran says: “We do not call anything in the Quran, or in comparable Arabic speech, figurative. We call figurative only what exceeds the bounds of moderation, such as the exaggeration found in poets’ praise and invective

, elegies, and martial verse”—it is clear that, if distinguishing between literal and figurative usage is a valid terminological convention, this convention is more deserving of acceptance than that of those who regard most speech as figurative, or even those who regard every restriction by an adjoining qualification as figurative.

Such a person thus regards as figurative His words:

“Pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to Allah by people—those who are able to make their way there.”

And His words: “Then seek clean earth.”

And His words: “Then the freeing of a believing slave.”

And His words: “Then fasting for two consecutive months.”

And His words: “Then from among your believing slave women whom your right hands possess.”

And His words: “And chaste women from among the believers and chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture before you, when you give them their dowries, seeking chastity, neither committing fornication nor taking secret lovers.”

And His words: “So woe to those who pray, who are heedless of their prayer.”

And His words: “Fight those who do not believe in Allah or the Last Day, nor regard as unlawful,” through to His words: “until they pay the jizyah in submission, humbled.”

And His words: “Then if he divorces her, she is not lawful for him thereafter until she marries another husband.”

And His words: “Do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated.”

And His words: “And do not have sexual relations with them while you are in devotional retreat in the mosques.”

And His words: “You shall have half of what your wives leave if they have no child.”

And His words: “But if you have a child, they shall have one-eighth.”

And His words: “The recompense for an evil deed is an evil deed like it.”

And His words: “Unless it is an immediate transaction that you conduct among yourselves.”

And His words: “For his parents, each shall have one-sixth of what he leaves if he has a child. But if he has no child and his parents inherit from him, his mother shall have one-third.”

And His words: “And whoever kills a believer

intentionally.” And His words:

“And whoever kills a believer by mistake must free a believing slave and pay compensation to the deceased’s family.”

And His words:

“To worship Allah, devoting my religion sincerely to Him.”

And His words:

“Do not kill the soul that Allah has forbidden, except by right.”

And His words:

“Except those who repent before you gain power over them.”

And His words:

“Unless they commit a clear indecency.”

And His words:

“Those who declare their wives unlawful to them by zihār, then go back on what they have said.”

And His words:

“And whoever does righteous deeds, whether male or female, while being a believer.”

And His words:

“They drank from it, except a few of them.”

And His words:

“And have no witnesses except themselves.”

And His words:

“You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills, in safety.”

There are countless similar examples, which could be enumerated only with difficulty.

Whoever regards all this as figurative, holding that in all these and similar expressions the Arabs use words in senses other than those for which they were originally coined, advances a claim whose falsity is self-evident. His position also entails that most speech is figurative, since the same consequence follows for every unrestricted expression to which a qualification is added.

Sentences are of two kinds: nominal and verbal. A nominal sentence is fundamentally composed of a subject and predicate. It would therefore follow that whenever its subject and predicate are modified, an exception is introduced, or a circumstantial qualifier is added, the sentence becomes figurative.

His position also entails that when kāna (“was”) and its related verbs, inna (“indeed”) and its related particles, or zanantu (“I thought”) and its related verbs are introduced into the sentence, changing its meaning and grammatical inflection, it becomes figurative. For a qualification may occur at the beginning of a sentence, in its middle, or at its end

, especially in constructions with zanantu (“I thought”). For they say: Zaydun muntaliqun (“Zayd is setting out”) and Zaydan muntaliqan zanantu (“Zayd was setting out, I thought”). Thus, when the verb comes first, it must govern the case of its objects; when it comes in the middle, its grammatical government may be suspended; and when it comes last, suspension is preferable, although government remains permissible. For when the object precedes the verb, the verb’s grammatical government is weakened. They therefore strengthen it by introducing a preposition, just as they strengthen the government of the active participle because it is weaker than the verb, as in His words:

“They stand in awe of their Lord.”

And His words:

“If you can interpret dreams.”

And His words:

“And they are indeed enraging us.”

His position also entails that a verbal sentence becomes figurative when qualified by a verbal noun modified by an adjective, indicating a number, or specifying a particular kind of action, as in His words:

“Flog them with eighty lashes.”

And His words:

“And that Allah may grant you a mighty victory.”

The same applies to adverbial expressions of place and time, and to all the prepositional phrases that qualify a verb, as in His words:

“Then wipe your faces and hands with it.”

And His words:

“Upon guidance from their Lord.”

And His words:

“And that those who believe follow the truth from their Lord.”

And His words:

It should also be known that Ibn ʿAqīl, despite going to great lengths here to refute those who say that there is no figurative language in the Quran, elsewhere defends the position that there is no figurative language at all, whether in the Quran or elsewhere. is eternal; and no part of what is eternal precedes another, for precedence and subsequence are attributes of that part of it which comes into being in time.’”

I say:

He has thus treated this expression as univocal, denoting a shared meaning like other univocal terms. In each instance, however, it has a distinctive element determined by its particular context, as in his example of blackness. Yet this very point refutes his argument for figurative language.

He said:

“Among the proofs of figurative language is what its proponents claim to be one of their strongest arguments against those who deny it: the words of the Most High,

‘Monasteries, churches, synagogues, and mosques in which Allah’s name is frequently mentioned would surely have been demolished,’

and His words,

‘Then they found there a wall that wanted to collapse, so he set it upright.’

In Arabic, salawāt means either supplications or the prescribed acts of prayer. Neither can be described as being demolished, and an inanimate object cannot possess will.

If it is said:

‘It was part of Arabic usage to call a place of prayer a prayer. Indeed, the words, “And the places of prostration belong to Allah,” have been explained as referring to the bodily parts used in prostration. Moreover, although a wall has no will, it is not impossible for Allah to produce will in it without bringing particular structures into existence.’

The reply is:

‘This is a claim about the original assignment of meanings to words, for prayer is not known to have originally meant

anything but supplication; in Islamic law, its meaning was expanded or transferred to the prescribed acts. As for buildings, no transmitted evidence from the Arabs establishes this usage. Even if they are called ‘prayers,’ this is merely a metaphor, because they are places of prayer. Were Allah to create will in a wall, that would not make it willing, just as creating speech in it would not make it a speaker.’”

As for his statement that “the Word of Allah” refers to Jesus himself, there is no doubt that, in Arabic, a verbal noun may denote its object, as when they say, “This is a dirham minted by the ruler.” Another example is His saying:

“This is Allah’s creation.”

Similarly, what is commanded is called a “command”; what is brought about by power is called “power”; that through which mercy is shown is called “mercy”; and what is created through the word is called a “word.” Such wording, however, is used only with accompanying indications that clarify the intended meaning, as in His saying:

“O Mary, Allah gives you good news of a word from Him, whose name is the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, honoured in this world and the Hereafter, and among those brought near to Him.”

He thus made clear that the word is the Messiah. Yet it is well known that the Messiah himself is not speech.

“She said, ‘My Lord, how can I have a child when no man has touched me?’ He said, ‘Thus Allah creates whatever He wills. When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, “Be,” and it is.’”

When she expressed astonishment at having a child, He explained that He—glory be to Him—creates whatever He wills: when He decrees a matter, He only says to it, “Be,” and it is. This indicates that this child is among the things Allah creates by His saying:

“Be,” and it is.

Hence Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: “Jesus was created through ‘Be’; he is not ‘Be’ itself.”

Hence He says in another verse:

“Indeed, the likeness of Jesus before Allah is that of Adam: He created him from dust, then said to him, ‘Be,’ and he was.”

He thus clarified His meaning: Jesus was created through “Be”; he is not himself the word “Be” or any other such speech.

Likewise, He says:

“Hajj is [during] well-known months.”

It is understood that He did not mean that acts are periods of time; rather, He intended to state the time of Hajj. Hence He says immediately afterwards:

“So whoever undertakes Hajj during them…”

The Hajj undertaken during those months is not the months themselves. It is therefore clear that, by saying “months,” He did not mean the act itself. Rather, He clarified His intent through His words, making clear that the expression does not indicate that acts are periods of time.

Likewise, He says:

“Rather, righteousness is [in] one who fears Allah.”

When He said:

“Righteousness is not that you enter houses from the back; rather, righteousness is [in] one who fears Allah,”

the wording indicated that His meaning was: rather, righteousness is fear of Allah. Such usage therefore occurs only alongside something that clarifies the intended meaning. In that case, the expression is used with a qualification that clarifies what is intended here, just as it is used elsewhere with a qualification that clarifies what is intended there.

The two meanings have something in common, yet also differ. This is comparable to names that are synonymous yet distinct, such as al-sārim (the keen-edged sword), al-muhannad (the sword of Indian steel), and al-sayf (the sword). They share a reference to the same entity and, in this respect, resemble univocal terms. Yet each is distinguished by indicating a particular meaning, so they resemble terms with distinct meanings. The names of Allah, His Messenger, and His Book belong to this category.

Likewise, an expression made definite by the definite article referring to something already known denotes, in each instance, what the addressee recognizes, either through prior familiarity or through the preceding wording. Although what is intended in one instance is not what is intended in another, the two have both a shared element and a distinguishing element. Thus Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, We have sent to you a Messenger as a witness over you, just as We sent to Pharaoh a messenger.”

“But Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger.”

And Allah Most High says:

“Do not make the Messenger’s calling among you like your calling one another.”

Both passages contain the word “messenger” with the definite article. However, the familiar, known referent in the former is the messenger sent to Pharaoh, namely Moses, peace be upon him. In the latter, the familiar, known referent for those addressed by His words, “Do not make the Messenger’s calling among you,” is Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Both usages are literal, and the term is univocal. It is made definite by the article in both passages, but the understood reference in one passage differs from that in the other. This is one of the factors through which an expression conveys meaning: the definite article conveys its meaning only when the addressee knows the familiar referent.

The same applies to demonstratives, such as “this,” “these,” and “those.” In each instance, a demonstrative denotes only what is being indicated there. There must therefore be a situational or verbal indication clarifying that what is being indicated is something other than the demonstrative expression itself. The intended meaning is conveyed only through that indication together with the demonstrative expression, just as, with the definite article, the intended meaning is conveyed only through the article itself

and the familiar referent. This manner of conveying meaning cannot be called figurative; otherwise, the signification of demonstratives, indeed of pronouns, the definite article referring to something already known, and other such expressions would also have to be figurative. No rational person would say this. If an ignorant person does say it, this shows that he has not understood how expressions convey meaning. He imagines that literal expressions convey meaning without these factors, which are indispensable to their signification.

Indeed, no expression conveys meaning except in conjunction with other expressions and the circumstances of the speaker, whose customary use of such speech must be known. Merely hearing an expression without knowing the speaker and his customary usage conveys nothing, for expressions signify intentionally and deliberately: they convey what the speaker intends them to convey, rather than signifying by themselves. One must therefore know what the speaker must intend by them. Hence, this cannot be known through hearing alone, but through reason together with hearing.

Understanding what expressions signify thus involves both hearing and reason. This is called fiqh (understanding). Accordingly, someone who grasps their meaning is said to understand, while someone who does not grasp it is said not to understand. Allah Most High says:

“What is the matter with these people that they can hardly understand any statement?”

And Allah Most High says:

“He found, on the near side of the two mountains, a people who could hardly understand speech.”

And He says:

“There is nothing that does not glorify Him with praise, but you do not understand their glorification.”

translated_text:
He also said—may Allah have mercy on him:

Section: The Foundations of Knowledge and Religion

Allah Most High said:

“Your allies are none but Allah, His Messenger, and those who believe,”

up to His words:

“Whoever takes Allah, His Messenger, and those who believe as allies—indeed, the party of Allah will prevail.”

He also said:

“Honor belongs to Allah, His Messenger, and the believers.”

And He said:

“Obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you.”

The testimony recited in prayer includes:

“All greetings, prayers, and good things are for Allah. Peace be upon you, O Prophet, and Allah’s mercy and blessings. Peace be upon us and upon Allah’s righteous servants.”

These are the principles that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb instructed Shurayh to follow when he said: “Judge according to what is in the Book of Allah. If no ruling is found there, then according to what is in the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah. If no ruling is found there, then according to what the people have agreed upon.” Another version reads: “Then according to the judgments of the righteous.”

Likewise, Ibn Masʿūd said:

“Whoever is asked about a matter should give a ruling according to what is in the Book of

Allah. If no ruling is found there, then according to what is in the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah. If no ruling is found there, then according to what the people have agreed upon.”

Something similar has also been reported from Ibn ʿAbbās and others. Hence the scholars said: “The Book, the Sunnah, and consensus.” This is because He made obedience to them obligatory when there is no disagreement, and commanded that matters be referred back to Allah and the Messenger only when there is disagreement. This provides evidence on two grounds: the obligation to obey them, and the fact that referring back to the Book and the Sunnah is obligatory only when there is disagreement. It follows that, in the absence of disagreement, this is not obligatory, though it is permissible, because their agreement is evidence of conformity with the Book and the Sunnah.

He also commanded loyalty to them. Loyalty entails agreement and adherence, just as enmity entails opposition and estrangement. If you agree with someone in everything, you are loyal to him in everything. If you agree with him in most matters, you are loyal to him in most matters. In the matter under dispute, however, you have not shown him loyalty, even if you have not shown him enmity.

As for commands to follow the Book and the Sunnah, they are exceedingly numerous, such as His words:

“Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord.”

“So follow it and fear Allah.”

“And followed the light that was sent down with him.”

And:

“They follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet.”

“Obey Allah and obey the Messenger.”

“We did not send any messenger except to be obeyed by Allah’s permission.”

“But no, by your Lord, they do not believe”—and the rest of the verse.

“Refer it back to Allah and the Messenger.”

“And this is My path, perfectly straight, so follow it.”

“Whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it.”

“It is not for a believing man or a believing woman…”

“So let those who oppose his command beware.”

Such passages are numerous.

As for following the early generations, several verses provide evidence. First are those already mentioned, such as His words, “and those in authority”; “if you disagree”; “and the believers”; and:

“Honor belongs to Allah, His Messenger, and the believers.”

If the believers were to depart from truth and guidance, they would not then possess honor in that respect, because falsehood and misguidance are not part of the faith by which honor is merited. Honor is conditional upon faith, as He says:

“Do not lose heart or grieve, for you will have the upper hand if you are believers.”

Another is His saying:

“Guide us to the straight path—the path of those You have blessed, not those who have incurred Your anger, nor those who have gone astray.”

He commanded us to ask Him for guidance to their path. He also said:

“Those will be with the ones whom Allah has blessed”—and the rest of the verse, which contains the evidence.

Another is His saying:

“Follow the path of those who turn to Me.”

The believers among the early generations turned to Him; hence their path must be followed.

Another is His saying:

“Follow those who ask no reward of you and are rightly guided.”

The early generations were likewise.

Another is His saying:

“And follows a path other than that of the believers.”

Whoever departs from their consensus

has indeed followed a path other than theirs.

Another is His saying:

“Thus We have made you a just community, so that you may be witnesses over mankind and the Messenger may be a witness over you.”

And His saying:

“So that the Messenger may be a witness over you, and you may be witnesses over mankind.”

The people of Jesus said:

“Then record us among the witnesses.”

This occurs in Āl ‘Imrān and al-Mā’idah, for ours is the role of bearing witness, while theirs is worship without bearing witness. The community described as “just” is upright and the best. Witnesses over mankind must be knowledgeable and just, like the Messenger. Hence, he said concerning a funeral, “It is assured! It is assured!” He also said:

“You are Allah’s witnesses on earth.”

And he said:

“You will soon be able to distinguish the people of Paradise from the people of Hell by the praise or blame they receive.”

It is thus known that their testimony concerning persons and actions is accepted. If they could testify to what is untrue, they would not have been designated witnesses without qualification.

Another is His saying:

“You are the best community brought forth for mankind: you enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and believe in Allah.”

This verse contains several proofs, such as His words, “the best community,” and His words, “you enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong.” They must therefore enjoin everything right and forbid everything wrong. Correctness in rulings is right, and error is wrong.

Another is His saying:

“Fear Allah and be with the truthful.”

Another is the saying of Allah’s intimate friend:

“My Lord, grant me sound judgment and join me with the righteous.”

And Joseph’s saying:

“Let me die as a Muslim and join me with the righteous.”

Another is His saying:

“The first forerunners among the Emigrants and the Helpers, and those who followed them in righteousness—Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him.”

Divine pleasure is incompatible with their unanimously agreeing upon and persisting in a sin or error, for that would call for pardon instead.

Another is His saying:

“Then We gave the Book as an inheritance to those of Our servants whom We chose.”

And His saying:

“And peace be upon His servants whom He has chosen.”

This provides evidence in two respects. First, choosing implies purification, which is incompatible with unanimously agreeing upon and persisting in sin and error. Second, the greeting of peace upon them implies their freedom from flaws, just as He pronounced peace upon the messengers, upon Noah, and upon the Messiah.

Another is His saying:

“Indeed, the allies of Allah will have no fear, nor will they grieve.”

Another is His saying:

“Then Allah, by His permission, guided those who believed to the truth concerning which they differed.”

This indicates that His guidance extends to every matter. And His saying:

“Allah is the Protector of those who believe; He brings them out of darkness into light.”

This implies that He brings them out of every darkness.

Another is His saying:

“It is He who sends blessings upon you, and whose angels pray for you, to bring you out of darkness into light.”

And His saying:

“It is He who sends down clear signs upon His servant to bring you out of darkness into light.”

Another is His saying:

“Hold firmly to the rope of Allah all together, and do not be divided.”

And similar verses commanding unity and forbidding division.

Shaykh al-Islām Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked about a statement frequently made by jurists: “This is contrary to analogy,” referring to rulings established by a scriptural text, by the statements of the Companions or some of them, or even, at times, by consensus. Examples include their statements that purifying water into which an impurity has fallen is contrary to analogy; (*) indeed, that even purifying impure matter is contrary to analogy; that performing ablution after eating camel meat is contrary to analogy; that breaking the fast through cupping is contrary to analogy; and that advance-payment sales are contrary to analogy. They likewise describe leasing, transfers of debt, contractual manumission, profit-sharing investment partnerships, sharecropping, tending orchards for a share of their yield, loans, the validity of the fast of someone who breaks it forgetfully, and continuing an invalidated Hajj—all these and other rulings—as contrary to analogy. Is this claim correct or not? And can sound analogy conflict with a scriptural text?

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds. The fundamental point to understand here is that “analogy” is an ambiguous term encompassing both sound and unsound analogy. Sound analogy is that which the Sharia has prescribed, and it consists in placing on an equal footing

like cases and distinguishing between unlike cases. The former is direct analogy, and the latter inverse analogy. This is part of the justice with which Allah sent His Messenger. An example of sound analogy is when the legal cause on which the ruling in the original case depends is present in the new case, without any countervailing factor in the latter preventing that ruling from applying. The Sharia never prescribes anything contrary to such analogy.

The same applies to analogy based on the absence of a relevant distinction: that is, when there is no difference between the two cases that carries weight in the Sharia. The Sharia does not prescribe anything contrary to such analogy. Wherever the Sharia singles out a particular category for a ruling that distinguishes it from comparable categories, that category must possess a characteristic that warrants its distinctive ruling and precludes treating it on an equal footing with others. Yet this distinguishing characteristic may be apparent to some people and not to others. It is not a condition of sound, balanced analogy that everyone should recognize its validity. Thus, when someone regards something in the Sharia as contrary to analogy, it is contrary only to the analogy he has formed in his own mind, not to sound analogy as it actually stands.

Whenever we know that a scriptural text runs contrary to an analogy, we know with certainty that the analogy is unsound. This means that the case addressed in the text differs from those cases thought to resemble it by a characteristic that warranted the Lawgiver’s singling it out for that ruling. There is therefore nothing in the Sharia that contradicts sound analogy, though it does contain rulings contrary to unsound analogy, even if some people do not recognize its unsoundness.

We shall now illustrate this with examples mentioned in the question. Those who said that profit-sharing investment partnerships, orchard-tending partnerships, and sharecropping agreements run contrary to analogy assumed that these contracts belong to the category of hire contracts, since they involve work in return for compensation. Hire contracts require both the compensation and the work provided in return to be known. When they saw that the work involved in these contracts was unspecified and the profit unknown, they said that they ran contrary to analogy. This was their mistake: these contracts belong to the category of partnerships, not exchange contracts in the strict sense, which require both countervalues to be known. Partnerships constitute a different category from exchange contracts, even if they are said to contain an element of exchange.

Likewise, partition constitutes a different category from exchange contracts in the strict sense, although it contains an element of exchange—so much so that some jurists have considered it a sale subject to the conditions governing sales in the strict sense.

To clarify this: work undertaken for financial gain falls into three types.

The first is where the work itself is the object of the contract, is clearly specified, and can be performed as agreed. This is a binding hire contract.

The second is where the work itself is the object of the contract, but is unspecified or uncertain. This is a reward contract, which is revocable, not binding. The reward may be an undivided share of what the work yields, and its amount may be unknown, provided that this uncertainty does not prevent its delivery. For example, the military commander may say, “Whoever points out a fortress shall have one-third of what it contains,” or tell a raiding party he dispatches, “You shall have one-fifth or one-quarter of the spoils you take.”

The scholars differed concerning a slain enemy’s personal effects: is the slayer entitled to them by virtue of the revealed law, as al-Shāfiʿī held, or only through an express stipulation, as Abū Hanīfa and Mālik held? These are two views, both reported from Ahmad. Those who make this entitlement conditional upon a stipulation place it in this category.

Another instance of this category is offering a physician a reward for curing a patient, which is permissible. Likewise, the Companions of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, accepted a flock that had been offered to them for curing a clan’s chief. One of them recited over him for healing until he recovered, and they took the flock. The reward was for the recovery, not for the recitation. By contrast, hiring a physician under a binding contract to bring about recovery would not be permissible, because recovery is beyond his control: Allah may cure the patient, or He may not. This and similar cases permit a reward contract, but not a binding hire contract.

The third type is where the work itself is not the objective; rather, the objective is the financial return. This is the profit-sharing investment partnership. If this is called a reward contract granting a share of what the work yields, the disagreement is merely terminological. Rather, this is a partnership: one contributes the benefit of his labor, and the other the benefit of his capital. Whatever profit Allah allots is shared between them in undivided proportions. This is the form of sharecropping that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prohibited. They used to stipulate that the owner should receive the crop from a particular plot—namely, what grew alongside the large watercourses, at the heads of the smaller irrigation channels, and similar places. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prohibited this.

For this reason, al-Layth ibn Saʿd and others said:

“What he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prohibited is something that anyone with discernment concerning the lawful and unlawful would, upon examining it, recognize as impermissible”—or words to that effect.

He thus explained that this prohibition follows from sound legal analogy. If a similar condition were stipulated in a profit-sharing investment partnership, it would not be permissible, because partnerships are founded upon justice between the two partners. If one is assigned profit to the exclusion of the other, this is not just. By contrast, when each has an undivided share, they share in both gain and loss. If there is a profit, they share in the gain; if there is no profit, they share in being deprived of it: the benefit of one party’s labor is lost just as the benefit of the other’s capital is lost. For this reason, financial loss is borne by the capital, since this corresponds to the loss of the benefit of the worker’s labor.

For this reason, the correct view is that an invalid profit-sharing investment partnership requires payment of the customary share of profit, not the customary wage. The worker is therefore given the share of profit customarily given to someone like him: one half, one third, or two thirds. As for awarding him a fixed sum for which the owner is liable, as in employment and reward contracts, those who advocate this are mistaken. Their error arises from assuming that this is an employment contract, and so awarding him customary remuneration when it is invalid, just as they award him the stipulated payment when it is valid. What demonstrates the error of this view is that the worker might work for ten years: if he were awarded the customary wage, he would receive several times the original capital. Yet under a valid partnership, he is entitled only to a share of the profit, if there is any profit. How, then, could he be entitled under an invalid partnership to several times what he would receive under a valid one?

Likewise, those who deemed sharecropping and orchard-tending partnerships invalid assumed that they were employment contracts with unknown remuneration, and therefore invalidated them. Some of them upheld those arrangements for which there was a need, such as orchard-tending partnerships involving trees, since trees cannot be leased, whereas land can. They permitted sharecropping when ancillary to orchard-tending, either without further restriction or only when the open land constituted one third. All this rests on the assumption that the evidence requires sharecropping to be invalid, and that it was permitted only because of need.

Anyone who gives the matter due consideration will recognize that sharecropping is farther removed from injustice and gambling than leasing land for a specified rent payable as a binding liability. Leasing for an unknown rent—for example, renting someone a house in return for whatever money the tenant earns in his shop—is a form of gambling and is therefore impermissible. Profit-sharing investment partnerships, orchard-tending partnerships, and sharecropping, however, involve no gambling whatsoever; rather, they are among the most equitable arrangements.
